answer:
Proposal for Fasudil (Rho kinase inhibitor; Sigma-Aldrich Cat. No. F5635)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Fasudil is a small‐molecule, synthetic isoquinoline derivative that functions as a Rho‐associated coiled‐coil forming kinase (ROCK) inhibitor. Originally discovered and subsequently developed for clinical use in the treatment of cerebral vasospasm following subarachnoid hemorrhage, fasudil represents one of the earliest examples of ROCK inhibitors entering the clinic (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). As a member of the ROCK inhibitor class, it has been synthesized and formulated to target the ATP‐binding pocket of both ROCK isoforms (ROCK1 and ROCK2), thereby effectively competing with ATP and suppressing the kinase activity that is normally responsible for phosphorylating downstream molecular substrates such as the myosin light chain (MLC) and LIM kinase (Catral et al., 2024; Xiao et al., 2022). The compound’s synthesis generally follows established medicinal chemistry protocols for heterocyclic compounds and includes derivatization steps that yield a potent inhibitor with an IC₅₀ for ROCK inhibition in the submicromolar range, which in the context of retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) function has been postulated to be around 300 nM (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Xiao et al., 2022). Fasudil’s chemical structure and its physicochemical properties allow for formulation into ophthalmic preparations, such as intravitreal injections or potentially sustained-release depot systems, making it an interesting candidate for repurposing in ocular diseases. This class of compounds has historically been used to modulate cytoskeletal dynamics, vascular tone, and cellular contractility in both vascular and neural tissues, and the same properties are being leveraged now to target the pathological stiffening and impaired phagocytic function of RPE cells in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Croze et al., 2014; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016).

Therapeutic History:  
Fasudil’s therapeutic history spans multiple clinical and preclinical applications that underscore its broad efficacy in modulating ROCK-mediated pathways. Clinically, fasudil has been approved and widely used in Japan since 1995 for the treatment of cerebral vasospasm after subarachnoid hemorrhage, owing to its vasodilatory and anti-contractile properties (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). Its clinical use has expanded into experimental paradigms beyond cerebral applications; for instance, fasudil has shown promise in ocular conditions such as diabetic macular edema, where intravitreal administration in combination with bevacizumab demonstrated feasibility and tolerability, and where its ability to modulate inflammatory responses and vascular permeability were beneficial (Mateos-Olivares et al., 2021; Rothschild et al., 2017). Furthermore, other members of the ROCK inhibitor class have been investigated for ocular applications, including glaucoma and even experimental models of photoreceptor synapse stabilization following retinal detachment (Townes-Anderson et al., 2017; Yamaguchi et al., 2017). Although fasudil itself has not yet been directly applied in clinical trials for dry AMD, its mechanism of action and safety profile in ocular tissues have been well documented in multiple studies. Animal studies in diabetic retinopathy models have also demonstrated that fasudil can reverse detrimental cytoskeletal changes and restore barrier integrity in RPE cells (Rothschild et al., 2017). Additionally, preclinical data indicate that ROCK inhibitors can improve wound repair responses and prevent epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) in RPE cells, which is a hallmark of cellular dysfunction in geographic atrophy – the advanced stage of dry AMD (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021; Moura-Coelho et al., 2019). Collectively, while fasudil’s historic use has largely focused on vascular and diabetic complications, its repurposing for dry AMD is supported by mechanistic parallels in RPE cytoskeletal plasticity, phagocytosis, and anti-inflammatory modulation (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Yamaguchi et al., 2017).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, fasudil acts by binding to the ATP-binding site of ROCK enzymes, thereby competitively inhibiting their kinase activity (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). Under normal cellular conditions, active ROCK phosphorylates several substrates including the myosin light chain (MLC) and myosin phosphatase target subunit 1 (MYPT1), which leads to enhanced actomyosin contractility, stabilization of actin stress fibers, and formation of focal adhesions (Catral et al., 2024; Rothschild et al., 2017). In the context of age-related retinopathies, there is mounting evidence that hyperactivity of the ROCK pathway leads to increased contractile force within the RPE cytoskeleton. This hypercontractility contributes to reduced cellular flexibility and impairs the formation of the phagocytic cups that are critical for the internalization of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) – a process that is essential for retinal homeostasis and visual cycle maintenance (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021; Rothschild et al., 2017). Fasudil’s inhibition of ROCK thereby mitigates these cytoskeletal alterations by decreasing the phosphorylation levels of downstream targets, which in turn reduces actomyosin contraction and promotes a more plastic and dynamic actin architecture (Catral et al., 2024; Xiao et al., 2022).

Furthermore, ROCK inhibition has been shown to enhance cell adhesion and reduce apoptotic signaling in stressed RPE cells, thereby improving wound repair and the overall cellular microenvironment (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021; Moura-Coelho et al., 2019). Biochemical experiments have demonstrated that when ROCK activity is suppressed, RPE cells exhibit a reduction in stress fiber formation and an increase in the formation of normal cell–cell junctions, which is crucial for the maintenance of the outer blood-retinal barrier (Rothschild et al., 2017). In addition to its effects on the actin cytoskeleton, fasudil and other ROCK inhibitors have been reported to modulate inflammatory and fibrotic pathways by reducing the phosphorylation of Smad 2/3 in response to TGF-β1 signaling; this effect may further protect RPE cells from deleterious pro-fibrotic and inflammatory cascades that are known to exacerbate dry AMD pathology (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Moura-Coelho et al., 2019). Several studies also indicate that ROCK inhibition promotes RPE differentiation and pigmentation, as evidenced by increased expression of key proteins such as RPE65, which is indispensable for the visual cycle and meso-zeaxanthin biosynthesis (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021). Given that oxidative stress in the aging retina exacerbates ROCK activation, fasudil’s ability to mitigate these effects through cytoskeletal remodeling and anti-inflammatory actions underlies its proposed mechanism of action in improving POS internalization in dry AMD (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Rothschild et al., 2017).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis for repurposing fasudil for dry AMD is that inhibition of ROCK in the RPE will lead to normalization of abnormal cytoskeletal tension, thereby enhancing the formation of phagocytic cups required for efficient POS internalization (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021; Rothschild et al., 2017). In aged RPE cells from patients with dry AMD, persistent ROCK hyperactivity is thought to cause increased actomyosin contraction; this leads to a “stiff” cytoskeletal state that hinders membrane dynamics essential for phagocytosis (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Rothschild et al., 2017). By reducing ROCK-mediated phosphorylation of MLC and other substrates, fasudil is expected to relieve this contractility, restore a more flexible actin network, and ultimately allow for enhanced phagocytic function. Preclinical studies have already demonstrated that use of ROCK inhibitors like Y-27632 can increase phagocytic activity by RPE cells, leading to improved clearance of POS debris – a key function that deteriorates in dry AMD (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021; Croze et al., 2014).

In the proposed assay, RPE cells under oxidative stress—an in vitro proxy for the aging microenvironment seen in dry AMD—will be treated with fasudil. The anticipated outcome is that fasudil will enhance cytoskeletal plasticity, thereby facilitating the formation of phagocytic cups and improving the uptake of POS, as measured by quantifiable phagocytosis assays (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021; Rothschild et al., 2017). Moreover, fasudil’s reported effects in enhancing cell adhesion and promoting a balanced extracellular matrix deposition are expected to provide additional benefits to RPE cell morphology and barrier integrity, indirectly supporting improved phagocytic function (Moura-Coelho et al., 2019). Given that key RPE-specific genes and proteins involved in phagocytosis, including integrin αvβ5 and MFG-E8, are expressed in these cells, normalization of the cytoskeletal machinery via ROCK inhibition is likely to translate into a functional recovery of POS clearance capacity (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021; Croze et al., 2014). Thus, the overall effect of fasudil treatment is expected to counteract the age-associated impairment in phagocytosis, reduce accumulation of waste material such as drusen, and potentially slow the progression of retinal degeneration in dry AMD (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016).

Overall Evaluation:  
In summary, the repurposing of fasudil for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration is supported by a substantial mechanistic rationale and a body of preclinical evidence indicating that ROCK inhibition can positively modulate RPE cellular function. The strengths of fasudil as a therapeutic candidate include its well-established clinical safety profile—stemming from decades of use in cerebrovascular conditions in Japan—as well as its robust capacity to modulate actin-cytoskeletal dynamics, reduce excessive cell contraction, and enhance processes such as cell adhesion and phagocytosis among RPE cells (Catral et al., 2024; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). The ability of fasudil to normalize the abnormal, stiff cytoskeletal state present in aged RPE cells is particularly compelling given the central role of impaired POS internalization in the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021; Rothschild et al., 2017).

Moreover, similar ROCK inhibitors have demonstrated promising effects in ocular models of retinal degeneration and diabetic retinopathy, where the restoration of RPE function and cytoskeletal composition has correlated with improved retinal architecture and cell survival (Moura-Coelho et al., 2019; Rothschild et al., 2017). Fasudil’s potential to also attenuate inflammatory and fibrotic signaling pathways via downstream effects on TGF-β/Smad signaling may add further benefit by curbing the detrimental microenvironment that exacerbates RPE dysfunction in dry AMD (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Moura-Coelho et al., 2019). The proposed mechanism—centered on relieving ROCK-induced actomyosin contraction and restoring the phagocytic capacity of RPE cells—addresses a key pathophysiological deficit in dry AMD, namely the impaired clearance of photoreceptor outer segments that leads to drusen accumulation and subsequent cell degeneration (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021; Rothschild et al., 2017).

However, there are also some weaknesses and challenges associated with using fasudil as a treatment for dry AMD. A major concern is the relatively nonselective nature of fasudil compared to more recently developed ROCK inhibitors that offer isoform specificity (e.g., selective ROCK2 inhibitors) (Alexander, 2017; Yamaguchi et al., 2017). Since ROCK signaling is implicated in multiple cellular processes beyond RPE cytoskeletal dynamics—including vascular regulation, neuronal survival, and immune cell polarization—a nonselective inhibitor may inadvertently affect these other pathways, potentially leading to off-target effects. In particular, the downregulation of thrombospondin 1 (THBS1) observed with some ROCK inhibitors, which is associated with anti-angiogenic processes, could theoretically predispose patients to neovascular complications if not carefully controlled (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021; Catral et al., 2024).

Another potential limitation is the pharmacokinetic profile of fasudil in ocular tissues. Fasudil is known to have a short plasma half-life (approximately 0.3 hours), although its active metabolite, hydroxyfasudil, has a moderately longer half-life (approximately 2.9 hours) (Futterknecht et al., 2024; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). For effective treatment of dry AMD—where chronic, sustained modulation of ROCK activity may be necessary—injection strategies such as intravitreal administration or depot formulations may be required to maintain therapeutic levels over an extended period. Although intravitreal delivery of fasudil has been demonstrated in diabetic macular edema and other experimental models (Rothschild et al., 2017), further studies will be needed to optimize the dosage, frequency, and formulation for the specific demands of long-term retinal therapy in dry AMD.

Furthermore, while the preclinical evidence regarding the benefits of ROCK inhibition in RPE cells is promising, there remains a lack of direct clinical data demonstrating the efficacy of fasudil in patients with dry AMD. Most studies to date have focused on the use of ROCK inhibitors in models of diabetic retinopathy, neovascular AMD, or other retinal conditions, and the translation of these findings to the dry, atrophic form of AMD is not yet fully established (Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016; Rothschild et al., 2017). This gap underscores the need for focused, well-designed clinical trials and further preclinical studies using models that accurately recapitulate the pathophysiology of dry AMD.

Moreover, it will be essential to monitor whether the positive effects on cytoskeletal plasticity and phagocytosis translate into meaningful clinical endpoints such as improved visual acuity or slowed progression of geographic atrophy. Biomarkers of RPE health, phagocytic activity, and retinal integrity will need to be identified and validated in the context of fasudil treatment (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021; Croze et al., 2014).

In conclusion, the available literature strongly supports the mechanistic rationale for using fasudil to target ROCK-mediated dysfunction in RPE cells, which is a critical aspect of dry AMD pathogenesis (Catral et al., 2024; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016). Its established safety profile in other clinical scenarios, coupled with evidence from preclinical models demonstrating improved cytoskeletal regulation, enhanced phagocytic capacity, and attenuated inflammation in retinal cells, makes fasudil a promising therapeutic candidate for repurposing in dry AMD (Moura-Coelho et al., 2019; Rothschild et al., 2017). Nonetheless, challenges related to drug-specific pharmacokinetics, the risk of off-target effects due to its nonselectivity, and the current lack of direct clinical evidence in dry AMD warrant cautious further investigation. The next steps should involve optimization of ocular delivery methods—potentially through sustained-release formulations—and the initiation of preclinical studies in animal models of dry AMD to assess functional outcomes. If these studies prove successful, they would pave the way for early-phase clinical trials aimed at evaluating the efficacy, safety, and tolerability of fasudil in patients with dry AMD (Rothschild et al., 2017; Yamaguchi et al., 2017).

Overall, while significant work remains to be done, the integration of biochemical, cellular, and clinical data from the broader ROCK inhibitor literature provides a compelling argument for further evaluation of fasudil as a potential repurposed treatment for dry AMD. The strategy to inhibit ROCK in RPE cells to restore cytoskeletal dynamics, enhance phagocytosis, and reduce oxidative and inflammatory stress fits well with current understanding of dry AMD pathophysiology and represents an innovative approach that could address a critical unmet need in AMD therapeutics (Bailey-Steinitz, 2021; Catral et al., 2024; Halasz & Townes-Anderson, 2016).

answer:
Proposal for Rapamycin (mTORC1 inhibitor; LC Laboratories Cat. No. R-5000)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Rapamycin is a naturally derived macrolide initially isolated from the bacterium Streptomyces hygroscopicus and belongs to the class of mTOR (mammalian target of rapamycin) inhibitors. This compound, originally discovered for its immunosuppressive properties, has evolved into a prominent therapeutic candidate across several fields including oncology, immunology, and neurodegeneration. Its chemical derivation and structural complexity allow for potent and selective inhibition of the mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1). Rapamycin is widely used in clinical settings as an immunosuppressant following organ transplantation and has been repurposed for other indications based on its ability to modulate intracellular signaling pathways that regulate cellular growth, survival, and autophagy. As such, its potential application in dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) is based on a body of work indicating that targeting mTORC1 can restore autophagic and lysosomal function in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells—a crucial factor given that RPE dysfunction is central to AMD pathogenesis (Falcão et al., 2024, 2025).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, rapamycin has been extensively used and investigated in various clinical and preclinical settings. Its initial clinical use as an immunosuppressive agent in organ transplant patients laid the groundwork for understanding its mechanisms of action and safety profile in humans. Beyond its immunosuppressive applications, rapamycin has been evaluated for its anti-proliferative effects in several types of cancer and for its capability to extend lifespan in model organisms; these studies underscore the drug’s pleiotropic effects on cellular metabolism and autophagy. Specifically regarding ocular therapeutics, preclinical studies on retinal degenerative diseases such as retinitis pigmentosa and glaucoma have demonstrated that mTOR modulation by rapamycin can exert neuroprotective properties in retinal tissues (Wang et al., 2022; Chang et al., 2022). In the realm of AMD, several investigations have focused on the role of autophagy and lysosomal degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) in RPE cells, where rapamycin has been shown to promote autophagy and decrease the buildup of toxic aggregates, such as lipofuscin (Falcão et al., 2024). Moreover, clinical studies and safety evaluations—in particular, intravitreal injections in non-human primates—have provided encouraging data regarding the ocular safety profile of rapamycin, thus supporting its further exploration as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD (Falcão et al., 2024; Chang et al., 2022).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, rapamycin exerts its effects by binding to the intracellular receptor FKBP12 (FK506-binding protein 12). This drug–FKBP12 complex then interacts with mTORC1, leading to its allosteric inhibition. Under normal anabolic conditions, active mTORC1 phosphorylates several downstream targets, including the transcription factor EB (TFEB). TFEB is sequestered in the cytosol in its phosphorylated state, thus preventing the transcription of genes associated with lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy. When rapamycin inhibits mTORC1, the phosphorylation of TFEB is reduced, permitting its nuclear translocation. Once inside the nucleus, TFEB initiates the transcription of numerous genes involved in autophagy and lysosomal function, thereby enhancing the cell’s capacity to degrade and recycle cellular debris such as accumulated photoreceptor outer segments (Falcão et al., 2024, 2025).

In the context of retinal pigment epithelium, mTORC1 normally integrates growth factor signals, nutrient availability, and stress responses to tightly regulate cellular homeostasis. The inhibition of mTORC1 by rapamycin thus releases the “brake” on autophagy, as evidenced by increased expression of autophagic markers such as LC3-II and lysosomal proteins such as LAMP1. This cascading effect leads to an enhanced intracellular clearance system (phagolysosomal flux), which is particularly critical for RPE cells that are responsible for the daily degradation of shed POS. Several studies have demonstrated that rapamycin-treated RPE cells exhibit improved POS degradation, a reduction in lipofuscin-like granules, and overall restoration of lysosomal function (Falcão et al., 2024). Moreover, the molecular signatures observed in rapamycin-treated cells mimic those seen under conditions of caloric restriction, further supporting the notion that mTORC1 inhibition can activate protective autophagic pathways (Davis, 2015; Falcão et al., 2024). This advanced understanding of rapamycin’s mechanism of action provides a compelling rationale for its application in dry AMD, where the accumulation of toxic protein aggregates and dysregulated autophagy are key pathological features (Falcão et al., 2024).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis driving the evaluation of rapamycin in dry AMD is that its inhibition of mTORC1 will lead to the activation of TFEB by reducing its cytosolic phosphorylation state, thereby promoting nuclear translocation. In iPSC-derived RPE models, this induction of TFEB activity is expected to upregulate a host of autophagy and lysosomal genes, which in turn should enhance the cellular degradation of photoreceptor outer segments—an essential process in maintaining retinal homeostasis (Falcão et al., 2024, 2025). Accordingly, the anticipated in vitro effects upon rapamycin treatment include a robust increase in autophagic flux evidenced by elevated levels of LC3-II and LAMP1, paired with improved processing and clearance of POS debris. This effect is crucial because impaired clearance mechanisms contribute to the accumulation of lipofuscin and other cellular waste materials in RPE cells, both of which are hallmarks of dry AMD pathology (Falcão et al., 2024).

Supporting this expected outcome are observations from previous studies where rapamycin has been associated with a reduction in autofluorescent granules and a restoration of normal cellular clearance dynamics in RPE cells (Falcão et al., 2024). Additionally, safety assessments performed through intravitreal administration in non-human primates have demonstrated that rapamycin can be delivered to the retina with minimal adverse events, thereby underpinning its feasibility for clinical translation (Falcão et al., 2024; Chang et al., 2022). Importantly, the hypothesis that rapamycin can act at IC₅₀ values as low as approximately 0.1 nM in RPE cells further reinforces the potential sensitivity and efficacy of this candidate in modulating the pathway of interest. Given the expression of mTOR, TFEB, LC3, and LAMP1 in RPE cells—and the established role of these proteins in the autophagic and lysosomal clearance of POS—the expected improvement in autophagic turnover should directly translate into enhanced cell function and potentially mitigate the progression of dry AMD (Wang et al., 2022; Intartaglia et al., 2022).

Overall Evaluation:  
Rapamycin emerges as a robust and mechanistically sound therapeutic candidate for dry AMD based on its established ability to inhibit mTORC1 and consequently activate autophagy and lysosomal gene expression through TFEB nuclear translocation. One of the major strengths of this candidate lies in the well-characterized molecular mechanism that connects mTORC1 inhibition with enhanced clearance of POS debris—a process that is fundamentally disrupted in dry AMD. The convergence of multiple lines of evidence, ranging from biochemical assays that show increased LC3-II and LAMP1 expression in rapamycin-treated RPE cells to preclinical safety data in non-human primates, bolsters confidence in its potential utility (Falcão et al., 2024, 2025).

Furthermore, the multifaceted benefits of mTORC1 inhibition extend beyond autophagy induction; rapamycin also offers neuroprotective and anti-inflammatory effects, both of which are advantageous in the treatment of retinal degenerative diseases (Chang et al., 2022). The leverage of TFEB activation not only addresses the aberrant accumulation of toxic cellular debris but may also promote a broader upregulation of lysosomal biogenesis, thereby preempting further functional decline of RPE cells. These properties make rapamycin a strong candidate for mitigating early events in AMD pathogenesis, particularly in the context of experimental iPSC-RPE models where enhanced phagocytic capacity can be directly measured.

Nevertheless, several challenges and potential weaknesses require careful consideration. Despite its promising mechanism and preclinical rationale, clinical trials evaluating rapamycin in the context of ocular diseases have yielded mixed results, with some studies documenting only marginal improvements in visual function and others noting issues related to the drug’s solubility and delivery (Marchesi et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2022). In advanced AMD, where the disease pathology is more complex and multifactorial, rapamycin’s efficacy might be limited, and there is a need for precise dosing strategies to balance mTORC1 inhibition with the preservation of physiological mTOR functions that are crucial for RPE cell survival (Wang et al., 2022; Chang et al., 2022). Additionally, the potential for off-target effects or immunosuppressive consequences linked to systemic exposure—although minimized by intravitreal delivery—necessitates further investigation into long-term safety profiles (Wang et al., 2022).

Another potential limitation is the inherent complexity of autophagy regulation in the RPE, which can be influenced by factors such as oxidative stress, metabolic dysfunction, and age-related changes in lysosomal function. While rapamycin is effective in reactivating autophagic pathways under controlled experimental settings, its impact within the pathogenic environment of a diseased retina, particularly if inflammatory processes are simultaneously active, may be less predictable (Davis, 2015; Falcão et al., 2024). Moreover, the therapeutic window for achieving beneficial rapamycin concentrations without incurring adverse events is not yet fully defined, underscoring the importance of pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic studies specifically tailored to ocular tissues (Falcão et al., 2024).

Taken together, the current body of evidence suggests that rapamycin’s capacity to restore autophagic homeostasis in RPE cells represents a solid mechanistic foundation for its use in dry AMD. Its ability to upregulate autophagy and lysosomal function through TFEB activation directly addresses known defects in the clearance pathways of RPE cells—a critical factor in the pathogenesis of dry AMD. Moreover, the safety data from preclinical intravitreal delivery studies provide additional incentive to advance this candidate further along the translational pipeline. However, given the mixed outcomes observed in some clinical contexts and the challenges related to drug formulation and optimal dosing, further comprehensive studies are warranted to clarify its efficacy in early versus advanced stages of AMD (Mei et al., 2022).

In conclusion, rapamycin as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD shows significant promise from both a mechanistic and translational standpoint. Its well-documented ability to inhibit mTORC1, thereby releasing TFEB and ramping up autophagic and lysosomal gene expression, positions it uniquely to tackle the underpinnings of RPE dysfunction characteristic of dry AMD. While preclinical data support its efficacy and safety with intravitreal administration in non-human primates, challenges remain regarding its formulation, potential off-target effects, and the delineation of its therapeutic window in human subjects. Consequently, while rapamycin’s molecular mechanism and early experimental results are highly encouraging, further studies—especially those that integrate pharmacokinetic profiling, dose optimization, and long-term outcome measurements in relevant in vivo models—are essential before definitive conclusions can be drawn regarding its clinical utility for dry AMD (Mei et al., 2022; Si et al., 2023).

Overall, the strengths of rapamycin include its robust and well-characterized action on mTORC1, its downstream activation of autophagic and lysosomal pathways via TFEB, and supportive preclinical safety data in ocular models. In contrast, its weaknesses lie in the variable efficacy observed in clinical studies, formulation challenges due to low solubility, and the need for careful dosing to avoid potential adverse effects related to systemic immunosuppression. These considerations collectively argue for the continued investigation of rapamycin as a therapeutic option for dry AMD with a focus on optimizing delivery strategies and characterizing its long-term impact on retinal structure and function (Wang et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2025).

hypothesis: AAV2-hTLR4 decoy peptide (Gene therapy research vector)
answer:
Proposal for AAV2-hTLR4 decoy peptide (Gene therapy research vector)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
The candidate under review is an AAV2-hTLR4 decoy gene therapy vector engineered to express a soluble form of the Toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4) decoy peptide. This gene therapy approach is synthetically designed by leveraging the adeno-associated virus serotype 2 (AAV2) as a delivery vector to the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). The decoy peptide is derived from the extracellular domain of TLR4 and is modified to be secreted into the subretinal space. Its design intends to bind and sequester danger-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs) that would normally interact with endogenous TLR4 receptors on RPE cells. In doing so, the decoy receptor limits the activation of proinflammatory cascades that are implicated in the pathogenesis of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD). The therapeutic falls within the class of gene therapy compounds designed to modulate innate inflammatory signaling. Gene therapy for ocular diseases has a history of success given the immune-privileged nature of the eye and the precise targeting achievable using AAV2 vectors, as evidenced by previously approved treatments for inherited retinal dystrophies. This candidate leverages a similar platform but repurposes it to attenuate chronic sterile inflammation by acting as a molecular sink for DAMPs, thus aiming to preserve RPE homeostasis and its critical phagocytic functions (Klettner & Roider, 2021; Mulfaul, Rhatigan, & Doyle, 2018).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, modulation of TLR signaling has been extensively studied in the context of inflammatory and degenerative diseases. Multiple preclinical studies have emphasized the role of TLR4 in mediating retinal inflammation and degeneration in AMD. Experimental evidence has demonstrated that activation of TLR4 in RPE cells leads to the release of proinflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α and IL-1β, and that the chronic engagement of TLR4 by DAMPs present in drusen contributes to RPE dysfunction and photoreceptor loss (Klettner & Roider, 2021; Titi-Lartey, Mohammed, & Amoaku, 2022). Moreover, genetic association studies have identified specific TLR4 variants as risk factors for AMD, thereby underpinning its significance as a therapeutic target (Brandli, Vessey, & Fletcher, 2024). Although direct clinical evidence using a TLR4 decoy has not yet been reported specifically for dry AMD, analogous strategies using decoy receptors have been applied in other inflammatory contexts to attenuate signaling by competitively inhibiting ligand-receptor interactions. Additionally, the use of AAV2 as a gene delivery vehicle has been validated by successful clinical trials in ocular gene therapy, including previous applications such as AAV2-mediated delivery of RPE65 for Leber congenital amaurosis and AAV2-VMD2-hMERTK for MERTK-associated retinitis pigmentosa; these precedents illustrate both safety and efficacy in targeting retinal cells (Inana et al., 2018; Ramlogan-Steel et al., 2019). Thus, while the AAV2-hTLR4 decoy candidate is novel with respect to its direct application for dry AMD, it builds on a substantial body of preclinical evidence implicating TLR4 in AMD as well as on the proven track record of AAV2-based ocular gene therapies.

Mechanism of Action:  
The fundamental mechanism of the AAV2-hTLR4 decoy therapy entails the intracellular delivery of a transgene encoding a soluble form of TLR4 that is secreted by transduced RPE cells. Under normal pathological conditions, various DAMPs—including but not limited to 7-ketocholesterol, oxidized lipids, amyloid-β peptides, and HMGB1—accumulate in the subretinal space as a result of chronic cellular stress and drusen formation, triggering TLR4-mediated inflammatory responses (Klettner & Roider, 2021; Titi-Lartey, Mohammed, & Amoaku, 2022). Endogenous TLR4 on RPE cells, upon binding these DAMPs, initiates downstream signaling cascades via both the MyD88-dependent and TRIF-dependent pathways. This leads to activation of transcription factors such as NF-κB and IRF3, which in turn stimulate the production of proinflammatory cytokines including TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-8, all of which have been implicated in the inflammatory milieu of AMD (Mulfaul, Rhatigan, & Doyle, 2018; Brandli, Vessey, & Fletcher, 2024).  

By expressing a soluble decoy form of TLR4, the candidate therapy competitively binds the available DAMPs in the subretinal space before they engage the membrane-bound receptors on RPE cells. This sequestration of DAMP ligands reduces the activation of the endogenous TLR4 signaling cascade. Notably, several experimental studies have suggested that chronic TLR4 activation in the RPE is associated not only with increased inflammatory cytokine production, but also with the downregulation of essential receptors involved in phagocytosis, namely MERTK and αvβ5 integrin. These receptors are crucial for the clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) from the RPE, and their reduced expression contributes to impaired phagocytosis and further retinal degeneration (Brandli, Vessey, & Fletcher, 2024). Therefore, the decoy is expected to provide a dual benefit: it dampens pathological inflammation mediated by cytokine overproduction and helps maintain the levels of phagocytic receptors essential for RPE function.  

At the molecular level, the decoy receptor binds DAMPs through its extracellular ligand-binding domains, effectively neutralizing these molecules by preventing them from binding to the transmembrane TLR4 that would trigger inflammatory signal transduction. The transgene is delivered using an AAV2 vector, which is known for its high tropism for RPE cells and its capacity to achieve long-term transgene expression with minimal immunogenicity. Studies using AAV2 vectors in retinal tissues have confirmed robust gene expression with a favorable safety profile, making this vector a suitable choice for chronic diseases such as dry AMD (Ramlogan-Steel et al., 2019; Inana et al., 2018).  

Furthermore, preserving normal RPE phagocytic functions by preventing the downregulation of receptors like MERTK is critical, as there is evidence that TLR4-mediated inflammation interferes with these functions, potentially creating a detrimental feedback loop that exacerbates degeneration (Klettner & Roider, 2021; Mulfaul, Rhatigan, & Doyle, 2018). Consequently, the blockade of TLR4 activation via the decoy molecule should lead to a more balanced inflammatory response and maintain proper RPE functionality in clearing POS, thereby slowing the progression of AMD.

Expected Effect:  
The primary expected outcome of administering the AAV2-hTLR4 decoy gene therapy is a marked reduction in the chronic inflammatory state observed in dry AMD. In experimental settings such as RPE explant cultures, expression of the soluble TLR4 decoy is anticipated to lead to a significant reduction in the levels of key proinflammatory cytokines, particularly TNF-α and IL-1β, which are known mediators of retinal inflammation and degeneration (Brandli, Vessey, & Fletcher, 2024; Klettner & Roider, 2021). By limiting the availability of DAMPs that would otherwise activate endogenous TLR4, the therapy is expected to attenuate the downstream NF-κB activation and the resultant cytokine cascade. This reduction in inflammation should, in turn, preserve or even restore the expression of phagocytic receptors such as MERTK and αvβ5 integrin on the RPE (Inana et al., 2018; Brandli, Vessey, & Fletcher, 2024).  

The maintenance of these receptors is critical because they mediate the phagocytosis of POS, a process essential for retinal homeostasis and visual function. In the context of AMD, compromised phagocytosis leads to an accumulation of debris and further cellular stress, thereby perpetuating a cycle of inflammation and degeneration. Therefore, through the preservation of MERTK and integrin αvβ5 expression, the decoy therapy is hypothesized to support normal POS clearance, thereby improving RPE cell health and reducing the progression of retinal degeneration (Mulfaul, Rhatigan, & Doyle, 2018; Titi-Lartey, Mohammed, & Amoaku, 2022).  

In addition to the biochemical assays and ex vivo RPE explant studies that are likely to show a decrease in inflammatory mediator levels, in vivo models of retinal degeneration may demonstrate improved structural and functional outcomes following treatment. This might include reduced RPE atrophy, diminished formation of drusen-like deposits, and stabilization or improvement in retinal morphology on imaging studies. Functional assessments could show attenuation of visual decline over time in animal models, mirroring the clinical goal of preserving vision in dry AMD patients. The broad immunomodulatory effect of the decoy is therefore expected not only to dampen the deleterious inflammatory response but also to contribute to the long-term maintenance of retinal tissue integrity and function (Klettner & Roider, 2021).

Overall Evaluation:  
In summary, the AAV2-hTLR4 decoy gene therapy candidate represents a promising therapeutic approach for dry AMD owing to its targeted mechanism to modulate innate inflammatory signaling. Among the key strengths of this candidate is its strong mechanistic rationale. A wealth of preclinical evidence highlights TLR4’s central role in AMD pathogenesis, where DAMP-induced TLR4 activation contributes to chronic inflammation and the detrimental downregulation of phagocytic receptors (Klettner & Roider, 2021; Titi-Lartey, Mohammed, & Amoaku, 2022). By employing a soluble decoy receptor to intercept DAMPs, this approach offers a targeted method to mitigate the adverse inflammatory cascade while simultaneously preserving critical RPE functions necessary for photoreceptor outer segment clearance (Brandli, Vessey, & Fletcher, 2024).  

Another significant strength is the use of an AAV2 vector for gene delivery. AAV2 is one of the most extensively studied and clinically validated gene therapy vectors for ocular applications, with a proven record of safety and efficacy in several retinal disorders (Ramlogan-Steel et al., 2019; Inana et al., 2018). The subretinal delivery of AAV2-based therapies has been demonstrated to produce sustained transgene expression with minimal immunogenicity, a feature particularly advantageous in treating chronic conditions such as dry AMD. This platform further benefits from its ability to transduce non-dividing cells, such as RPE, and achieve long-term expression, which is critical for a disease that requires prolonged therapeutic intervention.  

On the other hand, there are several challenges and potential weaknesses that warrant careful consideration. One notable concern is the inherent redundancy in Toll-like receptor signaling. Although TLR4 is a critical mediator of inflammatory responses in the retina, other TLRs such as TLR2 and TLR3 have also been implicated in AMD pathogenesis (Mulfaul, Rhatigan, & Doyle, 2018; Brandli, Vessey, & Fletcher, 2024). As such, an approach that solely targets TLR4 may not address the entire spectrum of innate immune activation in the diseased retina. This redundancy might diminish the overall efficacy of the decoy if compensatory mechanisms via other receptors persist.  

Additionally, TLR4 is known to play a dual role in RPE physiology. While its activation under pathological conditions exacerbates inflammation and cellular dysfunction, TLR4 is also involved in the normal phagocytic clearance of POS (Brandli, Vessey, & Fletcher, 2024). Consequently, complete inhibition of TLR4 signaling could unintentionally compromise physiological processes, leading to adverse effects on retinal homeostasis. Achieving the appropriate balance between inhibiting pathological inflammation and preserving essential immune functions will be a central challenge in the optimization of this therapeutic candidate.  

Another potential weakness relates to the immunological response elicited by the AAV2 vector itself. Although AAV2 has been shown to be relatively non-immunogenic in the ocular environment, there remains a risk of dose-dependent immune reactions, particularly if high levels of transgene expression occur. Pre-existing neutralizing antibodies to AAV2 in some patient populations could also limit the efficacy of the therapy (Ramlogan-Steel et al., 2019). Moreover, while early-phase clinical trials with other AAV2-based treatments have demonstrated favorable safety profiles, long-term data will be necessary to fully evaluate the risk of inflammatory complications or vector-related toxicity in the context of a decoy receptor that is intended to modulate immune signaling.  

From a mechanistic perspective, while the therapeutic hypothesis is compelling, the direct experimental evidence supporting a reduction in TNF-α and IL-1β levels in RPE explants using a TLR4 decoy is still limited. Most of the current evidence is derived from mechanistic studies that have established a correlation between TLR4 activation and proinflammatory cytokine production in AMD (Klettner & Roider, 2021; Titi-Lartey, Mohammed, & Amoaku, 2022; Brandli, Vessey, & Fletcher, 2024). As such, further in vitro and in vivo studies will be necessary to confirm that the AAV2-mediated delivery of the TLR4 decoy convincingly modulates these inflammatory pathways without adversely affecting normal RPE functions.  

Overall, the AAV2-hTLR4 decoy gene therapy candidate offers a novel and rational approach to treating dry AMD by directly targeting a central component in the inflammatory cascade. Its strengths lie in its targeted sequestration of DAMPs, the potential to preserve RPE phagocytic receptor expression, and the well-established safety of AAV2 vector delivery in the eye (Mulfaul, Rhatigan, & Doyle, 2018; Klettner & Roider, 2021). However, issues such as potential compensatory mechanisms by other TLRs, the dual role of TLR4 in both pathological and physiological contexts, and possible vector immunogenicity underscore the need for comprehensive preclinical validation. The candidate is promising, but further investigation into dosing, delivery route, and long-term expression is essential to ensure that the therapeutic benefits outweigh any risks in the clinical setting of dry AMD (Mulfaul, Rhatigan, & Doyle, 2018; Klettner & Roider, 2021).  

In conclusion, while the AAV2-hTLR4 decoy represents a highly innovative approach to modulating innate immunity in dry AMD, its future success will depend on rigorous preclinical studies that confirm its ability to selectively dampen pathological inflammation without disrupting normal RPE functions. The convergence of mechanistic insights on TLR4 signaling in AMD pathogenesis and the proven capabilities of AAV2 gene therapy creates a strong rationale for further development of this candidate. Continued evaluation through biochemical assays, RPE explant studies, and animal models of retinal degeneration is recommended to refine dosing strategies and assess long-term safety and efficacy prior to advancing into clinical trials.

answer:
Proposal for Nicotinamide Riboside (NR; ChromaDex TruNiagen)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Nicotinamide riboside (NR) is a naturally occurring derivative of vitamin B3 that was originally isolated from milk and later recognized for its role as an NAD⁺ precursor. NR belongs to the class of NAD⁺‐boosting compounds and is structurally a pyridine riboside with a glycosidic bond linking nicotinamide to ribose; this bond has proven to be chemically labile, which has driven innovations in its synthesis and stabilization (Zhang et al., 2020; Braidy et al., 2019). Recent advances in synthetic methods have enabled the production of purer, more thermally and chemically stable forms, such as borate-stabilized NR, although commercial formulations like NR chloride (ChromaDex TruNiagen) are widely used owing to their proven oral bioavailability (Biţă et al., 2023). As a member of the NAD⁺ precursor family that also includes nicotinamide and nicotinic acid, NR has been repurposed for its potential to restore intracellular NAD⁺ levels, a vital coenzyme in redox reactions and as a substrate for enzymes such as sirtuins and PARPs; these properties have been harnessed in research aimed at improving mitochondrial function and addressing age-related degeneration (Zhang et al., 2020; Cimaglia et al., 2020).

Therapeutic History:  
NR has a robust preclinical and early clinical history as a nutritional supplement with demonstrated efficacy in boosting NAD⁺ levels systemically. Prior biochemical studies have documented that oral NR supplementation raises circulating NAD⁺ and associated metabolites in both murine and human subjects, with repeated dosing regimens showing increases in NAD⁺ of up to 100% above baseline without causing adverse events such as flushing or liver toxicity—side effects that have been problematic with other niacin derivatives (Airhart et al., 2017; Conze et al., 2019). Furthermore, NR has been shown to ameliorate metabolic deficits in various disease models, including mouse models of diet-induced obesity, neurodegeneration, peripheral neuropathy, and even light-induced retinal degeneration, where systemic treatment with NR improved retinal outcomes in mice (Zhang et al., 2020; Biţă et al., 2023). Although NR has not been directly tested in clinical trials for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or in dedicated experiments on retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) phagocytosis, the accumulated evidence from related ocular studies and from the broader literature on NAD⁺ restoration suggests that its application in retinal degenerative conditions is plausible (Jadeja et al., 2020; Cimaglia et al., 2020).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, NR is rapidly taken up by cells and phosphorylated by nicotinamide riboside kinases (NRK1 and NRK2) to produce nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN), which is subsequently converted to NAD⁺ by NMN adenylyltransferases (NMNATs) (Zhang et al., 2020; Jadeja et al., 2020). NAD⁺ is a key metabolic hub that is required for essential cellular processes, including fueling mitochondrial ATP production via glycolysis, the tricarboxylic acid cycle, and oxidative phosphorylation, while also serving as a critical substrate for sirtuin deacetylases (notably SIRT1 and SIRT3) and poly(ADP-ribose) polymerases (PARPs) that mediate DNA repair and stress responses (Braidy et al., 2019; Biţă et al., 2023). In the context of the RPE, diminished NAD⁺ availability is linked to compromised mitochondrial bioenergetics, impaired autophagy/mitophagy, increased oxidative stress, and defective phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS), all of which contribute to the etiology of dry AMD (Jadeja et al., 2020). NR supplementation is proposed to elevate intracellular NAD⁺ levels above the physiological threshold, thereby stimulating sirtuin activity (particularly SIRT3 in mitochondria), stabilizing mitochondrial membrane potential, promoting efficient mitophagy, and reducing reactive oxygen species (ROS) production (Cimaglia et al., 2020; Biţă et al., 2023). Additionally, by restoring the NAD⁺/NADH balance, NR may directly support energy-dependent processes such as phagocytosis in RPE cells, where the clearance of aged POS is critically energy demanding (Zhang et al., 2020).

Expected Effect:  
In the proposed hypothesis for dry AMD, exogenous NR supplementation is expected to boost NAD⁺ levels in RPE cells, an effect that should be observable at an effective concentration (EC₅₀) in the range of approximately 100 µM in vitro (Zhang et al., 2020). This increase in NAD⁺ is anticipated to enhance mitochondrial respiration and activate sirtuin-dependent pathways that promote mitochondrial biogenesis and repair. In turn, improved mitochondrial function provides the necessary ATP for energy-dependent cellular functions, particularly the phagocytic clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS), which is impaired in dry AMD. Preclinical studies have indicated that NAD⁺ precursors, including nicotinamide and NMN, can correct defects in mitochondrial respiration and restore normal phagocytic activity in RPE models; NR, being an orally bioavailable NAD⁺ precursor with favorable safety profiles, is predicted to act similarly by reducing oxidative stress–induced damage to the phagocytic machinery and enhancing mitophagy to clear damaged mitochondria (Cimaglia et al., 2020; Jadeja et al., 2020; Hawkins et al., 2024). In animal models of retinal degeneration, NR supplementation has been linked to improved functional outcomes, supporting the notion that similar mechanisms may be relevant in the context of dry AMD, where RPE dysfunction underlies photoreceptor degeneration (Zhang et al., 2020). Thus, the expected effect is a dual benefit in RPE cells: increased energy production to drive POS phagocytosis and enhanced resistance to oxidative damage through improved mitochondrial quality control, ultimately helping to preserve RPE function and slow dry AMD progression (Conze et al., 2019).

Overall Evaluation:  
NR is an attractive candidate for repurposing in dry AMD due to its unique combination of advantages. Among its strengths is its origin as a naturally occurring, orally bioavailable NAD⁺ precursor that has a long record of safe use in human nutritional studies; clinical trials have repeatedly demonstrated its ability to significantly elevate systemic NAD⁺ levels without dose-limiting adverse effects such as flushing or hepatotoxicity, which are common to other niacin derivatives (Airhart et al., 2017; Conze et al., 2019). Its mechanism of action is well understood at the biochemical level: by feeding into the NAD⁺ salvage pathway, NR supports key cellular functions including mitochondrial respiration, DNA repair, and stress signaling via sirtuins and PARPs—pathways that are critically compromised in the aging RPE and in dry AMD (Braidy et al., 2019; Biţă et al., 2023). Additionally, preclinical data have shown that NAD⁺ restoration via NR or related precursors can ameliorate mitochondrial dysfunction and improve phagocytic activity in retinal tissues, providing a plausible molecular rationale for its use in maintaining RPE health (Zhang et al., 2020).

On the other hand, there are significant challenges that must be acknowledged. Despite promising preclinical evidence in various models of retinal degeneration, direct application of NR in the context of dry AMD has not yet been rigorously evaluated in dedicated clinical trials, leaving a gap between the compelling mechanistic rationale and the demonstration of clinical efficacy (Jadeja et al., 2020; Lee et al., 2024). The concentration required (EC₅₀ ≈ 100 µM) and the extent of NR’s penetration into the RPE in the human eye remain to be fully elucidated; tissue-specific pharmacokinetics may differ from those observed in systemic circulation, and there remains the possibility that presystemic metabolism (conversion to nicotinamide, for example) could limit the amount of NR available for direct uptake by the RPE (Damgaard & Treebak, 2023; Mehmel et al., 2020). Furthermore, while the drug’s safety profile is established in the context of metabolic and neurodegenerative indications, the unique microenvironment of the retina—with its high oxygen consumption and exposure to light-induced oxidative stress—may present unforeseen responses that require careful validation in animal models and early-phase clinical studies (Gemae et al., 2024; Jadeja et al., 2020).

In summary, NR (ChromaDex TruNiagen) holds considerable promise as a repurposed therapeutic for dry age-related macular degeneration. Its ability to safely boost NAD⁺ levels, improve mitochondrial function, and reduce oxidative stress aligns well with the pathophysiological needs of the RPE in dry AMD. Strengths of the candidate include its natural origin, established safety and bioavailability profiles in humans, and robust preclinical evidence supporting NAD⁺ repletion as a strategy for enhancing mitochondrial quality and phagocytic function. However, the absence of direct clinical trials in dry AMD and the need for targeted studies to confirm effective RPE delivery and functional restoration of POS clearance remain important considerations. Overall, NR merits further investigation in preclinical RPE models and carefully designed clinical trials to assess its efficacy in mitigating the progression of dry AMD (Zhang et al., 2020; Cimaglia et al., 2020; Airhart et al., 2017; Conze et al., 2019; Jadeja et al., 2020).

Proposal for Hydroxypropyl-β-cyclodextrin (HPβCD; Sigma-Aldrich Cat. No. C0926)

Below is a detailed evaluation of hydroxypropyl‐β‐cyclodextrin (HPβCD) as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD). The report is organized into several sections that describe the candidate’s origin, therapeutic history, molecular mechanism, expected effects in the context of RPE (retinal pigment epithelium) pathology, and an overall evaluation of its potential utility in dry AMD.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Hydroxypropyl‐β‐cyclodextrin (HPβCD) is a chemically modified derivative of β-cyclodextrin, a cyclic oligosaccharide originally discovered as a naturally occurring compound that forms toroidal structures with a hydrophilic exterior and a hydrophobic interior. The modification with hydroxypropyl groups improves its aqueous solubility and reduces toxicity, making it more suitable for biomedical applications. HPβCD belongs to the cyclodextrin family, which has been widely used as drug carriers and excipients due to their ability to form inclusion complexes with a range of lipophilic molecules. The development of HPβCD was driven by the need to improve the solubility and stability of lipophilic drugs, and its ability to modulate cholesterol homeostasis has led to its investigation in several disorders characterized by lipid accumulation. Notably, HPβCD has been studied in the context of cholesterol‐storage diseases such as Niemann–Pick type C disease by virtue of its capacity to extract cholesterol from intracellular membranes. Its synthesis involves partial substitution of hydroxyl groups on the parent β-cyclodextrin with hydroxypropyl moieties, thus expanding its inclusion complexation repertoire and enabling it to interact with lipophilic substrates such as cholesterol and bisretinoids. This candidate’s prior use in ocular studies, especially those addressing cholesterol dyshomeostasis and lipofuscin clearance, provides a strong rationale for its repurposing in dry AMD, where abnormal lipid accumulation in the RPE is a core pathology (Nociari, Kiss, & Rodriguez-Boulan, 2017).

Therapeutic History:  
HPβCD, as well as its parent cyclodextrin compounds, have been used extensively in both biomedical research and preclinical studies focused on lipid storage disorders. In Niemann–Pick type C models, for example, cyclodextrins have demonstrated efficacy in reducing cholesterol accumulation in lysosomes by sequestering cholesterol and promoting its efflux from cells. This cholesterol‐removal capability has led to its evaluation in animal models that exhibit retinal cholesterol dyshomeostasis. Several studies have provided evidence for HPβCD’s beneficial effects on lysosomal function in various cell types; in fibroblasts from Niemann–Pick patients, for instance, HPβCD treatment restored autophagy and reduced intracellular lipid buildup (Moruno-Manchon et al., 2016; Nixon, 2016). Moreover, in a mouse model of retinal cholesterol dyshomeostasis, HPβCD treatment produced significant reductions in retinal cholesterol content and reduced pathological deposits at critical interfaces such as the photoreceptor outer segment (POS)–RPE boundary (El-Darzi, Mast, Petrov, & Pikuleva, 2021; El-Darzi et al., 2023).  
In retinal models more directly related to AMD pathogenesis, cyclodextrins have been shown to decrease A2E, a major bisretinoid that accumulates in the RPE with age, by directly forming inclusion complexes with lipofuscin components (Nociari et al., 2017). Additionally, in cultured human cells and in animal studies, cyclodextrins have demonstrated a capacity to modulate lysosomal acidity and enhance the clearance of aggregated or indigestible material. Some reports, however, caution that cyclodextrins may act predominantly through cholesterol depletion rather than by stimulating lysosomal biogenesis via transcription factor EB (TFEB) (Gaspar, Mathieu, & Alvarez, 2017). Furthermore, studies using patient‐derived iPSC‐RPE cells, particularly in the context of Bietti’s crystalline dystrophy, have shown that cyclodextrin treatment rescues lysosomal pH defects and reinstates autophagic flux, which is directly relevant to dry AMD pathophysiology (Hata et al., 2018). Although HPβCD has not been formally trialed in dry AMD patients to date, its cumulative use in preclinical ocular models suggests that its repurposing for AMD is both a viable and promising strategy (El-Darzi et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action:  
The molecular basis for HPβCD’s therapeutic potential in retinal diseases rests on its multifaceted ability to interact with lipid and retinoid components within the RPE’s lysosomal compartment. One of the key pathological features of dry AMD is the accumulation of toxic bisretinoids such as A2E within lysosomes, which contributes to impaired phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments and eventual cellular dysfunction (Nociari et al., 2017). HPβCD is thought to ameliorate this situation via several interrelated mechanisms:  

1. Direct Extraction and Complexation of Lipofuscin Precursors:  
HPβCD’s hydrophobic cavity allows it to form inclusion complexes with lipophilic compounds. Several reports have provided computational and experimental evidence that β-cyclodextrins form complexes with A2E and other bisretinoids, effectively “solubilizing” these compounds within their cavity. This extraction mechanism leads to a reduction of lipofuscin accumulation in the lysosomes, which is a critical step since lipofuscin impairs lysosomal enzyme activation such as that of cathepsin D (Nociari et al., 2017). The formation of a 2:1 cyclodextrin–A2E complex has been predicted by in silico models, suggesting that each cyclodextrin can accommodate an arm of the A2E molecule, thereby reducing lipofuscin toxicity (Nociari et al., 2017).  

2. Cholesterol Depletion and Modulation of Lysosomal Lipid Homeostasis:  
HPβCD is well known for its ability to extract free and esterified cholesterol from cellular membranes. In the context of dry AMD, cholesterol accumulation contributes to lysosomal dysfunction by perturbing the activity of the vacuolar-type H⁺-ATPase (v-ATPase), leading to lysosomal alkalinization which in turn reduces cathepsin D activity. By depleting excess cholesterol from the POS and RPE, HPβCD can facilitate the restoration of lysosomal acidity. This cholesterol depletion has been documented in several animal models in which HPβCD treatment led to significant reductions in retinal cholesterol levels and improved ultrastructural characteristics of the RPE (El-Darzi et al., 2021). Additionally, this depletion is likely to relieve the inhibition of v-ATPase activity and promote effective autophagosome–lysosome fusion, thereby enhancing overall lysosomal function (Hata et al., 2018; Gaspar et al., 2017).

3. Activation of Autophagy and TFEB-Mediated Lysosomal Biogenesis:  
In many contexts of lysosomal storage and lipid overload, cellular homeostasis can be restored by triggering autophagy. HPβCD has been shown to induce autophagy by upregulating TFEB, a master transcriptional regulator that governs lysosomal biogenesis and autophagic pathways. Activation of TFEB leads to increased expression of genes involved in lysosome formation, acidification, and function. In experimental models, HPβCD has been reported to promote TFEB translocation to the nucleus, thereby enhancing lysosome-mediated degradation of accumulated substrates such as lipofuscin components (Moruno-Manchon et al., 2016; Nociari et al., 2017). It should be noted that not all studies find TFEB upregulation in all cell types; for instance, some human fibroblast studies have highlighted a cholesterol-mediated mechanism with no direct evidence of TFEB activation (Gaspar et al., 2017). Thus, the net effect of HPβCD may stem from a combination of direct removal of toxic aggregates and improvements in autophagic flux via restored lysosomal pH, rather than relying solely on TFEB-mediated biogenesis.

4. Enhancement of Lysosomal Exocytosis:  
A less widely discussed but complementary mechanism involves the induction of calcium-dependent lysosomal exocytosis. HPβCD has been shown in some studies to promote the exocytosis of lysosomal contents, thereby facilitating the clearance of undegraded material from the cell. This process may help eliminate toxic lipofuscin and other aggregated compounds that accumulate in RPE cells over time (Nociari et al., 2017).  

5. Restoration of Cathepsin D Activity and POS Degradation:  
Cathepsin D is a critical lysosomal protease involved in the degradation of photoreceptor outer segment (POS) material within RPE cells. Accumulated lipofuscin and cholesterol can raise lysosomal pH and directly interfere with cathepsin D maturation and activity. By extracting excess cholesterol and lipofuscin precursors, HPβCD is expected to normalize lysosomal pH and thereby restore cathepsin D function. This restoration is key to improving POS degradation efficiency, which is compromised in dry AMD and contributes to the progressive degeneration of RPE cells (Gaspar et al., 2017; Nixon, 2016). Although direct measurements of enhanced cathepsin D activity following HPβCD treatment in AMD models are not extensively reported in the current literature, the underlying biochemical interactions support the hypothesis that a more acidic lysosomal environment will favor proper cathepsin D activation (El-Darzi et al., 2023; Nociari et al., 2017).

Expected Effect:  
Based on the integrated mechanisms described above, the expected therapeutic effect of HPβCD in dry AMD models is multifold. First, by forming inclusion complexes with A2E and related lipofuscin precursors, HPβCD is expected to lower the intracellular burden of these toxic compounds in RPE lysosomes. This direct extraction would lead to a decrease in the accumulation of lipofuscin, which is known to exacerbate oxidative stress and inflammation in the RPE (Nociari et al., 2017). Second, through its cholesterol-extracting properties, HPβCD should mitigate lipid overload within the RPE cell membranes and lysosomes. This reduction in cholesterol content is predicted to relieve the inhibition on the lysosomal v-ATPase, thereby restoring the acidic pH necessary for optimal lysosomal enzyme function. Consequently, cathepsin D activity should be reinstated, enhancing the capacity of RPE cells to degrade phagocytosed POS material (El-Darzi et al., 2021; Hata et al., 2018). Third, if HPβCD additionally promotes autophagy via TFEB nuclear translocation and increased lysosome biogenesis, there would be an overall improvement in the turnover of cellular debris and a reinforcement of the cell’s degradative machinery. In turn, these improvements should lead to enhanced clearance of damaged proteins, lipids, and photoreceptor debris, thereby reducing RPE cell stress and dysfunction—a primary drive behind dry AMD pathology (Moruno-Manchon et al., 2016; Nociari et al., 2017).  
Furthermore, because lipofuscin accumulation is directly linked to impaired clearance of POS and chronic inflammation, reducing its burden should indirectly improve the visual cycle. Improvements in RPE function would likely translate to better photoreceptor support and potentially slow the progression of macular degeneration, which is critically important in managing dry AMD. In sum, the expected effect of HPβCD is a synergistic improvement in lysosomal function mediated by both direct chemical extraction of toxic substances and indirect enhancement of cellular clearance pathways (Gaspar et al., 2017; Hata et al., 2018).

Overall Evaluation:  
Hydroxypropyl-β-cyclodextrin presents several compelling strengths as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Its well-documented ability to extract cholesterol and lipophilic toxins from cells has been validated in several preclinical models, and its potential for restoring lysosomal pH and, consequently, lysosomal enzyme activity is particularly attractive in the context of AMD’s impairment of RPE degradative functions (El-Darzi et al., 2021; Nociari et al., 2017). The multifaceted mechanism of action—ranging from direct complexation with A2E to cholesterol depletion and potential activation of autophagy via TFEB—addresses several interconnected pathological processes that drive dry AMD progression. Moreover, cyclodextrins’ extensive history of use in other lipid storage disorders provides a valuable precedent for their clinical repurposing and supports the feasibility of translating these findings into an ocular application (Hata et al., 2018).  

However, several weaknesses and challenges must be considered. There is some inconsistency in the literature regarding the ability of HPβCD to activate TFEB, with certain studies reporting a predominantly cholesterol-mediated mechanism without marked transcriptional upregulation of lysosomal biogenesis (Gaspar et al., 2017). This indicates that the beneficial effects may depend on the specific cellular context and disease model. Additionally, while preclinical evidence in models of retinal cholesterol dyshomeostasis and lipofuscin accumulation is promising (El-Darzi et al., 2021; El-Darzi et al., 2023), there remains a need for more direct studies in AMD models—preferably in vitro studies using primary RPE cells or in vivo studies in well-established dry AMD animal models such as the Abca4−/− or other relevant transgenic lines. The dosing issue is also a consideration; in some studies, effective lipofuscin clearance required higher concentrations of HPβCD, which in turn may introduce off-target effects or toxicity concerns that have been noted in other cyclodextrin applications, such as ototoxicity in systemic administration (Gaspar et al., 2017). Moreover, while its ability to cross blood–retina barriers has been demonstrated in some contexts (El-Darzi et al., 2021; El-Darzi et al., 2023), ensuring sufficient local concentration in the RPE to achieve the desired lysosomal effects without eliciting adverse systemic effects remains an important translational challenge.

In conclusion, the cumulative evidence from biochemical, cellular, and preclinical studies supports the hypothesis that HPβCD has considerable potential as a repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD. Its dual action in directly binding and extracting toxic lipofuscin precursors and in correcting cholesterol-mediated lysosomal dysfunction addresses two key pathogenic pathways in dry AMD. While additional research is needed to optimize dosing, verify the mechanism in AMD-specific models, and fully assess safety profiles in the ocular context, the strengths of HPβCD—derived from its proven track record in modulating lipid metabolism and lysosomal function—make it a promising candidate for further development (El-Darzi et al., 2021; Gaspar et al., 2017). The proposed clinical strategy aiming to lower A2E levels, restore lysosomal pH and cathepsin D activity, and enhance POS degradation is well supported by the current literature, and thus HPβCD merits strong consideration for inclusion in the dry AMD therapeutic pipeline.

Overall, while some mechanistic nuances remain to be elucidated, particularly regarding the relative contributions of TFEB activation versus cholesterol extraction, the convergence of preclinical findings and the candidate’s established utility in lysosomal storage disorders provide a solid foundation for advancing HPβCD toward clinical evaluation in dry AMD. Continued investigation into its pharmacokinetics, local retinal bioavailability, and long-term effects on RPE function, along with careful dose optimization in relevant AMD animal models, will be essential next steps in validating its therapeutic value (El-Darzi et al., 2021; Gaspar et al., 2017).

This comprehensive review indicates that HPβCD stands as a promising repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD with several strengths that are directly aligned with the pathophysiological challenges of the disease, while also highlighting areas that require further investigation to ensure a safe and effective translation from preclinical models to clinical application (Hata et al., 2018; Nociari et al., 2017).
