Proposal for Tauroursodeoxycholic Acid (TUDCA; Sigma-Aldrich Cat. No. T0261)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Tauroursodeoxycholic acid (TUDCA) is the taurine-conjugated form of ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA), a hydrophilic secondary bile acid generated by microbial metabolism and hepatic conjugation, and long used in hepatobiliary disease pharmacotherapy as a cytoprotective bile salt scaffold (class: bile acids; subclass: hydrophilic ursane bile acids/taurine conjugates) (Cabrera et al., 2019). As a small amphipathic molecule, TUDCA exhibits chemical-chaperone activity that stabilizes nascent polypeptides, reduces protein misfolding/aggregation burden, and modulates unfolded protein response (UPR) signaling, thereby lowering endoplasmic reticulum (ER) stress across cell types (e.g., hepatocytes, epithelial cells, neurons) (Kusaczuk, 2019). In vitro and in vivo ocular studies identify TUDCA as a broadly neuroprotective agent that rescues photoreceptors and retinal cells in multiple injury paradigms, consistent with multimodal actions that include mitigation of ER stress, inhibition of mitochondrial pathway apoptosis, reduction of reactive oxygen species (ROS), and anti-inflammatory effects (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Win et al., 2021). In retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) models, TUDCA directly promotes phagocytosis via Mer tyrosine kinase (MerTK) activation and restores phagocytic function under oxidative stress, implicating a direct action on the canonical RPE phagocytic machinery (Murase et al., 2015). Delivery to ocular tissues is feasible with systemic dosing and local routes; related UDCA crosses the human blood–retinal barrier, and TUDCA tissue distribution has been quantified after intravitreal, systemic, and suprachoroidal administration in large animals (Daruich et al., 2021; Olsen et al., 2020).

Therapeutic History  
Clinically, the UDCA/TUDCA class is established in hepatology; mechanistic reviews document antiapoptotic activity via inhibition of mitochondrial cytochrome c release, stabilization of mitochondrial membranes, attenuation of ER stress via chaperone actions, increases in glutathione pools, and activation of survival kinases (p38/ERK/MAPK/PI3K), with a translational safety track record that has motivated evaluation in neurodegenerative disorders (Cabrera et al., 2019). In ophthalmology, preclinical data repeatedly show that systemic or local TUDCA protects retina across models: it preserves photoreceptors in genetic (rd10, P23H, Rpgr knockout) and injury models (retinal detachment, light damage), decreases ER stress and apoptosis markers (e.g., caspase-3), and improves electroretinography (ERG) function (Win et al., 2021; Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021). In diabetic retinopathy–like models and vascular stress paradigms, TUDCA or UDCA reduces vascular permeability, inflammation, and ER stress, and in retinal endothelial cells these effects require the bile acid receptor TGR5, supporting receptor-mediated protection in the retina (Lenin et al., 2023). In RPE models (ARPE-19 and primary human RPE), TUDCA protects against H₂O₂-induced oxidative injury and thapsigargin-induced ER stress, improves viability, suppresses apoptosis, and activates antioxidant defenses, while also reversing oxidative-stress–induced phagocytic dysfunction via MerTK/FAK signaling (Alhasani et al., 2020; Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021). Although these mechanistic actions align with pathogenic axes in dry age-related macular degeneration (dAMD), no clinical trials in dAMD are referenced in the supplied context; the current evidence base is preclinical and translational (e.g., drug distribution and barrier penetration) rather than RPE/dAMD clinical efficacy (Olsen et al., 2020; Daruich et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action  
ER proteostasis and unfolded protein response modulation  
- Chemical chaperoning: TUDCA stabilizes folding intermediates, reduces aberrant protein–protein interactions, promotes ATF6-driven folding capacity, and prevents UPR malfunction, thereby attenuating ER stress signaling (downregulating BiP/GRP78, ATF4/eIF2α, XBP1 splicing, and CHOP in multiple models) (Kusaczuk, 2019). In ARPE-19 cells, TUDCA reduces thapsigargin-induced CHOP expression and spliced XBP1, with parallel decreases in apoptosis and improved survival, linking chaperone action to UPR attenuation in RPE (Alhasani et al., 2020). Across retinal systems, TUDCA repeatedly lowers ER stress signatures, and the retina-relevant pathophysiology of UPR–mitochondrial crosstalk (IRE1/JNK pro-apoptotic routing, CHOP-mediated death, PERK’s protective vs. maladaptive bifurcation) underscores why ER stress relief is mechanistically central in RPE and photoreceptors (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Alhasani et al., 2020).

Mitochondrial membrane stabilization and anti-apoptotic signaling  
- Intrinsic apoptosis blockade: TUDCA inhibits Bax translocation, preserves mitochondrial outer membrane integrity, prevents cytochrome c release, and suppresses caspase activation (caspase-3/7), thereby interrupting the mitochondrial execution cascade and preserving oxidative phosphorylation capacity (Alhasani et al., 2020; Cabrera et al., 2019). In neuronal and isolated mitochondrial systems, co-incubation with TUDCA prevents amyloid-β–induced mitochondrial membrane perturbation, preserves redox state and protein conformation of the outer membrane, and limits cytochrome c release—convergent evidence for direct mitochondrial membrane stabilization and preservation of electron transport chain function under proteotoxic/oxidative stress (Khalaf et al., 2022). TUDCA upregulates survival signaling (PI3K/Akt → Bad phosphorylation; ERK/MAPK) and inhibits stress kinases (JNK/c-Jun), further shifting the balance away from mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization (MOMP) and toward survival (Cabrera et al., 2019; Win et al., 2021).

Antioxidant and anti-inflammatory reprogramming  
- NRF2 axis and redox control: In RPE oxidative injury models, TUDCA reduces intracellular ROS and malondialdehyde (MDA), restores NRF2 expression, upregulates antioxidant enzymes (SOD1, catalase, GPX1, NQO1, GCLM), elevates reduced glutathione (GSH), and rescues SOD/catalase activities—features of a robust antioxidant response that stabilizes mitochondrial redox homeostasis (Alhasani et al., 2020). Suppression of inflammatory signaling (decreased IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α transcription and secretion) further reduces secondary mitochondrial injury and death receptor cross-talk (Alhasani et al., 2020). Such antioxidant/anti-inflammatory shifts are consistent with TUDCA-induced NRF2 pathway enhancement reported across tissues and with the known linkage between persistent UPR activation and pro-inflammatory cytokine induction in RPE (Alhasani et al., 2020; Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021).

RPE phagocytic machinery activation  
- MerTK/FAK signaling and POS uptake: TUDCA increases MerTK phosphorylation in a concentration-dependent manner, maintains FAK phosphorylation under oxidative stress, and restores H₂O₂-impaired RPE phagocytosis in both ARPE-19 and primary human RPE, supporting a direct effect on RPE’s canonical POS ingestion machinery (MerTK–FAK–integrin axis) (Murase et al., 2015). Functional assays demonstrate increased uptake and lysosomal digestion of photoreceptor outer segments (pHrodo® and FITC readouts), indicating rescue of both recognition/engulfment and downstream processing (Murase et al., 2015). Notably, in the MerTK rescue paradigm GRP78 was not altered by TUDCA, implying that the pro-phagocytic effect can occur independently of a measurable reduction in ER stress under those specific conditions and may involve upstream integrin/FAK/Src signaling that converges on MerTK (Murase et al., 2015).

Bile acid receptors and signaling in the retina  
- TGR5-dependent protection: In diabetic and inflammatory retinal models, TUDCA reduces ER stress markers (GRP78, IRE1α, sXBP1, CHOP), inflammation, and vascular permeability; these endothelial barrier and anti-inflammatory effects require TGR5 expression in retinal endothelial cells and correlate with functional rescue in vivo (ERG, optokinetic responses), suggesting a receptor-mediated component that is present in the retina (Lenin et al., 2023). Although FXR appears less relevant in retina, additional candidate receptors (TGR5, α5β1 integrin, S1PR2, PXR, GR/mineralocorticoid receptor) have been implicated at the transcript/protein level in ocular tissues, providing plausible upstream routes for TUDCA’s signaling (Daruich et al., 2022; Win et al., 2021).

Mechanistic integration in AMD biology  
- In RPE, ER stress and mitochondrial dysfunction reinforce each other: UPR activation (IRE1/JNK, ATF4–CHOP) promotes mitochondrial apoptosis and ATP decline; mitochondrial impairment (Δψm loss, ROS) feeds back to exacerbate ER stress and can drive epithelial–mesenchymal transition seen in early dAMD (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Alhasani et al., 2020). TUDCA’s combined actions—chemical chaperoning of ER proteostasis, MOMP blockade/cytochrome c retention, redox control via NRF2, and restoration of MerTK/FAK-dependent phagocytosis—directly map onto these intersecting failure modes and therefore represent a coherent, biologically grounded therapeutic hypothesis for dAMD (Alhasani et al., 2020; Cabrera et al., 2019; Murase et al., 2015).

Important mechanistic gaps for dAMD  
- Despite strong plausibility, direct RPE bioenergetics readouts (ATP levels, oxygen consumption rate, mitochondrial membrane potential) after TUDCA in dAMD-relevant stress paradigms are not reported in the provided RPE studies and remain a central evidentiary gap for this indication (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021). Likewise, while TUDCA rescues phagocytosis and activates MerTK, there are no data here on cathepsin transcription, maturation, or activity in RPE phagolysosomes after TUDCA, precluding claims about normalization of lysosomal proteases in dAMD RPE (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Murase et al., 2015).

Expected Effect  
In a dAMD-relevant RPE assay comprising oxidative and/or ER stress with phagocytosis readouts, the following effects are expected based on the compiled evidence:

- ER stress attenuation and reduced UPR-driven apoptosis: TUDCA should lower CHOP and spliced XBP1 levels and decrease TUNEL/caspase-3/7 activation, improving viability under thapsigargin or oxidative stress, consistent with chemical chaperone–mediated UPR modulation (Alhasani et al., 2020).  
- Mitochondrial preservation and anti-apoptosis: TUDCA should suppress Bax translocation/cytochrome c release and maintain mitochondrial membrane integrity, thereby reducing mitochondrial pathway apoptosis and preserving the proton motive force needed for oxidative phosphorylation; while these endpoints have not yet been quantified in RPE with Seahorse or JC-1 in the supplied reports, they are supported mechanistically in retina/neuronal systems and hepatocyte models (Cabrera et al., 2019; Khalaf et al., 2022).  
- Antioxidant reset via NRF2: TUDCA should reduce ROS/MDA, restore NRF2 expression, increase GSH, and upregulate antioxidant enzymes (SOD, CAT, GPX1, NQO1, GCLM), consistent with lower oxidative injury to mitochondrial lipids/proteins and stabilized respiratory capacity (Alhasani et al., 2020).  
- Restoration of RPE phagocytosis via MerTK/FAK: Under oxidative stress (H₂O₂), TUDCA is expected to restore POS ingestion/digestion as measured by pHrodo®/FITC assays, accompanied by increased MerTK phosphorylation and maintenance of FAK signaling, potentially via upstream integrin activation; this rescues both recognition/engulfment and lysosomal processing phases (Murase et al., 2015).  
- Anti-inflammatory effects: TUDCA should reduce IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α at mRNA/protein levels in RPE challenged by H₂O₂, limiting cytokine-driven mitochondrial impairment and secondary UPR activation (Alhasani et al., 2020).  
- Putative receptor mediation: In endothelial/retinal contexts, TUDCA’s ER-stress and barrier benefits require TGR5; although RPE-specific TGR5 dependency is not demonstrated in the supplied texts, receptor-mediated contributions in the retinal environment are plausible and testable (Lenin et al., 2023).  

Expression and pathway presence in RPE are well established for MerTK, integrins (e.g., αvβ5), and FAK—core components of the POS phagocytosis cascade targeted by TUDCA in RPE cells (Murase et al., 2015).  

Dosing and assay considerations:  
- In ARPE-19, 100 µM TUDCA improved survival under 750 µM H₂O₂; higher concentrations (200–500 µM) impaired viability, indicating a window for benefit (Alhasani et al., 2020).  
- In phagocytosis assays, TUDCA increased MerTK phosphorylation at high concentration (1 mM) and improved phagocytosis at lower concentrations (≥ 0.1 µM) under non-H₂O₂ conditions, suggesting multiple dose-dependent mechanisms (direct vs. upstream integrin-mediated pathways) (Murase et al., 2015).  

Endpoints to include for hypothesis validation:  
- ER stress/UPR: GRP78/BiP, sXBP1, CHOP, ATF4, eIF2α-P, ATF6 targets (Alhasani et al., 2020; Kusaczuk, 2019).  
- Mitochondrial bioenergetics: Δψm (JC-1/TMRM), oxygen consumption rate and extracellular acidification rate (Seahorse), cellular ATP (luminescent readout), cytochrome c release/Bax translocation (Cabrera et al., 2019; Khalaf et al., 2022).  
- Redox/inflammation: ROS (DCFH-DA), MDA (TBARS), GSH, NRF2 targets, cytokine ELISAs (Alhasani et al., 2020).  
- Phagocytosis: MerTK/FAK phosphorylation, POS binding/engulfment/digestion (pHrodo®/FITC), and key lysosomal proteolysis markers; importantly, add cathepsin D/B/L maturation/activity assays to address the specific lysosomal arm of the hypothesis, which remains untested in the provided literature (Murase et al., 2015; Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021).  

Overall Evaluation  
Summary judgment  
TUDCA is a mechanistically coherent, repurposable candidate for dAMD that targets central RPE failure modes—ER proteostasis breakdown, mitochondrial injury/apoptosis, oxidative and inflammatory stress—and functionally restores a defining RPE task (POS phagocytosis) via MerTK/FAK signaling under oxidative insult (strengths: convergent mechanistic breadth and direct RPE function rescue) (Alhasani et al., 2020; Cabrera et al., 2019; Murase et al., 2015). However, two critical evidence gaps must be addressed to de-risk the program for dAMD: (1) lack of direct demonstration that TUDCA preserves RPE mitochondrial bioenergetics and ATP production under dAMD-relevant stress, and (2) absence of data that TUDCA normalizes lysosomal cathepsin expression/maturation/activity downstream of phagosome–lysosome fusion (weaknesses: missing bioenergetic and lysosomal endpoints underpinning the hypothesis) (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021).  

Strengths  
- Mechanistic fit to dAMD pathophysiology: TUDCA reduces ER stress/UPR effectors (CHOP, sXBP1), blocks mitochondrial pathway apoptosis (Bax/cytochrome c/caspase-3), induces NRF2-driven antioxidant programs, and suppresses inflammatory cytokines—all directly relevant to the ER–mitochondria redox loop that destabilizes RPE in early AMD (Alhasani et al., 2020; Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021).  
- Direct RPE functional efficacy: Restoration of POS phagocytosis via MerTK activation and FAK stabilization under oxidative stress offers a clear, disease-relevant mechanism to preserve outer segment turnover and RPE homeostasis (Murase et al., 2015).  
- Mitochondrial stabilization plausibility: Strong cross-system evidence shows TUDCA preserves mitochondrial membrane structure, limits cytochrome c release, and blocks permeability transition–like events, which would support ATP maintenance under stress (albeit not yet measured in RPE) (Khalaf et al., 2022; Cabrera et al., 2019).  
- Retinal in vivo activity and barrier access: Systemic TUDCA protects photoreceptors and retinal function in multiple rodent disease models; related UDCA crosses the human blood–retinal barrier, and ocular delivery platforms achieve retinal distribution in large animals, supporting translational feasibility (Win et al., 2021; Daruich et al., 2021; Olsen et al., 2020).  
- Receptor-mediated tractability: TGR5 dependency for retinal endothelial barrier/inflammation effects offers a defined receptor axis for pharmacodynamic biomarkers in vivo, complementing MerTK/FAK functional readouts in RPE (Lenin et al., 2023).  

Weaknesses and risks  
- Mitochondrial bioenergetics unproven in RPE: No ATP, OCR/ECAR, or Δψm data in stressed RPE after TUDCA are provided; this is a pivotal gap because preservation of energy production is central to the proposed disease-modifying effect in dAMD (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021).  
- Lysosomal protease (cathepsin) claims unsupported: While TUDCA rescues phagocytosis and MerTK signaling, there are no data here that TUDCA restores cathepsin expression/maturation/activity in RPE; the stated hypothesis reference to “alleviates ER stress–induced downregulation of MERTK and cathepsins” is not substantiated in the supplied sources and should be considered unverified for RPE/dAMD (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021; Murase et al., 2015).  
- Dose–mechanism tension: In RPE phagocytosis assays, MerTK phosphorylation was robust at 1 mM, whereas phagocytosis enhancement occurred at ≥ 0.1 µM, suggesting indirect upstream mechanisms at low doses and raising questions about clinically relevant concentrations for direct MerTK phosphorylation (Murase et al., 2015).  
- Heterogeneity of mechanistic readouts: In one RPE phagocytosis study, GRP78 was not changed by TUDCA during rescue, indicating ER stress reduction is not required for the pro-phagocytic effect in that setting; mechanism may differ across contexts (Murase et al., 2015).  
- Evidence quality and generalizability: Several RPE-focused studies are from lower-tier journals, and many mechanistic claims derive from non-RPE systems; rigorous replication with polarized primary human RPE and in dAMD-relevant in vivo models is needed (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021).  

Decision framework and next experiments  
Given the favorable mechanistic alignment and preclinical retinal efficacy, TUDCA merits advancement to a focused preclinical validation plan tailored to dAMD, gated by resolution of the bioenergetics and lysosomal gaps:  

- Bioenergetics/mitochondria (must-have): In human primary, polarized RPE under defined oxidative and ER stress (e.g., low-dose H₂O₂, tunicamycin/thapsigargin), quantify Δψm (TMRM), OCR/ECAR (Seahorse), cellular ATP, cytochrome c release, and Bax translocation with and without TUDCA; include NRF2 dependency (siRNA) to map antioxidant mediation (Alhasani et al., 2020; Cabrera et al., 2019).  
- Phagolysosomal proteolysis (must-have): In POS ingestion assays, measure cathepsin D/B/L maturation (pro-/mature forms), activity (fluorogenic substrates), lysosomal pH and degradative capacity; test whether TUDCA normalizes these under ER/oxidative stress and whether effects require MerTK or integrin/FAK signaling (Murase et al., 2015).  
- ER–mitochondria crosstalk mapping (should-have): Track UPR arms (IRE1/JNK, PERK/eIF2α/ATF4, ATF6) alongside mitochondrial readouts to define causal sequence; test whether TUDCA biases PERK toward pro-survival signaling and reduces CHOP/TRB3 induction (Alhasani et al., 2020; Kusaczuk, 2019).  
- In vivo dAMD-relevant model (should-have): In RPE mitochondrial/oxidative stress models (e.g., sodium iodate low-dose; cigarette-smoke–derived oxidants), test systemic and local TUDCA dosing for RPE structure/function (autofluorescence, OCT, ERG) and RPE phagocytosis biomarkers, plus mitochondrial/UPR markers (Win et al., 2021; Olsen et al., 2020).  
- Pharmacology/PK/PD (must-have): Link ocular exposure (vitreous/choroid/RPE) to effect using delivery modalities with translational potential (oral UDCA as a proxy crossing BRB; suprachoroidal implant pharmacokinetics); incorporate PD markers (retinal ER stress proteins, NRF2 targets) (Daruich et al., 2021; Olsen et al., 2020; Lenin et al., 2023).  

Positioning in dAMD  
If the above gaps are closed positively, TUDCA would be positioned as a proteostasis–mitochondria stabilizer that preserves RPE phagocytic function and metabolic sufficiency—an upstream, disease-modifying approach complementary to complement modulation and to anti-angiogenic strategies (the latter relevant if geographic atrophy coexists with incipient neovascularization) (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021). The MerTK/FAK rescue of phagocytosis provides a strong functional anchor for mechanism-based biomarkers, while the antioxidant/UPR signatures support PD tracking in early-phase clinical translation (Murase et al., 2015; Alhasani et al., 2020).

Go/no-go conclusion  
- Go for preclinical dAMD validation with a clear focus on mitochondrial bioenergetics and lysosomal protease function in RPE, using polarized human RPE and in vivo oxidative/ER-stress models that recapitulate early dAMD (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021).  
- No-go for cathepsin-centered claims until direct RPE evidence is generated; likewise, refrain from asserting ATP rescue in RPE until OCR/ATP/Δψm data are obtained (Bilbao-Malavé et al., 2021).  

On balance, TUDCA is a high-priority repurposing candidate with strong mechanistic plausibility and supportive retinal efficacy, but it requires targeted, RPE-centric bioenergetics and lysosomal validation to meet decision-grade standards for a dAMD program (Cabrera et al., 2019; Win et al., 2021; Murase et al., 2015; Alhasani et al., 2020).

Proposal for Nicotinamide (Vitamin B3; Sigma-Aldrich Cat. No. N4126)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Nicotinamide, a water‐soluble form of vitamin B3, is a naturally occurring compound that plays a critical role in cellular metabolism by serving as a precursor for nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD⁺) synthesis. It is available both through dietary sources and chemical synthesis and has been produced at high purity for research purposes (Sigma-Aldrich Cat. No. N4126). Nicotinamide belongs to the vitamin B3 class of compounds, which have been extensively used as nutritional supplements and metabolic regulators; these compounds are well recognized for their role in the salvage pathway that replenishes NAD⁺ levels in cells. The therapeutic candidate under consideration is repurposed with the hypothesis that at a concentration of 10 mM, nicotinamide will boost intracellular NAD⁺ pools and enhance the activity of NAD⁺‐dependent enzymes, such as sirtuins, leading to improved mitochondrial function and increased deacetylation of autophagy regulators. Such effects are expected to restore phagocytic function, specifically the photoreceptor outer segment (POS) degradation, in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cultures pertinent to dry age‐related macular degeneration (Gemae et al., 2024; Jadeja et al., 2018).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, nicotinamide has been investigated in various preclinical and clinical settings for its potential neuroprotective effects and its capacity to modulate cellular metabolism. In the context of ocular health, several studies have demonstrated that nicotinamide supplementation can enhance NAD⁺ levels and improve mitochondrial function in retinal cells. Preclinical studies have reported that this vitamin not only supports retinal ganglion cell health in glaucoma models but also shows promise in improving photoreceptor and RPE function in models of age-related macular degeneration (Gemae et al., 2024). Although there remains limited direct clinical experience with nicotinamide in dry AMD, the compound has been a subject of interest in related ocular conditions due to its favorable safety profile and widespread use in other age-related and mitochondrial dysfunction settings (Gemae et al., 2024). More recent investigations have focused on its ability to rescue mitochondrial deficits and restore autophagic flux in RPE cells, with data indicating that in models of CFH Y402H iPSC-RPE, nicotinamide can ameliorate lysosomal processing and POS degradation problems (Gemae et al., 2024; Jadeja et al., 2018). This body of evidence, compounded with its extensive historical use as a nutritional supplement, supports the rationale for repurposing nicotinamide as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD (Gemae et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action:  
At a molecular level, nicotinamide exerts its effects primarily through its role as a key precursor in the NAD⁺ salvage pathway. In this pathway, nicotinamide is converted to nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) via the enzyme nicotinamide phosphoribosyltransferase (NAMPT), and subsequently to NAD⁺ by NMN adenylyltransferase. NAD⁺, in turn, is an essential co-factor for numerous enzymes involved in energy metabolism and cellular homeostasis, most notably the sirtuin family of NAD⁺-dependent deacetylases (Gemae et al., 2024; Jadeja et al., 2018). Sirtuins, such as SIRT1 and SIRT3, play a pivotal role in mitochondrial biogenesis, oxidative phosphorylation, and regulation of autophagy by deacetylating key transcription factors and enzymes that control metabolic stress responses (Gemae et al., 2024). In RPE cells, increased NAD⁺ levels facilitate the activation of these sirtuins, which then deacetylate a range of targets including histones and autophagy regulators, leading to improved mitochondrial structure and function, enhanced energy production, and the promotion of efficient autophagic and lysosomal degradation pathways (Gemae et al., 2024). Furthermore, the improved mitochondrial function translates into a better cellular energy state, providing the necessary ATP required for high-energy processes such as POS phagocytosis. Experimentally, administration of nicotinamide has been shown to yield a two-fold increase in NAD⁺ levels in ARPE-19 cells, thereby confirming its ability to augment the cellular bioenergetic capacity (Hazim et al., 2022). This mechanism also intersects with the regulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, as enhanced mitochondrial function and sirtuin activity contribute to lower oxidative stress, a known contributor to cellular senescence and dysfunction in the aging retina (Gemae et al., 2024).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis driving the current proposal is that nicotinamide, administered at a concentration of 10 mM in vitro, will significantly increase NAD⁺ levels in RPE cells, thereby enhancing sirtuin activity and downstream mitochondrial function. This boost in NAD⁺ is expected to promote deacetylation of autophagy regulators, which will, in turn, normalize the autophagic flux and facilitate the effective degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) by the RPE. In models of dry AMD, where phagocytosis deficits and impaired proteostasis are key pathological features, the restoration of autophagy and mitochondrial activity is anticipated to ameliorate cellular senescence and maintain retinal homeostasis (Gemae et al., 2024; Jadeja et al., 2018). Data from previous studies suggest that in aging RPE, reduced NAMPT expression is linked to decreased NAD⁺ levels and compromised SIRT1 function, leading to cellular senescence and defective mitochondrial dynamics (Jadeja et al., 2018). By contrast, nicotinamide supplementation helps to reverse these effects, as evidenced by restored NAD⁺ content and reactivation of sirtuins that enable degradation of accumulated defective cellular components, thereby improving lysosomal enzyme processing and phagocytosis (Jadeja et al., 2018). Moreover, enhanced mitochondrial metabolism has been correlated with improved RPE differentiation and the maintenance of a polarized epithelial phenotype, critical factors in ensuring effective POS phagocytosis and overall retinal health (Hazim et al., 2022). Thus, the expected outcome is that nicotinamide treatment will correct metabolic impairments, reduce oxidative stress, and restore phagocytic efficiency in dry AMD cultures, which are all essential for halting or even reversing disease progression (Gemae et al., 2024; Jadeja et al., 2018).

Overall Evaluation:  
Nicotinamide emerges as a highly promising therapeutic candidate for the treatment of dry AMD based on its multi-faceted mechanism of action and extensive preclinical evidence supporting its role in maintaining retinal health. One of the primary strengths of nicotinamide is its excellent safety profile and widespread historical use as a nutritional supplement, which significantly lowers the risk associated with its repurposing (Gemae et al., 2024). Its ability to augment NAD⁺ levels and activate sirtuins directly addresses several key pathological processes in dry AMD, including mitochondrial dysfunction, oxidative stress, and impaired autophagy. Experimental findings have consistently shown that increased NAD⁺ levels, mediated by nicotinamide or its analogues such as NMN, correlate with reduced cellular senescence and improved lysosomal and mitochondrial function in RPE cells (Jadeja et al., 2018).

Moreover, the convergence of multiple lines of evidence—from studies detailing NAMPT decline in aging RPE, to those demonstrating the restoration of NAD⁺ and sirtuin activity by nicotinamide—provides a robust biochemical rationale for its use in combating dry AMD (Gemae et al., 2024). The ability of nicotinamide to enhance mitochondrial respiration in ARPE-19 cells and primary human fetal RPE cells further underscores its potential in promoting a healthy, polarized RPE phenotype capable of efficient POS phagocytosis (Hazim et al., 2022). These studies also suggest that improved mitochondrial metabolism is closely linked to enhanced proteostasis and autophagic clearance of damaged cellular components—an outcome that is particularly relevant given the known deficits in autophagy and lysosomal processing observed in dry AMD (Gemae et al., 2024).

However, while the preclinical data are encouraging, several challenges must be acknowledged. One potential weakness lies in the translation of in vitro findings to in vivo therapeutic efficacy. The concentration of 10 mM nicotinamide used in cell culture experiments may not directly correspond to achievable or sustainable therapeutic levels in the human retina. Moreover, while nicotinamide is known to boost NAD⁺ synthesis, there is a nuanced balance in its effects on sirtuin activity; in certain contexts, excessive nicotinamide has been reported to inhibit sirtuins, suggesting that dosing and timing will be critical parameters that require careful optimization (Will-Orrego, 2020). There is also the inherent challenge of the multifactorial nature of dry AMD, where mitochondrial dysfunction and impaired autophagy are only parts of a complex network of pathological events that include inflammatory signaling, extracellular matrix alterations, and genetic predispositions. Thus, while nicotinamide addresses several of these pathways, it may need to be combined with other therapeutic agents to achieve a comprehensive treatment effect (Gemae et al., 2024; Will-Orrego, 2020).

Another important consideration is the need for more extensive clinical studies. Although nicotinamide’s safety profile is well established in the context of dietary supplementation and its use in other neurological and ocular conditions, robust clinical trials specifically targeting dry AMD are lacking (Gemae et al., 2024; Lin, 2020). Future research will need to focus not only on the pharmacokinetics and optimal dosing strategies in human subjects but also on precise biomarkers indicating the restoration of NAD⁺ metabolism, mitochondrial function, and POS phagocytosis. Furthermore, mechanistic studies that dissect the interactions between nicotinamide-driven NAD⁺ elevation and the downstream modulation of autophagy regulators will be essential to confirm the proposed mode of action and to identify any potential off-target effects.

Overall, the repurposing of nicotinamide for dry AMD presents several compelling advantages. Its established safety, low cost, and known biochemical mechanisms strongly support its potential as a therapeutic candidate. Preclinical evidence indicates that nicotinamide not only restores NAD⁺ levels but also reactivates sirtuin pathways, thereby mitigating mitochondrial dysfunction and defective autophagy that are central to the pathogenesis of dry AMD. These effects could translate into improved cellular proteostasis and enhanced POS phagocytosis, ultimately preserving retinal integrity and visual function (Gemae et al., 2024; Jadeja et al., 2018). Nevertheless, the path forward will require careful dose optimization and rigorous clinical validation to ensure that the in vitro benefits observed translate into meaningful clinical outcomes. In summary, despite the challenges associated with translating cell-based results into human therapy, nicotinamide remains an attractive candidate whose mechanism, historical use, and preclinical successes justify further investigation as a potential treatment for dry AMD (Jadeja et al., 2018; Lin, 2020).

hypothesis: Mini-FH (Recombinant FH CCP1-4/19-20; Tel-Aviv University research reagent)
answer:
Proposal for Mini-FH (Recombinant FH CCP1-4/19-20; Tel-Aviv University research reagent)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Mini‐FH is a rationally engineered, recombinant protein therapeutic derived from human complement factor H (FH) by selectively fusing its N-terminal complement control protein (CCP) modules 1–4 with its C-terminal CCP modules 19–20 (Kamala et al., 2021; de Boer et al., 2020). This minimal construct is synthesized through recombinant DNA methodologies that allow for expression in suitable heterologous systems such as yeast, insect cells, or mammalian cell lines; its design takes full advantage of recent advances in protein engineering guided by high‐resolution structural data (Dobo et al., 2018; Makou et al., 2013). Belonging to the class of engineered biologics—or “modular complement regulators”—Mini‐FH represents a more manufacturable, compact alternative to full‐length FH (≈155 kDa), reducing the molecular weight to roughly 40–45 kDa, which is expected to facilitate improved tissue and cellular penetration (Kamala et al., 2021; de Boer et al., 2020). This therapeutic candidate is designed to recapitulate the dual functionality of native FH: the CCP1–4 region provides regulatory activity through decay‐accelerating and cofactor functions against the alternative pathway (AP) C3 convertase, while the CCP19–20 region confers selective binding to surface‐associated ligands, including C3b/C3d and glycosaminoglycans, thereby anchoring the inhibitor to host membranes (Merle et al., 2015; Biggs et al., 2022). In essence, Mini‐FH is synthesized as a fusion protein that retains critical complement regulatory activities in a smaller, more agile molecule; this design underscores a broader trend in drug development toward developing “miniaturized,” high‐potency biologics that can overcome limitations of full‐length proteins in terms of tissue distribution and immunogenicity (Dobo et al., 2018; Makou et al., 2013).

Therapeutic History:  
The use of complement regulators as therapeutic agents has a long history in clinical research, particularly for diseases driven by dysregulation of the AP of complement. Engineered FH fragments like Mini‐FH have been the subject of extensive biochemical and preclinical evaluation, with studies demonstrating that constructs consisting of CCP1–4/19–20 exhibit enhanced binding to C3 fragments and improved decay‐accelerating activity compared to native FH on a per‐molecule basis (Kamala et al., 2021; de Boer et al., 2020). Preclinical in vitro assays, such as surface plasmon resonance (SPR) and hemolytic assays, have confirmed that Mini‐FH binds C3b with high affinity and competitively inhibits AP convertase formation by both displacing factor B and accelerating convertase decay (Dobo et al., 2018; Biggs et al., 2022). Moreover, animal studies, including those involving FH‐deficient mice, have provided compelling evidence for the in vivo activity of such engineered constructs, wherein administration of Mini‐FH or homodimeric variants (e.g., HDM-FH) reduced complement deposition and ameliorated tissue pathology in models of complement‐mediated kidney disease (de Boer et al., 2020; Kamala et al., 2021). Although direct clinical trials of Mini‐FH specifically for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) have not yet been reported, related compounds such as full‐length recombinant FH (GEM103) have entered phase-2 clinical testing for AMD, thereby validating the concept of using FH‐based molecules to restore complement homeostasis in ocular diseases (Kamala et al., 2021; Dobo et al., 2018). Additionally, engineered versions of FH, including dimerized variants designed to enhance serum half-life and tissue binding, have shown promising preclinical efficacy in non-ocular models such as paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH) and C3 glomerulopathy, further suggesting that the underlying mechanism is broadly applicable to complement‐mediated disorders (de Boer et al., 2020; Biggs et al., 2022).

Mechanism of Action:  
The mechanism of action of Mini‐FH relies on its ability to simultaneously exploit the dual functionalities of FH through its modular design. The N-terminal CCP1–4 domain comprises the core regulatory region that mediates AP control by binding directly to C3b. This interaction competitively prevents the binding of factor B (FB), thereby inhibiting the formation of the pro-convertase C3bB complex and effectively blocking the assembly of the C3 convertase (C3bBb) (Merle et al., 2015; Kamala et al., 2021). In addition, CCP1–4 exerts decay-accelerating activity by accelerating the dissociation of Bb from the C3bBb complex; it also provides a binding platform for factor I (FI), thereby functioning as a cofactor that promotes the proteolytic cleavage of C3b to inactive iC3b (Kamala et al., 2021; de Boer et al., 2020). Complementing this, the C-terminal CCP19–20 domains of Mini‐FH are involved in high-affinity ligand recognition. These domains bind to the thioester-containing domain (TED) of C3b as well as to C3d fragments, which are present at sites of previous complement activation, and they interact with glycosaminoglycans (GAGs) and sialic acid residues on host cell surfaces (Merle et al., 2015; Biggs et al., 2022). This binding not only increases the overall avidity of the interaction by engaging multiple sites on a single C3b molecule but also serves to target the regulatory activity specifically to host surfaces that are decorated with complement activation products—a critical factor in distinguishing self from non-self (Dobo et al., 2018; Makou et al., 2013). Furthermore, by engaging in a dual binding mode, Mini‐FH effectively “bridges” the regulatory and recognition functions that in full-length FH are partially masked by the intervening CCP modules, thus resulting in a higher potency per molecule (Kamala et al., 2021; Dobo et al., 2018). Structural studies, including crystallographic analysis of complexes such as C3b:Mini-FH:FI, substantiate that Mini-FH engages two spatially distinct sites on C3b and even recruits FI through additional contacts involving CCP2–3, which further enhances its complement inhibitory function (Biggs et al., 2022). The overall consequence of these molecular interactions is the efficient disruption of the AP amplification loop, thereby reducing the cascade of complement activation products and ultimately limiting tissue damage driven by uncontrolled complement activity (Kamala et al., 2021; Dobo et al., 2018).

Expected Effect:  
In the context of dry AMD, the hypothesis posits that Mini-FH will competitively bind to C3b deposited on the surfaces of retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells and within Bruch’s membrane, specifically restoring local complement regulation by the alternative pathway (Kamala et al., 2021; de Boer et al., 2020). The expected mechanism is that, upon intravitreal administration, Mini-FH will localize to the subretinal space where excessive complement activation is known to occur as a result of FH deficiency or dysfunction associated with the Y402H polymorphism. Once there, the CCP1–4 segment of Mini-FH is anticipated to exert decay-accelerating and cofactor activities that promote the inactivation of C3b—inhibiting the formation and persistence of the C3 convertase (C3bBb) and thereby interrupting the amplification of the cascade (de Boer et al., 2020; Dobo et al., 2018). This biochemical activity is expected to result in a reduction of downstream complement components such as C5b–9 (the membrane attack complex) and inflammatory mediators like C3a and C5a, which are implicated in the chronic inflammation observed in dry AMD (Kamala et al., 2021; Dobo et al., 2018).

From a cellular perspective, by limiting complement activation on RPE surfaces, Mini-FH is expected to reduce the formation and accumulation of drusen-like deposits—extracellular aggregates that have been associated with inappropriate complement activity and are a hallmark of AMD pathology (Dobo et al., 2018; Makou et al., 2013). In addition, the engagement of CCP19–20 with surface-bound C3b/C3d and GAGs should enhance the targeted accumulation of Mini-FH on the RPE and in Bruch’s membrane, areas that are known hotspots for complement dysregulation in AMD (Merle et al., 2015; Biggs et al., 2022). This targeted binding not only localizes the regulatory function where it is most needed but may also facilitate secondary beneficial effects; for example, by mitigating complement-mediated cytotoxicity, Mini-FH may indirectly improve the phagocytic function of the RPE. Efficient post-phagocytosis is critical for the daily clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS), and disruption of this process is a contributing factor in the progression of AMD (Kamala et al., 2021; Dobo et al., 2018). Preclinical experiments in RPE explant models or murine AMD models that have been exposed to Mini-FH are thus expected to demonstrate a decrease in C3 deposition and complement activation markers, accompanied by restoration of normal RPE phagocytic capacity (de Boer et al., 2020; Dobo et al., 2018). Moreover, due to its relatively small size when compared to full-length FH, Mini-FH is predicted to have superior tissue penetration, which is essential for reaching the deeper layers of Bruch’s membrane and the subretinal space, where the pathological complement activation predominantly occurs (Kamala et al., 2021; Dobo et al., 2018).

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating the potential of Mini-FH (Recombinant FH CCP1–4/19–20) as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, several key strengths and challenges emerge. One of the primary strengths of Mini-FH is its rational design based on a deep understanding of FH architecture and function. By incorporating the most critical regulatory and recognition domains into a single, compact molecule, Mini-FH offers enhanced potency on a per-molecule basis and efficient competitive binding to C3b. The enhanced decay-accelerating activity and ability to serve as a cofactor for FI-mediated C3b inactivation have been well documented in preclinical assays, including SPR and hemolysis studies (Kamala et al., 2021; de Boer et al., 2020). These features are especially promising given that dysregulated complement activation is a central element of AMD pathogenesis. Furthermore, Mini-FH’s smaller size relative to full-length FH suggests improved penetration into ocular tissues such as Bruch’s membrane and the subretinal space, where therapeutic intervention is most needed (Dobo et al., 2018; de Boer et al., 2020).

Another significant strength is the translational rationale supported by biochemical and preclinical animal studies. Engineered FH fragments, including Mini-FH variants, have demonstrated efficacy in reducing complement activity in murine models of complement dysregulation, such as C3 glomerulopathy and PNH, which supports the concept that restoring control over the AP can ameliorate tissue damage (Kamala et al., 2021; Biggs et al., 2022). The fact that full-length recombinant FH (GEM103) is already being evaluated clinically for AMD further bolsters the therapeutic validity of targeting the complement cascade in ocular diseases (Kamala et al., 2021; Dobo et al., 2018). Moreover, the diverse strategies employed in the development of similar biologics (e.g., dimerized forms of Mini-FH or fusion constructs with additional targeting domains) point to an active area of research and innovation that is likely to yield clinically effective solutions (Makou et al., 2013; Dobo et al., 2018).

Nevertheless, several weaknesses and challenges warrant careful consideration. Although Mini-FH has demonstrated robust in vitro complement regulatory activity, its reduced size relative to the full-length molecule may also come with a trade-off, such as a potential reduction in FI cofactor activity under certain conditions (de Boer et al., 2020; Kamala et al., 2021). This diminished cofactor activity might necessitate higher dosing to achieve complete complement inhibition, which in turn could impact the safety profile and overall therapeutic index in the delicate ocular environment. Immunogenicity remains another concern; engineered proteins can sometimes elicit anti-drug antibodies (ADAs), and although intravitreal delivery benefits from the eye’s relative immune privilege, long-term administration in a chronic disease like AMD may eventually overcome this barrier (Kamala et al., 2021; Biggs et al., 2022). In addition, while animal model data in non-ocular systems are promising, the unique anatomy and microenvironment of the retina—especially the dynamics of RPE function, Bruch’s membrane characteristics, and POS phagocytosis—present additional layers of complexity that have not yet been fully addressed by preclinical studies specific to this application (Kamala et al., 2021; Dobo et al., 2018).

There is also the challenge of ensuring consistent manufacturing and high-yield recombinant production of a complex, multi-domain protein like Mini-FH. Although advances in recombinant expression systems have made it feasible to produce such proteins at scale, the retention of full activity, appropriate post-translational modifications, and proper folding is critical for therapeutic efficacy and must be established within a robust quality control framework (Makou et al., 2013). Furthermore, the pharmacokinetic profile of Mini-FH, including its half-life on ocular tissues and systemic clearance if any, requires detailed investigation; alterations in inter-domain linker length or structural flexibility could impact tissue distribution and drug retention at the target site (Kamala et al., 2021; Dobo et al., 2018).

From a mechanistic standpoint, while Mini-FH is designed to restore regulation by competitively binding to C3b and facilitating its inactivation, the downstream consequences of complement repression in the retina are multifaceted. In dry AMD, chronic complement dysregulation not only drives inflammation but also contributes to impaired phagocytosis of POS by the RPE. Although preclinical evidence suggests that restoring complementary control can indirectly improve RPE function (Kamala et al., 2021), the exact molecular pathways linking complement inhibition to improved POS clearance have not been fully elucidated, necessitating further mechanistic studies in retinal model systems (Dobo et al., 2018).

In summary, Mini‐FH represents a highly promising therapeutic candidate for dry AMD due to its engineered dual functionality—providing both potent AP convertase regulatory activity and targeted binding to complement‐deposited surfaces—as well as its potential for superior tissue penetration given its compact molecular size (Kamala et al., 2021; de Boer et al., 2020). Its mechanism of action is well supported by structural, biochemical, and preclinical data, and the conceptual framework is further validated by ongoing clinical evaluations of full‐length recombinant FH in AMD. However, while the biochemical rationale and preclinical models lend strong support to the therapeutic strategy, challenges remain in translating these findings to the complex ocular environment; these include ensuring sufficient FI cofactor activity, managing potential immunogenicity, optimizing intravitreal delivery parameters, and confirming that the beneficial effects observed in kidney or systemic models are recapitulated in retinal tissues (de Boer et al., 2020; Dobo et al., 2018).

However, several critical issues must be addressed before advancing Mini‐FH as a clinical candidate for dry AMD. First, direct evidence from retinal model systems is required to confirm that the biochemical potency of Mini‐FH translates into meaningful therapeutic outcomes in the context of RPE integrity, Bruch’s membrane function, and POS phagocytosis (de Boer et al., 2020; Dobo et al., 2018). Second, while the immune privileged status of the eye may mitigate ADA risk, long-term intravitreal delivery studies need to be conducted to establish both safety and sustained efficacy over the chronic course of AMD (Kamala et al., 2021; Biggs et al., 2022). Third, the pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic profiles in the ocular milieu must be rigorously characterized to determine the optimal dosing regimen, ensuring that Mini‐FH reaches and remains active at the target site without eliciting off-target effects (Kamala et al., 2021; Dobo et al., 2018). Finally, manufacturing consistency and scalability remain practical challenges for any complex recombinant protein therapeutic, and these aspects must be optimized early in the development process to facilitate clinical translation (Makou et al., 2013).

In conclusion, Mini‐FH (Recombinant FH CCP1–4/19–20) is a state-of-the-art, mechanistically driven therapeutic candidate that harnesses the targeted complement inhibitory potential of engineered FH fragments for the treatment of dry AMD. Its design leverages the strengths of both the N-terminal regulatory and C-terminal recognition domains, offering a potent means to counteract the dysregulated complement activation underlying AMD pathology. While the preclinical data from non-ocular models are very promising, targeted studies in retinal systems are necessary to confirm its efficacy and safety in the context of dry AMD. Based on the comprehensive literature review, Mini‐FH represents a compelling candidate with strong scientific rationale and significant translational potential, but further preclinical work specifically focused on retinal endpoints is essential before progressing to clinical trials. The balance between enhanced C3b binding and potential trade-offs in FI cofactor activity, along with considerations of immunogenicity and optimal delivery strategies, will be critical determinants of its ultimate clinical success in alleviating the burden of dry AMD (Kamala et al., 2021; Dobo et al., 2018; de Boer et al., 2020; Biggs et al., 2022).

hypothesis: AM580 (Retinoic acid receptor α agonist; Cayman Chemical Cat. No. 10007915)
answer:
Proposal for AM580 (Retinoic acid receptor α agonist; Cayman Chemical Cat. No. 10007915)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
AM580 is a fully synthetic retinoid compound designed as a highly selective agonist for the retinoic acid receptor α (RARα). Its chemical structure—a derivative of naphthalene and benzoic acid—was rationally engineered to confer two key properties: a more rigid molecular architecture compared with the natural ligand all‐trans retinoic acid (ATRA) and a marked preferential binding to RARα over other retinoid receptor subtypes (RARβ and RARγ) (Garattini et al., 2007; Martin et al., 1992). The molecule’s chemical name, 4-(5,6,7,8-tetrahydro-5,5,8,8-tetramethyl-2-naphthalenyl)carboxamido]benzoic acid, reflects its derivation from a series of modifications intended to enhance receptor selectivity and bioactivity (Martin et al., 1992). AM580 belongs to the broader class of retinoids—compounds that are either natural derivatives of vitamin A or synthetically modified analogues—which function as ligands for nuclear hormone receptors. Retinoids have been exploited in various fields of medicine due to their ability to modulate cellular differentiation, proliferation, and apoptosis by activating retinoic acid receptor (RAR) and retinoid X receptor (RXR) pathways (Cras et al., 2010; Martin et al., 1992). In the case of AM580, its design emphasizes selective RARα activation, as demonstrated by its 30-fold higher binding affinity for RARα compared to RARβ and RARγ (Teng et al., 1996; Martin et al., 1992), making it an excellent molecular tool for dissection of RARα-specific biological responses.

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, retinoids have been at the forefront of differentiation therapy, with ATRA being successfully employed in the treatment of acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) (Garattini et al., 2007; Garattini et al., 1997). However, the clinical use of natural retinoids like ATRA has been limited by drawbacks such as isomerization, rapid metabolism, and broad receptor engagement leading to unnecessary side effects (Drowley et al., 2020; Cras et al., 2010). These limitations spurred the development of receptor subtype–selective ligands, among which AM580 emerged as a leading RARα-selective agonist (Martin et al., 1992). Beyond oncology, synthetic retinoids have been investigated in a variety of contexts including dermatology and even cardiovascular applications (Nagy et al., 2012; Petrukhin, 2013); however, more recent studies have explored the potential ocular applications of retinoid receptor agonists. In particular, a growing body of literature has begun to examine the effects of RAR agonists on retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells. Preclinical studies have demonstrated that activation of RARα in RPE cells by compounds such as AM580 can modulate epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT) and improve cellular functions relevant to retinal homeostasis (Kobayashi et al., 2021). Although not previously approved as an ocular therapeutic, the compound’s use in research settings—including those investigating phagocytic processes in the RPE—provides a promising precedent for repurposing it for conditions like dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Kobayashi et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action:  
The mechanism of action of AM580 is well delineated at the molecular level. As an RARα agonist, it binds with high affinity to the ligand-binding domain of RARα, a nuclear receptor that functions as a ligand-dependent transcription factor. Upon ligand binding, the receptor undergoes a conformational change that results in the dissociation of co-repressor complexes and the recruitment of co-activators and other transcriptional machinery. This ligand-induced activation facilitates the heterodimerization of RARα with retinoid X receptor (RXR), followed by binding to retinoic acid response elements (RAREs) in the promoter regions of target genes (Garattini et al., 2007; Teng et al., 1996).  
Notably, AM580’s structural modification—featuring a polar amide linkage—enhances its selectivity for RARα by promoting specific hydrogen bonding interactions within the receptor’s binding pocket that are not available in RARβ or RARγ (Teng et al., 1996). Once activated, RARα modulates a variety of downstream genes. Among these, studies have recently indicated that selective RARα activation can lead to the upregulation of milk fat globule epidermal growth factor 8 (MFGE8) in RPE cells (Unknown Reference). MFGE8 plays a critical role in facilitating the bridging of phosphatidylserine (exposed on the shed photoreceptor outer segments (POS)) to integrin receptors—specifically αvβ5—which are expressed on the RPE, thereby promoting efficient phagocytosis (Drowley et al., 2020; Kobayashi et al., 2021). Consequently, AM580’s engagement of RARα is expected to not only drive transcriptional changes related to RPE differentiation and anti-fibrotic responses but also directly enhance phagocytic clearance mechanisms essential for retinal health (Kobayashi et al., 2021). In additional preclinical settings, RARα agonism via AM580 has been implicated in modulating transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-β) signaling pathways, which further supports its capacity to inhibit aberrant EMT—a process implicated in retinal scarring and progression of dry AMD (Kobayashi et al., 2021).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis under evaluation posits that AM580, by selectively activating RARα at an effective concentration (EC₅₀ ~50 nM as observed in RPE cell assays), will stimulate the transcription of the MFGE8 gene. Upregulation of MFGE8 is crucial because this glycoprotein acts as a “molecular bridge” by binding to phosphatidylserine on POS and to integrin receptors such as αvβ5 on the RPE. Under normal conditions, MFGE8 is an essential mediator of RPE phagocytosis, facilitating the daily clearance of spent outer segments—a process that is impaired in dry AMD (Kobayashi et al., 2021; Nagy et al., 2012). Evidence from preclinical studies, including those using Mertk-deficient RPE models, suggests that AM580 treatment can lead to increased MFGE8 levels and a concomitant improvement in POS uptake (Kobayashi et al., 2021). Thus, in the assay proposed by the team, AM580 is expected to restore or enhance the phagocytic capacity of RPE cells by boosting MFGE8 expression. This improved clearance mechanism would help reduce the accumulation of POS debris and lipofuscin—a buildup known to contribute to RPE dysfunction and the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Kobayashi et al., 2021; Drowley et al., 2020). Furthermore, secondary effects such as the inhibition of deleterious EMT processes—which are associated with fibrosis and the progression of dry AMD—may also be realized, thereby preserving or restoring a more differentiated, functional RPE phenotype (Kobayashi et al., 2021).

Overall Evaluation:  
AM580 represents a compelling therapeutic candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD, based on several lines of evidence gathered from the literature. Its primary strength lies in its high degree of selectivity for RARα. This receptor selectivity is critical because it allows for target‐specific modulation of gene expression, potentially reducing the broad side effects observed with natural retinoids like ATRA that activate multiple receptor subtypes (Garattini et al., 2007; Martin et al., 1992; Teng et al., 1996). The structural optimization of AM580 not only confers potent agonistic activity but also provides a pharmacological tool for dissecting the specific roles of RARα in retinal biology, particularly within the RPE. Preclinical studies have underscored the utility of RARα activation in modulating key processes such as cellular differentiation, inhibition of EMT, and enhancement of phagocytic function in RPE cells (Kobayashi et al., 2021; Nagy et al., 2012).  
However, several potential challenges must also be acknowledged. Retinoid compounds are notorious for their complex pharmacokinetics and potential for off-target effects, including teratogenicity, as evidenced by prior studies of AM580 in teratogenicity models (Elmazar et al., 2001). The delicate balance between efficacy and safety remains a critical issue, particularly for a condition such as dry AMD where long-term treatment is anticipated. Furthermore, while the preclinical evidence supporting the induction of MFGE8 by RARα activation is promising, the available data remain largely confined to in vitro studies and select animal models. Clinical validation in human subjects is still lacking, and the translation of dose levels, tissue penetration, and metabolic stability from the laboratory to the clinic remains an open question (Kobayashi et al., 2021; Drowley et al., 2020). Another concern is that AM580, while selective, does retain some activity at RARβ and RARγ at higher concentrations (Teng et al., 1996), an effect that may have unpredictable consequences on cell signaling in the complex microenvironment of the RPE. Moreover, the retinoid system is intricately linked with multiple signaling pathways, and long-term modulation may lead to compensatory mechanisms or unforeseen adverse outcomes.  
In summary, the repurposing of AM580 for dry AMD is supported by a robust molecular rationale—its ability to selectively activate RARα is directly linked to the upregulation of MFGE8 and, consequently, the enhancement of POS phagocytosis in RPE cells. This mechanism directly addresses a critical defect in dry AMD pathology, namely the impaired clearance of photoreceptor debris, which is a central driver of retinal degeneration (Garattini et al., 2007; Kobayashi et al., 2021). The preclinical literature offers promising evidence that selective RARα modulation can exert beneficial effects on RPE physiology, including the prevention of EMT and restoration of phagocytic function (Kobayashi et al., 2021; Drowley et al., 2020). Despite these strengths, the transition from preclinical studies to clinical application will require careful attention to pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic factors, as well as rigorous safety assessments to mitigate risks typical of retinoid therapies. Overall, while challenges remain, AM580’s unique properties render it a promising candidate that merits further investigation in the context of dry AMD, with the potential to fill a significant therapeutic gap in the management of this debilitating condition (Martin et al., 1992; Teng et al., 1996; Kobayashi et al., 2021).

Proposal for Zinc Sulfate (ZnSO₄; Sigma-Aldrich Cat. No. Z0251)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Zinc sulfate (ZnSO₄; Sigma-Aldrich Cat. No. Z0251) is an inorganic salt that dissociates readily in aqueous solutions to yield zinc ions (Zn²⁺) and sulfate anions. Zinc sulfate is a well‐characterized compound produced via chemical synthesis and has been used for decades as a nutritional supplement to treat zinc deficiency. It belongs to the class of trace mineral supplements, and, more broadly, to inorganic therapeutic agents. In many clinical and veterinary practices, zinc sulfate has been utilized as a dietary supplement to support immune function, antioxidant defenses, and wound healing. Its broad therapeutic use is partly validated by its inclusion in complex formulations—for example, in the Age-Related Eye Disease Study (AREDS) protocol for age-related macular degeneration (AMD) where zinc supplementation was associated with a reduction in disease progression risk (Qin, 2007). Zinc sulfate has also found application in ophthalmic preparations due to extensive ocular safety data supporting its use; indeed, zinc sulfate eye drops have been evaluated for ocular safety in early-phase clinical trials (Qin, 2007). This candidate is particularly attractive for repurposing since its manufacturing and formulation are well established, and its molecular properties as a zinc donor could potentially address deficiencies in zinc-dependent enzymatic processes observed in dry AMD.

Therapeutic History  
Historically, the use of zinc in medical treatments dates back to its role as an essential trace element in numerous biological systems. In the context of ocular diseases, mounting evidence has implicated zinc deficiency in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) dysfunction and the pathogenesis of dry AMD. Preclinical studies in animal models have demonstrated that zinc-deficient conditions lead to significant pathological consequences in the RPE, including increased lipofuscin accumulation and impaired phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) (Julien et al., 2011). In vitro studies using ARPE-19 cells have similarly shown that disruption of zinc homeostasis produces lysosomal dysfunction which contributes to the build-up of toxic metabolic by-products associated with AMD pathology (Rajapakse et al., 2017). Moreover, several investigations have shown that zinc supplementation can rescue lysosomal acidification deficits and restore autophagic flux in RPE cells exposed to toxic compounds such as A2E—a bisretinoid that accumulates abnormally in dry AMD (Choi et al., 2024). Although many of these reports have employed zinc ionophores (e.g., ClioQ, 1H10) to facilitate zinc delivery into cells, they highlight a fundamental therapeutic rationale: zinc is an essential cofactor for proper lysosomal enzyme function, and its supplementation can reverse key features of cellular dysfunction associated with dry AMD (Choi et al., 2024). Clinical approaches, particularly those emerging from the AREDS trials, have also shown that high-dose zinc supplementation (typically delivered as zinc oxide or zinc sulfate) can slow the progression of AMD (Qin, 2007). While these formulations primarily aimed to address generalized zinc deficiency and oxidative stress, they establish a precedent for the repurposing of zinc salts—specifically zinc sulfate—in ocular disorders such as dry AMD.

Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, zinc acts as an indispensable cofactor for a multitude of enzymes, including the zinc-dependent cathepsins B and L. Cathepsins are lysosomal proteases critical for the degradation of phagocytosed POS, autophagic cargo, and other intracellular substrates that accumulate over time. In the RPE, the efficient clearance of POS is a daily and metabolically demanding process; thus, any impairment in cathepsin activity can lead to the accumulation of undegraded material, contributing to the formation of lipofuscin and subsequent cellular toxicity (Julien et al., 2011; Choi et al., 2024). Zinc ions contribute structurally and catalytically to the proper folding and activity of these cathepsins. Under conditions of zinc deficiency or altered intracellular zinc distribution—as has been observed in aged RPE and AMD patients—the activity of cathepsin B and L becomes suboptimal, leading to lysosomal dysfunction (Julien et al., 2011; Rajapakse et al., 2017).

Several reports have demonstrated that exposure to bisretinoids such as A2E leads to dose-dependent cell death and lysosomal alkalinization in ARPE-19 cells; this in turn impairs the activity of lysosomal hydrolases that require an acidic environment for optimal function (Choi et al., 2024). Zinc supplementation, when delivered intracellularly via ionophores in these models, restored lysosomal acidification and enabled the reactivation of the degradative machinery, including zinc-dependent enzymes (Choi et al., 2024). This reacidification is crucial because lysosomal proteases, including cathepsin B/L, demonstrate maximal catalytic activity at a pH of approximately 4.5–5.0—a condition that is disrupted in diseased RPE cells (Choi et al., 2024). Moreover, zinc has been shown to influence autophagy dynamics: in models where A2E treatment led to an arrest in autophagic flux (evidenced by increased p62 and LC3-II levels), zinc supplementation was able to reduce p62 levels and partially restore proper autophagic turnover (Choi et al., 2024). These observations suggest that zinc not only acts as a structural cofactor for lysosomal enzymes but also indirectly supports the maintenance of lysosomal pH homeostasis and autophagic function. The proposal under evaluation extends this line of reasoning by hypothesizing that direct supplementation with Zn²⁺—provided in the form of zinc sulfate—could similarly restore cathepsin B/L activity in RPE cells, thereby improving phagolysosomal enzyme function and photoreceptor outer segment degradation in dry AMD models (Choi et al., 2024).

Expected Effect  
Based on the aforementioned mechanistic rationale, the expectation is that ZnSO₄ supplementation will elevate intracellular Zn²⁺ concentrations in RPE cells, thereby reconstituting the proper activity of zinc-dependent enzymes. In the context of dry AMD, where lysosomal dysfunction is a key pathological feature, the restoration of cathepsin function is anticipated to improve the degradation of POS. Successful clearance of POS is critical to prevent the buildup of lipofuscin and other deleterious aggregates that contribute to RPE degeneration (Rajapakse et al., 2017). In cell-based assays—such as those using ARPE-19 cells exposed to A2E—the addition of zinc sulfate is hypothesized to act by increasing the bioavailability of Zn²⁺, which in turn would lead to several interrelated outcomes: (1) reacidification of lysosomes as zinc supports proton pump function and stabilizes lysosomal membranes, (2) enhanced enzymatic activity of cathepsins B and L, leading to improved proteolytic clearance, and (3) restoration of autophagic flux as evidenced by decreased p62 accumulation and normalized LC3-II turnover (Choi et al., 2024; Rajapakse et al., 2017). Furthermore, improved phagolysosomal function would likely reduce the intracellular accumulation of A2E and other toxic by-products, ultimately leading to increased cell viability and better overall RPE function. It is important to note that although many of the existing studies have utilized zinc ionophores to deliver Zn²⁺ into cells, the existing ocular safety profile for zinc sulfate formulations (as evidenced by previous clinical studies using zinc sulfate eye drops) supports the feasibility of adapting ZnSO₄ for this application (Qin, 2007). Moreover, gene expression studies confirm that RPE cells express high levels of cathepsin B and L, and their dysfunction correlates with AMD pathogenesis; thus, elevating Zn²⁺ levels may have a directly beneficial impact on these key enzymatic pathways (Julien et al., 2011).

Overall Evaluation  
The repurposing of zinc sulfate as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD rests on several well-founded observations. First, there is a robust body of preclinical evidence indicating that zinc supplementation can restore lysosomal function in RPE cells challenged with A2E-induced toxicity, which is a well-characterized in vitro model of dry AMD (Choi et al., 2024). This evidence includes improvements in lysosomal pH, reductions in A2E accumulation, and restored autophagic flux. Second, clinical data from large-scale studies such as AREDS have established that zinc supplementation—albeit delivered in a different form than zinc sulfate—confers a statistically significant reduction in the progression risk of AMD (Qin, 2007). Third, mechanistic studies have underlined the pivotal role of zinc as a cofactor for cathepsin B and L, enzymes that are crucial for the phagolysosomal degradation of POS. In the diseased state, reductions in zinc availability or disruptions in zinc homeostasis result in diminished cathepsin activity, impaired clearance of cellular debris, and subsequent lipofuscin accumulation (Julien et al., 2011; Rajapakse et al., 2017).

Despite these strengths, the candidate does have notable limitations. A significant concern is that most of the supportive in vitro studies have used zinc ionophores (such as ClioQ or 1H10) to ensure efficient intracellular delivery of zinc (Choi et al., 2024). Zinc sulfate, being a simple salt, does not possess intrinsic ionophore properties, which may limit its immediate cellular uptake and availability to lysosomal compartments. This suggests that while ZnSO₄ has a favorable safety profile and is easily formulated, its efficacy in rescuing intracellular cathepsin activity may be contingent on formulation strategies that enhance cellular uptake, such as combining it with a permeation enhancer or designing specialized delivery vehicles. Additionally, direct evidence linking zinc sulfate supplementation to the restoration of cathepsin B/L activity in RPE cells is currently inferred from studies using alternative zinc delivery methods rather than from studies employing ZnSO₄ directly (Rajapakse et al., 2017). Therefore, while the hypothesis is strongly supported by mechanistic reasoning and parallel evidence from related studies, targeted experiments specifically using ZnSO₄ in models of dry AMD are necessary to confirm its therapeutic potential.

Another consideration is the multifactorial nature of AMD pathogenesis. While lysosomal dysfunction and cathepsin impairment are certainly central features, AMD is also driven by oxidative stress, inflammation, and complement dysregulation. Zinc exerts broader antioxidant effects partly through its involvement in metallothionein systems and by modulating the activity of antioxidant enzymes (Rajapakse et al., 2017). Thus, while restoring cathepsin activity represents a compelling mechanistic target, zinc sulfate supplementation might also confer additional benefits that go beyond enzyme cofactor replacement. However, these pleiotropic effects may complicate the interpretation of the therapeutic outcomes, making it challenging to ascribe clinical benefits solely to the restoration of cathepsin activity.

In summary, zinc sulfate represents a promising therapeutic candidate for dry AMD on several fronts. Its inherent ability to donate Zn²⁺, a cofactor crucial for the activity of lysosomal proteases such as cathepsins B and L, forms the basis of its proposed mechanism of action. Preclinical evidence indicates that zinc supplementation can restore lysosomal pH, reduce A2E accumulation, and enhance autophagic flux in RPE cells—key elements that underpin the pathological cascade of dry AMD (Choi et al., 2024). Moreover, clinical trial data from studies using zinc compounds, including those with zinc sulfate formulations as ocular drops, further underscore the potential efficacy and safety of zinc-based therapies in AMD (Qin, 2007). Nevertheless, the translational success of ZnSO₄ hinges on addressing the challenge of effective cellular uptake. Without the use of an ionophore or an advanced delivery system, there is a risk that ZnSO₄ may not achieve the intracellular zinc concentrations required to modulate cathepsin activity and, by extension, lysosomal function in a robust manner. Additionally, while mechanistic studies have provided indirect evidence linking zinc levels to cathepsin function in RPE cells (Julien et al., 2011), direct validation of the therapeutic hypothesis with ZnSO₄ remains limited.  

Strengths of the candidate include its well-established production, favorable safety profile in ocular applications, and substantial supporting evidence from both preclinical and clinical studies that underscore the importance of zinc in maintaining lysosomal integrity and protease function (Choi et al., 2024; Rajapakse et al., 2017). The repurposing strategy is bolstered by a strong theoretical rationale: correction of zinc deficiency in the RPE should restore cathepsin effectiveness and thereby improve the degradation of POS, a function known to be compromised in dry AMD (Choi et al., 2024).

Conversely, weaknesses include the fact that most experimental paradigms demonstrating zinc’s benefits have relied on assisted delivery mechanisms (ionophores) and have not been directly replicated with zinc sulfate alone. This introduces uncertainty regarding the bioavailability of zinc ions when administered as ZnSO₄ in the intended therapeutic context. Furthermore, AMD is a complex, multifactorial disease, and while addressing lysosomal enzyme dysfunction is promising, it remains only one aspect of the overall pathology. Without addressing complementary pathological mechanisms such as chronic oxidative stress and inflammation, zinc sulfate alone may not suffice as a standalone therapy. Finally, the lack of direct evidence from ZnSO₄-specific studies in relevant dry AMD models (as opposed to studies using zinc ionophores) highlights the need for further targeted research before progressing to clinical trials.

Overall, the evaluation of zinc sulfate as a potential therapeutic candidate for dry AMD reveals a strong theoretical foundation conditioned on its role as a zinc donor to rescue Zn-dependent cathepsin activity in the RPE. The candidate leverages a well-known mechanism where zinc acts both structurally and catalytically within lysosomal proteases, and clinical data from related zinc supplementation studies provide an encouraging backdrop. However, the translational challenges concerning the effective delivery of Zn²⁺—particularly in the absence of an ionophore—must be carefully addressed. In conclusion, zinc sulfate exhibits considerable potential as part of a multifaceted therapeutic strategy targeting lysosomal dysfunction in dry AMD, with the caveat that further studies are needed to optimize its delivery, validate its mechanism in precise AMD models, and integrate it effectively within a broader therapeutic regimen that tackles the multifactorial nature of the disease (Choi et al., 2024; Qin, 2007).
