Proposal for Homotaurine (GABA analogue; Tocris Cat. No. 0388)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Homotaurine is a small-molecule GABA analogue that was originally investigated for its potential neuroprotective properties in Alzheimer’s disease due to its ability to interact with inhibitory neurotransmitter receptors. Although originally isolated from marine algae as a natural sulfonated amino acid derivative, the synthetic production of homotaurine has allowed for its repurposing and pharmacological refinement for various clinical indications. As a member of the GABAergic modulator class, it is designed to mimic the activity of the endogenous neurotransmitter γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA), thereby affecting neuronal excitability and cellular homeostasis. In particular, homotaurine is postulated to activate GABAA receptors, which are ligand-gated chloride channels that normally contribute to membrane hyperpolarization and dampening of excitatory input. This class of compounds has been widely explored for neuroprotective purposes and has been utilized in clinical trials for Alzheimer’s disease, where an acceptable safety profile was established. The fact that homotaurine has progressed to advanced clinical stages in Alzheimer’s research supports its tolerability and widespread bioactivity, making it an attractive candidate for repurposing in ocular diseases such as dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Carullo et al., 2020).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, homotaurine has been primarily evaluated in the context of Alzheimer’s disease, where its anti-aggregation properties and potential to interfere with amyloid-β deposition were of paramount interest. Its prior clinical examination, which concluded with a favorable safety record, provides a solid foundation for its repurposing in other neurodegenerative conditions. Although there is no direct record of homotaurine being used to treat dry AMD, other compounds that modulate GABAergic signaling have been investigated in retinal degenerative models. For example, several studies have documented the expression of GABA receptor subunits, including those of the GABAA family, in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, suggesting that pharmacological targeting of these receptors may have therapeutic implications in diseases associated with retinal dysfunction (Arellano et al., 2025). Furthermore, inhibitory neurotransmitters such as GABA have been implicated in maintaining proper cellular excitability and synaptic balance in the retina; alterations in their regulation are associated with excitotoxicity and neurodegeneration in retinal conditions including macular degeneration (Pavan & Dalpiaz, 2018; Schur et al., 2018). In a similar vein, preclinical studies have used GABA modulators to rescue or protect RPE and photoreceptor function in models of retinal degeneration and light-induced injury (Schur et al., 2018). Thus, while direct clinical evidence for homotaurine in dry AMD is lacking, its antecedents in the GABAergic drug class and the known vulnerability of RPE cells to excitotoxic calcium overload position it as a promising candidate for therapeutic repurposing.

Mechanism of Action:  
The hypothesized mechanism of action of homotaurine in dry AMD rests on its ability to activate GABAA receptors expressed on RPE cells. Under physiological conditions, GABAA receptors are heteropentameric chloride channels that, upon binding GABA, permit chloride influx and hyperpolarize the cell membrane. This hyperpolarization ordinarily serves to counteract excessive excitation and limit voltage-gated calcium channel opening. In the context of RPE function, maintaining a tight regulation of intracellular calcium is paramount because calcium levels directly influence cytoskeletal reorganization, phagosome trafficking, and lysosomal fusion events necessary for the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) (Nagymihaly et al., 2021). Several studies have documented that RPE cells not only express GABAA receptor subunits, such as GABAAα1, but that receptor activation in these cells can modify intracellular calcium concentrations, thereby modulating a host of calcium-dependent cellular processes—including phagocytosis (Arellano et al., 2025).

In dry AMD, the RPE’s phagocytic capacity is compromised, leading to the accumulation of lipofuscin and other toxic by-products, which in turn further disrupt cellular function and promote oxidative stress (Si et al., 2023; Inana et al., 2018). Homotaurine’s binding to GABAA receptors is expected to stabilize the membrane potential and reduce the abnormal Ca²⁺ influx that occurs during excitotoxic stress. This reduction in calcium entry is anticipated to alleviate downstream effects such as dysregulated cytoskeletal dynamics and impaired lysosomal trafficking. Cytoskeletal reorganization is essential for phagosome motility; proper F-actin dynamics direct the trafficking of phagosomes toward lysosomal compartments where degradation occurs (Inana et al., 2018; Nagymihaly et al., 2021). Moreover, studies have demonstrated that inflammatory mediators present in AMD, including TNF-α and interleukin-1β, modulate GABAA receptor expression and function, suggesting that modulation of these receptors could be a viable strategy to counteract inflammation-driven excitotoxicity (Arellano et al., 2025). In addition, the excitotoxic environment generated by imbalanced glutamate/GABA signaling in the retina can be mitigated by restoring the inhibitory tone through GABAA receptor activation. The specific EC₅₀ of approximately 10 µM for homotaurine indicates that it has the potential to achieve receptor activation within a therapeutic window that is plausible in an ocular formulation (Carullo et al., 2020; Arellano et al., 2025). Taken together, the combined modulation of calcium influx, along with the stabilization of cytoskeletal and lysosomal pathways, constitutes a comprehensive molecular strategy that homotaurine may employ to rescue impaired POS degradation in dry AMD.

Expected Effect:  
The proposed assay in ARPE-19 cells—a well-established in vitro model for RPE function—aims to evaluate whether homotaurine, via activation of GABAA receptors, can restore impaired photoreceptor outer segment (POS) phagocytosis under conditions of glutamate-induced stress. RPE cell dysfunction in dry AMD is characterized by diminished phagocytosis and lysosomal degradation of POS, leading to the pathological accumulation of lipofuscin, which further impedes cellular function (Si et al., 2023; Inana et al., 2018). By engaging GABAA receptors, homotaurine is expected to “rescue” this vital phagocytic process by normalizing intracellular Ca²⁺ dynamics—thus preventing excitotoxicity—and by ensuring the proper reorganization of actin filaments or other cytoskeletal elements that are essential for efficient phagosome motility (Nagymihaly et al., 2021).

Experimental evidence in related studies supports that compounds with similar mechanisms (i.e., GABA modulators and taurine-related molecules) are capable of influencing intracellular calcium signaling and can enhance the uptake and processing of POS in RPE cells (Arellano et al., 2025; López-Colomé et al., 1994). Under normo-physiological conditions, RPE cells efficiently internalize shed POS through receptor-mediated pathways involving CD36, MerTK, and αVβ5 integrin, initiating a cascade that is dependent on well-regulated intracellular Ca²⁺ fluctuations (Nagymihaly et al., 2021). In a stress state, glutamate excess drives excitotoxic Ca²⁺ entry that may dysregulate these processes. By antagonizing this excitotoxic cascade, homotaurine is anticipated to reduce the aberrant Ca²⁺ load, thereby restoring the dynamic equilibrium that supports both cytoskeletal integrity and lysosomal trafficking. This mechanism is supported by studies showing that dysregulation of Ca²⁺ not only impairs phagosome motility but also has deleterious effects on downstream lysosomal fusion and degradation, ultimately impacting cellular clearance mechanisms (Si et al., 2023; Nowak et al., 2025). Thus, the expected effect is a measurable enhancement in POS uptake as well as improved degradation kinetics in RPE cells subjected to glutamate-induced stress, which would correlate with potential therapeutic efficacy in dry AMD. Furthermore, since the underlying pathology of dry AMD involves chronic oxidative stress and accumulation of metabolic by-products, a pharmacological intervention that can restore intracellular homeostasis has far-reaching implications for halting or even reversing disease progression (Arellano et al., 2025).

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating homotaurine for dry age-related macular degeneration, several critical observations emerge. One of the key strengths of homotaurine is its well-documented safety profile from Alzheimer’s clinical trials, which lowers the translational hurdles when repurposing the compound for ocular administration. The fact that homotaurine is a GABA analogue that activates GABAA receptors—a receptor class that is expressed on RPE cells and critically involved in regulating intracellular Ca²⁺—provides a strong mechanistic rationale for its application in dry AMD (Arellano et al., 2025). By potentially mitigating excitotoxic Ca²⁺ influx, homotaurine could restore normal cytoskeletal dynamics and lysosomal trafficking, both of which are indispensable for the effective degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (Nagymihaly et al., 2021).

Among the strengths, the following points are notable:  
1. The candidate’s mechanism directly addresses a central pathology of dry AMD—namely, impaired RPE phagocytosis and lysosomal dysfunction—which leads to toxic lipofuscin accumulation (Si et al., 2023; Inana et al., 2018).  
2. Activation of GABAA receptors by homotaurine could normalize Ca²⁺ handling within RPE cells, thereby alleviating the excitotoxic stress that is linked to altered cytoskeletal assembly and defective phagosome trafficking (Arellano et al., 2025; Inana et al., 2018).  
3. The compound’s history in Alzheimer’s trials suggests a favorable safety margin and known pharmacokinetic properties that may be adapted for ocular use, thus enhancing its potential for rapid clinical translation (Carullo et al., 2020).  
4. Preclinical evidence from other studies involving GABA modulators and related compounds shows that interfering with aberrant neurotransmitter signaling in the retina can elicit neuroprotective and phagocytosis-enhancing effects (Schur et al., 2018).

Conversely, some weaknesses and uncertainties remain that necessitate further investigation:  
1. Although the proposed EC₅₀ of approximately 10 µM for homotaurine is within a plausible therapeutic window for GABAA receptor activation, the actual pharmacodynamic response in RPE cells—especially in the diseased microenvironment of dry AMD—remains to be rigorously quantified (Arellano et al., 2025).  
2. The retinal microenvironment in dry AMD is complex, characterized not only by excitotoxic stress but also by chronic oxidative stress, inflammation, and altered expression of multiple receptor types. In such a context, GABAA receptor activation could be affected by altered ionic gradients, potentially leading to reversed or atypical receptor responses as has been documented in other retinal degenerations (Arellano et al., 2025; Telegina et al., 2022).  
3. While indirect evidence supports the role of GABAergic modulation in restoring phagocytic function, there is a paucity of direct data demonstrating that homotaurine can specifically enhance POS uptake in ARPE-19 cells under injurious conditions. This gap necessitates additional in vitro studies to detail its effects on cytoskeletal reorganization, vesicular trafficking, and lysosomal fusion dynamics (Si et al., 2023; Nagymihaly et al., 2021).  
4. The exact downstream signaling pathways that link GABAA receptor activation to the observed improvements in phagocytic function must be delineated further. For example, the interplay between calcium channel deactivation, actin cytoskeleton stabilization, and the regulation of key phagocytic receptors (e.g., MerTK, αvβ5 integrin) remains incompletely characterized in the context of GABAergic modulation (Nagymihaly et al., 2021).  
5. Finally, the translational leap from in vitro findings in ARPE-19 cells to a robust therapeutic effect in human dry AMD patients is non-trivial. Aging RPE cells in vivo exhibit additional layers of complexity, including altered gene expression profiles, metabolic imbalances, and possible shifts in receptor isoforms, all of which might influence the responsiveness to homotaurine (Nowak et al., 2025; Si et al., 2023).

Overall, homotaurine represents a scientifically sound and mechanistically plausible candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration. Its potential to activate GABAA receptors on RPE cells, thereby reducing excitotoxic calcium influx and normalizing the intracellular processes that govern cytoskeletal dynamics and lysosomal trafficking, aligns well with the pathophysiological underpinnings of AMD (Arellano et al., 2025). Given the favorable safety data from Alzheimer’s trials and the breadth of preclinical evidence supporting the neuroprotective effects of GABAergic modulation in retinal contexts, homotaurine merits further exploration. Prior to clinical application, however, detailed mechanistic studies using ARPE-19 cells and appropriate animal models of dry AMD must be conducted. These studies should focus on quantifying calcium flux, cytoskeletal dynamics, phagosome motility, and lysosomal fusion efficiency upon homotaurine treatment under pathologically relevant conditions. Additionally, it will be important to investigate potential off-target effects and to determine whether combinatorial therapies that address oxidative stress and inflammation might synergize with homotaurine’s mechanism. In summary, while challenges remain, the repurposing of homotaurine for dry AMD offers a promising therapeutic avenue worthy of investment and further preclinical validation (Arellano et al., 2025; Si et al., 2023; Carullo et al., 2020).

Proposal for AMY-101 (Compstatin analog Cp40; Peptide, catalog no. Peptidotech P-1234)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
AMY-101 is a third-generation compstatin analogue built on the Cp40 scaffold, a cyclic, disulfide-constrained peptide discovered through iterative structure–activity optimization of the original compstatin hit identified by phage display against C3/C3b in 1996 (initial macrocycle I[CVVQDWGHHRC]T) (Lamers et al., 2022). Key potency-improving modifications en route to Cp40 include N-methylation of Trp and insertion of sarcosine, which rigidify the backbone and substantially increase binding affinity to C3; Cp40 (y-I[CV(1Me)WQDWSarAHRC]mI) binds a defined pocket between MG4/MG5 on the β-chain of C3/C3b with subnanomolar affinity and high selectivity for human and nonhuman primate (NHP) C3, while sparing other species, thereby necessitating NHP for translational in vivo work (Lamers et al., 2022). Mechanistically, compstatins are protein–protein interaction inhibitors: they occupy a substrate-binding site on C3 that prevents association with the C3 convertases, blocking convertase-mediated cleavage of native C3, and thereby interrupting the amplification loop and downstream effector generation (C3a, C3b, C5a, and membrane attack complex) independent of the initiating pathway (Lamers et al., 2022; Mastellos et al., 2019).

Compstatin analogues comprise a class of synthetic macrocyclic peptides that target the central node of complement activation at C3, distinguishing them from terminal-pathway blockers (e.g., C5 antibodies) and alternative-pathway–restricted inhibitors (e.g., factor D), which have shown mixed outcomes in complex complement-driven diseases such as age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Mastellos et al., 2019; Cerniauskas et al., 2020). Clinically, the compstatin platform has matured to produce both a PEGylated bivalent C3 inhibitor (pegcetacoplan/APL-2) approved for paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH) and non-PEGylated Cp40-derived candidates such as AMY-101 in human trials, establishing class translatability and safety management paradigms for chronic C3 inhibition (Lamers et al., 2022; Mastellos et al., 2019).

For ophthalmic translation, medicinal chemistry on Cp40 has produced fourth-generation, non-PEGylated lysine-extended derivatives (Cp40-KK, Cp40-KKK) with markedly improved solubility and favorable intraocular retention after intravitreal (IVT) administration in NHPs; these scaffolds maintain subnanomolar C3 affinity and exhibit retinal tissue engagement and co-localization with C3, suggesting target-driven distribution in ocular compartments (Hughes et al., 2020). Within the compstatin clinical lineage, earlier intravitreal compstatin (POT-4) and the PEGylated derivative APL-2/pegcetacoplan provided clinical benchmarks in geographic atrophy (GA), albeit with formulation-dependent considerations (e.g., PEG-associated risks) that motivate PEG-free ocular candidates such as AMY-101 or next-generation Cp40 analogues tailored for ocular delivery (Cerniauskas et al., 2020; Hughes et al., 2020; Lamers et al., 2022).

Therapeutic History  
Compstatin peptides have undergone extensive preclinical characterization and early clinical translation across complement-driven indications. Systemically, Cp40/AMY-101 blocked intravascular hemolysis and C3b opsonization in primate models and attenuated alloimmune responses and downstream B/T cell activation in transplantation models, demonstrating potent complement control and immunomodulatory ripple effects in vivo (Lamers et al., 2022). AMY-101 progressed through a first-in-human phase 1 trial (single and multiple ascending doses; subcutaneous and intravenous) with acceptable safety, no serious adverse events, and pharmacodynamic evidence of complement pathway modulation in healthy volunteers (Amyndas Pharmaceuticals S.A., 2017), and subsequently achieved local-delivery efficacy in a randomized, double-blind, split-mouth Phase IIa study for gingival inflammation with durable anti-inflammatory responses and no drug-induced immunogenicity detected (Hasturk et al., 2021). In the periodontal trial, AMY-101 reduced clinical indices (modified gingival index, bleeding on probing) and decreased matrix metalloproteinases (MMP-8, MMP-9) in gingival crevicular fluid, with effects persisting up to 90 days after the three weekly local injections, supporting local tolerability, biomarker responsiveness, and sustained pharmacodynamic action (Hasturk et al., 2021).

Within ophthalmology and AMD, multiple lines of evidence support the clinical plausibility of C3-directed strategies. Early intravitreal compstatin (POT-4) dosing in a primate model was associated with disappearance of drusen deposits, and PEGylated C3 inhibition (APL-2/pegcetacoplan) reduced GA lesion growth in Phase II and has achieved efficacy signals in Phase III, representing the first successful complement intervention in GA and validating the target class for dry AMD (Cerniauskas et al., 2020; Lamers et al., 2022). Conversely, downstream or pathway-restricted modulation disappointed: anti-C5 agents (eculizumab, LFG316) and alternative pathway blockade at factor D (lampalizumab) failed to deliver clinical benefit in GA, bolstering the rationale for upstream C3 control that addresses both opsonization and effector generation (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). Although AMY-101 itself has not yet been reported in human ocular trials in the provided context, Cp40-class derivatives have been tailored for ocular use and evaluated in NHPs after single IVT injections, achieving prolonged C3-saturating vitreous concentrations and retinal/choroidal target engagement for over three months—exposure metrics compatible with infrequent intravitreal maintenance regimens (Hughes et al., 2020).

Critically, human iPSC-derived RPE models carrying the common CFH Y402H high-risk variant establish a mechanistic and phenotypic bridge to AMD and provide in vitro evidence that Cp40 reverses disease-relevant pathology, particularly lysosome/autophagy defects and complement-driven lysosomal overburden, thereby directly supporting the translational concept for dry AMD (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). The RPE findings are reinforced by the broader AMD complement literature: complement activation on photoreceptor outer segments drives monocyte-dependent retinal atrophy, factor H genetics (including Y402H) modulates ocular alternative pathway activity, and complement deposition in Bruch’s membrane/sub-RPE space contributes to drusen biogenesis and RPE stress—elements that are mechanistically addressable by C3 blockade (Mastellos et al., 2019).

In sum, compstatin-class agents have an extensive preclinical pedigree and emergent clinical validation. For AMD specifically, the class has ocular proof-of-concept (POT-4) and clinical validation of C3 inhibition (pegcetacoplan), and Cp40 analogues demonstrate prolonged ocular PK in NHP; AMY-101 contributes human safety and local-delivery experience that supports translational risk management but requires dedicated ocular development for dry AMD (Cerniauskas et al., 2020; Lamers et al., 2022; Hughes et al., 2020).

Mechanism of Action  
C3 sits at the convergence of the classical, lectin, and alternative complement pathways; its cleavage by C3 convertases (C4b2b for CP/LP and C3bBb for AP) produces the anaphylatoxin C3a and the opsonin C3b, which seeds an amplification loop by forming additional alternative pathway convertases on activating surfaces (Mastellos et al., 2019). Persistent generation and deposition of C3b (and downstream C5b-9) under dysregulated conditions fuels inflammatory tissue damage and membrane injury; thus, targeting C3 offers initiation-independent suppression of both opsonization and effector generation (C3a, C5a, MAC), addressing multiple pathogenic modalities concurrently (Lamers et al., 2022; Mastellos et al., 2019).

Compstatins, including Cp40/AMY-101, are substrate-protecting inhibitors that bind to a defined site on C3/C3b (between MG4 and MG5 of the β-chain) and prevent the binding of native C3 to the active convertase, thereby blocking C3 turnover and the AP amplification cycle regardless of initiating pathway (Lamers et al., 2022). This binding mode is supported by co-crystallographic and kinetic analyses, and SAR has established critical roles for N-methylated Trp and charged residues (Asp7, Arg12) in affinity and solubility (Lamers et al., 2022). Unlike some PEGylated bivalent constructs that display altered target preference and weaker affinity to soluble C3, monovalent PEG-free Cp40 binds strongly to both soluble and surface-bound C3/C3b, preserving potency where soluble target is abundant (e.g., in plasma and vitreous), a beneficial profile for local ocular delivery (Lamers et al., 2022).

In human iPSC-RPE carrying CFH Y402H, C3 overactivation and increased C3 turnover correlate with multiple autophagy–lysosome abnormalities: increased expression of autophagosome markers (LC3-II, p62, ATG12–ATG5), expansion and activation of late endosomal/lysosomal/exosomal compartments (LAMP1, CD63; increased Lysotracker), reduced lysosomal functional readouts (decreased Cathepsin D expression/activity), swollen lysosome-like vesicles, lysosomal membrane fragility (elevated galectin-8 recruitment), and extracellular deposition of Cathepsin D in ApoE-positive drusen-like material (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). Mechanistic links are twofold: (1) excessive extracellular C3 activation increases surface C5b-9 (MAC) formation, which is internalized to lysosomes and triggers lysosomal membrane permeabilization with cathepsin leakage; (2) intracellular C3–autophagy crosstalk via ATG16L1 and cathepsin-mediated C3 activation may perturb autophagy flux, compounding lysosomal stress (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). In this model, Cp40 reduces C3 turnover (biochemical ELISA/MSD readouts) and diminishes C3b and C5b-9 deposition on and within RPE, leading to restoration of lysosomal pH/function and autophagic flux (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). Specifically, Cp40 treatment increases Cathepsin D expression/activity, reduces lysosome size and swelling, stabilizes lysosomal membranes (reduced galectin-8/LAMP co-localization), normalizes melanosome content (increased mature type 4 melanosomes), and decreases the volume of drusen-like deposits on transwells—collectively, a reversal of RPE disease phenotypes (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).

Importantly, the RPE data underscore that “tuning” C3 is necessary: stable shRNA knockdown of C3 (~85% reduction) did not restore melanosome/lysosome number and increased stress vacuoles indicative of a detrimental effect, whereas pharmacologic Cp40-mediated control of C3 turnover (not wholesale depletion) was beneficial—consistent with C3’s homeostatic roles in tissue clearance and immune surveillance (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). Rapamycin-driven autophagy activation failed to correct lysosomal deficits in the same AMD-RPE model, underscoring that upstream removal of complement burden may be required to re-enable autophagic clearance in complement-dysregulated RPE (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).

For ophthalmic PK/PD, next-generation Cp40 derivatives (Cp40-KK, Cp40-KKK) demonstrate prolonged vitreous residence and target engagement after single IVT injection in cynomolgus NHPs, measured by a sensitive SPR-based competition assay that recovers peptide from C3 complexes by heat dissociation and quantifies active inhibitor; ocular C3 levels were assayed in parallel (Hughes et al., 2020). Following a 0.5 mg IVT dose, Cp40-KKK maintained C3-saturating vitreous concentrations over three months (~200 nM during month 1; ~100–120 nM by month 3) and co-localized with C3 in retinal/choroidal tissue, suggesting target-driven retention and possible depot release; intraocular C3 concentrations measured were ~0.1–2 nM, implying inhibitor:target ratios sufficient for sustained pharmacodynamic coverage (Hughes et al., 2020). Only ~0.2% of the initial dose remained unbound in vitreous by day 14, consistent with rapid clearance of free peptide and prolonged persistence of target-bound pools (Hughes et al., 2020). These PK relationships, combined with AMY-101’s subnanomolar C3 affinity and prolonged plasma half-life (>60 h), support the feasibility of durable local complement control via IVT compstatin analogues without PEGylation (Lamers et al., 2022; Hasturk et al., 2021; Lamers et al., 2022).

Expected Effect  
In the proposed iPSC-RPE assay, AMY-101/Cp40 is expected to bind native C3 in the extracellular milieu and block its convertase-mediated cleavage, thereby suppressing both C3a/C3b generation and downstream terminal-pathway activation, including formation and lysosomal internalization of C5b-9 complexes that exacerbate lysosomal membrane permeabilization and cathepsin leakage in complement-dysregulated RPE (Lamers et al., 2022; Cerniauskas et al., 2020). The RPE model provides direct biochemical and cell-biological readouts that respond to C3 inhibition: Cp40 reduced C3 turnover (C3b/iC3b/C3c in supernatants), decreased surface and lysosomal C3b and C5b-9, and restored lysosomal functional markers (Cathepsin D expression and activity), organelle morphology (reduced lysosomal swelling; increased mature melanosomes), and membrane integrity (decreased galectin-8 recruitment), with associated reductions in drusen-like deposit burden—outcomes that would be expected for AMY-101 under similar conditions (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).

Given the measured RPE complement activity and the presence of C3 in ocular compartments, PD monitoring can include extracellular C3 fragment profiling (e.g., MSD capture for C3a domain detecting C3b; ELISA for C3b/iC3b/C3c), surface and lysosomal C5b-9 immunostaining (e.g., co-localization with LAMP markers), and lysosomal/autophagy endpoints such as LAMP1/CD63 expression, LysoTracker signal, LC3-II and p62 accumulation, Cathepsin D protein/activity, and galectin-8–based lysosomal damage assays (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). In the referenced RPE studies, effective Cp40 exposure used 6 µM for seven days with media change mid-course—a regimen that achieved robust biochemical and morphological rescue; potency in cellular systems is governed by high target abundance and convertase dynamics and may not mirror biochemical IC₅₀ values, but AMY-101’s subnanomolar C3 affinity and the low-nanomolar ocular C3 concentrations measured in NHP vitreous suggest that pharmacologically relevant free drug levels in the assay will saturate target (Cerniauskas et al., 2020; Hughes et al., 2020; Lamers et al., 2022). We note that no direct IC₅₀ for Cp40/AMY-101 in RPE culture is provided in the cited work; therefore, the proposed IC₅₀ value (~0.5 µM) cannot be confirmed from the current context and dosing should be guided empirically by the established 6 µM exposure used to reverse phenotypes in the Y402H model (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).

Regarding photoreceptor outer segment (POS) processing, impaired lysosomal function in RPE is causally linked to defective POS degradation; complement activation on POS can drive monocyte-dependent retinal atrophy, providing disease-relevant context for expecting that restoration of lysosomal flux via C3 inhibition would secondarily improve POS handling (Mastellos et al., 2019; Cerniauskas et al., 2020). However, the provided RPE studies did not explicitly report POS uptake/degradation assays in Cp40-treated cells, so POS-specific rescue should be treated as a testable hypothesis rather than an established outcome; lysosomal/autophagy restoration and reduced complement burden provide a mechanistic basis for such improvement (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).

For translational extrapolation to IVT dosing paradigms, ocular PK from Cp40-KK/KKK in NHP indicates that non-PEGylated Cp40 analogues can achieve multi-month C3-saturating exposure (retinal/choroidal co-localization with C3), which, combined with AMY-101’s high-affinity binding and absence of PEG (avoiding anti-PEG immunogenicity and PEG-related tissue effects), supports feasibility of infrequent dosing with a favorable mechanistic risk–benefit profile (Hughes et al., 2020; Lamers et al., 2022).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
– Mechanistic centrality and breadth of action at C3: AMY-101 directly blocks the C3 convertase–substrate interaction, upstream of opsonization and effector generation, thereby intercepting multiple pathogenic drivers operative in dry AMD (C3b deposition, C3a/C5a-mediated inflammation, and MAC-mediated membrane injury), in contrast to pathway-restricted or terminal-pathway agents that have underperformed in GA (Lamers et al., 2022; Mastellos et al., 2019; Cerniauskas et al., 2020). By protecting C3 from cleavage rather than inhibiting a specific convertase assembly, AMY-101 exerts initiation-independent control, appropriate for the complex and mixed complement activation modes present in AMD (Hasturk et al., 2021).  
– Direct human RPE disease-model evidence: In Y402H iPSC-RPE, Cp40 suppressed C3 turnover and downstream C5b-9 deposition, relieved lysosomal overburden and membrane fragility, restored Cathepsin D expression/activity and melanosome maturation, and reduced drusen-like deposits—an unusually comprehensive, mechanistically coherent rescue of AMD-relevant cellular pathology that maps directly onto the hypothesized mode of action for AMY-101 (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).  
– Ocular PK/translational feasibility: Single IVT dosing of Cp40 lysine-extended derivatives in NHPs yielded >90 days of C3-saturating intraocular exposure with retinal/choroidal target engagement and co-localization, supporting achievable, infrequent dosing intervals for a PEG-free compstatin platform; methods to quantify ocular drug and C3 (SPR competition; ELISA) and retinal localization are validated and can be deployed for PD monitoring (Hughes et al., 2020).  
– Clinical precedent for the target class in GA and systemic safety: Pegcetacoplan’s efficacy in reducing GA growth validates C3 inhibition in dry AMD; prolonged systemic C3 inhibition has an acceptable safety profile with appropriate vaccination and monitoring, and AMY-101 itself showed favorable safety, lack of anti-drug antibodies, and durable local efficacy in a human local-delivery setting (periodontal disease) (Lamers et al., 2022; Hughes et al., 2020; Hasturk et al., 2021).  
– PEG-free design: Non-PEGylated Cp40 analogues avoid PEG-associated liabilities (anti-PEG antibodies, tissue vacuolation, and potential association with CNV conversion observed in a subset of GA patients on PEGylated C3 inhibitors), while maintaining strong affinity for soluble C3—attributes favorable for chronic ocular use (Hughes et al., 2020; Lamers et al., 2022).

Weaknesses and Gaps  
– No human ocular clinical data for AMY-101: Despite compelling RPE in vitro data and NHP ocular PK for related derivatives, AMY-101 lacks reported human ocular PK/safety and clinical efficacy data in AMD in the provided context; bridging studies will be required to confirm ocular tolerability, immunogenicity, and dosing intervals specific to AMY-101 (Lamers et al., 2022; Hughes et al., 2020).  
– Species specificity constrains preclinical breadth: Compstatins bind human/NHP C3 with high specificity, precluding meaningful small-animal efficacy studies beyond surrogate approaches; this increases reliance on NHP for ocular PK/PD and toxicity packages and complicates broader in vivo AMD model validation (Lamers et al., 2022).  
– POS degradation not yet demonstrated under Cp40 in RPE: Although lysosomal/autophagy restoration strongly predicts improved POS clearance, the provided RPE studies did not report POS uptake/degradation assays post-Cp40; this is an essential disease-relevant endpoint to include in the next-stage validation (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).  
– Need to balance complement suppression: Stable C3 knockdown in the RPE model exacerbated stress phenotypes, underscoring the necessity for controlled pharmacologic inhibition rather than depletion; clinical protocols must monitor for under/over-suppression and preserve homeostatic complement roles in the immunoprivileged ocular environment (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).  
– Potential safety/biology caveats with C3 blockade in the eye: Theoretical risks include modulation of macrophage polarization that might favor neovascularization and the necessity to maintain anti-infective surveillance locally; although systemic experience with vaccination mitigates infectious risk, ocular-specific risks and CNV conversion propensity must be assessed prospectively for PEG-free C3 inhibitors (Mastellos et al., 2019; Hughes et al., 2020). Patient stratification (“complotype”) and baseline complement activity vary with age/sex and genetics (e.g., CFH), necessitating biomarker-driven inclusion and response frameworks in trials (Mastellos et al., 2019).

Decision-grade Assessment and Development Plan  
– Scientific validity: Strong. The AMD-RPE disease biology is directly addressed by AMY-101’s mechanism, with robust iPSC-RPE rescue data for Cp40 spanning biochemical, organellar, and deposit readouts; the mechanism integrates with known complement–lysosome–autophagy crosstalk and MAC-induced lysosomal permeabilization (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).  
– Translational feasibility: Good, with defined tasks. Ocular PK/PD in NHPs for Cp40 derivatives is compelling and suggests IVT dosing intervals of 2–3 months; AMY-101 has favorable systemic/local safety credentials and is PEG-free (Hughes et al., 2020; Hasturk et al., 2021). The absence of human ocular data for AMY-101 is a remediable gap.  
– Comparative landscape: Favorable. Factor D and C5 failures in GA argue for upstream intervention; C3 inhibition has shown clinical benefit (pegcetacoplan), placing AMY-101 in a validated mechanistic class, with potential safety advantages from PEG-free design and strong affinity to soluble C3 (Cerniauskas et al., 2020; Lamers et al., 2022).  
– Key risks: Ocular safety (immunogenicity, inflammation, CNV conversion), pharmacodynamic over-suppression, and unknowns around long-term retinal tissue distribution with AMY-101 (as distinct from Cp40-KKK). These will be addressed with staged NHP toxicology/PK, dosing optimization, and clinical biomarker surveillance (Hughes et al., 2020; Mastellos et al., 2019).

Recommended studies before IND for dry AMD  
1) In vitro translational package in human iPSC-RPE (Y402H and non-risk): reproduce Cp40 rescue with AMY-101 under identical conditions (6 µM; 7-day dosing), including biochemical C3 turnover (C3b/iC3b/C3c), surface/lysosomal C5b-9, LAMP1/CD63, LysoTracker, LC3-II, p62, galectin-8, Cathepsin D expression and activity, melanosome quantitation, and drusen-like deposit volume (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). Add POS feeding assays (pulse–chase of isolated POS) to quantify phagosome–lysosome fusion kinetics and rhodopsin degradation as POS-specific endpoints (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).  
2) Ocular PK and PD in cynomolgus NHPs with AMY-101: single- and multiple-dose IVT, vitreous/tissue levels by SPR competition assay, vitreous C3 fragments and C3:drug ratios, retinal/choroidal co-localization, and depot behavior versus Cp40-KKK; include dose ranging (≥0.5 mg) and extended sampling to ≥90 days (Hughes et al., 2020).  
3) Ocular safety/toxicology: GLP IVT studies (single and repeat-dose) evaluating inflammation, IOP, ERG, OCT/FAF, histopathology (RPE, choroid, retina), and immunogenicity (anti-drug antibodies intraocular/systemic) with correlation to drug levels and C3 suppression; monitor for CNV risk signals (Mastellos et al., 2019; Hughes et al., 2020).  
4) Biomarker strategy: translate RPE/animal biomarkers to clinical sampling—aqueous/vitreous C3 fragments, C5a, sC5b-9; imaging biomarkers (FAF for lipofuscin; OCT for outer retinal integrity; autofluorescent deposit quantification) to track pharmacodynamic effects on deposit burden and RPE health (Cerniauskas et al., 2020; Hughes et al., 2020).  
5) Patient stratification plan: incorporate CFH Y402H and broader complotype profiling in trial design, with baseline complement activity and demographic modifiers (age, sex) to enrich for responders and appropriately power efficacy analyses (Mastellos et al., 2019).

Conclusion  
AMY-101 (Cp40) is a mechanistically precise, high-affinity C3 inhibitor whose action is well matched to the complement-driven lysosomal/autophagy pathology observed in dry AMD RPE biology; Cp40 has already demonstrated reversal of Y402H RPE disease phenotypes across orthogonal readouts, and Cp40-class ocular PK in NHPs supports infrequent IVT dosing without PEG, addressing practical treatment constraints (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). The class has clinical validation in GA (pegcetacoplan) and an increasingly reassuring safety dossier for chronic C3 inhibition, while AMY-101 itself exhibits favorable human safety and local-delivery performance in non-ocular indications (Lamers et al., 2022; Hasturk et al., 2021). The principal development gaps—human ocular PK/safety for AMY-101 and POS-specific efficacy readouts—are tractable with focused preclinical and early clinical work. Taken together, the weight of mechanistic, cellular, and translational evidence supports advancing AMY-101 into an ophthalmic development path for dry AMD with a high likelihood of mechanistic efficacy and a manageable risk profile under a biomarker-driven, stratified clinical strategy (Cerniauskas et al., 2020; Lamers et al., 2022; Mastellos et al., 2019).

Proposal for Metformin (AMPK agonist; Sigma-Aldrich Cat. No. D150959)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Metformin is a well‐established biguanide originally derived from the natural compound galegine found in Galega officinalis. Over decades of development, it has been chemically optimized and synthesized into its modern, orally administrable form. Today, metformin is classified within the antidiabetic drug class and is routinely used to treat type 2 diabetes mellitus. Its discovery as an antihyperglycemic agent was serendipitous, and subsequent structural modifications have resulted in a drug with an excellent safety profile and pleiotropic effects beyond blood glucose regulation. As a small synthetic molecule available from reputable suppliers such as Sigma‐Aldrich (Cat. No. D150959), metformin has been repurposed in recent years for potential applications outside of metabolic diseases, including neurodegeneration and retinal degenerative disorders. This candidate belongs to a class of compounds that have historically been used for systemic metabolic control, but emerging evidence also suggests that their ability to activate AMPK—a critical cellular energy sensor—can be exploited to modulate autophagy and mitochondrial function in non‐metabolic tissues, including the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Zhao et al., 2020).

Therapeutic History:  
Clinically, metformin has long been the first-line treatment for type 2 diabetes due to its robust glucose-lowering capability and favorable long-term risk profile. The extensive clinical use of metformin in diabetic populations has allowed researchers to retrospectively observe its pleiotropic effects on other organ systems. Notably, retrospective epidemiological studies have demonstrated that diabetic patients treated with metformin exhibit a lower incidence of age-related macular degeneration (AMD) compared to non-users, suggesting potential protective effects in the retina (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Huang et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2020). Furthermore, preclinical studies investigating metformin in vitro have shown that it protects human RPE cells against oxidative stress-induced damage, largely mediated by stimulation of the AMPK pathway (Zhao et al., 2020). In addition, in vivo models employing metformin have provided evidence of its ability to mitigate light-induced photoreceptor loss and retinal degeneration, supporting the hypothesis that its molecular targets in the RPE could be leveraged against dry AMD (Dang et al., 2021; Miyagishima et al., 2021). Although metformin has not been established as a conventional treatment for AMD, its proven use in modulating metabolic pathways, along with demonstrable effects on autophagy, mitochondrial function, and inflammation in retinal cells, provides the rationale for repurposing it in the context of dry AMD (Vessey et al., 2022; Buonfiglio et al., 2024).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, metformin exerts its primary pharmacological effects by inhibiting mitochondrial electron transport chain complex I, which leads to a reduction in ATP production and a concomitant increase in the AMP/ATP ratio. This energetic shift results in the activation of AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK), a master regulator of cellular metabolism and autophagy (Zhao et al., 2020). Activated AMPK phosphorylates several downstream targets that collectively restore energy homeostasis; among these targets are key regulators of autophagy, including the inhibition of mTOR and the direct phosphorylation of ULK1, which initiates autophagosome formation (Zhao et al., 2020; Dang et al., 2021). One important biochemical hallmark of this autophagy induction is the conversion of cytosolic LC3-I to its lipidated, membrane-bound form LC3-II, which has been used extensively as a marker to assess autophagy flux in RPE cell studies (Zhao et al., 2020). Additionally, metformin’s activation of AMPK influences mitochondrial biogenesis through upregulation of transcription co-activators such as PGC-1α, thereby promoting the generation of new, functionally active mitochondria (Dang et al., 2021; Sekar et al., 2023). These mechanisms are particularly relevant in the context of dry AMD, where RPE metabolic dysfunction is a key pathological feature. Moreover, metformin has been shown to modulate lipid metabolism, notably by enhancing cholesterol efflux via the AMPK/LXR pathway, which can reduce intracellular lipid accumulation—a contributor to drusen formation in AMD (Dang et al., 2021). Additional anti-inflammatory effects are mediated through suppression of NLRP3 inflammasome activation and modulation of VEGF signaling, further contributing to the overall cytoprotective profile of metformin in the retina (Dang et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2020).

Expected Effect:  
Based on the proposed hypothesis and existing evidence, it is expected that metformin will activate AMPK in RPE cells, thereby promoting autophagy and mitochondrial biogenesis. In practical terms, treatment with metformin is anticipated to lead to a measurable increase in LC3-II formation, a reduction in intracellular lipid accumulation, and restoration of ATP levels in RPE cells—specifically in models employing CFH Y402H iPSC-RPE cells, which serve as a relevant in vitro model of AMD (Zhao et al., 2020). The enhanced autophagic flux, as indicated by increased LC3-II levels and decreased p62 levels, will facilitate the clearance of damaged organelles, including dysfunctional mitochondria. This process of mitophagy is expected to improve overall mitochondrial homeostasis, thereby restoring the energetic capacity required for efficient phagocytosis and degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS). Given that efficient POS degradation by RPE cells is critical for photoreceptor renewal and retinal health, the metformin-induced restoration of energy balance and autophagic function could lead to improved visual function. Importantly, AMPK is expressed in RPE cells and has been shown to be a crucial mediator of autophagy and mitochondrial quality control in these cells, ensuring that metformin’s mechanism of action is well-targeted to the cellular environment affected in dry AMD (Miyagishima et al., 2021; Zhou & Xue, 2024). Furthermore, several in vivo studies support the notion that metformin can rescue mitochondrial function and enhance cellular clearance mechanisms, which are expected outcomes of its use in dry AMD models (Sekar et al., 2023; Zhou & Xue, 2024).

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating metformin as a drug candidate for treating dry age-related macular degeneration, there are several notable strengths. First, metformin’s well-established safety profile from decades of clinical use for type 2 diabetes offers an advantageous starting point for repurposing—its known pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic properties facilitate its potential translation to ophthalmic indications (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Zhang et al., 2020). Second, robust preclinical data support metformin’s ability to activate AMPK and promote autophagy, two pathways intimately involved in the maintenance of RPE health. Activation of AMPK has been repeatedly shown to enhance LC3-II formation, reduce oxidative stress, restore mitochondrial membrane potential, and upregulate mitochondrial biogenesis, all of which are critical to counteracting the metabolic deficits seen in AMD (Zhao et al., 2020; Dang et al., 2021; Sekar et al., 2023). Third, epidemiological studies have suggested that metformin use correlates with a reduced incidence of AMD, lending clinical relevance to its potential protective effects in the retina (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Huang et al., 2023). Fourth, the ability of metformin to modulate lipid metabolism, particularly by promoting cholesterol efflux and thereby reducing drusen-associated lipid accumulation, represents another beneficial mechanism targeting a fundamental aspect of AMD pathology (Dang et al., 2021).

However, several weaknesses and challenges must also be considered. Although many preclinical and retrospective clinical studies point toward a beneficial role of metformin in retinal health, direct prospective evidence in dry AMD patients remains limited. Some of the data originate from studies published in journals of variable quality, and there exists heterogeneity in the responses observed across different model systems, including patient-derived RPE cells where metformin’s effects may vary (Augustin & Atorf, 2023). Moreover, while metformin is effective in activating AMPK systemically at standard doses used for diabetes, the optimal dosing regimen, route of administration, and tissue-targeting strategies necessary to achieve effective concentrations in the retinal tissue remain to be determined. The possibility that metformin’s efficacy may depend on specific genetic or metabolic backgrounds of patients—such as differences in CFH status or other AMD-related risk factors—also raises concerns about patient heterogeneity in clinical trials (Miyagishima et al., 2021; Augustin & Atorf, 2023). Additionally, while the expected restoration of autophagy and mitochondrial biogenesis is promising, the precise quantitative changes in LC3-II, ATP levels, lipid accumulation, and POS degradation need rigorous validation under controlled experimental conditions before definitive conclusions can be drawn (Zhao et al., 2020; Zhou & Xue, 2024). Finally, potential systemic side effects such as gastrointestinal disturbances, rare occurrences of lactic acidosis, and vitamin B12 deficiency, albeit infrequent, may need consideration when repurposing metformin for chronic ocular use, especially in non-diabetic populations (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Brown et al., 2019).

Overall, metformin represents a promising therapeutic candidate for dry AMD due to its multifaceted effects on enhancing autophagy, improving mitochondrial biogenesis, and restoring cellular energy metabolism in RPE cells. Its safety profile and broad availability further support its potential for rapid clinical translation. Nonetheless, the candidate’s ultimate success will depend on careful dose optimization, robust clinical trial designs that account for inter-patient variability, and further mechanistic studies to precisely delineate the quantitative biochemical improvements—such as LC3-II increase, lipid clearance, ATP restoration, and enhanced POS degradation—in preclinical AMD models (Augustin & Atorf, 2023; Zhao et al., 2020). The convergence of epidemiological, biochemical, and preclinical data thus supports proceeding with further validation studies, while also highlighting the need to address remaining uncertainties regarding tissue-specific drug delivery and long-term outcomes in the context of dry AMD (Dang et al., 2021; Vessey et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2020).

answer:
Proposal for Fenofibrate (PPARα agonist; Sigma-Aldrich Cat. No. F6020)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Fenofibrate is a synthetic fibrate originally developed and approved as a lipid‐lowering agent that acts primarily as a peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor alpha (PPARα) agonist. It was discovered through efforts to develop compounds that could enhance fatty acid oxidation and thereby reduce triglyceride levels and improve lipid profiles in patients with dyslipidemia. As a member of the fibrate class of drugs, fenofibrate and its active metabolite, fenofibric acid, have been classically used in cardiometabolic conditions such as hyperlipidemia, where they improve lipid profiles by increasing high-density lipoprotein (HDL) levels and lowering triglycerides. The compound available as Sigma-Aldrich Cat. No. F6020 is representative of these agents and has been extensively studied in preclinical models of metabolic stress. Its chemical design enables it to bind to PPARα, a nuclear receptor that modulates gene expression of enzymes central to fatty acid β-oxidation and lipid homeostasis. In the context of retinal disorders, fenofibrate has been pursued as a repurposing candidate owing to its robust safety profile and its potential to address the dysregulation of lipid metabolism observed in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells. Several studies have suggested that by activating PPARα, fenofibrate may help reduce lipid overload and mitigate the accumulation of toxic by-products such as A2E (a major fluorophore in lipofuscin) that contribute to RPE dysfunction in age-related macular degeneration (Wang et al., 2023; Ren et al., 2022).  

Therapeutic History:  
Fenofibrate has a long clinical history as an antihyperlipidemic agent with a well-established safety profile in patients with cardiovascular risk factors. In addition to its widespread use in metabolic disorders, a significant body of preclinical research has documented the potential benefits of fenofibrate in retinal diseases. Several studies have demonstrated that fenofibrate can ameliorate retinal abnormalities induced by high-fat diets and excessive lipid exposure. For instance, experimental models of fat-induced RPE injury have shown that fenofibrate reduces oxidative stress and inflammatory mediators, thereby protecting RPE integrity through mechanisms such as upregulation of the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway (Wang et al., 2023). In diabetic retinopathy—a condition that, while distinct from dry AMD, shares underlying processes related to oxidative stress, lipid peroxidation, and inflammatory cascades—fenofibrate has been explored for its protective effects on the retina, contributing to improvements in vascular permeability and barrier function of the outer blood–retina barrier (Fu et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2023). Although fenofibrate’s potential use in dry AMD has not been as widely investigated as its role in diabetic retinopathy, the documented protective effects on RPE under conditions of lipid overload, as well as its ability to downregulate markers of oxidative stress (e.g., NOX4 and 3‐nitrotyrosine) and inflammatory cytokines (such as TNFα and ICAM1), support its candidacy for repurposing in dry AMD (Ren et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023). It is noteworthy that while clinical data in diabetic populations (e.g., FIELD study outcomes) have driven considerable interest in fenofibrate’s ocular effects, direct applications to dry AMD remain exploratory and are based largely on preclinical findings that show promise for reducing lipotoxic damage in the RPE.

Mechanism of Action:  
Fenofibrate exerts its pharmacological effects primarily through the activation of PPARα, a nuclear receptor that, upon ligand binding, dimerizes with the retinoid X receptor and binds to specific PPAR response elements in promoter regions of target genes. This leads to the transcriptional upregulation of a variety of genes involved in lipid uptake, fatty acid transport, and β-oxidation, ultimately promoting the catabolism of long-chain fatty acids. In RPE cells, robust expression of PPARα is critical for maintaining homeostasis in the face of high lipid loads and oxidative stress. Activation of PPARα by fenofibrate has been shown to enhance mitochondrial and peroxisomal fatty acid oxidation, thereby reducing intracellular lipid accumulation and possibly the generation of toxic lipid peroxidation products such as A2E, a primary component of the lipofuscin granules that accumulate with age in RPE cells (Ren et al., 2022).

Beyond its classical role in lipid metabolism, fenofibrate has also been reported to engage additional cellular signaling pathways that contribute to its cytoprotective effects. In several preclinical studies, fenofibrate and fenofibric acid have been observed to activate the PI3K/AKT pathway in RPE cells, which is well recognized for its roles in cell survival and stress response. The activation of PI3K/AKT signaling by fenofibrate leads to enhanced cell survival signals, mitigates oxidative damage, and downregulates inflammatory mediators in fatty acid–challenged RPE cells (Wang et al., 2023). Moreover, fenofibrate has been implicated in reducing the expression of pro-oxidant enzymes such as NADPH oxidase 4 (NOX4) and in decreasing levels of markers of oxidative stress like 3-nitrotyrosine (3-NT) in palmitic acid-treated RPE models (Wang et al., 2023). These actions collectively contribute to mitigation of oxidative injury—a central component of dry AMD pathogenesis.

In addition, some studies have proposed that fenofibrate may exert ancillary effects through mechanisms independent of PPARα activation. For example, evidence suggests that fenofibrate might function as an iron chelator, thereby reducing intracellular free iron levels, which in turn could diminish the generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and blunt the aberrant activation of the canonical Wnt/β-catenin pathway—a pathway implicated in various ocular pathologies including AMD (Mandala et al., 2020). This suppression of iron-induced oxidative stress and its associated downstream signaling cascades may further contribute to the preservation of RPE cell function under conditions of chronic oxidative insult.

Another mechanism of potential interest is fenofibrate’s impact on inflammatory signaling. Classical anti-inflammatory effects have been verified through its ability to inhibit nuclear factor-kappa B (NF-κB) activity, thereby reducing the transcription of a host of pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines that might contribute to retinal degeneration (Garcia-Ramírez et al., 2016; Fu et al., 2020). Although direct evidence for improved phagocytosis or lysosomal function in the context of dry AMD is not yet abundant in the literature provided, it has been hypothesized that by reducing lipid overload and oxidative stress, fenofibrate could indirectly improve lysosomal pH stability and optimize the function of cathepsin D—a key lysosomal protease involved in the degradation of photoreceptor outer segment (POS) fragments (as hypothesized in Tang et al. IOVS 2024). Given that proper autophagic flux and phagocytic processing are essential for RPE homeostasis and that their impairment is a hallmark of dry AMD, the restoration of these cellular processes via improved metabolic and intracellular signaling pathways is an attractive proposition (Ren et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis for the repurposing strategy of fenofibrate in dry AMD is that its activation of PPARα in RPE cells—achievable at concentrations with an EC₅₀ of approximately 2 µM—will promote a metabolic shift toward enhanced fatty acid oxidation. This shift is expected to lower the intracellular lipid load and decrease the accumulation of lipofuscin, a complex mixture of lipid-protein aggregates that includes A2E, which is thought to contribute directly to RPE cell dysfunction and subsequent photoreceptor degeneration. In vitro data from models using palmitic acid to induce lipotoxic stress in RPE cells suggest that fenofibrate can restore cellular homeostasis by activating survival pathways such as PI3K/AKT and by suppressing overexpressed stress markers and inflammatory cytokines (Wang et al., 2023).

According to the proposed mechanism, activation of PPARα should lead to the upregulation of genes involved in fatty acid β-oxidation, resulting in improved clearance of lipid-rich photoreceptor outer segments. The improvement in lipid processing not only reduces the overall lipid burden within RPE cells but is also expected to restore lysosomal function—specifically, normalizing lysosomal pH and enhancing cathepsin D activity. These changes should facilitate more efficient phagocytosis and degradation of photoreceptor outer segment debris, thereby mitigating the accumulation of cytotoxic lipofuscin deposits.

Furthermore, by lowering intracellular lipid accumulation and reducing oxidative stress through enhanced PI3K/AKT signaling and potential NF-κB inhibition, fenofibrate is expected to decrease the production of inflammatory cytokines and chemokines that contribute to chronic inflammation in the retina. Since inflammation is a driving force behind the progression of dry AMD, such a decrease would synergize with improved autophagy and phagocytosis to stabilize or even improve RPE function. In preclinical models, the application of fenofibrate in conditions simulating high dietary fat has been shown to restore aspects of RPE cell viability and function, lending indirect support to its potential efficacy in dry AMD (Wang et al., 2023). Although the precise effects on A2E reduction and lipofuscin clearance have yet to be fully elucidated, the cumulative data on fenofibrate’s capacity to improve lipid metabolism and reduce oxidative and inflammatory stress suggest that the compound could address multiple maladaptive processes that underlie dry AMD.

Overall Evaluation:  
When evaluating fenofibrate as a repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD, several strengths and potential weaknesses become apparent. On the strengths side, fenofibrate benefits from an extensive clinical safety record, as it is already in widespread use as a lipid-lowering agent in patients with dyslipidemia. This established safety profile, along with known pharmacokinetics, provides an important advantage when considering rapid repurposing for ocular indications. Moreover, its well-documented efficacy in modulating lipid metabolism through PPARα activation is a significant asset, given that dysregulated lipid handling is a central aspect of dry AMD pathogenesis. Preclinical studies have convincingly demonstrated that fenofibrate can attenuate RPE injury induced by fat overload by reducing oxidative stress markers, enhancing protective signaling pathways (e.g., PI3K/AKT), and suppressing inflammatory cytokines (Wang et al., 2023). Additionally, the possibility that fenofibrate might also act through mechanisms independent of PPARα—such as iron chelation and suppression of Wnt/β-catenin signaling—broadens its therapeutic potential in addressing the multifactorial nature of RPE degeneration (Mandala et al., 2020).

Another critical strength is the hypothesized ability of fenofibrate to improve lysosomal function and promote the phagocytosis of lipid-rich photoreceptor outer segments. Although the direct evidence for improvement in autophagy or direct clearance of lipofuscin and A2E is not yet fully established in the context of dry AMD studies, mechanistic insights from fenofibrate’s action in reducing cellular oxidative stress and lipid droplet accumulation provide a plausible basis for such effects (Ren et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023). The proposed cellular effects—activation of PPARα leading to upregulation of genes related to fatty acid oxidation, restoration of lysosomal pH, and normalization of cathepsin D activity—could collectively improve RPE function and delay the progression of dry AMD. The EC₅₀ value of roughly 2 µM as suggested in the hypothesis is within a physiologically relevant range based on in vitro findings in other RPE models, and may be achievable in ocular tissues with appropriate drug delivery strategies.

However, there are also notable weaknesses and uncertainties that must be addressed. First, while fenofibrate’s benefits have been clearly documented in models of diabetic retinopathy and fat-induced RPE injury, there remains a relative paucity of direct evidence for its efficacy in models that specifically recapitulate the pathophysiological features of dry AMD. Dry AMD is characterized by a complex interplay of factors including drusen formation, chronic inflammation, and impaired phagocytosis, and the literature provided does not offer conclusive data demonstrating that fenofibrate can reduce lipofuscin accumulation or enhance the clearance of photoreceptor outer segments in these contexts (Wang et al., 2023). In other words, while fenofibrate effectively modulates the metabolic state of RPE cells in fat-induced injury models, its impact on the accumulation of A2E and other lipofuscin components remains largely hypothetical at this stage.

Another potential weakness is related to the complexity of AMD pathogenesis. Dry AMD involves not only metabolic and inflammatory dysregulation at the level of the RPE but also changes in Bruch’s membrane, choroidal perfusion, and immune cell infiltration. As such, a therapeutic candidate targeting primarily RPE lipid metabolism and oxidative stress may need to be combined with other interventions or may not be sufficient as a monotherapy to address all pathogenic aspects of the disease. Further, the off-target effects of fenofibrate—such as its potential to act through PPARα-independent pathways—could complicate its clinical profile in the eye, where fine-tuning of multiple overlapping cellular pathways is critical (Mandala et al., 2020; Garcia-Ramírez et al., 2016).

Moreover, although fenofibrate has excellent systemic safety and pharmacokinetics, its ocular penetration, bioavailability in the retina, and long-term effects specifically on the RPE have not been comprehensively evaluated in the context of dry AMD. Optimization of drug delivery to the posterior segment of the eye is a well-known challenge, and while fenofibrate’s lipophilic nature could be advantageous for retinal penetration, formulation and dosing strategies would require careful investigation.

In summary, fenofibrate represents a compelling candidate for repurposing in dry AMD based on its ability to activate PPARα and improve lipid metabolism, as well as its demonstrated capacity to reduce oxidative stress and inflammation in RPE cells under conditions of lipid overload. Its long-standing clinical use and excellent safety record provide a strong foundation for further preclinical and eventually clinical studies in the context of ocular degenerative diseases. Nonetheless, a critical gap in the current literature is the direct demonstration that fenofibrate can lower A2E levels and enhance the phagocytosis of lipid-rich photoreceptor outer segments—a key mechanism underlying its hypothesized benefit in dry AMD. Addressing this gap through targeted in vitro and in vivo studies using dry AMD models will be essential. Should these studies confirm that fenofibrate improves lysosomal function, normalizes RPE phagocytosis, and reduces lipofuscin accumulation, it would represent a major advance in the treatment options for dry AMD.

Overall, fenofibrate’s potential lies in its multifaceted mechanisms of action. By combining improved fatty acid oxidation, antioxidant defenses, anti-inflammatory effects, and possibly even modulation of cellular iron levels and aberrant signaling pathways, fenofibrate could serve as a powerful therapeutic to modify the progressive degeneration of the RPE seen in dry AMD. However, additional mechanistic studies and preclinical validations are necessary before this candidate can be confidently advanced in clinical trials for dry AMD. Future research should aim to delineate the concentrations required for ocular efficacy, assess drug delivery methods that maximize retinal bioavailability, and determine whether the cellular effects observed in diabetic retinopathy and fat-induced injury models translate to the unique pathophysiological environment of dry AMD (Fu et al., 2020; Garcia-Ramírez et al., 2016; Mandala et al., 2020; Ren et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023).

In conclusion, while fenofibrate is a promising candidate for repurposing in dry AMD therapy, its ultimate success will depend on the ability to generate robust, direct evidence that supports its hypothesized effects on RPE lipid metabolism, lysosomal function, and phagocytic clearance of toxic lipofuscin components. The existing data on fenofibrate’s systemic and retinal protective effects provide an encouraging starting point; however, the transition from preclinical promise to clinical efficacy in the context of dry AMD remains contingent on focused investigations into these key areas. The strengths of fenofibrate—its established safety profile, multiple beneficial metabolic actions, and evidence from related retinal models—are balanced by the need for more specific, AMD-targeted research to fully validate its repurposing potential (Fu et al., 2020; Garcia-Ramírez et al., 2016; Mandala et al., 2020; Ren et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023).
