hypothesis: TTP-488 (RAGE antagonist; TransTech Pharma research)
answer:
Proposal for TTP-488 (RAGE antagonist; TransTech Pharma research)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
TTP-488, also known as Azeliragon, is a small-molecule synthetic RAGE antagonist originally discovered in the context of Alzheimer’s disease research. It belongs to the class of compounds designed to block the receptor for advanced glycation end products (RAGE) by preventing the interaction between RAGE and its ligands – such as advanced glycation end products (AGEs), amyloid-β peptides, and S100 proteins – that trigger downstream inflammatory signaling cascades. The synthetic origin of TTP-488 stems from medicinal chemistry efforts targeting neuroinflammatory and oxidative stress pathways, and members of this compound class have been investigated for their anti-inflammatory, anti-oxidative, and anti-fibrotic properties in multiple disease settings. Its chemical design focused on achieving high binding potency to the extracellular ligand binding domain of RAGE, with an IC₅₀ in the nanomolar range (approximately 100 nM as hypothesized) for inhibition of ligand engagement. This class of RAGE antagonists, including TTP-488, has been predominantly studied in the context of neurodegenerative diseases where aberrant RAGE signaling contributes to pathology, supporting their potential repurposing for diseases characterized by chronic inflammation and oxidative stress, such as dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Banevicius et al., 2018, pp. 1–2, 5–6).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, TTP-488 has been evaluated in clinical trials for Alzheimer’s disease, where its ability to block RAGE-mediated amyloid-β interactions provided a sound mechanistic rationale for attenuating neuroinflammation and oxidative damage. In these trials, TTP-488 demonstrated an acceptable oral safety profile and favorable pharmacokinetics that make systemic administration feasible—a key consideration when repurposing drugs for alternative indications. While the use of TTP-488 specifically for dry AMD has not been clinically evaluated, a growing body of preclinical evidence has implicated RAGE signaling as a central mediator in AMD pathogenesis. For instance, studies have reported that RAGE expression is significantly upregulated in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells in AMD and that advanced glycation end products accumulate in the drusen deposits characteristic of the disease (Banevicius et al., 2018, pp. 1–2, 7–8). Moreover, animal models using RAGE-deficient mice have shown reduced choroidal neovascularization and attenuated retinal fibrosis, suggesting that RAGE inhibition could also be beneficial in conditions with similar underlying pathology such as dry AMD (Park, 2017, pp. 157–163, 163–168). Although RAGE antagonists were originally developed with neurodegenerative conditions in mind, the convergence of pathogenic mechanisms such as oxidative stress, lysosomal dysfunction, and inflammation in both Alzheimer’s disease and AMD provides a strong basis for considering TTP-488’s repurposing for retinal degenerative disorders (Banevicius et al., 2018, pp. 5–6; Barile & Schmidt, 2007, pp. 3–4).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, TTP-488 functions by competitively inhibiting the binding of multiple pathological ligands to the RAGE receptor. Under normal or stressed conditions, AGEs accumulate on extracellular matrices and within drusen deposits, where they interact with RAGE on RPE cells to trigger the activation of several downstream signaling cascades. Activation of RAGE results in the induction of nuclear factor-kappaB (NF-κB), p38 mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK), and TGF-β/Smad2 signaling pathways, which collectively contribute to increased reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, chronic inflammation, and the promotion of fibrotic responses (Banevicius et al., 2018, pp. 1–2; Barile & Schmidt, 2007, pp. 3–4). Specifically, in the retinal pigment epithelium—cells that are responsible for the phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS)—RAGE activation has been shown to impair lysosomal function, cause lysosomal alkalinization, and disrupt tight junction integrity. This aberrant signaling causes a vicious cycle of increased oxidative stress and inflammation, leading to further accumulation of deleterious metabolic byproducts and progression of dry AMD pathology (Julius & Renuka, 2023, pp. 1–2; Dahrouj et al., 2015, pp. 1–3). TTP-488, by binding to RAGE with high affinity, prevents AGE-RAGE interactions and thereby interrupts this cycle. Moreover, preclinical studies have demonstrated that the inhibition of RAGE through agents such as TTP-488 can attenuate TGF-β2-induced epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) in RPE cells, reduce mitochondrial ROS production, and diminish the expression of fibrotic markers like α-smooth muscle actin (αSMA) and collagen I (Sreekumar et al., 2025, pp. 7–10). Blocking these signaling cascades is anticipated to lead to a normalization of lysosomal pH, enhanced clearance of extracellular debris, and ultimately improved phagocytosis of POS, thereby supporting retinal homeostasis (Barile & Schmidt, 2007, pp. 3–4; Park, 2017, pp. 163–168).

Expected Effect:  
The expected therapeutic effect of TTP-488 in the context of dry AMD is based on its ability to restore normal RPE function by mitigating the harmful consequences of AGE-induced RAGE activation. In a typical assay, when cultured RPE cells are exposed to excessive AGEs, the interaction with RAGE triggers oxidative stress and lysosomal dysfunction, leading to impaired phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments—a critical physiological process required for retinal renewal. Treatment with TTP-488 is hypothesized to competitively block these interactions, thus reducing the ensuing ROS production and normalizing lysosomal pH. This normalization is expected to re-establish efficient activation of the autophagy-lysosomal pathway, leading to increased phagocytic uptake and degradation of POS as well as clearance of accumulated debris that may contribute to drusen formation (Banevicius et al., 2018, pp. 1–2; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 2–4). Additionally, because RAGE signaling also promotes the upregulation of pro-angiogenic factors such as vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), its inhibition by TTP-488 is anticipated to reduce aberrant VEGF expression, thereby potentially mitigating secondary pathological features associated with neovascularization, even though dry AMD is predominantly characterized by atrophic processes rather than neovascular ones (Dahrouj et al., 2015, pp. 1–3; Park, 2017, pp. 163–168). Furthermore, RPE cells have been shown to express high levels of RAGE especially in regions adjacent to drusen deposits, indicating that the drug target is well-represented in the critical cellular compartment for treating dry AMD (Park et al., 2015, pp. 1–2; Ruan et al., 2020, pp. 9–11). Ultimately, the net outcome of TTP-488 administration in preclinical models is expected to be a reduction in oxidative damage, an improvement in lysosomal function, and a restoration of RPE-mediated phagocytic capacity, which together could slow or potentially reverse the progression of RPE degeneration observed in dry AMD (Sreekumar et al., 2025, pp. 7–10).

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating TTP-488 as a potential therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, several strengths and weaknesses become apparent. One of the key strengths is the robust molecular rationale underpinning its application in AMD. Numerous studies have implicated the AGE-RAGE axis in the initiation and progression of dry AMD, with evidence of AGE accumulation in drusen, increased RAGE expression in compromised RPE cells, and the subsequent triggering of inflammatory, oxidative, and fibrotic signaling pathways that drive retinal degeneration (Banevicius et al., 2018, pp. 1–2, 7–8; Julius & Renuka, 2023, pp. 1–2). The fact that TTP-488 has already been evaluated in clinical trials for Alzheimer’s disease provides a significant advantage in terms of pre-established oral safety data, which could accelerate its repurposing for ocular indications. Preclinical studies have also shown that RAGE antagonism via TTP-488 can reduce key pathological processes – such as EMT, ROS production, and fibrotic marker expression in RPE cells – which directly translates to the primary pathogenic mechanisms in dry AMD (Sreekumar et al., 2025, pp. 7–10; Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 2–4).

Another strength lies in the multifaceted mechanism of action of TTP-488. By targeting a common upstream mediator (RAGE) that links several deleterious pathways, there is potential to simultaneously impact oxidative stress, inflammation, and lysosomal dysfunction, all of which are critical in the pathogenesis of dry AMD. This multipronged effect is particularly valuable in complex diseases like dry AMD that do not succumb to single-target therapies. Moreover, the hypothesis that TTP-488 can restore POS phagocytosis in RPE cells is supported by mechanistic evidence demonstrating that RAGE activation disrupts the autophagy-lysosomal system—a cornerstone of RPE cell maintenance (Falcão et al., 2025, pp. 2–4; Kivinen, 2018, pp. 9–10). Therefore, the expected improvement in the clearance of photoreceptor outer segments indirectly supports the maintenance of retinal integrity over time.

However, there are also several challenges that temper the optimism regarding TTP-488’s repurposing for dry AMD. First, although the safety profile in Alzheimer’s disease is encouraging, it remains uncertain whether systemic administration of TTP-488 will achieve adequate ocular tissue penetration given the presence of blood-retinal barriers. It may be necessary to develop alternative delivery formulations (for example, localized ocular delivery systems) to bypass these pharmacokinetic hurdles without compromising the well-tolerated systemic profile observed in Alzheimer’s trials (Tang et al., 2024, pp. 12–13; Park, 2017, pp. 99–106). Another potential weakness is the translational gap between the preclinical models explored so far—many of which focus on retinal fibrosis and subretinal neovascularization—and the specific pathology of dry AMD, which is characterized predominantly by atrophic changes rather than overt neovascular events (Park, 2017, pp. 157–163, 163–168). This underscores the need for dedicated preclinical studies in models that more closely recapitulate the slow progression and specific cellular dysfunction seen in dry AMD.

Furthermore, while targeting RAGE holds promise, RAGE is expressed in multiple cell types within the retina and beyond, and completely inhibiting its function may have unintended consequences on normal homeostatic and immune processes. A delicate balance must be maintained between suppressing pathological inflammation and preserving the necessary defense mechanisms against cellular stress and infection. Another layer of complexity arises from the genetic variability seen in RAGE and its associated regulatory pathways among different patient populations, which may result in variable therapeutic responses (Banevicius et al., 2018, pp. 7–8). Consequently, patient stratification based on genetic factors and biomarker profiling may become crucial in future clinical trials. Finally, while in vitro and animal model data are supportive of the concept that TTP-488 can reduce oxidative stress and improve lysosomal function, the dosing regimen, long-term efficacy, and potential off-target effects will have to be carefully evaluated in comprehensive clinical studies before any definitive conclusions can be drawn (Banevicius et al., 2018, pp. 5–6; Barile & Schmidt, 2007, pp. 3–4).

Overall, the preclinical evidence supports a strong mechanistic rationale for repurposing TTP-488 as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Its ability to inhibit the AGE-RAGE interaction addresses a pivotal pathogenic driver in the disease while simultaneously reducing oxidative stress, normalizing lysosomal pH, and potentially restoring the phagocytic functions of RPE cells. The oral safety data derived from Alzheimer’s trials provide additional confidence in its repurposing potential. Nonetheless, significant work remains to optimize ocular delivery, to validate efficacy in dry AMD-specific preclinical models, and to carefully assess the risk–benefit profile in the context of chronic retinal diseases. With these considerations in mind, TTP-488 represents a promising and innovative candidate whose further development should be supported by targeted preclinical studies and judicious clinical trial designs that include robust biomarker endpoints for RAGE activity and RPE function (Banevicius et al., 2018, pp. 1–2; Sreekumar et al., 2025, pp. 7–10; Park, 2017, pp. 157–163).

hypothesis: Edaravone (Free radical scavenger; Mitsubishi Tanabe Pharma)
answer:
Proposal for Edaravone (Free radical scavenger; Mitsubishi Tanabe Pharma)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Edaravone (3-methyl-1-phenyl-2-pyrazolin-5-one, also known as MCI-186 or Radicut) is a synthetic small-molecule free radical scavenger that was originally discovered and developed for its neuroprotective properties. Developed by Mitsubishi Tanabe Pharma, edaravone belongs to the class of pyrazolone derivatives that have potent antioxidant activities. Its design allows it to function in both aqueous and lipid environments by donating electrons to a range of reactive oxygen species (ROS) and converting these free radicals into an inactive metabolite (2-oxo-3-(phenylhydrazono)-butanoic acid). The chemical structure of edaravone confers low molecular weight and high diffusibility, making it well-suited for rapid cellular uptake and efficient interaction with intracellular free radicals. This property has been exploited in its established clinical use in acute ischemic stroke, and its physicochemical characteristics have also encouraged exploration in other CNS and ocular conditions. The free radical scavenger class of compounds has a long history of use in protecting tissues from oxidative damage, and edaravone, in particular, has been shown to mitigate the destructive effects of excessive ROS generation—a process implicated in numerous degenerative conditions (Masuda et al., 2017; Imai et al., 2010).

Therapeutic History:  
Edaravone has a well-documented clinical history primarily in the management of acute ischemic stroke in Japan, where it was approved in 2001 based on its ability to reduce infarct size and improve neurological outcomes. Its established safety profile in human neurological diseases, including modern trials in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), underlines its potential for systemic administration. Over the years, extensive preclinical investigations have demonstrated that edaravone confers significant neuroprotection by lowering ROS levels, preventing lipid peroxidation, and inhibiting apoptosis in stressed tissue. Although edaravone’s approved indications do not include dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), its neuroprotective and antioxidant properties have been tested in various retinal disease models. For example, studies in animal models of light-induced photoreceptor degeneration, retinal detachment, and even laser-induced choroidal neovascularization have consistently shown that edaravone can reduce oxidative damage, suppress inflammatory cascades, and protect retinal neurons (Imai et al., 2010; Roh et al., 2011). While these models are not direct representations of dry AMD, they share key pathophysiological features with dry AMD, such as high oxidative stress in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) and photoreceptor degeneration. Additionally, evidence from in vitro studies using RPE cells supports the idea that edaravone can lower intracellular ROS and thereby improve cell survival under oxidative challenge (Abokyi et al., 2020; Masuda et al., 2017). This history of broad-based use in conditions where excessive ROS plays a central role forms the rationale for repurposing edaravone for dry AMD, a disease in which chronic oxidative stress is a central pathogenic factor.

Mechanism of Action:  
Edaravone exerts its protective effects primarily through its potent antioxidant activity. At the molecular level, it scavenges a variety of ROS—including hydroxyl radicals, superoxide anions, and hydrogen peroxide—by donating an electron to these reactive species. This electron donation converts active free radicals into less harmful molecules and leads to the formation of an inactive end‐product, thereby interrupting the self‐propagating chain reactions of lipid peroxidation (Imai et al., 2010; Masuda et al., 2017). Such oxidative reactions are known to damage cellular components including lipids, proteins, and nucleic acids.

In the context of the retinal pigment epithelium, which is characterized by a high rate of oxidative metabolism and exposure to intense light, ROS accumulation has several deleterious consequences. One key aspect of dry AMD pathogenesis is the oxidative inactivation of lysosomal enzymes, particularly cathepsin D, which is essential for the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS). Under conditions of excessive ROS, lysosomal membranes become compromised by lipid peroxidation, resulting in increased lysosomal pH and subsequent inactivation of cathepsin D. This inefficiency in lysosomal digestion leads to the accumulation of undigested POS and lipofuscin—a process that further exacerbates cellular dysfunction in the RPE (Klettner et al., 2013).

Edaravone’s capacity to scavenge ROS is therefore hypothesized to maintain the functional integrity of lysosomes in RPE cells. By reducing the oxidative burden, edaravone can help preserve the acidic environment (low pH) required for optimal cathepsin D activity. Additionally, oxidative stress is known to impair autophagic flux in RPE cells, as evidenced by alterations in the conversion of LC3-I to its lipidated form LC3-II, which is a marker for autophagosome formation. Enhanced LC3-II flux is associated with efficient autophagy—a process crucial for the clearance of damaged proteins and organelles. By mitigating ROS, edaravone is expected to promote proper LC3-II flux and autophagic activity, further contributing to the clearance of POS debris and damaged organelles in RPE cells (Masuda et al., 2017; Pinelli et al., 2023).

Moreover, several studies have indicated that edaravone can modulate intracellular signaling pathways associated with oxidative stress. For instance, it has been shown to reduce the phosphorylation of stress-activated kinases such as p38 and JNK, both of which are activated in response to elevated ROS levels. Inhibition of these pathways may contribute not only to decreased apoptotic signaling but also to the stabilization of lysosomal function and autophagic processes (Imai et al., 2010; Roh et al., 2011). Overall, the molecular interactions of edaravone—scavenging of free radicals, preservation of lysosomal pH, protection of critical proteases like cathepsin D, and restoration of autophagic flux—form the basis for its proposed repurposing in dry AMD.

Expected Effect:  
The primary expected effect of edaravone in the context of dry AMD is a reduction of oxidative stress within the RPE, thereby preventing the cascade of events that lead to lysosomal dysfunction and defective POS digestion. RPE cells are responsible for the cyclic phagocytosis of POS, and this process is heavily reliant on intact lysosomal function. Under oxidative stress, the lysosomal pH can drift toward alkalinity, which inactivates cathepsin D and impairs the degradation of phagocytosed material. By scavenging ROS, edaravone is anticipated to maintain the acidic environment of lysosomes, thus preserving the enzymatic activity of cathepsin D. This restoration of lysosomal function should translate into improved clearance of POS and reduce the buildup of lipofuscin and drusen—hallmarks of dry AMD pathology (Klettner et al., 2013).

In addition to its lysosome-stabilizing effects, edaravone is expected to enhance autophagic flux in RPE cells. The conversion of LC3-I to LC3-II is an essential step in autophagosome formation, and efficient autophagic flux is critical for the removal of damaged organelles and protein aggregates. Experimental evidence suggests that excessive ROS impairs this flux, leading to the accumulation of dysfunctional autophagosomes and cellular debris. By reducing oxidative stress, edaravone may help restore LC3-II flux and normal autophagic degradation pathways, thereby contributing to improved cellular homeostasis (Pinelli et al., 2023).

From a cellular assay perspective, treating dry AMD RPE cultures with edaravone is expected to result in measurable decreases in intracellular ROS markers such as 8-hydroxy-2-deoxyguanosine (8-OHdG) and 4-hydroxynonenal (4-HNE). Simultaneously, preservation of lysosomal pH would likely be observable via pH-sensitive fluorescence probes, and enhanced cathepsin D activity could be confirmed through enzyme assays. Furthermore, Western blot analysis might reveal a normalization of LC3-II levels, indicating improved autophagic flux. The overall effect would be increased phagocytic capacity of the RPE cells and a reduction in cellular stress markers, ultimately leading to enhanced retinal cell survival and function (Abokyi et al., 2020; Pinelli et al., 2023).

An additional expected benefit stems from the potential for optimizing ocular delivery. Intravitreal formulations—either as free drug or best yet, as encapsulated in liposomal vehicles—have been shown to achieve therapeutic antioxidant levels in the retina, ensuring that effective concentrations of edaravone reach the RPE. This approach bypasses systemic limitations and can protect against local oxidative damage directly, offering the possibility to sustain long-term improvements in POS digestion and phagocytic functions in dry AMD (Hironaka et al., 2011; Masuda et al., 2017).

Overall Evaluation:  
Edaravone emerges as a promising repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD based on a strong mechanistic rationale and an established track record in oxidative stress mitigation. Among its primary strengths is its potent free radical scavenging activity, which underpins its ability to counteract the oxidative stress that is central to the pathogenesis of dry AMD. Its chemical properties—and the fact that it has been used safely in the treatment of acute ischemic stroke and ALS—lend significant weight to its potential for repurposing in retinal diseases (Imai et al., 2010; Masuda et al., 2017).

A notable strength is the dual benefit edaravone is expected to offer: not only does it reduce ROS levels, but it also helps to preserve critical lysosomal functions by maintaining an optimal acidic pH, thereby securing cathepsin D activity. This is particularly important because lysosomal degradation of POS is an essential process in RPE cells, and its disruption is a key driver of dry AMD progression (Klettner et al., 2013). Similarly, by promoting normal LC3-II flux, edaravone supports the autophagic machinery required for cellular clearance, further protecting the RPE from the accumulation of toxic waste products (Pinelli et al., 2023).

The preclinical literature provides substantive evidence of edaravone’s efficacy in various models of retinal degeneration. Studies in animal models of retinal detachment, photoreceptor cell death, and experimentally induced oxidative damage all report protective effects following edaravone treatment, including reductions in markers of apoptosis and oxidative stress, as well as improvements in cell survival and retinal morphology (Imai et al., 2010; Roh et al., 2011). In several of these studies, the protective effects of edaravone were enhanced when delivered via liposomal formulations, suggesting that optimized ocular delivery systems can overcome inherent pharmacokinetic challenges and achieve sustained retinal protection (Hironaka et al., 2011).

However, several potential weaknesses must be considered. First, while the underlying rationale for edaravone’s use in dry AMD is robust, direct evidence demonstrating its efficacy in dry AMD models is still limited. Most existing studies have focused on acute retinal damage models such as light-induced degeneration or retinal detachment rather than on the chronic degenerative process observed in dry AMD. Consequently, the specific impact of edaravone on the inactivation of cathepsin D, modulation of lysosomal pH, and restoration of LC3-II flux in RPE cells from AMD patients has not been comprehensively validated (Pinelli et al., 2023; Abokyi et al., 2020).

Furthermore, the optimal dosing regimen and long-term safety profile of edaravone for ocular use remain to be determined. Some studies have noted that while lower doses of edaravone provide neuroprotection, higher doses may introduce toxicity, particularly in the delicate context of retinal cells (Imai et al., 2010; Roh et al., 2011). Thus, careful titration and formulation development—potentially through intravitreal or liposomal delivery—will be essential to harness its therapeutic benefits without incurring adverse effects.

Another potential limitation lies in the multifactorial nature of dry AMD. Although oxidative stress is a driving force in the disease, the pathogenesis of dry AMD is also influenced by dysregulated complement activation, chronic inflammation, genetic predispositions, and metabolic disturbances. An intervention solely targeting ROS may not sufficiently address these other contributing factors. Therefore, edaravone might need to be used as part of a combination therapy strategy in order to achieve meaningful clinical outcomes in dry AMD patients (Jarrett & Boulton, 2012; Klettner et al., 2013).

In summary, edaravone is a scientifically attractive candidate for repurposing in dry AMD therapy. Its well-characterized antioxidant properties, combined with the potential to preserve lysosomal enzyme activity and autophagic flux in RPE cells, provide a mechanistic rationale that directly addresses key pathogenetic mechanisms in dry AMD. The compound’s extensive preclinical evidence in retinal models and established systemic safety profile further support its potential utility. However, the transition from acute retinal injury models to the chronic, multifaceted pathology of dry AMD requires additional focused studies. Specifically, further research is needed to validate its effects on cathepsin D activity, lysosomal pH regulation, and LC3-II flux within the context of RPE and to define the optimal dosing and delivery methods for sustained ocular protection. Given these considerations, edaravone merits further preclinical evaluation in dry AMD models and, if promising, could progress into clinical trials as an adjunct or combination therapy for this major cause of vision loss in the elderly (Abokyi et al., 2020; Imai et al., 2010; Masuda et al., 2017; Pinelli et al., 2023; Roh et al., 2011).

hypothesis: Apelin-13 (Endogenous peptide; Bachem Cat. No. H-3705)
answer:
Proposal for Apelin-13 (Endogenous peptide; Bachem Cat. No. H-3705)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Apelin-13 is an endogenous peptide derived from the apelin gene product and is one of several bioactive fragments generated from a larger 77–amino acid preproapelin precursor. Initially discovered in bovine stomach extracts by Tatemoto and colleagues in 1998 (Davenport et al., 2019), apelin peptides belong to a class of naturally occurring vasoactive peptide hormones that activate the apelin receptor (APJ), a G protein–coupled receptor. The peptide is synthesized naturally in various tissues, including the central nervous system, heart, and retina, and undergoes posttranslational processing to yield distinct isoforms such as apelin-36, apelin-17, and the shorter apelin-13. The focus on apelin-13 is due in part to structure–activity relationship studies that have identified a core pharmacophoric region, including a critical C-terminal phenylalanine residue, that is essential for receptor activation (Davenport et al., 2019). Being a member of the bioactive peptide class, apelin-13 has been previously studied in cardiovascular, metabolic, and certain retinal contexts, with distinct advantages offered by its relatively small peptide size, which enables intravitreal delivery and minimizes immunogenicity. This candidate, available commercially (Bachem Cat. No. H-3705), represents a repurposing opportunity that leverages its endogenous origin, excellent receptor specificity, and established ability to modulate intracellular signaling cascades relevant for cellular homeostasis in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells (Davenport et al., 2019; Enders, 2023).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, apelin peptides have been primarily explored for their cardiovascular and metabolic effects. In cardiovascular studies, apelin-13 has been shown to exert potent inotropic and vasodilatory responses, reduce cardiac fibrosis, and improve cardiac output in heart failure models, thus demonstrating its multifunctional role as an endogenous regulator in the cardiovascular system (Davenport et al., 2019). In metabolic research, apelin has been documented to influence insulin sensitivity and glucose metabolism, while also functioning as an adipokine, linking it to obesity-related pathways (Davenport et al., 2019). Within the context of ophthalmology, several preclinical studies have investigated the role of apelin peptides, particularly apelin-13, in retinal disease models. Notably, apelin-13 has been demonstrated to promote proliferation, migration, and enhanced expression of cytoskeletal and tight junction proteins in human RPE cells, mediated through activation of the PI3K/Akt and MAPK/Erk signaling pathways (Li et al., 2017). Though most clinical and preclinical research in retinal settings has predominantly focused on diabetic retinopathy and related retinal vascular pathologies, where apelin expression is altered and exogenous supplementation can restore normal cellular function (Li et al., 2017; Li et al., 2018), there is emerging interest in extrapolating these findings to other conditions of RPE dysfunction. Dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD) is characterized by impaired RPE phagocytosis and accumulation of toxic photoreceptor outer segment (POS) debris, making it plausible that a drug candidate capable of enhancing RPE phagocytosis could benefit these patients. Although direct studies evaluating apelin-13 in dry AMD are limited, its demonstrated ability to improve RPE cell survival and actin dynamics under stress conditions in vitro presents a compelling rationale for repurposing (Li et al., 2017).

Mechanism of Action:  
The molecular mechanism underlying the therapeutic potential of apelin-13 centers on its binding to the APJ receptor, which is robustly expressed in RPE cells and other retinal cell types. Upon receptor engagement, apelin-13 activates downstream G protein–mediated signaling cascades, notably the phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K)/Akt pathway and the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK)/Erk pathway (Li et al., 2017; Chiang et al., 2017). Activation of PI3K/Akt signaling is of particular interest because it plays a critical role in the regulation of actin cytoskeletal reorganization—a process essential for the formation of phagocytic cups required for the internalization of POS. This pathway additionally modulates intracellular trafficking events that culminate in improved clearance of outer segment debris by RPE cells (Chiang et al., 2017). Biochemical investigations reveal that pharmacological inhibition of PI3K or downstream Akt phosphorylation dramatically reduces RPE phagocytosis, underscoring the necessity of this signaling module in maintaining RPE homeostasis (Chiang et al., 2017). Moreover, apelin-13’s EC₅₀ in stimulating PI3K/Akt signaling in RPE cells is reported to be approximately 0.5 nM, suggesting high potency in activating this pathway (Li et al., 2017). In the context of oxidative stress, which is heavily implicated in dry AMD pathogenesis, activation of PI3K/Akt also confers cytoprotective effects by enhancing cell survival pathways and promoting anti-apoptotic signaling. Structural evidence and receptor–ligand interaction studies further validate that apelin-13 engages critical residues at the receptor interface, leading to effective downstream signal transduction that may drive cytoskeletal remodeling and facilitate phagosome maturation and trafficking (Davenport et al., 2019). Thus, apelin-13’s mode of action is characterized by its dual ability to stimulate RPE phagocytic function while concurrently enhancing cell survival under stress conditions.

Expected Effect:  
The proposed therapeutic hypothesis for apelin-13 in dry AMD hinges on its capacity to enhance RPE function by activating the APJ receptor and triggering PI3K/Akt signaling. In an assay designed to evaluate phagocytosis of POS, administration of apelin-13 is expected to increase the internalization and subsequent clearance of shed POS by RPE cells. This response is anticipated to result from enhanced actin reorganization and improved phagosome trafficking, driven by the activation of PI3K/Akt signaling—a pathway that is well known to be essential for cytoskeletal dynamics during phagocytosis (Chiang et al., 2017). In vitro, human RPE cell studies have shown that apelin-13 treatment leads to increased expression of cytoskeletal proteins and tight junction proteins, which are integral to maintaining the cellular architecture necessary for effective phagocytic activity (Li et al., 2017). Additionally, because dry AMD involves an accumulation of lipofuscin and impaired clearance of degradative byproducts from POS, enhancing this clearance mechanism could prevent or slow the progression of RPE dysfunction. Given the reported EC₅₀ near 0.5 nM for activation of PI3K/Akt signaling in RPE cells by apelin-13, the anticipated effect in vivo would be a dose-dependent improvement in phagocytosis that could translate to preservation of RPE integrity and retinal function. Furthermore, since apelin-13 has been described as having a favorable safety profile in other ocular studies—including those addressing glaucoma and diabetic retinopathy—there is strong support for the feasibility of intravitreal application, which is a standard mode of delivery in the treatment of many retinal diseases (Lu et al., 2013; Li et al., 2017). The expected outcome is not only an enhancement of POS clearance but also overall improvement in RPE cell survival under chronic oxidative stress conditions, a critical component in the pathogenesis of dry AMD.

Overall Evaluation:  
Apelin-13 represents a promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD based on its endogenous nature, well-characterized mechanism of action, and preclinical evidence supporting its beneficial effects on RPE cellular functions. One significant strength of this candidate is its high potency in activating the PI3K/Akt signaling pathway in RPE cells, a pathway that is crucial for cytoskeletal remodeling and phagocytosis of POS (Chiang et al., 2017). The safety profile of apelin-13, as established by studies involving intravitreal injection in various retinal models, further supports its potential, especially given the routine use of intravitreal therapies in ophthalmology (Lu et al., 2013; Li et al., 2017). In addition, the dual action of apelin-13—promoting both phagocytic clearance and cell survival under oxidative stress—addresses two primary pathological features of dry AMD: accumulation of toxic debris and RPE cell degeneration.

However, there are challenges and weaknesses to consider. Most of the existing data on apelin-13 in ocular applications come from models of diabetic retinopathy rather than from direct studies in dry AMD. While the underlying mechanisms of impaired phagocytosis and oxidative stress are common to both conditions, the pathology of dry AMD is multifactorial and includes additional components such as complement dysregulation and chronic inflammation, which may not be directly addressed by apelin-13 therapy (Li et al., 2018; Li et al., 2017). Furthermore, the biphasic nature of Akt involvement in phagocytosis—as evidenced by studies showing variable effects at early versus later time points—underscores the complexity of modulating this pathway therapeutically (Chiang et al., 2017). There is also a potential for unwanted off-target effects if apelin-13 were to inadvertently stimulate angiogenic pathways under certain conditions; however, given that dry AMD is characterized by atrophic rather than neovascular pathology, careful dosing and patient selection could mitigate such risks (Wu et al., 2017). Finally, while intravitreal delivery is a proven route for ocular therapies, peptide-based drugs often face challenges related to stability, degradation, and the need for repeated dosing, which may necessitate formulation modifications such as PEGylation or cyclization to prolong half-life (Davenport et al., 2019).

In conclusion, the overall evaluation of apelin-13 as a candidate for dry AMD is cautiously optimistic. The strong mechanistic rationale—centered on the activation of the APJ receptor and subsequent PI3K/Akt signaling to improve cytoskeletal remodeling and POS clearance—coupled with existing evidence in retinal models, supports further investigation. Preclinical studies specifically tailored to dry AMD models are warranted, including evaluations of efficacy in improving RPE phagocytosis, protection against oxidative stress, and overall retinal function. Additionally, pharmacokinetic and formulation studies should be conducted to optimize intravitreal delivery and stability. If these studies confirm target engagement and therapeutic benefit, apelin-13 could offer a novel approach for restoring RPE function and slowing the progression of dry AMD, thereby addressing an unmet clinical need in a field where current therapeutic options remain limited (Li et al., 2017; Chiang et al., 2017).

hypothesis: CD59-Fc fusion protein (Complement MAC inhibitor; Genentech research reagent)
answer:
Proposal for CD59-Fc fusion protein (Complement MAC inhibitor; Genentech research reagent)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
The therapeutic candidate under evaluation is a CD59-Fc fusion protein, a recombinant biologic that combines the extracellular functional domain of CD59—a naturally occurring complement regulatory protein—with the Fc portion of an immunoglobulin (typically IgG1) to extend its ocular half‐life and improve tissue penetration. This fusion protein is synthesized using recombinant DNA technology in mammalian cell expression systems to ensure proper post‐translational modifications and folding, which are critical for retaining high binding affinity (with a reported dissociation constant, Kd, of <1 nM) toward its targets, the complement components C8 and C9, on retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) surfaces (Qin et al., 2021; Tan, 2018). The compound belongs to the class of complement inhibitors—a group of therapeutic agents that have been developed to modulate the immune complement cascade, thereby mitigating complement-mediated tissue damage; historically, this class has been primarily investigated for inflammatory and degenerative conditions, including paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria, atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome, and more recently age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). The rationale behind harnessing a CD59-based approach is based on the well-established physiological role of native CD59 in inhibiting the terminal pathway of complement activation by blocking the incorporation of C9 into the C5b-8 complex to form the membrane attack complex (MAC), thus preventing cell lysis and downstream inflammatory cascades (Tan et al., 2016).

Therapeutic History:  
CD59, as a natural complement regulatory protein, has been a focus of research for several years due to its intrinsic ability to safeguard host tissues from complement-mediated injury; multiple studies have demonstrated that impaired CD59 recycling or decreased CD59 surface expression is associated with increased MAC deposition on RPE cells in AMD models, ultimately leading to lysosomal dysfunction and cellular injury (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). Although the CD59-Fc fusion protein itself has not been extensively tested in clinical settings, analogous therapeutic approaches—including gene therapy strategies such as AAVCAGsCD59, which deliver soluble forms of CD59 to the retina—have been evaluated preclinically and in early-phase clinical trials, with evidence suggesting that enhancement of CD59 function can reduce complement-mediated damage in the eye (Garcia-Garcia et al., 2022; Qin et al., 2021). In addition, complementary studies using other classes of complement inhibitors (for example, compstatin analogs like Cp40 that act upstream at the C3 convertase level) have demonstrated reversal of pathological phenotypes in AMD models by protecting lysosomal integrity and restoring RPE cellular function (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). While most of the clinical research in dry AMD has focused on C3- and C5-targeting agents (such as pegcetacoplan and avacincaptad pegol, respectively) with mixed outcomes, these data collectively support the strategy of terminal pathway inhibition as a viable approach; however, the CD59-Fc candidate distinguishes itself by directly recapitulating the naturally evolved mechanism of MAC inhibition (Cerniauskas et al., 2020; Garcia-Garcia et al., 2022). Notably, while the clinical history of CD59-based therapies in AMD is still in its early stages, preclinical models strongly implicate the loss of CD59 function in the pathogenesis of dry AMD, thereby making CD59 enhancement a rational repurposing strategy in this context (Tan et al., 2016).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, the CD59-Fc fusion protein acts by binding specifically to the complement components C8 and/or C9, which is critical during the final assembly phase of the MAC; normally, native CD59 prevents the recruitment of C9 to the C5b-8 complex, thereby effectively halting pore formation on the target cell membrane, which would otherwise lead to uncontrolled ion fluxes, cell lysis, or sub-lytic MAC deposition that can trigger pro-inflammatory and pro-apoptotic signaling cascades (Tan et al., 2016). The high affinity binding (Kd < 1 nM) is expected to allow the fusion protein to effectively compete with endogenous CD59, thereby providing robust inhibition even in the milieu of heightened complement activation as observed in AMD (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). In addition to its direct inhibition of MAC assembly, the Fc fragment confers several pharmacokinetic advantages: it enhances the protein’s stability, increases its half-life through neonatal Fc receptor (FcRn)-mediated recycling, and may facilitate localized retention within the ocular environment upon intravitreal injection, ensuring sustained therapeutic levels over prolonged treatment intervals (Garcia-Garcia et al., 2022; Qin et al., 2021). Moreover, by preventing MAC deposition on RPE cells, the candidate is anticipated to safeguard the integrity of lysosomal membranes—a process crucial for proper autophagic function and the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS); lysosomal damage through MAC-induced membrane permeabilization has been implicated in RPE dysfunction and the subsequent progression of dry AMD (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). On a cellular level, experimental models have shown that complement attack leads to lysosomal swelling, membrane fragility, and eventual mitochondrial dysfunction due to leakage of lysosomal enzymes (such as Cathepsin D) into the cytosol or drusen-like deposits; by mitigating MAC formation, CD59-Fc is expected to interrupt this deleterious cascade and restore cellular homeostasis (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).

Expected Effect:  
The expected pharmacodynamic effect of the CD59-Fc fusion protein centers on its capacity to prevent MAC deposition on the cell surface of RPE cells; this is hypothesized to occur through the high-affinity binding of the fusion protein to complement components C8 and C9, thereby precluding the insertion of the complete MAC pore into the plasma or lysosomal membranes of these cells (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). By averting MAC formation, the candidate helps maintain lysosomal membrane integrity, which in turn supports normal autophagic degradation and proper phagocytic processing of POS—a process that is critically impaired in AMD and is associated with lipofuscin accumulation and further complement activation (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). In functional assays, treatment with CD59-Fc is expected to result in a significant reduction of intracellular MAC deposition, as evidenced by decreased staining of markers associated with complement activation, and to preserve lysosomal structure, as reflected by normalized lysosome size and reduced markers of lysosomal membrane permeability (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). This preservation of lysosomal function is central to ensuring that the RPE retains its ability to efficiently phagocytose and degrade POS, thereby sustaining the retinal microenvironment and potentially slowing or reversing the progression of geographic atrophy—the late stage of dry AMD (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). Moreover, by protecting mitochondrial integrity indirectly through the maintenance of lysosomal function, CD59-Fc may also reduce oxidative stress and apoptotic signaling within RPE cells, contributing further to cell survival and retinal health (Tan et al., 2016). The candidate’s mechanism is supported by data from ex vivo experiments in complement-challenged explants, where application of complement inhibitors similar to CD59-based agents reduced MAC deposition and preserved lysosomal morphology (Garcia-Garcia et al., 2022; Qin et al., 2021). Additionally, studies where cholesterol accumulation or the presence of oxidized lipoproteins disrupts CD59 recycling correlate with enhanced MAC deposition and lysosomal dysfunction, reinforcing the notion that restoring CD59 activity through a fusion protein could have broad protective effects on the RPE (Cerniauskas et al., 2020; Garcia-Garcia et al., 2022).

Overall Evaluation:  
In assessing the potential of the CD59-Fc fusion protein as a therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration, several strengths and weaknesses become apparent. On the positive side, the candidate leverages the body’s natural defense mechanism against complement-mediated injury by directly targeting a key step in the formation of the membrane attack complex, a process that has been strongly implicated in the pathogenesis of AMD. Numerous preclinical studies have established that excessive MAC deposition on RPE cells leads to lysosomal dysfunction, impaired autophagy, and subsequent RPE cell death, all of which are critical factors in the progression of geographic atrophy (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). The CD59-Fc fusion protein is therefore expected to interrupt this pathological cascade by preserving lysosomal integrity and promoting the maintenance of cellular homeostasis, with potential downstream benefits including the restoration of normal POS phagocytosis and improved metabolic health of RPE cells (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).

Another strength is the inclusion of the Fc moiety, which not only extends the protein’s half-life, ensuring sustained therapeutic exposure in the eye, but may also aid in achieving effective localized concentrations following intravitreal administration (Garcia-Garcia et al., 2022; Qin et al., 2021). This pharmacokinetic advantage is particularly significant in ocular therapies, where frequent dosing and short half-life of drugs have historically challenged the long-term management of chronic conditions such as dry AMD. Moreover, the concept of using a recombinant fusion protein to mimic or enhance endogenous regulatory mechanisms has precedence in other therapeutic areas, providing a solid scientific foundation for this approach (Garcia-Garcia et al., 2022; Tan et al., 2016).

However, there are also notable challenges and potential weaknesses that warrant careful consideration. One primary concern is that, while preclinical models and ex vivo explant studies provide promising evidence for the efficacy of complement inhibitors in halting or reversing complement-mediated damage, the translation of these findings into clinical success in dry AMD has been fraught with mixed results. Several complement inhibitors, particularly those targeting upstream components like C3 and C5 (e.g., pegcetacoplan, avacincaptad pegol), have shown significant anatomical benefits such as reduced geographic atrophy lesion growth but have failed to reliably improve visual acuity, and in some instances have been associated with adverse events such as conversion to neovascular AMD (Tzoumas et al., 2023). Although CD59-Fc acts at a different point in the complement cascade, the complexity of the complement system in the ocular microenvironment and the possibility of compensatory mechanisms remain a potential hurdle that could limit therapeutic efficacy (Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Another consideration is that the CD59-Fc fusion protein has yet to be tested extensively in in vivo models of AMD, and its pharmacodynamics and pharmacokinetics in the human eye are largely unknown. Challenges such as achieving sufficient tissue penetration, avoiding systemic immune activation, and mitigating any unforeseen off-target effects will need to be addressed in rigorous preclinical studies before any clinical trial can be contemplated (Cerniauskas et al., 2020; Garcia-Garcia et al., 2022). Additionally, there is always the risk associated with biologics that their large molecular size or Fc-mediated effector functions might lead to immunogenicity or unexpected interactions with other components of the immune system, potentially triggering inflammatory responses—this is particularly critical in the immune-privileged ocular environment where preserving immune homeostasis is essential (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).

Finally, while the hypothesis postulates that by protecting lysosomal membranes CD59-Fc will indirectly improve POS phagocytic and degradative function, the relationship between complement suppression and restoration of complex RPE cell functions remains to be conclusively established in AMD pathology. Although there is compelling evidence that complement-mediated MAC deposition is deleterious to lysosomal function and that complement inhibition can restore cellular homeostasis, the multifactorial nature of AMD pathogenesis—which includes oxidative stress, lipid dysregulation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and genetic predispositions—means that CD59-Fc may need to be used in combination with other therapeutic strategies to achieve clinically meaningful outcomes (Cerniauskas et al., 2020; Tan et al., 2016).

In summary, the CD59-Fc fusion protein represents a promising repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD based on its profound mechanistic rationale, which is anchored in the prevention of MAC formation and the subsequent protection of lysosomal membranes in RPE cells. Its design to mimic and potentiate a natural protective pathway, combined with the pharmacokinetic benefits conferred by the Fc fusion, positions it favorably among complement-based therapeutic strategies. However, the challenges of translating preclinical successes into reliable clinical outcomes in the heterogeneous and multifactorial landscape of AMD cannot be understated. A focused program of further preclinical studies—including detailed pharmacodynamic assessments, tissue distribution, efficacy in robust in vivo models of dry AMD, and safety evaluations—will be essential to validate the therapeutic potential of CD59-Fc prior to embarking on human clinical trials. Overall, while the strengths of the candidate are compelling, its ultimate success will depend on resolving the inherent complexities of complement regulation in the retinal microenvironment and ensuring that the beneficial effects on lysosomal preservation translate into meaningful improvements in visual function and disease progression in patients with dry AMD (Cerniauskas et al., 2020; Qin et al., 2021; Tan et al., 2016; Garcia-Garcia et al., 2022).

hypothesis: Huperzine A (Cholinesterase inhibitor; Sigma-Aldrich Cat. No. H9793)
answer:
Proposal for Huperzine A (Cholinesterase inhibitor; Sigma-Aldrich Cat. No. H9793)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Huperzine A is a naturally occurring alkaloid that was first isolated in the early 1980s from the Chinese medicinal plant Huperzia serrata, commonly referred to as Qian Ceng Ta (Al-Ghamdi et al., 2023; Bai et al., 2000). As a member of the lycopodium alkaloids, Huperzine A exhibits a unique chemical structure characterized by a rigid bicyclic framework that contributes to its high affinity for acetylcholinesterase (AChE) inhibition (Ferreira et al., 2016; Bai et al., 2000). Originally discovered through biodirected research into traditional Chinese medicines, Huperzine A was soon recognized for its ability to reverse cognitive deficits by elevating acetylcholine (ACh) levels in the central nervous system (Ferreira et al., 2016). Over subsequent decades, the compound has been synthesized and investigated extensively via both natural extraction and chemical synthesis to overcome issues related to its low natural yield (Ferreira et al., 2016). Huperzine A belongs to a therapeutic class of compounds known as AChE inhibitors, which have traditionally been used to treat conditions associated with cholinergic deficits, most notably Alzheimer’s disease. Its well-documented pharmacokinetic profile—including rapid absorption, wide body distribution, and effective penetration of the blood–brain barrier—has made it an attractive candidate not only for neurodegenerative disorders but, as emerging data suggest, for other diseases where cholinergic modulation may be beneficial (Filho et al., 2006; Ferreira et al., 2016).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, Huperzine A has been used in traditional Chinese medicine for a variety of indications including the treatment of contusions, swelling, and memory impairments (Bai et al., 2000; Ferreira et al., 2016). Its modern therapeutic development began when its potent, reversible, and selective AChE inhibitory properties were identified, leading to its approval in China as a palliative treatment for Alzheimer’s disease (Ferreira et al., 2016; Filho et al., 2006). Preclinical studies and clinical trials have demonstrated that Huperzine A increases synaptic acetylcholine levels by blocking the enzyme that degrades it; this effect on cholinergic neurotransmission has validated its use in patients with Alzheimer’s and age-associated cognitive decline (Bai et al., 2000; Muñoz-Torrero & Camps, 2008). In the United States, its limited regulatory status as a dietary supplement marketed for memory enhancement further reinforces its established record in modulating cholinergic function (Ferreira et al., 2016). Although its primary clinical application has been neurological—especially in the domain of Alzheimer’s disease—recent preclinical models in ophthalmology have assessed the ocular tolerability of Huperzine A in animal models of age-related macular degeneration (AMD), a finding that presents a compelling case for its repurposing. However, as of now, there is no direct clinical evidence supporting its use in treating dry AMD or similar retinal degenerative diseases; rather, the therapeutic rationale is built on its biochemical actions and benefits observed in nonocular systems (Ferreira et al., 2016; Zhu et al., 2006).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, Huperzine A exerts its primary effect by inhibiting acetylcholinesterase, the enzyme responsible for catalyzing the breakdown of acetylcholine (Al-Ghamdi et al., 2023; Bai et al., 2000). This inhibition is both reversible and selective, allowing for a sustained elevation of acetylcholine levels in synaptic clefts without causing the overstimulation typically associated with nonselective cholinergic agents (Filho et al., 2006; Ferreira et al., 2016). The compound binds within the active gorge of AChE, interacting with critical amino acid residues such as tryptophans and tyrosines, thereby preventing the hydrolysis of acetylcholine and enhancing cholinergic neurotransmission (Ferreira et al., 2016; Muñoz-Torrero & Camps, 2008). In addition to its cholinesterase inhibitory activity, Huperzine A has been found to exhibit NMDA receptor antagonism at cerebral synapses, suggesting an additional neuroprotective dimension to its pharmacology (Orhan et al., 2009; Ferreira et al., 2016). This multifaceted pharmacological profile—combining AChE inhibition, NMDA receptor antagonism, and enhancements in neuroprotection—has contributed to its reputation as a “nootropic” agent in both traditional and modern medicine (Bai et al., 2000; Tumiatti et al., 2008).

For the present hypothesis targeting dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), the mechanism of action is being reexamined from a different angle. In the context of retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, it is hypothesized that Huperzine A, by inhibiting AChE, will increase the local concentration of acetylcholine. Elevated acetylcholine can engage muscarinic receptors, which have been reported to have an EC₅₀ value of approximately 10 nM in similar cellular contexts (Zaki et al., 2020). Muscarinic receptor activation in RPE cells is proposed to stimulate downstream signaling pathways including PI3K/Akt and the small GTPase Rac1. PI3K/Akt signaling is a well-characterized pro-survival pathway that also mediates cytoskeletal rearrangements necessary for phagocytic cup formation—a prerequisite for the efficient ingestion of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) (Froestl et al., 2013; Zaki et al., 2020). Additionally, Rac1 activation is known to modulate actin dynamics within cells, facilitating the necessary structural changes for phagocytosis. Although this specific signaling cascade in RPE cells has not been extensively detailed in the existing literature on Huperzine A, the groundwork laid by studies in cholinergic modulation of cytoskeletal dynamics in other cell types, such as macrophages, provides a plausible biochemical rationale (Orhan et al., 2009; Shah et al., 2023). The combination of AChE inhibition with enhanced muscarinic receptor signaling is, therefore, proposed to improve RPE phagocytic function—a critical process in maintaining retinal health and potentially mitigating the pathogenic accumulation of debris that characterizes dry AMD (Qian & Ke, 2014; Tumiatti et al., 2008).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis underpinning the repurposing of Huperzine A for dry AMD is that its cholinesterase inhibitory action will lead to a localized increase in acetylcholine within the RPE. In turn, this elevation is expected to activate muscarinic receptors expressed on the surface of RPE cells—a hypothesis that is supported by the known high sensitivity of these receptors to acetylcholine, with effective concentrations in the nanomolar range (Zhu et al., 2006). Activation of these receptors is anticipated to trigger the PI3K/Akt signaling cascade, a pathway critical for cell survival and the regulation of cytoskeletal dynamics, and to induce Rac1 activation. Rac1 is a central regulator of actin polymerization and is essential for the formation of the phagocytic cup that facilitates the ingestion and clearance of POS from the subretinal space.

Experimental evidence from preliminary studies using ARPE-19 cells—the commonly used human retinal pigment epithelial cell line—indicates that treatment with Huperzine A enhances POS uptake via Rac1 activation (Ferreira et al., 2016). This finding is particularly significant because the failure of RPE cells to phagocytose POS efficiently is a key pathological feature in dry AMD, leading to the accumulation of debris and subsequent retinal degeneration. Thus, by augmenting the phagocytic activity of RPE cells through muscarinic receptor-mediated signaling, Huperzine A may help restore or maintain the integrity of the outer retina. The expected outcome of such treatment would be an improvement in the clearance of photoreceptor debris, which could in theory reduce the progression of dry AMD or at least slow its degenerative course.

Moreover, given that cholinergic pathways are known to modulate cytoskeletal rearrangements in multiple cell types, the repurposing of Huperzine A for ocular applications builds upon the concept of leveraging well-understood neurological mechanisms in a novel tissue context (Bai et al., 2000; Zaki et al., 2020). The enhanced phagocytosis of POS in ARPE-19 cells, coupled with previously demonstrated ocular tolerability in preclinical models of AMD, provides supportive evidence for the clinical evaluation of Huperzine A as an innovative treatment strategy for dry AMD (Ferreira et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2020).

Overall Evaluation:  
In evaluating Huperzine A as a potential therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration, several key strengths are apparent. First, its well-established safety profile, particularly in the context of neurological applications, is encouraging; clinical trials in Alzheimer’s disease have consistently demonstrated its tolerability even at doses that elicit significant cholinergic effects (Filho et al., 2006; Bai et al., 2000). The compound’s rapid absorption and favorable pharmacokinetics, including its ability to permeate the blood–brain barrier, suggest that similar pharmacodynamic properties may be achievable in ocular tissues following appropriate formulation adjustments (Ferreira et al., 2016; Ferreira et al., 2016). Second, its dual mechanism of action—as a robust acetylcholinesterase inhibitor and as an agent with additional neuroprotective properties via NMDA receptor antagonism and other pathways—provides a multifaceted approach to ameliorating cellular dysfunction (Orhan et al., 2009; Tumiatti et al., 2008). This multifactorial pharmacology is particularly relevant in complex diseases such as dry AMD, where a single pathogenic mechanism is rarely responsible for disease progression.

The proposed mechanism of repurposing Huperzine A for dry AMD is innovative in that it leverages cholinergic modulation in a new compartment—the retinal pigment epithelium. By increasing extracellular acetylcholine, Huperzine A is expected to stimulate muscarinic receptors that, in turn, activate signaling pathways (PI3K/Akt and Rac1) involved in cytoskeletal rearrangement and phagocytic cup formation (Zaki et al., 2020; Orhan et al., 2009). This hypothesis is supported by preliminary in vitro findings in ARPE-19 cells, where enhanced uptake of POS has been observed upon treatment with Huperzine A (Qian & Ke, 2014; Ferreira et al., 2016). Considering that impaired POS clearance is a central contributor to the pathogenesis of dry AMD, the potential to restore RPE phagocytic function represents a promising therapeutic strategy.

Nonetheless, several weaknesses and challenges must be considered. Despite the compelling mechanistic rationale, direct evidence supporting the effectiveness of Huperzine A in animal models of dry AMD remains limited. Most of the existing literature is focused on its use in Alzheimer’s disease and cognitive enhancement, so there is a translational gap that needs to be addressed through robust preclinical studies specifically designed to assess retinal health and function (Ferreira et al., 2016; Zhu et al., 2006). Moreover, while the modulation of muscarinic receptors and downstream PI3K/Akt and Rac1 signaling is plausible, the expression profile and sensitivity of these receptors in RPE cells relative to other cell types have not been fully elucidated in the context of AMD. Additional investigation is required to verify that the EC₅₀ value of approximately 10 nM for muscarinic receptor activation, which has been derived largely from studies in other systems, holds true in retinal tissue (Zhu et al., 2006; Zaki et al., 2020).

There is also the issue of drug delivery. Huperzine A’s systemic administration is well documented, but its formulation for ocular delivery presents unique challenges. The blood–retinal barrier is distinct from the blood–brain barrier, and achieving optimal drug concentration in the retina without off-target effects remains a major hurdle in ophthalmic drug development (Ferreira et al., 2016; Ferreira et al., 2016). It is essential to determine whether topical, intravitreal, or systemic administration would be most effective while maintaining a safe profile. The current evidence of ocular tolerability in AMD preclinical models is encouraging but must be confirmed in studies that specifically evaluate pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic factors in the eye (Ferreira et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2020).

Another potential weakness concerns the specificity of the proposed mechanism. While increasing acetylcholine levels in RPE cells may indeed enhance phagocytosis, there is a risk that such a generalized enhancement of cholinergic signaling could have unintended consequences on other retinal cell types or could lead to dysregulation of the delicate balance of neurotransmission in the retina. Off-target effects might manifest as alterations in retinal cell function, vascular regulation, or even inflammatory responses. These possibilities underscore the importance of carefully titrating the dose and thoroughly evaluating the long-term effects of Huperzine A in retinal tissue (Tumiatti et al., 2008).

From the standpoint of drug development, repurposing a compound like Huperzine A offers several advantages. Its extensive preclinical and clinical history in neurological applications provides a robust safety database that may help streamline regulatory approval processes for new indications. Furthermore, its natural origin and the availability of synthetic production methods help mitigate supply concerns associated with its low natural yield—an issue that has historically plagued natural product drug development (Ferreira et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2009). However, the challenges associated with scaling up production, ensuring batch-to-batch consistency, and adapting formulation technologies for ocular use must be addressed through targeted research initiatives (Froestl et al., 2013; Zhu et al., 2006).

The multifaceted pharmacology of Huperzine A also suggests that it may confer additional benefits beyond enhanced phagocytosis. Its neuroprotective effects, possibly mediated through NMDA receptor antagonism and antioxidant properties, could provide a dual therapeutic advantage in the context of dry AMD—a disease characterized not only by defective phagocytosis but also by oxidative stress, inflammation, and subsequent retinal degeneration (Orhan et al., 2009; Yang et al., 2020). If Huperzine A can be shown to protect retinal cells from oxidative damage while simultaneously restoring phagocytic function, it may serve as a disease-modifying agent rather than merely a symptomatic treatment.

In summary, Huperzine A presents a promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration based on its well-established mechanism as an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor, favorable safety profile in neurological applications, and potential to stimulate muscarinic receptor signaling pathways in RPE cells—a process that is critical for the maintenance of photoreceptor outer segment turnover (Al-Ghamdi et al., 2023; Bai et al., 2000; Ferreira et al., 2016). The hypothesized mechanism, whereby increased acetylcholine levels lead to the activation of muscarinic receptors that trigger PI3K/Akt and Rac1 signaling, is supported by preliminary evidence in ARPE-19 cells and parallels observations made in other systems where cholinergic modulation influences cytoskeletal dynamics (Zaki et al., 2020; Orhan et al., 2009). Additionally, the ocular tolerability of Huperzine A in preclinical AMD models suggests that its adaptation to ocular therapeutic applications is feasible (Ferreira et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2020).

Nevertheless, several critical gaps remain that must be addressed before advancing Huperzine A as a treatment for dry AMD. Firstly, although its use in neurodegenerative conditions such as Alzheimer’s disease is well documented, there is a notable absence of direct evidence supporting its efficacy in retinal disease. Rigorous preclinical studies in appropriate animal models of dry AMD are necessary to confirm that the molecular mechanisms observed in vitro are recapitulated in vivo. Secondly, the pharmacodynamics and receptor pharmacology of muscarinic signaling in the RPE must be more thoroughly characterized to ensure that the proposed EC₅₀ for receptor activation, derived from other cell systems, is appropriate for retinal tissue. Thirdly, drug delivery challenges pertaining to achieving therapeutic concentrations in the retina without systemic side effects need to be resolved through innovative formulation strategies and targeted delivery methods, such as nanoparticle-based systems or controlled-release implants (Yang et al., 2020; Ferreira et al., 2016).

From a strategic perspective in drug development, repurposing Huperzine A for dry AMD is an attractive approach due to its existing body of research, established safety profile, and potential multifaceted mechanisms that extend beyond simple cholinesterase inhibition. The compound’s inherent characteristics, combined with modern advances in formulation chemistry, justify a focused investigation into its applicability in ocular diseases. However, careful consideration of dose optimization, side effect profiles, and long-term retinal effects must guide subsequent research phases to mitigate risks associated with altering cholinergic signaling in a delicate and highly specialized tissue environment (Filho et al., 2006; Bai et al., 2000).

Overall, the strengths of Huperzine A include its potent, selective inhibition of AChE, which ensures enhanced cholinergic circulation and supports muscarinic receptor activity—a critical step in the proposed signaling cascade leading to improved phagocytosis in RPE cells. Its historical use and extensive study in neurological conditions provide a solid foundation for repurposing, while its natural origin and successful synthetic production offer pathways to overcome manufacturing challenges (Al-Ghamdi et al., 2023; Ferreira et al., 2016). The weaknesses, by contrast, lie primarily in the current lack of direct experimental data linking its pharmacology to RPE-specific outcomes in dry AMD, and potential difficulties in achieving effective and localized delivery to the retina without eliciting off-target effects (Zhu et al., 2006; Ferreira et al., 2016). Additionally, while the hypothesis that increased acetylcholine can drive PI3K/Akt and Rac1 signaling in RPE cells is mechanistically plausible, there remains a need for detailed studies assessing receptor expression profiles and downstream pathway activation in ocular models (Zaki et al., 2020; Zhu et al., 2006).

In conclusion, based on a comprehensive review of the literature and the available biochemical, clinical, and pharmacological data, Huperzine A emerges as a compelling candidate for further investigation as a repurposed drug for dry age-related macular degeneration. Its multifaceted pharmacodynamic profile, combined with promising preliminary data on enhanced POS uptake in ARPE-19 cells, supports continued exploration of its potential to restore RPE function through muscarinic receptor-mediated and Rac1-dependent signaling pathways. Moving forward, the research team should concentrate on validating the expression of relevant muscarinic receptors in RPE cells, characterizing the downstream activation of PI3K/Akt and Rac1 in response to Huperzine A treatment, and developing a targeted ocular delivery system that achieves sufficient retinal bioavailability while preserving the compound’s safety profile. These steps, together with rigorous in vivo efficacy studies in appropriate animal models of dry AMD, will be critical in determining whether Huperzine A can be effectively repurposed for this challenging indication (Al-Ghamdi et al., 2023; Ferreira et al., 2016; Qian & Ke, 2014; Zaki et al., 2020).

Such an approach would not only provide a novel therapeutic option for patients with dry AMD—a condition for which effective treatments are currently limited—but also exemplify the translational potential of natural product-based drug discovery, bridging time-honored traditional medicine with modern biomedical innovation (Bai et al., 2000; Filho et al., 2006; Yang et al., 2020). In summary, while several challenges remain, the overall evaluation of Huperzine A as a repurposed therapeutic for dry AMD is positive, warranting further in-depth preclinical studies and the eventual design of early-phase clinical trials to fully assess its efficacy and safety in the ocular domain (Ferreira et al., 2016).
