Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Celastrol is a naturally occurring pentacyclic triterpenoid compound originally isolated from the root extracts of Tripterygium wilfordii Hook F, commonly known as the “Thunder God Vine” (Gu et al., 2018; Cascao et al., 2017). This compound belongs to the quinone methide triterpenoid class, a group of bioactive natural products that have been used in traditional Chinese medicine for centuries to alleviate inflammatory, autoimmune, and neurodegenerative disorders (Law, 2022; Chan et al., 2024). Celastrol’s unique chemical structure, characterized by electrophilic centers that enable covalent interactions with nucleophilic cysteine residues on target proteins, confers upon it a multi-targeted mechanism of action. Its triterpenoid nature places it among a class of compounds known for their broad anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and anticancer properties, which have been applied in diverse preclinical settings ranging from rheumatoid arthritis and Crohn’s disease to neurodegenerative conditions such as Parkinson’s disease (Bian et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2019). The candidate under consideration, provided by Santa Cruz Biotech (Cat. No. sc-204268), is being evaluated for repurposing in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), a disease characterized by chronic inflammation, oxidative stress, and impairment in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) function (Zhang et al., 2019; Du et al., 2019).

Therapeutic History:  
Celastrol’s therapeutic history spans several decades and includes extensive preclinical research across multiple disease models. Historically, extracts from Tripterygium wilfordii have been utilized in traditional medicine for conditions marked by inflammation and autoimmunity. Modern biochemical investigations have validated celastrol’s anti-inflammatory and antioxidant actions, particularly through its ability to suppress proinflammatory cytokine production by inhibiting the NF-κB pathway (Zhang et al., 2019). In ocular research, celastrol has been shown to provide significant protection in models of retinal injury. For example, in studies using human ARPE-19 cells—a widely accepted in vitro model for RPE—the compound has demonstrated cytoprotective effects against hydrogen peroxide-induced oxidative stress, reducing reactive oxygen species (ROS) production, autophagy, and apoptosis while enhancing cell survival (Du et al., 2019). Additionally, preclinical animal studies have demonstrated that celastrol can protect retinal ganglion cells from optic nerve crush–induced degeneration, underscoring its neuroprotective potential within ocular tissues (Kyung et al., 2015; Law, 2022). Although direct clinical evaluations in dry AMD are few, the compound’s efficacy in analogous retinal degenerative conditions, including its ability to modulate inflammatory responses and oxidative stress in retinal cells, provides a compelling rationale for its repurposing in dry AMD (Zhao et al., 2022; Gu et al., 2018). Moreover, its application in other chronic inflammatory diseases and early-phase clinical investigations in rheumatoid arthritis have established proof-of-concept that celastrol can be used safely at carefully controlled dosages, although challenges with bioavailability and systemic toxicity have been repeatedly noted (Cascao et al., 2017).

Mechanism of Action:  
Celastrol exerts its cellular effects through a dual mechanism that targets two critical signaling pathways implicated in dry AMD pathogenesis: the nuclear factor-kappa B (NF-κB) pathway and the nuclear factor erythroid 2–related factor 2 (Nrf2) pathway. On the inflammatory front, celastrol inhibits the NF-κB signaling cascade. Under normal conditions, NF-κB is held inactive in the cytoplasm by inhibitory proteins (IκBs). Upon inflammatory stimulation, IκBs are phosphorylated and degraded, allowing NF-κB to translocate to the nucleus and induce transcription of proinflammatory cytokines such as interleukin-6 (IL-6), interleukin-8 (IL-8), and tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) (Zhang et al., 2019). Celastrol has been shown to block the phosphorylation of key regulatory proteins such as IKKα/β and IκBα, thereby preventing nuclear translocation of the p65 subunit and subsequent activation of inflammatory gene transcription in RPE cells (Zhang et al., 2019). This results in a marked reduction in cytokine secretion—a finding that is crucial for attenuating the chronic inflammatory milieu present in dry AMD. Simultaneously, celastrol activates the Nrf2 signaling pathway. Under oxidative stress conditions, Nrf2 dissociates from its cytoplasmic chaperone Keap1 and translocates to the nucleus, where it binds to antioxidant response elements (ARE) and promotes the transcription of a battery of antioxidant enzymes such as heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1), NAD(P)H quinone oxidoreductase 1 (NQO1), and glutamate-cysteine ligase catalysis (Catanzaro et al., 2020; Du et al., 2019). Activation of Nrf2 not only enhances the antioxidant capacity of RPE cells but also supports cellular defense mechanisms against oxidative insults, which are central to the progression of dry AMD. Further contributing to its protective profile, celastrol has been implicated in modulating SIRT3 expression—a mitochondrial sirtuin involved in the regulation of metabolic and oxidative stress responses—and in promoting autophagy by upregulating markers such as LC3II/LC3I ratio and Beclin-1 (Du et al., 2019). The compound’s electrophilic properties permit it to form covalent adducts with target proteins, thereby impairing the activity of key proinflammatory mediators while simultaneously bolstering the cell’s intrinsic antioxidant machinery (Venkatesha & Moudgil, 2016; Law, 2022). This comprehensive modulation of both inflammatory and oxidative stress pathways underpins celastrol’s potential utility in preserving RPE function under the duress of chronic stressors typical of dry AMD.

Expected Effect:  
The primary hypothesis driving the repurposing of celastrol for dry AMD is that, at an effective concentration (approximately EC₅₀ ~1 µM), the compound will exert a dual molecular effect in RPE cells by inhibiting NF-κB and activating Nrf2. In an in vitro assay using ARPE-19 cells, celastrol is expected to reduce the expression and secretion of proinflammatory cytokines—such as IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF-α—by interfering with the phosphorylation events necessary for NF-κB activation (Zhang et al., 2019). This reduction in cytokine levels is crucial given that inflammatory mediators are known to downregulate the expression of phagocytic receptors such as MERTK, which are essential for the clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS). Impaired POS clearance leads to the accumulation of toxic cellular debris and lipofuscin, contributing significantly to RPE dysfunction and progression of dry AMD (Venkatesha & Moudgil, 2016; Zhang et al., 2019). Concurrently, the activation of the Nrf2 pathway by celastrol will upregulate antioxidant enzymes including HO-1, thereby enhancing the cell’s ability to neutralize ROS and mitigate oxidative damage (Catanzaro et al., 2020; Du et al., 2019). Enhanced antioxidant defenses contribute to the maintenance of mitochondrial integrity and facilitate proper lysosomal function and autophagic flux in the RPE. This is critical not only for cellular survival under oxidative stress but also for the preservation of proper phagocytic functions necessary for efficient POS clearance (Du et al., 2019). Additionally, studies indicate that improvements in mitochondrial function via SIRT3 upregulation—in part mediated by celastrol—may further support the energy-dependent processes underlying phagocytosis and intracellular recycling (Du et al., 2019). As a result, the expected outcomes in the proposed assay are multi-fold: a decrease in inflammatory signaling, an increase in cellular antioxidant capacity, preservation or restoration of phagocytic receptor expression (such as MERTK), and overall enhanced clearance of POS debris by RPE cells. Taken together, these effects would slow or even halt the degenerative processes characteristic of dry AMD, thereby preserving retinal structure and function.

Overall Evaluation:  
Celastrol represents a promising therapeutic candidate for dry AMD based on its multi-targeted mechanisms that directly address the disease’s central pathophysiological processes—namely, chronic inflammation and oxidative stress. One of the fundamental strengths of celastrol is its dual modulatory action. By inhibiting the NF-κB pathway, celastrol effectively lowers the production of proinflammatory cytokines that are linked to the downregulation of MERTK and disruption of RPE phagocytic function (Zhang et al., 2019). This mechanism is particularly relevant for AMD, where uncontrolled inflammation contributes not only to RPE degeneration but also to subsequent retinal dysfunction. Simultaneously, the activation of the Nrf2 pathway and upregulation of antioxidant enzymes such as HO-1 play a pivotal role in neutralizing the excessive oxidative stress that drives RPE cell damage in dry AMD (Catanzaro et al., 2020; Du et al., 2019). Additionally, the ability of celastrol to modulate SIRT3 expression and enhance autophagic processes provides further mechanistic support for its potential to restore the balance between cellular degradation pathways and survival, thereby supporting the clearance of photoreceptor outer segments and maintenance of retinal health (Du et al., 2019).  

From a therapeutic history perspective, celastrol has been extensively studied in preclinical models of inflammation, oxidative stress, and ocular diseases. Its protective effects in ARPE-19 cells, including reduced ROS production, decreased apoptosis, and improved autophagy, are particularly encouraging for its repurposing in dry AMD (Du et al., 2019). Moreover, in vivo studies demonstrating neuroprotective effects in retinal ganglion cell models and protection against light-induced retinal degeneration further underscore its potential ocular benefits (Kyung et al., 2015; Law, 2022). These data collectively suggest that celastrol’s mechanisms of action intersect effectively with the molecular dysfunctions observed in dry AMD, making it a candidate with strong scientific rationale for further investigation.

Despite these strengths, several weaknesses and challenges must be considered. A primary limitation of celastrol is its poor water solubility and low bioavailability, which have been highlighted as significant hurdles in its clinical development (Cascao et al., 2017; Chan et al., 2024). The narrow therapeutic window and potential systemic toxicity observed at higher doses necessitate careful dose optimization and the development of advanced drug delivery systems—such as nanocarriers or liposomal formulations—that could improve its ocular bioavailability and target specificity (Cascao et al., 2017; Cheng et al., 2021). Additionally, while there is a substantial body of data supporting celastrol’s anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects, most of these studies have been conducted in vitro or in non-AMD-specific animal models. Therefore, direct evidence of its efficacy in dry AMD models—particularly those that recapitulate the complex interplay between oxidative stress, inflammation, and impaired phagocytic function in the RPE—is still limited (Zhao et al., 2022; Gu et al., 2018).  

The hypothesis underlying the proposed research is compelling: by inhibiting NF-κB signaling and activating Nrf2-mediated antioxidant responses, celastrol could restore the balance between inflammation and cellular defense mechanisms in RPE cells, ultimately preserving the expression of phagocytic receptors like MERTK and enhancing lysosomal function. This restoration is expected to improve the clearance of photoreceptor outer segments, a process critically impaired in dry AMD (Venkatesha & Moudgil, 2016; Du et al., 2019). However, it is important to note that the actual in vitro and in vivo efficacy of celastrol in improving POS clearance and maintaining RPE function must be rigorously demonstrated through additional experiments. Furthermore, while there are encouraging indications regarding ocular safety from rodent models, the translation of these findings to human clinical settings involves further validation regarding pharmacokinetic properties, dosing regimens, and long-term safety profiles (Kyung et al., 2015; Gu et al., 2018).

In summary, celastrol offers a robust mechanistic rationale for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD by simultaneously targeting key pathological processes—chronic inflammation mediated by NF-κB and oxidative stress mitigated by Nrf2. The compound’s ability to enhance antioxidant defenses while suppressing deleterious inflammatory cascades holds considerable promise for preserving RPE function, maintaining photoreceptor outer segment clearance, and ultimately slowing the progression of retinal degeneration. Nonetheless, challenges related to its formulation, delivery, and potential systemic toxicity are significant and must be addressed through advanced drug development strategies and further preclinical testing in AMD-specific models. Given these considerations, celastrol stands as an attractive but complex candidate for dry AMD therapy, warranting a comprehensive research program to optimize its clinical potential while mitigating associated risks (Cascao et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2019).

Overall, the evidence supports continued investigation into celastrol’s application in dry AMD, particularly focusing on detailed pharmacodynamic studies in RPE systems, optimization of ocular delivery methods, and rigorous safety and efficacy evaluations in well-established dry AMD animal models. If these hurdles can be successfully overcome, celastrol may emerge as a valuable addition to the currently limited therapeutic arsenal available for the treatment of dry AMD, offering hope for addressing a significant unmet medical need in age-related retinal degeneration (Zhang et al., 2019; Du et al., 2019).

answer:
Proposal for Oncostatin M (Cytokine; R&D Systems Cat. No. 287-OM)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Oncostatin M (OSM) is a cytokine originally identified as a member of the interleukin‐6 (IL-6) family and is naturally produced by various immune cells. Recombinant OSM, as provided by R&D Systems (Cat. No. 287-OM), is synthesized using recombinant DNA technology and purified to ensure bioactivity. As a protein therapeutic, OSM belongs to the class of cytokine-based drugs, which have historically been harnessed for their abilities to modulate inflammatory responses, regulate cell differentiation, and promote tissue repair. The recombinant formulation offers high purity and biological consistency, which makes it an attractive candidate for repurposing in ocular diseases. Prior studies have shown that cytokines from the IL-6 family, including OSM, CNTF, and LIF, are capable of inducing cellular protective mechanisms in the retina and may influence inflammatory and repair pathways (Brown, 2015; Pacione, 2004).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, OSM has been investigated in various models of retinal degeneration where its administration was correlated with protection of retinal ganglion cells and photoreceptors. In a rat model of retinal degeneration, OSM injection led to a reduction in photoreceptor loss, suggesting its neuroprotective potential in ocular pathologies (Brown, 2015; Xia et al., 2011). Beyond the retina, evidence indicates that OSM can influence epithelial repair and barrier integrity in tissues affected by inflammation, as seen in studies of airway epithelial cells in diseases such as asthma and allergic rhinitis (Pothoven & Schleimer, 2017). In terms of specific use against dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), there is no direct clinical history of OSM application; however, the body of work on cytokine-based interventions in ocular diseases is promising and supports repurposing efforts. Notably, the success in using CNTF—a cytokine with mechanistic similarities to OSM—in clinical studies to preserve photoreceptors and improve retinal function underscores the potential of this class of agents for treating degenerative retinal disorders (Xia et al., 2011).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, the mechanism of action of OSM is initiated by its binding to the OSM receptor (OSMR), which forms a heterodimeric complex with the signal-transducing receptor subunit gp130. This receptor engagement prompts the recruitment of Janus kinases (JAKs), including Jak2 and Tyk2, leading to the phosphorylation of specific tyrosine residues on the receptor and subsequent activation of the Signal Transducer and Activator of Transcription 3 (STAT3) (Pacione, 2004; Richards, 2013). Once phosphorylated, STAT3 forms homodimers that translocate to the nucleus and bind to STAT-responsive elements in the promoter regions of target genes. Among the genes regulated by STAT3 are those implicated in the acute phase response, such as A2m, as well as genes like Cebpd, which are involved in immune and pro-inflammatory responses (Pacione, 2004).

In retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells—critical for maintaining photoreceptor health—the activation of STAT3 may have multiple beneficial effects. Studies have shown that OSM not only induces STAT3 phosphorylation in RPE cells, but also phosphorylates ERK1/2 MAP kinase, indicating a broad spectrum of signal transduction modulation that influences cell survival, differentiation, and cytoskeletal organization (Li et al., 2011). Given that cytoskeletal reorganization is essential for the formation of phagocytic cups and subsequent photoreceptor outer segment (POS) internalization, OSM-mediated STAT3 activation is hypothesized to contribute directly to these processes. It is important to note that similar effects have been observed with related IL-6 family cytokines in various epithelial models, supporting the notion that STAT3 signaling plays a pivotal role in establishing and maintaining epithelial barrier integrity (Richards, 2013; Pacione, 2004; Tiffen et al., 2008).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis proposed for repurposing OSM in dry AMD is that when administered at concentrations around the EC₅₀ (~0.1 nM), OSM will robustly activate STAT3 in RPE cells. This activation is expected to drive the transcription of genes that encode tight junction proteins and cytoskeletal elements critical for the morphological and functional integrity of the RPE layer. Enhanced expression of these genes would, in theory, facilitate reorganization of the cytoskeleton, thereby enabling the efficient formation of phagocytic cups. As phagocytosis of shed POS is a central function of the RPE—ensuring the renewal of the photoreceptor layer—improvements in this process may directly translate into enhanced retinal health and slow disease progression in dry AMD (Li et al., 2011; Richards, 2013).

Evidence from the literature suggests that STAT3 activation plays a role in cytoskeletal dynamics and barrier function. For example, in studies with human fetal RPE cells, OSM stimulation led to phosphorylated STAT3 accumulation, which is correlated with modifications in cell shape, inhibition of uncontrolled proliferation, and potentially enhanced phagocytosis (Li et al., 2011). Moreover, the beneficial effects witnessed in similar cytokine treatments, such as with CNTF, reinforce the notion that a shared signaling cascade involving STAT3 not only supports neuroprotection but also augments cellular processes essential for maintaining the RPE’s barrier functions and phagocytic competence (Xia et al., 2011; Mori et al., 2024). However, while the expected induction of tight junction and cytoskeletal gene expression is mechanistically plausible based on the STAT3 pathway, direct evidence linking OSM-induced gene expression specifically to enhanced phagocytic cup formation in RPE cells remains to be conclusively established and would benefit from further in vitro and in vivo validation (Pothoven & Schleimer, 2017; Pacione, 2004).

Overall Evaluation:  
The repurposing of Oncostatin M for the treatment of dry AMD is supported by a mechanistic rationale that draws on its established role in STAT3-mediated cellular signaling and its previous demonstrations of neuroprotective effects in retinal degeneration models. One of the key strengths of OSM as a candidate lies in its ability to activate STAT3—a transcription factor that governs a spectrum of genes involved in cell survival, cytoskeletal reorganization, and barrier integrity. This is highly relevant in the context of dry AMD, where RPE dysfunction and impaired phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments contribute to disease progression (Brown, 2015; Pacione, 2004). Additionally, the availability of a high-quality recombinant form, combined with prior research in ocular models showing evidence of photoreceptor protection and potential enhancement of retinal function, renders OSM an attractive prospect for repurposing (Xia et al., 2011; Mori et al., 2024).

Despite these strengths, several challenges and potential weaknesses warrant consideration. First, although OSM-induced STAT3 activation is well documented, its downstream effects on tight junction proteins and the cytoskeletal apparatus within RPE cells have not been conclusively demonstrated in the context of dry AMD. There is some concern that while low to moderate doses of OSM may promote cellular repair and barrier stabilization, higher concentrations—or chronic overexpression—might induce epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) and compromise barrier integrity, as seen in other epithelial tissues (Pothoven & Schleimer, 2017). This dual nature of OSM’s action necessitates careful dosing and thorough characterization of its effects on RPE function to avoid adverse outcomes such as enhanced inflammation or unwanted EMT that could exacerbate retinal degeneration.

Furthermore, specific studies in human RPE cells indicate that while OSM robustly activates STAT3 and ERK1/2 pathways, it can also lead to inhibitory effects on cell proliferation and survival, suggesting that its impact on cell dynamics is highly context-dependent (Li et al., 2011; Tiffen et al., 2008). This raises questions regarding the optimal balance between achieving sufficient STAT3 activation to drive cytoskeletal and tight junction gene expression and avoiding potential cytostatic or cytotoxic effects that may impair overall RPE health. There is also a need to determine whether the upregulation of target genes such as A2m and Cebpd—documented in other cellular contexts—translates into functional improvements in POS internalization and maintenance of the RPE barrier in the specific setting of dry AMD (Pacione, 2004).

Moreover, while studies in rat models of retinal degeneration have shown that OSM can reduce photoreceptor loss and promote the regeneration of outer segments (Järgen et al., 2017), these effects have not been directly linked to changes in RPE phagocytic activity or tight junction integrity. Given that dry AMD involves chronic, low-grade inflammation and oxidative stress, it is essential to ascertain whether OSM’s systemic inflammatory modulation would have beneficial or deleterious effects over the longer term. The balance between its regenerative potential and the possibility of promoting inflammatory cascades or pathological angiogenesis (despite some reports of reduced pathological neovascularization) must be rigorously tested in preclinical models that faithfully recapitulate the multifactorial nature of dry AMD pathology (Pothoven & Schleimer, 2017; Mori et al., 2024).

Another aspect to consider is the cross-talk between OSM-mediated STAT3 signaling and other cellular pathways that regulate cytoskeletal dynamics and cellular adhesion in the RPE. For instance, the cytokine’s ability to modulate both the ERK1/2 MAP kinase pathway and STAT family proteins suggests that it operates at a nodal point that could influence diverse cellular functions. This complexity, while offering an opportunity to address multiple pathological processes simultaneously, also raises the possibility of off-target effects that could undermine the therapeutic goal. Detailed dose-response studies and time-course experiments will be imperative to delineate the precise window in which OSM functions as a promoter of barrier integrity and efficient phagocytosis, rather than triggering pathological changes detrimental to RPE function (Li et al., 2011; Tiffen et al., 2008).

In terms of translational potential, the strategy of repurposing an existing recombinant cytokine such as OSM offers significant advantages, including the possibility of leveraging existing manufacturing, formulation, and regulatory data. This could expedite the transition from preclinical studies to early-phase clinical trials in patients with dry AMD. Nonetheless, the preclinical evidence specific to dry AMD remains preliminary, and further research is needed to systematically assess OSM’s effects on RPE cell morphology, tight junction formation, cytoskeletal organization, and phagocytic efficiency. It would be beneficial to conduct detailed in vitro experiments using human RPE cell lines or primary RPE cultures, evaluating not only short-term signaling events (e.g., STAT3 phosphorylation kinetics) but also long-term outcomes such as maintenance of the barrier phenotype and resistance to oxidative or inflammatory stress. Such studies could be complemented by in vivo investigations in animal models that mimic the key features of dry AMD, thereby providing a more comprehensive understanding of the balance between beneficial and potentially harmful effects of OSM in the ocular environment (Li et al., 2011; Pacione, 2004).

Overall, Oncostatin M presents as an innovative and mechanistically plausible candidate for the treatment of dry AMD. Its ability to activate STAT3 is intrinsically linked to cytoskeletal reorganization and epithelial barrier maintenance, processes that are critical for proper RPE function and the clearance of shed POS. The preclinical data from retinal degeneration models, along with evidence from related cytokines, lend credence to the hypothesis that OSM could enhance POS internalization and overall retinal health when applied at carefully optimized concentrations (Brown, 2015; Xia et al., 2011). However, the candidate’s dualistic role in modulating epithelial barrier function—including the risk of inducing EMT and compromising cellular integrity at inappropriate doses—necessitates a cautious and methodical approach to further development (Pothoven & Schleimer, 2017).

In conclusion, while the repurposing of Oncostatin M for dry AMD is underpinned by compelling mechanistic insights and supportive data from alternative ocular applications, significant gaps remain in our understanding of its specific effects on RPE cells. Detailed investigations into the optimal dosing regimen, the kinetics of STAT3 activation, and the downstream transcriptional events governing tight junction and cytoskeletal gene expression are crucial. Only through rigorous preclinical evaluation—encompassing both in vitro mechanism-based assays and in vivo efficacy studies—can we validate whether OSM truly possesses the capacity to enhance phagocytic cup formation and POS internalization as hypothesized. The balance between therapeutic benefit and potential adverse effects must be carefully managed to harness the full potential of OSM as a treatment for dry age-related macular degeneration (Pacione, 2004; Li et al., 2011; Richards, 2013).

answer:
Proposal for Brexpiprazole (5-HT₁A agonist/5-HT₂A antagonist; Otsuka pharmaceutical)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Brexpiprazole is a synthetic, orally available fifth‐generation antipsychotic developed by Otsuka Pharmaceutical that belongs to the class of serotonin–dopamine activity modulators (SDAMs). It was discovered and developed as an improvement over earlier dopamine partial agonists in order to achieve balanced modulation of neurotransmission. Chemically, brexpiprazole was designed as a dihydrocarbostyril derivative that retains partial agonistic properties at dopamine D₂ receptors while simultaneously exhibiting potent partial agonism at serotonin 5-HT₁A receptors and antagonism at serotonin 5-HT₂A receptors (Das et al., 2016). This balanced receptor profile has been exploited primarily for psychiatric indications, but the receptor distribution of serotonin receptors is not limited to neuronal tissues. In particular, the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) expresses several serotonin receptor subtypes, and there is compelling biochemical evidence that serotonergic signaling influences inflammatory gene expression and cellular homeostasis in these cells (Biswal et al., 2015). As such, brexpiprazole’s well‐defined receptor interactions position it as a promising candidate to modulate pathological pathways in dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD).

Therapeutic History:  
Brexpiprazole has an established history for its use in central nervous system disorders. It has been approved for the treatment of schizophrenia and as an adjunct therapy in major depressive disorder owing to its favorable safety and tolerability profiles, which include a low risk of extrapyramidal side effects and modest metabolic liabilities (Das et al., 2016; Fabre et al., 2022). To date, however, no clinical trials or preclinical studies have directly examined brexpiprazole for the treatment of retinal degenerative conditions such as dry AMD. Nevertheless, multiple studies have investigated the therapeutic potential of 5-HT₁A receptor agonists in retinal models. For example, research utilizing 8-OH-DPAT—a prototypical 5-HT₁A agonist—demonstrated significant antioxidant protection in RPE cells, reduction in oxidative stress markers, and preservation of retinal architecture under conditions of mitochondrial oxidative stress (Biswal et al., 2015). Other compounds with selective 5-HT₁A agonist properties, such as tandospirone, have been evaluated in retinal models, albeit with mixed clinical outcomes (Buschini et al., 2015). This preclinical precedence establishes an indirect rationale for repurposing brexpiprazole in dry AMD even if direct ocular applications have not been previously explored.

Mechanism of Action:  
Brexpiprazole exerts its pharmacological effects primarily through dual modulation of serotonergic receptors. Its partial agonism at 5-HT₁A receptors, with reported potency in the low nanomolar range (EC₅₀ ~ 5 nM as hypothesized), is thought to trigger intracellular cascades that promote cellular survival and antioxidant defenses. Activation of the 5-HT₁A receptor in other tissues has been associated with upregulation of key antioxidant enzymes—including metallothionein-1 (MT-1), heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1), NADPH quinone oxidoreductase 1 (NqO1), catalase, and superoxide dismutase-1 (SOD1)—thereby mitigating oxidative stress and reducing mitochondrial damage (Biswal et al., 2015). In RPE cells—the cell type critical for photoreceptor outer segment (POS) clearance—the 5-HT₁A receptor is endogenously expressed, and its activation has been linked to attenuation of inflammatory signaling. Preclinical studies using other 5-HT₁A agonists in ARPE-19 cells have shown reductions in oxidative stress markers and inflammatory mediators, as well as preservation of tight junction proteins (Biswal et al., 2015).

Simultaneously, brexpiprazole’s antagonism at 5-HT₂A receptors may complement these effects by further modulating inflammatory responses. Blockade of 5-HT₂A receptors has been associated with reduced microglial activation and decreased complement deposition in the outer retina, contributing to neuroprotection in models of retinal degeneration (Biswal et al., 2015; Das et al., 2016). This dual receptor effect is proposed to result in an overall anti-inflammatory microenvironment in the RPE, which is crucial because chronic inflammation is a key pathological feature in dry AMD. Moreover, the compound’s modulation of serotonergic signaling may indirectly support the maintenance of phagocytic receptors such as MERTK and lysosomal enzymes like cathepsin D, which are essential for the normal clearance of POS (Biswal et al., 2015). Although direct studies with brexpiprazole in RPE cells are lacking, these mechanistic insights derived from similar 5-HT₁A agonists underpin the hypothesis that brexpiprazole could reduce production of pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g., IL-6 and TNF-α) and restore normal phagocytic and lysosomal function (Biswal et al., 2015).

Expected Effect:  
In an in vitro assay using ARPE-19 cells or isolated RPE cells under conditions of complement-induced stress, brexpiprazole is expected to act by modulating serotonergic receptor signaling to yield a multi-faceted protective effect. Specifically, its 5-HT₁A agonism should trigger intracellular survival pathways that result in the upregulation of antioxidant defenses analogous to the responses observed with 8-OH-DPAT in similar models (Biswal et al., 2015). This effect is anticipated to lead to a reduction in oxidative stress markers, such as 8-OH-deoxyguanosine or nitrotyrosine adducts, which are typically elevated in conditions of mitochondrial oxidative injury (Biswal et al., 2015).

Additionally, brexpiprazole is hypothesized to reduce the expression of key pro-inflammatory cytokines—specifically IL-6 and TNF-α—through receptor-mediated modulation of inflammatory signaling cascades. In a cell culture model where RPE cells are exposed to oxidative and complement-mediated insults, a drop in these cytokine levels would be indicative of an amelioration of stress-induced inflammatory responses (Biswal et al., 2015; Wright & Ambati, 2016). This anti-inflammatory effect is critical because uncontrolled inflammation not only perpetuates oxidative damage but also disrupts the barrier and phagocytic functions of the RPE.

Furthermore, the candidate is expected to preserve or restore the expression of MERTK, a receptor tyrosine kinase crucial for the phagocytosis of POS, as well as cathepsin D, a lysosomal protease necessary for the degradation of internalized material (Biswal et al., 2015; Fischer, 2016). Successful maintenance of these proteins would directly support the clearance functions of RPE cells, an essential element for retinal homeostasis that is compromised in dry AMD. This improved phagocytic capacity, coupled with reduced cytokine production, would likely result in overall preservation of RPE structure and function, as reflected in enhanced visual function in preclinical models (Biswal et al., 2015).

Moreover, although the clinical studies of other serotonergic compounds such as tandospirone have yielded mixed results—with at least one phase III trial for geographic atrophy being discontinued due to lack of efficacy (Buschini et al., 2015)—the favorable pharmacokinetic properties and established safety profile of brexpiprazole in other indications provide a strong rationale for its repurposing, particularly if its ocular penetration can be demonstrated in relevant preclinical models (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

Overall Evaluation:  
Brexpiprazole offers several attractive strengths as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. Its dual mechanism—partial agonism at 5-HT₁A receptors paired with antagonism at 5-HT₂A receptors—is well aligned with the emerging understanding of how serotonergic signaling influences retinal cell survival, oxidative stress, and inflammation (Biswal et al., 2015). The wealth of preclinical evidence supporting the role of 5-HT₁A receptor activation in reducing oxidative damage and preserving RPE function under stress conditions provides a sound mechanistic basis for expecting similar protective effects from brexpiprazole. In addition, the targeting of phagocytic receptor expression (i.e., MERTK) and lysosomal enzymes (i.e., cathepsin D) represents a novel strategy to address one of the fundamental dysfunctions in dry AMD: impaired clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (Biswal et al., 2015).

Brexpiprazole’s established safety profile and pharmacokinetics in psychiatric populations further underscore its potential for repurposing. Its high oral bioavailability and documented tolerability in long-term studies, along with evidence that similar compounds can penetrate ocular tissues when administered systemically, add to the candidate’s appeal (Das et al., 2016; Fabre et al., 2022). This is particularly relevant given the chronic nature of dry AMD and the need for therapies that can be safely administered over extended periods.

However, several significant weaknesses and gaps warrant cautious consideration. First, direct evidence linking brexpiprazole to improved RPE function—specifically, its effects on inflammatory signaling markers IL-6 and TNF-α, and on the preservation of MERTK and cathepsin D expression—remains theoretical and extrapolated from studies using other 5-HT₁A agonists like 8-OH-DPAT (Biswal et al., 2015). This means that while the underlying mechanistic hypothesis is plausible, there is a pressing need for targeted in vitro and in vivo studies focused on brexpiprazole in ocular models. In particular, experiments using ARPE-19 cells under conditions of oxidative or complement-induced stress must be conducted to confirm that brexpiprazole can indeed modulate cytokine levels and restore phagocytic function in these cells.

Another shortcoming is the uncertainty regarding ocular penetration. Although the systemic administration of 5-HT₁A agonists in animal models has led to beneficial retinal outcomes (Biswal et al., 2015), brexpiprazole’s distribution into ocular tissues has not been directly evaluated. It is essential to ascertain the extent to which brexpiprazole reaches the RPE at therapeutically relevant concentrations, particularly given that dosage regimens for psychiatric conditions may not be directly translatable to ocular therapy (Biswal et al., 2015).

Furthermore, while the anti-inflammatory hypothesis is supported by the general role of serotonergic signaling in RPE cells, the direct measurement of inflammatory cytokines and downstream phagocytic markers in response to brexpiprazole treatment remains to be demonstrated. Given that earlier clinical attempts using tandospirone for AMD were unsuccessful (Buschini et al., 2015), there is a need to critically assess whether brexpiprazole’s receptor profile confers advantages that overcome the limitations observed with other 5-HT₁A agonists. Additionally, potential off-target effects in the ocular environment—such as those arising from modulation of other receptor systems—must be thoroughly evaluated.

In summary, brexpiprazole presents a scientifically sound and innovative approach to the treatment of dry AMD by virtue of its serotonergic receptor modulation. Its dual action on 5-HT₁A and 5-HT₂A receptors is supported by a robust body of preclinical evidence indicating that 5-HT₁A receptor activation can reduce oxidative stress and inflammation in RPE cells, while also preserving essential functions like POS clearance (Biswal et al., 2015). The candidate’s excellent safety profile in psychiatric applications and potential for systemic administration further enhance its appeal. Nevertheless, the absence of direct experimental data linking brexpiprazole to improved phagocytosis, reduced IL-6 and TNF-α production, and maintained lysosomal enzyme expression in RPE cells represents a critical gap that must be addressed. As such, while the repurposing of brexpiprazole for dry AMD holds promise, a series of preclinical experiments—encompassing in vitro ARPE-19 cell assays, in vivo ocular pharmacokinetic studies, and efficacy models of retinal degeneration—are required before progressing to clinical trials. Overall, given the mechanistic rationale and the encouraging safety and pharmacological characteristics of brexpiprazole, further research is justified to validate its application in dry AMD, provided that the aforementioned knowledge gaps are systematically addressed (Das et al., 2016; Biswal et al., 2015).

hypothesis: CETP inhibitor anacetrapib (Evacetrapib analog; Merck research compound)
answer:
Proposal for CETP inhibitor anacetrapib (Evacetrapib analog; Merck research compound)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Anacetrapib is a synthetic small‐molecule inhibitor of cholesteryl ester transfer protein (CETP) originally developed by Merck as part of a class of compounds aimed at modulating lipid metabolism. This compound was identified and refined through extensive medicinal chemistry programs designed to target CETP’s lipid transfer function. As a member of the CETP inhibitor class, anacetrapib has been developed primarily for cardiovascular risk reduction by increasing high‐density lipoprotein cholesterol (HDL‐C) and lowering low‐density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL‐C), and its chemical structure and binding properties have been designed to disrupt the lipid‐transfer tunnel of the CETP enzyme (Gurfinkel & Joy, 2011; Tall & Rader, 2018). The proposed repurposing for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) is based on the rationale that by inhibiting CETP, the agent could raise local HDL levels in Bruch’s membrane (BrM) and improve reverse cholesterol transport, thereby reducing drusen‐like lipid accumulation and indirectly supporting retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) phagocytic capacity—a hypothesis derived from observed associations between CETP activity, local retinal lipid metabolism, and AMD pathogenesis (Betzler et al., 2020; Shughoury et al., 2022).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, CETP inhibitors have been evaluated extensively for their potential to address dyslipidemia and reduce atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease. Anacetrapib, in particular, has undergone large clinical trials such as the DEFINE and REVEAL studies, where its efficacy in raising HDL‐C by approximately 138% and reducing LDL‐C by 37–40% compared to placebo was demonstrated (Cheung et al., 2017; Tall & Rader, 2018). The class of CETP inhibitors also includes compounds such as torcetrapib, dalcetrapib, and evacetrapib—with torcetrapib’s development being terminated due to off‐target effects including blood pressure elevations, while anacetrapib and evacetrapib showed more favorable profiles in subsequent trials (Gurfinkel & Joy, 2011; Sirtori, 2011). Although these compounds were developed to address cardiovascular pathologies, genetic and mechanistic studies have implicated CETP and HDL metabolism in the ocular environment as well. Several genome‐wide association studies and Mendelian randomization studies have demonstrated a relationship between CETP gene variants, HDL levels, and AMD risk (Burgess & Davey Smith, 2017; Schmidt et al., 2020). Despite this, no CETP inhibitor has previously been used in a clinical setting for the treatment of dry AMD or similar ocular diseases, and the repurposing of anacetrapib for dry AMD represents a novel therapeutic direction inspired by preclinical studies in murine models that suggest potential benefits in the retinal context (Cheung et al., 2017).

Mechanism of Action:  
Anacetrapib functions by binding to CETP, thereby preventing the transfer of cholesteryl esters from HDL to apolipoprotein B‐containing lipoproteins (i.e., LDL, very‐low‐density lipoprotein [VLDL]) and the subsequent exchange of triglycerides in the opposite direction. At the molecular level, CETP normally operates via a tunnel‐mechanism or shuttle mechanism to facilitate the bidirectional lipid transfer between lipoproteins. Inhibition of CETP by anacetrapib results in the accumulation of cholesterol-rich, enlarged HDL particles and a concomitant reduction in the levels of atherogenic LDL particles (Gurfinkel & Joy, 2011; Sirtori, 2011). In the context of the retina, emerging evidence suggests that CETP is expressed not only systemically but also locally—in the retinal pigment epithelium, photoreceptor outer segments, and interphotoreceptor matrix (Shughoury et al., 2022; Cheung et al., 2017). The rationale is that CETP activity in Bruch’s membrane may normally lower HDL levels, thereby impairing the capacity for reverse cholesterol transport in this specialized extracellular matrix, which can lead to the accumulation of lipids and the formation of drusen. By inhibiting CETP, anacetrapib may restore or increase local HDL levels, improving the efflux of accumulated cholesterol and other lipids from the RPE and neighboring structures (Fan et al., 2017; Lin et al., 2022). Moreover, the resulting HDL particles may gain enhanced cholesterol efflux capacity, as evidenced by preclinical studies that show increased cholesterol removal from macrophages via ABCA1- and ABCG1-mediated pathways (Sirtori, 2011; Page et al., 2016). In addition, proper HDL particle composition under CETP inhibition could influence key inflammatory regulatory mechanisms through the carriage of complement factors, which are linked to AMD pathogenesis (Tricorache et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2015).

Expected Effect:  
In the proposed assay, treatment with anacetrapib is expected to increase HDL levels locally in Bruch’s membrane, thereby enhancing reverse cholesterol transport across the retinal layers. The improved cholesterol efflux from the RPE is postulated to mitigate the accumulation of drusen-like lipid deposits—a hallmark of dry AMD—and potentially restore critical cellular functions such as integrin localization and associated phagocytic receptor activity (Cheung et al., 2017; Schmidt et al., 2020). This restoration of lipid homeostasis is anticipated to reduce the build-up of oxidized lipids and other debris beneath the RPE, ultimately alleviating RPE dysfunction—a central component in the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Burgess & Davey Smith, 2017; Cheung et al., 2017). The mechanism relies on the observation that HDL not only serves as a cholesterol acceptor but also carries important complement regulatory proteins and inflammatory mediators; thus, its normalization in Bruch’s membrane could indirectly support the phagocytic activity of RPE cells and improve tissue homeostasis (Lin et al., 2022; Cheung et al., 2017). Gene expression studies have identified CETP expression in ocular tissues, reinforcing the notion that local CETP inhibition may directly influence lipid handling in the retina (Shughoury et al., 2022; Cheung et al., 2017). Ultimately, the expected outcomes in preclinical models—and, by extension, in clinical trials—are a measurable reduction in drusen burden, improvement in RPE functionality, and a potential delay or attenuation in the progression of dry AMD (Schmidt et al., 2020; Cheung et al., 2017).

Overall Evaluation:  
The repurposing of anacetrapib for the treatment of dry AMD presents a compelling opportunity, supported by a solid mechanistic hypothesis and a favorable human safety profile established in cardiovascular trials. Among the clear strengths is the extensive biochemical and clinical data on CETP inhibitors in the context of dyslipidemia; anacetrapib has demonstrated robust HDL‐C raising and LDL‐C lowering effects, with a tolerability profile superior to earlier CETP inhibitors such as torcetrapib (Gurfinkel & Joy, 2011; Tall & Rader, 2018). Furthermore, emerging evidence of CETP expression in ocular tissues and its potential role in modulating local lipid metabolism—combined with findings that suggest dysfunctional HDL composition may contribute to drusen formation—lends strong support to the therapeutic rationale (Shughoury et al., 2022; Cheung et al., 2017).

However, there are important weaknesses and challenges that must be addressed. First, the genetic and epidemiological data linking HDL cholesterol and AMD have been paradoxical; several Mendelian randomization studies have implicated HDL‐raising alleles, particularly those related to CETP modulation, with an increased risk for AMD (Betzler et al., 2020; Fan et al., 2017). This counterintuitive observation raises concerns that simply increasing HDL levels may not guarantee improved RPE function unless the quality and functionality of HDL particles are also enhanced (Schmidt et al., 2020; Lin et al., 2022). Second, while the cardiovascular applications of anacetrapib provide a strong safety signal, the ocular-specific pharmacodynamics and tissue distribution of the drug remain largely unexplored. It is conceivable that the systemic modulation of HDL might not translate into the desired local changes in Bruch’s membrane, particularly given the unique lipid microenvironment of the retina (Cheung et al., 2017; Cheung et al., 2017). Third, preclinical data demonstrating that anacetrapib can reduce BrM lipid burden and restore integrin localization in murine models, although promising, have yet to be validated extensively, and species differences in CETP expression and lipid metabolism could limit translatability to human patients (Cheung et al., 2017; Cheung et al., 2017). Lastly, the long-term consequences of altering CETP activity in the retina are unknown, and there exists a potential risk that chronic CETP inhibition could inadvertently disrupt local complement regulation or other aspects of retinal homeostasis, given the tight interplay between lipid metabolism and inflammation in AMD pathogenesis (Tricorache et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2015).

Overall, while the conceptual framework underlying the repurposing of anacetrapib for dry AMD is scientifically intriguing and supported by a convergence of genetic, biochemical, and preclinical mechanistic data, further investigation is needed to reconcile the paradoxical relationships observed in human genetic studies, to precisely characterize the local retinal pharmacokinetics of the drug, and to validate its effects on reverse cholesterol transport in the specific context of the retina. In summary, anacetrapib holds potential as a novel therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, but its ultimate success will depend on carefully designed preclinical studies and early-phase clinical trials that specifically address its ocular efficacy and safety profile (Burgess & Davey Smith, 2017; Schmidt et al., 2020; Lin et al., 2022).

hypothesis: Astrocyte-derived exosomes enriched for miR-146a (Research product)
answer:
Proposal for Astrocyte-derived exosomes enriched for miR-146a (Research product)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Astrocyte‐derived exosomes enriched for miR-146a are an innovative, biomimetic class of therapeutic agents that combine the natural properties of extracellular vesicles with the regulatory functions of microRNAs. Exosomes are nano‐sized vesicles (typically 40–160 nm in diameter) generated in the endosomal pathway and released by almost all cell types, including astrocytes, which are a fundamental component of the retinal microenvironment (Heo & Ryu, 2024). In this candidate, exosomes are isolated from retinal astrocytes and selectively engineered to become enriched with miR-146a, a microRNA known for its anti‐inflammatory and immunomodulatory properties. Because astrocytes are intimately involved in neuronal support and retinal homeostasis, their exosomes offer an inherent targeting advantage for diseased retinal regions, particularly in age-related macular degeneration (AMD) where the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) is compromised (Romero et al., 2024). The enrichment with miR-146a transforms these naturally secreted vesicles into a targeted drug delivery vehicle that can modulate specific intracellular pathways in the RPE. This approach falls within the broader therapeutic class of exosome‐based drug delivery systems, a class that has increasingly attracted attention for its ability to transport nucleic acids, proteins, and lipids with high specificity and minimal immunogenicity (Du & Palczewski, 2022). Exosome therapy has been previously explored in preclinical models for various retinal pathologies using different source cells, such as mesenchymal stem cells (MSCs) and RPE cells (Heo & Ryu, 2024; Liu et al., 2023). Engineering exosomes to carry therapeutic miRNAs like miR-146a exemplifies a precision medicine strategy in which the carrier is not only inert but provides its own biological effects derived from its cell of origin, contributing to the overall therapeutic profile.

Therapeutic History:  
While there is robust literature documenting the application of exosome-based therapies in ocular diseases, the specific use of astrocyte-derived exosomes enriched with miR-146a is a relatively novel proposition. In several studies, exosomes isolated from mesenchymal stem cells have been engineered to carry anti-inflammatory microRNAs, including miR-146a, and have shown neuroprotective effects in retinal degeneration models such as retinitis pigmentosa and diabetic retinopathy (Zhang et al., 2022). Moreover, astrocyte-derived exosomes have been explored for their intrinsic neuroprotective and anti‐angiogenic properties. For instance, retinal astrocyte-derived exosomes have been demonstrated to contain multiple anti-angiogenic molecules including endostatin, PEDF, and TIMP-1, which contribute to the suppression of choroidal neovascularization in laser-induced models (Mead & Chow, 2023; Romero et al., 2024). Although these studies primarily target neovascular AMD, their underlying mechanisms emphasize the utility of astrocyte-based exosome therapy in modulating critical retinal pathways. In the context of dry AMD, which is characterized by chronic RPE degeneration, oxidative stress, and complement system dysregulation, the strategy of utilizing exosomal delivery to target RPE dysfunction is supported by evidence that exosome‐mediated miRNA transfer can restore lysosomal function and reduce inflammatory cascades in retinal cells (ElShelmani et al., 2021; Guan et al., 2025). Additionally, complement dysregulation and increased complement factor expression are central features of dry AMD pathology, and prior studies have implicated exosomal cargo in modulating inflammatory and complement pathways (Guan et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2023). Although direct clinical or extensive preclinical experience with astrocyte-derived exosomes enriched for miR-146a in dry AMD is limited, the analogous applications of MSC-derived exosomes carrying miR-146a establish an important precedent and provide a mechanistic rationale for further investigation (Zhang et al., 2022; Berber et al., 2017).

Mechanism of Action:  
The therapeutic mechanism of this candidate operates at multiple molecular levels, integrating the known functions of both miR-146a and exosomal delivery systems. miR-146a is recognized as a key negative regulator of inflammation through its ability to target components in the Toll-like receptor (TLR) and nuclear factor-κB (NF-κB) signaling pathways. Specifically, miR-146a targets interleukin-1 receptor–associated kinase 1 (IRAK1) and TNF receptor-associated factor 6 (TRAF6), leading to a reduction in NF-κB activation and subsequent downregulation of pro-inflammatory cytokines (Berber et al., 2017; ElShelmani et al., 2021). In the context of dry AMD, complement overactivation has been identified as a pivotal event contributing to RPE degeneration. Complement factor H (CFH) and complement factor B (CFB) play significant roles in regulating the alternative complement pathway, and dysregulation of these factors leads to excessive complement activation, resulting in increased levels of complement fragments such as C3a that promote inflammation and lysosomal stress (ElShelmani et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2021). The proposed mechanism asserts that miR-146a, delivered via astrocyte-derived exosomes, can penetrate the RPE cell layer and downregulate the transcription and/or translation of complement components such as CFH and CFB. By limiting the production of these factors, miR-146a effectively reduces the downstream formation of the inflammatory anaphylatoxin C3a, alleviating lysosomal overload and preserving the acidic lysosomal environment necessary for optimal activity of degradative enzymes like cathepsin D (Heo & Ryu, 2024; Zhang et al., 2022). This modulation of complement activity is essential because aberrant complement activation in the RPE has been linked to photoreceptor outer segment (POS) accumulation and impaired phagocytosis, which are hallmarks of dry AMD progression (Romero et al., 2024; Sanghani et al., 2022). Furthermore, exosomes themselves possess intrinsic targeting and cell–cell communication properties; their membrane proteins, such as tetraspanins (CD63, CD81) and other surface markers, facilitate uptake by recipient cells and can mediate tissue-specific homing to the RPE (Liu et al., 2023; Romero et al., 2024). The combination of miR-146a’s molecular action on inflammatory and complement pathways with the natural delivery proficiency of astrocyte-derived exosomes creates a synergistic effect that is expected to restore lysosomal integrity and enhance functional POS degradation in high-risk CFH backgrounds (ElShelmani et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2022).

Expected Effect:  
The expected therapeutic effect in the treatment of dry AMD is multilayered. In vitro studies utilizing RPE cell cultures derived from patient lines with high-risk CFH expression are anticipated to show that treatment with miR-146a-enriched astrocyte exosomes results in a significant downregulation of complement factors, notably CFH and CFB. This downregulation would be reflected in reduced levels of the complement activation fragment C3a, which is known to exacerbate inflammation and lysosomal dysfunction in RPE cells (Romero et al., 2024; Berber et al., 2017). As a direct consequence of complement normalization, lysosomal integrity is expected to be maintained through the preservation of an acidic pH environment and the restoration of cathepsin D activity. Cathepsin D plays a critical role in the degradation of POS material taken up by RPE cells during the daily process of photoreceptor renewal (Liu et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2022). Enhanced clearance of POS is hypothesized to reduce the accumulation of toxic waste products and drusen formation, a defining characteristic of dry AMD. In addition, the anti-inflammatory action of miR-146a should attenuate the chronic low-grade inflammation observed in the retinal microenvironment, thereby mitigating further RPE and photoreceptor damage (Heo & Ryu, 2024; Liu et al., 2020).  
At the molecular level, the treatment is anticipated to modulate intracellular signaling cascades by reducing NF-κB–mediated transcription of pro-inflammatory cytokines, which in turn helps to suppress the local inflammatory milieu and prevent further complement activation (Berber et al., 2017; ElShelmani et al., 2021). The exosomal vehicle ensures that miR-146a is delivered in a protected and concentrated form, which maximizes cellular uptake and preserves functional integrity during circulation. Given their natural ability to cross biological barriers, these astrocyte-derived exosomes are expected to efficiently reach the RPE layer, and this targeted delivery is crucial for achieving the desired therapeutic outcomes with minimal off-target effects (Guan et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2023). Furthermore, the experimental assays based on RPE cell cultures and animal models of dry AMD are designed to evaluate both the biological activity of the delivered miR-146a and the restoration of lysosomal function. Expected readouts include a decrease in complement factor mRNA and protein levels, improved lysosomal enzyme activity (especially cathepsin D), reduced accumulation of POS debris, and ultimately, preservation of RPE and photoreceptor viability (Guan et al., 2025; ElShelmani et al., 2021). These effects, if validated, could translate into a slowing of disease progression or even a reversal of certain pathological features in dry AMD.

Overall Evaluation:  
The candidate therapeutic of astrocyte-derived exosomes enriched for miR-146a holds considerable promise for the treatment of dry AMD due to its innovative design and strong mechanistic rationale. One of the most significant strengths of this approach lies in its biomimetic nature. By harnessing exosomes derived from retinal astrocytes, the therapy benefits from inherent targeting properties that increase the likelihood of efficient delivery to the RPE, a key cell type implicated in dry AMD pathology (Romero et al., 2024; Mead & Chow, 2023). Furthermore, the use of miR-146a—an endogenous regulatory molecule with well-documented anti-inflammatory effects—adds an additional layer of specificity to the treatment by directly modulating the inflammatory milieu and complement dysregulation that are central to dry AMD (Berber et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2022). This dual action, combining restoration of lysosomal integrity through improved POS degradation and suppression of complement-mediated inflammation, addresses two critical pathogenic processes simultaneously.  

However, despite its notable strengths, several challenges and uncertainties remain. First, while the therapeutic concept is strongly supported by preclinical studies involving MSC-derived exosomes and by literature demonstrating the beneficial effects of exosomal miRNAs in retinal diseases (Zhang et al., 2022; Du & Palczewski, 2022), the specific application of astrocyte-derived exosomes enriched with miR-146a for dry AMD remains to be thoroughly evaluated. There is limited direct evidence in the literature showing that astrocyte-derived exosomes naturally enriched or engineered to carry miR-146a can downregulate complement factor expression in RPE cells in a clinically meaningful way (Liu et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2023). This represents a gap in knowledge that would need to be addressed through rigorous preclinical investigation, including detailed dose–response studies and assessments of long-term efficacy and safety.  

Another potential weakness lies in the scalability and reproducibility of exosome isolation from astrocytes. Exosome production can vary depending on the source, the culture conditions, and the methods used for enrichment and purification. Manufacturing a consistent and high-quality exosome product that meets clinical grade standards is a well-recognized challenge in the field of exosome therapeutics (Liu et al., 2023; Guan et al., 2025). In addition, while exosomes are known for their low immunogenicity, the possibility of immune reactions, especially when they are over-engineered or when administered repeatedly, cannot be entirely discounted and will require careful evaluation (Romero et al., 2024).  

From a mechanistic standpoint, although the theoretical framework linking miR-146a with the downregulation of complement factors CFH and CFB is compelling, the precise molecular interactions within RPE cells must be validated by robust in vitro and in vivo experiments. Detailed studies are needed to confirm the extent to which miR-146a directly modulates these complement components, and whether additional targets or off-target effects might complicate the therapeutic outcome (Zhang et al., 2022; Berber et al., 2017). Furthermore, while the restoration of lysosomal function and POS degradation is a promising endpoint, the complexity of lysosomal biology in the context of chronic degenerative diseases such as dry AMD means that multifactorial interventions might be necessary. It will be essential to demonstrate that the observed improvements in lysosomal enzyme activity (e.g., cathepsin D) translate into meaningful clinical benefits, such as slowed disease progression or improved visual function (ElShelmani et al., 2021; Romero et al., 2024).  

In summary, the concept of using astrocyte-derived exosomes enriched for miR-146a as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD is innovative, leveraging the natural targeting, biocompatibility, and multi-functional capabilities of exosomes along with the potent anti-inflammatory and complement‐modulating properties of miR-146a. The preclinical evidence derived from analogous studies using MSC-derived exosomes and the general literature on exosomal miRNA therapies in retinal diseases provides a solid foundation for this approach (Zhang et al., 2022; Heo & Ryu, 2024; Liu et al., 2023). Nevertheless, the strategy will require comprehensive validation, including optimization of exosome isolation and engineering protocols, detailed mechanistic studies in relevant cellular models, and robust in vivo efficacy assessments in dry AMD animal models before clinical translation can be considered. With targeted efforts to address these challenges, this therapeutic candidate could represent a significant advance in the treatment of dry AMD, offering a precision medicine approach that directly tackles both complement overactivation and lysosomal dysfunction at the cellular level (Du & Palczewski, 2022; Guan et al., 2025; ElShelmani et al., 2021).

Overall, the combination of bioengineered exosomes and miR-146a offers mechanistic specificity and a novel route of administration that may overcome many of the limitations inherent in current dry AMD therapies, particularly those related to anti-VEGF treatments which are primarily indicated for wet AMD. While further preclinical investigations are essential to fully elucidate the pharmacodynamics, safety profile, and therapeutic window of this candidate, the approach holds promise as a next-generation drug candidate for dry AMD that could potentially improve patient outcomes by preserving retinal structure and function through the reestablishment of homeostatic cellular processes (Mead & Chow, 2023; Sanghani et al., 2022; Song et al., 2024).
