hypothesis: Bardoxolone Methyl (CDDO-Me; Reata Pharmaceuticals)
answer:
Proposal for Bardoxolone Methyl (CDDO-Me; Reata Pharmaceuticals)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Bardoxolone methyl (also known as CDDO‐Me) is a fully synthetic derivative of the naturally occurring pentacyclic triterpenoid oleanolic acid. The parent molecule, oleanolic acid, is widely found in many plants and has been used for centuries in traditional medicine owing to its modest anti‐inflammatory and hepatoprotective properties. However, to overcome its relatively low intrinsic potency and poor pharmacokinetics, medicinal chemists modified oleanolic acid by introducing key structural changes. In particular, the synthesis of CDDO (2-cyano-3,12-dioxoolean-1,9-dien-28-oic acid) involved the installation of a cyano group at the C2 position and oxidation at positions C3 and C12, generating an electrophilic cyanoenone moiety; subsequent esterification at the C28 carboxyl group yielded bardoxolone methyl as the C28 methyl ester. These chemical modifications resulted in a molecule with two electrophilic Michael acceptor sites that are essential for its biological action, notably its ability to react reversibly with cysteine thiols in target proteins. Being part of the synthetic oleanane triterpenoids family, bardoxolone methyl falls into a class of compounds that has been extensively explored for their anti‐inflammatory, antioxidant, anticancer, and cytoprotective activities in various disease models (Borella et al., 2019).

This class of synthetic triterpenoids has historically been pursued to potentiate the natural but modest bioactivities of plant‐derived triterpenes such as oleanolic and ursolic acids. Early research aimed at enhancing anti‐inflammatory activity led to the discovery of potent derivatives such as CDDO, CDDO‐Im (the imidazolide derivative), and ultimately bardoxolone methyl. Their design was motivated by the need to generate highly potent, orally bioavailable agents capable of activating key cytoprotective pathways. The robust preclinical efficacy observed with these compounds in various models of oxidative stress, inflammation, and even tumorigenesis provided proof‐of‐concept for their use as drug candidates (Borella et al., 2019; Sakashita et al., 2021). Consequently, bardoxolone methyl has emerged as a leading representative of this chemical class, notable for its finely tuned electrophilic reactivity and its ability to induce a broad spectrum of protective gene products.

Therapeutic History:  
Bardoxolone methyl has a well‐documented history of investigation in both preclinical and clinical settings across various therapeutic indications. Originally developed for its potent anti‐inflammatory and antioxidant properties, it was first investigated in oncology where its pro‐apoptotic and antiproliferative effects were characterized in multiple cancer cell types such as pancreatic, colorectal, ovarian, and breast cancer. Early preclinical studies demonstrated that at nanomolar and low micromolar concentrations, CDDO and its derivatives could exert robust cytoprotective effects via the activation of the nuclear factor erythroid 2‐related factor 2 (Nrf2) pathway, as well as induce cell cycle arrest and trigger apoptosis in cancer cells (Borella et al., 2019; Tanase et al., 2022).

Following its anticancer exploration, a serendipitous clinical observation during early oncology trials revealed that patients treated with bardoxolone methyl experienced improved renal function, as measured by an elevation in the estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR). This finding prompted a pivot in therapeutic focus toward kidney diseases, particularly chronic kidney disease (CKD) associated with type 2 diabetes. The promising renoprotective data initially generated in Phase I oncology studies led to Phase II trials (such as the BEAM trial) where bardoxolone methyl displayed remarkable efficacy in increasing eGFR in CKD patients. However, in a subsequent Phase III study (the BEACON trial), concerns were raised after an unexpected increase in cardiovascular events, particularly heart failure, halted the trial. These mixed clinical outcomes have since spurred ongoing efforts to better understand and optimize the safety profile of bardoxolone methyl while leveraging its strong cytoprotective properties (Mathis & Cui, 2016; Sakashita et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2014).

Notably, while bardoxolone methyl has been extensively investigated in oncology and renal diseases, there is currently no record or published clinical trial data indicating that this compound has been used for treating dry age‐related macular degeneration (dry AMD) or similar ocular conditions. Nonetheless, its underlying mechanism—primarily Nrf2 activation—is highly relevant to the pathobiology of dry AMD, given that oxidative stress and proteostasis imbalance are central to RPE cell dysfunction. Thus, while previous therapeutic applications have focused on systemic diseases, the repositioning of bardoxolone methyl to an ocular indication represents a scientifically plausible and innovative strategy that builds on its earlier demonstrated biochemical activities in other organ systems (Borella et al., 2019; Sakashita et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action:  
Bardoxolone methyl’s primary mode of action is its potent and selective activation of the Keap1/Nrf2/ARE (antioxidant response element) pathway. Under basal conditions, Nrf2 is sequestered in the cytoplasm by its inhibitory binding partner Keap1, which targets Nrf2 for ubiquitination and subsequent proteasomal degradation. Bardoxolone methyl, owing to its electrophilic cyanoenone structure, covalently modifies reactive cysteine residues on Keap1 (including key sensors such as Cys151), thereby inhibiting its E3 ligase activity. This modification prevents the degradation of Nrf2, allowing it to accumulate and translocate into the nucleus (Hong et al., 2012; Mathis & Cui, 2016).

Once in the nucleus, Nrf2 dimerizes with small Maf proteins and binds to ARE sequences in the promoter regions of various cytoprotective genes. This leads to the transcriptional induction of a battery of antioxidant and phase II detoxification enzymes, including heme oxygenase-1 (HO-1), NAD(P)H quinone oxidoreductase 1 (NQO1), glutathione S-transferases, and several molecular chaperones involved in protein folding and proteostasis. Through these gene products, bardoxolone methyl exerts robust antioxidant, anti‐inflammatory, and cytoprotective effects that help mitigate oxidative stress and repair cellular damage (Mathis & Cui, 2020; Tanase et al., 2022).

In addition to Nrf2‐mediated gene induction, bardoxolone methyl has been shown to modulate other signaling pathways that contribute to its anti‐inflammatory profile. For instance, it can inhibit NF-κB signaling, which reduces the transcription of pro‐inflammatory cytokines, and also affect pathways involving JAK/STAT and PI3K/Akt/mTOR, all of which have been implicated in the control of cell proliferation, differentiation, and survival (Sporn et al., 2011). The dual capacity to both upregulate protective gene networks and downregulate inflammatory signaling is central to the pharmacological action of bardoxolone methyl and underscores its potential to modulate cellular processes that are dysregulated in conditions characterized by oxidative and proteostatic stress (Cores et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2014).

Furthermore, crystallographic and proteomic studies have provided molecular‐level evidence for the reversible Michael‐addition interaction between bardoxolone methyl and target cysteine residues on Keap1. This “dock and lock” mechanism ensures that the electrophilic reactivity of the compound is directed preferentially toward specific regulatory cysteines, thereby limiting non‐specific alkylation and supporting its relatively high potency as an Nrf2 activator (Borella et al., 2019; Zhou et al., 2014).

Expected Effect in Dry AMD:  
The hypothesis for repurposing bardoxolone methyl in dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) is grounded firmly in its ability to activate Nrf2 and thereby bolster the endogenous antioxidant defenses of the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). In the RPE, oxidative damage is a pivotal pathomechanism that contributes to the accumulation of lipofuscin, impairment of autophagic flux, and ultimately, decreased phagocytic clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS). As Nrf2 plays a critical role in maintaining redox homeostasis within the RPE, its activation is expected to alleviate oxidative and proteostatic stress, thereby protecting critical functions such as phagocytosis and lysosomal degradation.

At an effective concentration in the submicromolar range (with an EC₅₀ estimated around 0.1 µM), bardoxolone methyl is anticipated to induce the transcription of genes such as HO-1 and NQO1 as well as chaperone proteins that ensure proper protein folding and degradation. The upregulation of these cytoprotective proteins may protect phagocytic receptors from oxidative modifications and preserve lysosomal enzymatic activity, which is essential for the degradation of ingested POS. This action is particularly crucial because impaired phagocytic function contributes to the accumulation of toxic lipofuscin and other debris in RPE cells—a hallmark of dry AMD pathogenesis (Borella et al., 2019; Sakashita et al., 2021).

Moreover, the robust activation of Nrf2 by bardoxolone methyl can help counterbalance the deficit in endogenous antioxidant capacity observed in the RPE of patients with dry AMD, as Nrf2 deficiency has been shown experimentally to exacerbate lipofuscin accumulation and autophagy blockade. Preclinical studies in non‐ocular systems have consistently demonstrated that treatment with CDDO‐Me leads to a marked increase in the expression of antioxidant genes and proteins that are implicated in both oxidative stress management and the maintenance of proteostasis (Hong et al., 2012; Sporn et al., 2011). Extrapolating from these findings, it is reasonable to expect that treatment with bardoxolone methyl in dry AMD cultures would result in a more effective clearance of POS by correcting the underlying oxidative imbalance and restoring lysosomal function. It is also plausible that enhanced expression of chaperones and stress‐response proteins would contribute to improved recycling of degraded photoreceptor material, thereby reducing the burden of intracellular debris (Cores et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2014).

In addition, the effects of bardoxolone methyl on other signaling cascades—such as its inhibitory impact on NF-κB—could further reduce inflammatory responses within the RPE. Chronic inflammation is increasingly recognized as a contributing factor to AMD progression, and the suppression of pro‐inflammatory mediators would be expected to create a more favorable cellular environment for tissue repair and maintenance of RPE function (Sporn et al., 2011). Collectively, by activating Nrf2 and modulating inflammatory signaling pathways, bardoxolone methyl is expected to restore the cellular homeostasis of RPE cells, leading to enhanced phagocytosis of POS and potentially slowing or even reversing the degenerative processes characteristic of dry AMD.

Overall Evaluation:  
Bardoxolone methyl represents an innovative and promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age‐related macular degeneration, particularly given its well‐characterized ability to activate the Nrf2 pathway and trigger a potent antioxidant and proteostatic response. One clear strength of this compound is its robust preclinical and clinical profile in other indications; extensive studies in oncology and chronic kidney disease have established its capability to induce protective gene networks, coupled with a well‐defined mechanism of action that is directly applicable to combating oxidative stress—one of the central features of dry AMD pathogenesis (Borella et al., 2019).

From a mechanistic standpoint, bardoxolone methyl’s electrophilic structure enables it to interact in a highly regulated manner with the Keap1 protein. This interaction leads to the stabilization and nuclear translocation of Nrf2, culminating in the transcriptional activation of a spectrum of cytoprotective genes, including HO-1, NQO1, and various chaperones. These genes are known to be expressed in RPE cells and are essential for maintaining the integrity of phagocytic receptors and lysosomal enzymes that mediate POS clearance. Thus, the molecular rationale for its use in dry AMD is strong, as it addresses a fundamental aspect of RPE cell dysfunction (Mathis & Cui, 2016; Hong et al., 2012).

In terms of therapeutic history, while bardoxolone methyl has not previously been applied to ocular indications, its repositioning for dry AMD is scientifically warranted by the extensive evidence linking Nrf2 deficiency to the progression of RPE degeneration and lipofuscin accumulation. The previously observed benefits in non‐ocular systems, such as improvements in renal function via Nrf2 activation, support the idea that similar cytoprotective processes could be beneficial in the eye, particularly if local delivery or ocular formulation approaches can be developed to maximize efficacy while minimizing systemic exposure (Sakashita et al., 2021; Tanase et al., 2022).

Nevertheless, there are several challenges and weaknesses that must be carefully considered. First, the systemic use of bardoxolone methyl has been marred by significant cardiovascular safety concerns, as evidenced by the terminated BEACON trial in CKD patients. Although these adverse events were observed in a systemic context and might be mitigated by localized (for example, intravitreal) administration in the eye, they nonetheless raise caution regarding the compound’s off‐target effects and overall safety profile. The intrinsic electrophilicity that underlies its mechanism also bears the potential risk of non‐specific protein modification and cytotoxicity if not carefully controlled, particularly in a delicate tissue such as the retina (Mathis & Cui, 2016; Zhou et al., 2014).

Second, while preclinical ocular safety data are being cited as supportive evidence for repositioning, robust and comprehensive studies specific to retinal tissues and RPE cell models must be undertaken to confirm that the drug does not induce unintended damage or disrupt other vital functions of the retina. Pharmacokinetic challenges—such as achieving and maintaining an effective therapeutic concentration in the RPE without eliciting systemic exposure—will also need to be addressed. The EC₅₀ for Nrf2 activation in RPE is hypothesized to be approximately 0.1 µM, and this level must be reliably achieved in an ocular setting, ideally through controlled‐release formulations or targeted delivery systems (Cores et al., 2020).

An additional consideration is the complexity of dry AMD itself, which is influenced not only by oxidative stress and impaired autophagy but also by chronic low‐grade inflammation, complement dysregulation, and extracellular matrix alterations in Bruch’s membrane. Although bardoxolone methyl’s anti‐inflammatory effects via NF-κB inhibition are a potential asset, it remains to be determined how these multiple pathways will interact within the unique microenvironment of the retina. Tailored preclinical studies that specifically evaluate the compound’s impact on POS clearance, RPE phagocytosis, and lysosomal function in models of dry AMD are essential to validate the underlying hypothesis (Sporn et al., 2011; Zhou et al., 2014).

On the strength side, the repositioning of bardoxolone methyl is supported by its extensive clinical investigation in other indications. The existence of Phase I and II human data provides a valuable foundation regarding dosing, pharmacokinetics, and some aspects of safety, which can significantly de‐risk early translational studies in the ocular domain. The compound’s well‐documented capacity to activate Nrf2—a pathway known to be highly relevant in the aging RPE and in the pathogenesis of dry AMD—further underscores its potential utility. Moreover, the synthetic nature of bardoxolone methyl facilitates the possibility of further chemical optimization and the development of novel formulations (such as nanoparticle‐ or liposome‐based ocular delivery systems) that may enhance its safety and efficacy profile when administered locally (Borella et al., 2019; Borella et al., 2019; Sporn et al., 2011).

In summary, bardoxolone methyl appears to be a promising candidate for repurposing in dry age‐related macular degeneration based on its potent Nrf2‐activating properties and its capacity to upregulate antioxidant and proteostasis genes. These effects could theoretically restore and enhance the phagocytic function of RPE cells, thereby improving the clearance of photoreceptor outer segments and reducing lipofuscin accumulation—a central pathogenic feature of dry AMD. However, significant challenges remain, including addressing the compound’s systemic safety concerns, ensuring specific ocular delivery, and confirming efficacy and safety in relevant RPE and retinal models. Rigorous preclinical studies focusing on ocular pharmacodynamics, toxicity, and long‐term effects in models of dry AMD are warranted before advancing to clinical trials for this indication. While the repurposing hypothesis is scientifically sound and mechanistically compelling, the unique challenges of ocular drug development must be navigated cautiously (Mathis & Cui, 2016; Tanase et al., 2022; Zhou et al., 2014; Thomas, 2012; Dao et al., 2015).

Overall Evaluation:  
Bardoxolone methyl’s robust mechanistic action as an Nrf2 activator—coupled with its documented preclinical and early clinical efficacy in other indications—positions it as a highly attractive repurposed drug candidate for dry AMD. Its molecular design, derived from oleanolic acid and enhanced through strategic electrophilic modifications, underpins a powerful ability to upregulate antioxidant defenses and restore proteostasis. These actions directly address the cellular deficits observed in dry AMD, namely the accumulation of oxidative damage, impaired autophagy, and subsequent dysfunction of the RPE.  

Strengths of the candidate include:  
• A well‐characterized synthetic origin with clearly defined structure–activity relationships, ensuring potent Nrf2 activation at low concentrations (Borella et al., 2019).  
• Substantial preclinical data indicating its ability to induce cytoprotective gene networks such as HO-1, NQO1, and molecular chaperones that are crucial for maintaining RPE function (Mathis & Cui, 2016; Hong et al., 2012).  
• An extensive history in clinical testing in systemic diseases (oncology and CKD), which provides valuable information regarding dosing and pharmacokinetics that could inform ocular application (Zhou et al., 2014; Sakashita et al., 2021).  
• The underlying hypothesis is supported by evidence that Nrf2 deficiency exacerbates RPE dysfunction and lipofuscin accumulation, suggesting that restoring Nrf2 activity could ameliorate key pathological features of dry AMD.

Weaknesses and challenges include:  
• The previous systemic administration of bardoxolone methyl was associated with significant cardiovascular adverse events, and while local delivery to the eye may mitigate this risk, careful ocular safety studies are essential (Tanase et al., 2022; Mathis & Cui, 2016).  
• There is a paucity of data on the compound’s effects in retinal tissues specifically; it has not been previously tested in dry AMD or similar ocular models, necessitating robust preclinical validation in RPE cells and animal models (Borella et al., 2019; Sakashita et al., 2021).  
• The inherent electrophilic reactivity of bardoxolone methyl, while central to its mechanism, poses a risk of off‐target protein modification and possible cytotoxicity, particularly in the sensitive environment of the retina (Zhou et al., 2014; Cores et al., 2020).  
• Achieving the optimal therapeutic window in the eye may require innovative formulation strategies to ensure sustained, localized exposure at the low nanomolar range that is effective for Nrf2 activation without provoking adverse effects.  
• Given the multifactorial nature of dry AMD pathogenesis—encompassing oxidative stress, inflammation, and extracellular matrix alterations—it is critical to consider that Nrf2 activation alone may not fully address all aspects of the disease, implying that combination therapies or adjunctive treatments might ultimately be necessary (Sporn et al., 2011).

In conclusion, the repurposing of bardoxolone methyl for dry AMD is a scientifically sound and potentially transformative strategy, especially if its potent Nrf2 activation can be harnessed safely within the ocular milieu. Its capacity to induce elegant cytoprotective responses aligns well with the need to mitigate oxidative damage and restore autophagy in stressed RPE cells. Nonetheless, before committing significant resources to clinical trials in this indication, it is imperative to undertake thorough preclinical studies focused on ocular pharmacokinetics, toxicity, and efficacy in relevant models of dry AMD. These investigations will not only validate the underlying hypothesis but also inform the development of appropriate delivery systems to maximize local efficacy and minimize systemic risk. With these considerations addressed, bardoxolone methyl holds considerable promise as a repurposed therapeutic candidate that could significantly improve outcomes for patients suffering from dry age‐related macular degeneration (Mathis & Cui, 2016; Tanase et al., 2022; Zhou et al., 2014; Dao et al., 2015; Cuadrado et al., 2019).

hypothesis: Ibrutinib (BTK inhibitor; SelleckChem Cat. No. S2680)
answer:
Proposal for Ibrutinib (BTK inhibitor; SelleckChem Cat. No. S2680)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Ibrutinib is a fully synthetic small‐molecule inhibitor originally developed as an irreversible inhibitor of Bruton's tyrosine kinase (BTK). It achieves inhibition by covalently binding to the conserved Cys481 residue located within the ATP‐binding pocket of BTK, a key member of the TEC family of kinases. This irreversible binding results in permanent inactivation of BTK, thereby interrupting B‐cell receptor signaling as well as other downstream pathways that are critical for cell survival and proliferation (Xie et al., 2021). As a member of the broader class of tyrosine kinase inhibitors, ibrutinib is designed through refined organic synthesis strategies that optimize its selectivity and potency. Compounds of this chemical class have been extensively utilized in oncology, particularly for the treatment of B‐cell malignancies, where they serve to disrupt aberrant oncogenic signaling pathways. Ibrutinib is available commercially (e.g., SelleckChem Cat. No. S2680) and has been subject to rigorous clinical evaluation, ensuring that its chemical properties, including its irreversible binding mechanism and cell penetration capabilities, are well established in the literature (Xie et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, ibrutinib was developed and advanced clinically for hematologic cancers such as chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), mantle cell lymphoma (MCL), Waldenström’s macroglobulinemia (WM), and other B‐cell malignancies. Its success in these domains is attributed to its effective inhibition of BTK, a kinase that is critical for B‐cell receptor signaling and survival (Xie et al., 2021). Once approved by the U.S. FDA in 2013, it rapidly became a standard of care in oncology. Outside of its oncologic use, ibrutinib has been recognized for its immunomodulatory effects that extend to innate immune cells such as macrophages, dendritic cells, and, notably, microglia. Although the primary application of ibrutinib is in cancer therapy, there is emerging evidence and growing scientific interest suggesting that BTK plays a role in innate immune signaling pathways that contribute to chronic inflammatory states, including those implicated in age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Brandli et al., 2024). In pharmacovigilance studies, ocular adverse events—including uveitis, cataracts, and retinal disorders—have been identified among patients treated with ibrutinib, which indicates that the molecule penetrates ocular compartments and exerts biological effects there (Allouchery et al., 2021). However, despite these observations, ibrutinib has not been previously developed or marketed for the treatment of dry AMD or similar degenerative retinal diseases. Instead, its potential repurposing arises from the hypothesis that by modulating BTK-dependent inflammatory pathways in microglia and retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, ibrutinib might reduce deleterious inflammasome priming and cytokine production that contribute to the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Brandli et al., 2024; Korhonen, 2024).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, ibrutinib exerts its primary action by binding irreversibly to BTK, thereby preventing autophosphorylation and subsequent transmission of intracellular signals that lead to inflammation and cell survival. BTK is not only a critical mediator of B‐cell receptor signaling but is also expressed in cells of the innate immune system including microglia and RPE cells. Its activation is linked to the regulation of the NLRP3 inflammasome—a multiprotein complex that senses cellular stress, leading to the activation of caspase-1 and the maturation and release of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-1β and IL-18 (Brandli et al., 2024). There is accumulating evidence that BTK facilitates the priming of the NLRP3 inflammasome in response to various stimuli, including oxidative stress and the accumulation of deleterious protein aggregates, both of which are implicated in dry AMD pathogenesis. Experimental data suggest that inhibition of BTK by ibrutinib can lead to a reduction in IL-1β release, which in turn may lower downstream pro-inflammatory signals such as tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNFα) (Far et al., 2022; Allouchery et al., 2021). Moreover, the preservation of lysosomal cathepsin activity observed in ARPE-19 cells under inflammasome-stimulating conditions implies that BTK inhibition may also support the maintenance of RPE lysosomal integrity and phagocytic function. Such actions are critical for the clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) and prevention of drusen accumulation—a hallmark of dry AMD (Brandli et al., 2024; Allouchery et al., 2021). In summary, by covalently binding to BTK, ibrutinib not only halts aberrant immune cell signaling but also indirectly modulates inflammasome activity and associated inflammatory cytokine release in retinal cells (Xie et al., 2021; Brandli et al., 2024).

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis for the repurposing of ibrutinib in dry AMD revolves around its ability to inhibit BTK activity within microglia and RPE cells, thereby suppressing inflammasome priming and limiting the production of inflammatory mediators such as IL-1β and TNFα. In the context of an in vitro assay using ARPE-19 cells, it is anticipated that the application of ibrutinib (IC₅₀ ~0.5 nM) will result in a marked attenuation of inflammasome activation, as evidenced by reduced secretion of IL-1β and preserved lysosomal cathepsin activity (Brandli et al., 2024; Allouchery et al., 2021). The proposed mechanism by which ibrutinib exerts its therapeutic benefit in dry AMD is multifaceted. First, by inhibiting BTK, the compound is expected to downregulate the overactive NLRP3 inflammasome that plays a central role in the inflammatory cascade within the retinal pigment epithelium (Brandli et al., 2024; Korhonen, 2024). Second, by reducing the production of pro-inflammatory cytokines—especially TNFα—which have been shown to negatively impact the phagocytic ability of RPE cells, ibrutinib may help to maintain the clearance of photoreceptor outer segment debris. This is particularly important because impaired clearance mechanisms contribute to the accumulation of drusen and subsequent RPE degeneration in dry AMD (Brandli et al., 2024; Korhonen, 2024). Moreover, animal and clinical pharmacovigilance studies have provided evidence that ibrutinib is capable of crossing the blood-brain and blood-retinal barriers, suggesting that it can reach retinal tissues at therapeutically relevant concentrations. Although there is documented evidence of ocular adverse events in patients treated with ibrutinib for hematologic malignancies—including instances of uveitis and cystoid macular edema—such effects have been largely reported as unintended consequences rather than engineered therapeutic outcomes. In the current repurposing framework, the premise is that controlled intravitreal or local administration, possibly as a modified formulation, could harness the anti-inflammatory properties of ibrutinib while minimizing systemic exposure and the risk of ocular adverse events (Allouchery et al., 2021; Far et al., 2022). Ultimately, the expected effect is a preserved RPE function with enhanced ability to clear POS debris, thereby mitigating the degenerative progression typically observed in dry AMD (Korhonen, 2024; Brandli et al., 2024).

Overall Evaluation:  
Ibrutinib presents as a promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration due to its well-characterized molecular mechanism and its established clinical profile in oncology. One of the major strengths of ibrutinib lies in its potent and selective irreversible inhibition of BTK, a kinase implicated not only in B-cell malignancies but also in the pathogenesis of inflammatory retinal diseases through its role in NLRP3 inflammasome priming (Xie et al., 2021). The scientific rationale for its repurposing is supported by preclinical observations indicating that BTK inhibition leads to reduced IL-1β secretion and preservation of lysosomal function in RPE cells, which are essential for maintaining photoreceptor homeostasis and preventing drusen accumulation in dry AMD (Brandli et al., 2024; Allouchery et al., 2021). Furthermore, the demonstration that ibrutinib crosses the blood-retinal barrier underscores its potential utility in directly targeting retinal tissues, especially when administered via routes that ensure localized high concentrations with limited systemic exposure (Xie et al., 2021; Far et al., 2022).

However, there are several challenges and weaknesses associated with this therapeutic candidate. First, the ocular safety profile of ibrutinib is a matter of concern, as pharmacovigilance data have linked ibrutinib to a spectrum of adverse ocular events including cataracts, uveitis, and retinal disorders (Allouchery et al., 2021; Far et al., 2022). While these effects have so far been observed in the context of systemic cancer therapy, they raise important safety questions when considering chronic administration for a disease such as dry AMD that often requires long-term treatment. Second, the dosages and formulation required to achieve an anti-inflammatory effect in the retina, while concurrently minimizing cytotoxicity and other off-target effects, remain uncertain. Ibrutinib’s off-target inhibitory effects, such as its activity against VEGFR2, may impart vascular side effects that could further complicate its use in the delicate retinal environment (Allouchery et al., 2021). Third, the repurposing strategy relies heavily on the extrapolation of cellular and animal model data—such as the observed reduction of inflammasome activation and preservation of cathepsin activity in ARPE-19 cells—to the complex pathophysiology of human dry AMD. The heterogeneity of dry AMD pathogenesis, driven by a confluence of genetic, environmental, and age-related factors, means that successful translation from preclinical models to effective clinical outcomes is not guaranteed (Korhonen, 2024; Brandli et al., 2024). Additionally, while there is a robust theoretical framework underpinning BTK’s involvement in inflamed retinal microenvironments, direct evidence of ibrutinib’s efficacy in modulating microglial or RPE function specifically in the setting of dry AMD remains limited.

Despite these challenges, the mechanistic rationale for using a BTK inhibitor in dry AMD is compelling. The interplay between NLRP3 inflammasome activation, chronic low-grade inflammation, and RPE dysfunction is increasingly recognized as a pivotal driver of dry AMD progression (Brandli et al., 2024). If ibrutinib can effectively attenuate these inflammatory processes without incurring prohibitive adverse events, it may offer a novel therapeutic avenue for a disease area currently lacking effective treatment options. However, this necessitates a series of rigorous preclinical studies to characterize the dose-response relationship, evaluate retinal safety, and define the pharmacokinetic profile of ibrutinib when delivered via ocular routes. Moreover, any proposed clinical trial must incorporate comprehensive ophthalmologic monitoring given the known spectrum of ibrutinib-induced ocular side effects (Allouchery et al., 2021; Far et al., 2022).

In summary, while ibrutinib is primarily an approved oncologic agent, its underlying mechanism of inhibiting BTK—the kinase that modulates inflammasome priming in microglia and RPE cells—provides a strong scientific basis for its repurposing in dry AMD. The expected effects of reduced IL-1β and TNFα production, coupled with preserved lysosomal cathepsin activity and improved phagocytic function, align well with the therapeutic goals of mitigating chronic inflammation and preserving retinal integrity in dry AMD. Nevertheless, the potential ocular adverse effects and the challenges related to achieving a favorable therapeutic index in the retinal environment are significant concerns that must be addressed through further rigorous preclinical and clinical evaluations (Brandli et al., 2024; Allouchery et al., 2021). Overall, ibrutinib represents an intriguing candidate with a solid mechanistic rationale for dry AMD treatment; however, careful attention to formulation, dosing, and safety testing is warranted before advancing this repurposing strategy to later-stage clinical trials (Xie et al., 2021; Brandli et al., 2024; Korhonen, 2024).

Proposal for Ceapin-A7 (ATF6 pathway inhibitor; Sigma-Aldrich Cat. No. SML1922)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Ceapin-A7 is a small molecule inhibitor that belongs to the pyrazole amide class of compounds. It was originally discovered through high‐throughput cell‐based screening assays designed to identify modulators of the unfolded protein response (UPR), with an emphasis on selectively targeting the ATF6α signaling branch (Gallagher & Walter, 2016; Hetz et al., 2019). Structural optimization through structure–activity relationship (SAR) studies led to the development of Ceapin-A7 as a potent derivative with submicromolar inhibitory activity against ATF6α (Hetz et al., 2019). The molecule’s chemical origins are purely synthetic; its pyrazole amide core is complemented by additional substituents that optimize its binding affinity and selectivity. Traditionally, compounds in this chemical class have been explored as research tools to dissect the UPR pathways and have shown promise in modulating ER stress signaling in various cellular contexts (Gallagher & Walter, 2016). The compound’s design exploits the unique structure–function relationships of ATF6α, aiming to interfere with its normal intracellular trafficking rather than block downstream proteolysis directly, which marks a novel approach compared with many enzyme inhibitors developed for other targets.

Therapeutic History:  
To date, Ceapin-A7 has been mainly used as an investigative tool in cellular models to study mechanisms underlying ER stress and the UPR. Its ability to selectively inhibit ATF6α activation has been characterized in multiple cell lines, including human osteosarcoma U2-OS cells and HEK293 cells engineered to express tagged ATF6α constructs (Gallagher & Walter, 2016; Hetz et al., 2019). Although there is extensive preclinical evidence supporting its utility in modulating UPR signaling—all of which has been generated in the context of studies on cancer cells, neurodegeneration, and endothelial dysfunction—there is no historically established clinical or veterinary usage for Ceapin-A7 specifically in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or similar retinal degenerative diseases. However, the mechanistic insights gained from its application in other cell types have spurred investigations into repurposing Ceapin-A7 as a potential therapeutic candidate for correcting maladaptive ER stress responses in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, which plays a pivotal role in diseases such as dry AMD (Gallagher & Walter, 2016; Torres et al., 2019).

Mechanism of Action:  
Ceapin-A7 exerts its pharmacological action by selectively inhibiting the ATF6α branch of the UPR. Under normal ER stress conditions, ATF6α, a 90-kDa transmembrane protein located in the endoplasmic reticulum, undergoes a stress-induced conformational change that facilitates its packaging into COPII vesicles and subsequent trafficking to the Golgi apparatus. Once in the Golgi, ATF6α is cleaved sequentially by site-1 (S1P) and site-2 (S2P) proteases to release its N-terminal transcription factor domain, which then translocates to the nucleus to upregulate several chaperone and ER stress-related genes (Gallagher & Walter, 2016).

Ceapin-A7 intervenes at this critical transport step. Rather than inhibiting the proteolytic machinery directly, Ceapin-A7 selectively prevents the ER-to-Golgi trafficking of ATF6α. Mechanistic studies have demonstrated that upon treatment with Ceapin-A7, ATF6α is sequestered within the ER where it accumulates in discrete foci. Fluorescence microscopy analyses have shown that these foci do not colocalize with ER exit site markers such as SEC16 or SEC31A, indicating that the compound disrupts the selection of ATF6α into COPII vesicles (Gallagher & Walter, 2016).

One particularly novel aspect of Ceapin-A7’s mechanism is its induction of a neomorphic inter-organelle tether. Detailed proteomic and genome-wide CRISPR interference screening studies have revealed that Ceapin-A7 induces a physical interaction between the cytosolic domain of ATF6α and the peroxisomal transporter protein ABCD3 (Torres et al., 2019). This newly formed tether effectively anchors ATF6α within the ER and precludes its normal traffic to the Golgi. In addition, Ceapin-A7 appears to stabilize ATF6α in its oligomeric state, rather than allowing it to convert to the transport-competent monomeric form (Gallagher & Walter, 2016). The fact that these mechanistic events are reversible upon compound washout further indicates that Ceapin-A7 provides a transient yet highly specific method for modulating ATF6α activity without causing permanent alterations to the protein structure or its eventual capacity to function when the inhibitor is removed (Gallagher & Walter, 2016). Such high selectivity distinguishes Ceapin-A7 from broader ER stress inhibitors that often affect multiple UPR signaling branches.

Expected Effect:  
In the context of dry AMD, the hypothesized role of Ceapin-A7 is to inhibit chronic ATF6α overactivation in RPE cells, thereby rebalancing the UPR toward adaptive rather than pro-apoptotic responses. Chronic or overwhelming ER stress in RPE cells, as observed in AMD, is associated with decreased expression of genes critical for maintaining cellular homeostasis, including those linked to autophagy, lysosomal function, and the phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) (Gallagher & Walter, 2016). Because RPE cells are responsible for daily phagocytosis of POS, maintaining efficient lysosomal clearance is crucial for retinal health. In dry AMD, impaired phagocytosis leads to the buildup of toxic byproducts such as lipofuscin, which further exacerbates cellular dysfunction (Kubra et al., 2022; Benedetti et al., 2024).

The therapeutic hypothesis for Ceapin-A7 centers on its capacity to inhibit ATF6α at an IC₅₀ in the low micromolar range (approximately 2 µM, as proposed), thus reducing maladaptive UPR signaling. By preventing ATF6α from trafficking and undergoing proteolytic activation, Ceapin-A7 is expected to alleviate the chronic ER stress that drives RPE dysfunction. In a proposed assay—using ARPE-19 cells in conditions of induced ER stress (for instance, via tunicamycin treatment)—Ceapin-A7 should reduce the levels of cleaved, active ATF6α. This in turn is expected to restore the gene expression patterns associated with lysosomal enzyme production and phagocytic receptor synthesis, thereby enhancing the clearance of POS components (Gallagher & Walter, 2016).

Furthermore, because the ATF6 branch of the UPR is associated with the upregulation of chaperones like BiP/Grp78, persistent activation can lead to resource exhaustion and an imbalance that favors apoptotic signaling under chronic ER stress conditions (Gallagher & Walter, 2016). By selectively inhibiting this pathway, Ceapin-A7 might reduce excessive chaperone induction and allow cellular systems to shift toward a more balanced, adaptive stress response that promotes autophagy and lysosomal function. Importantly, RPE cells express ATF6, as evidenced by studies utilizing ARPE-19 and primary RPE cultures, making these cells appropriate targets for ATF6 modulation (Gallagher & Walter, 2016). Thus, the expected effect is a reestablishment of normal proteostasis in RPE cells via the restoration of adaptive autophagy, improved lysosomal enzyme activity, and enhanced phagocytic receptor expression, all of which are critical for the sustained clearance of photoreceptor outer segment debris and prevention of cytotoxic accumulation in dry AMD (Gallagher & Walter, 2016).

Overall Evaluation:  
Ceapin-A7 represents an innovative therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration due to its unique and selective mechanism of action targeting the ATF6α branch of the UPR. One of the main strengths of this compound is its ability to modulate a very specific aspect of cellular stress signaling. By preventing the ER-to-Golgi trafficking of ATF6α and thereby inhibiting its proteolytic activation, Ceapin-A7 offers a promising strategy for shifting the balance of UPR signaling toward adaptive autophagy instead of chronic, detrimental ER stress (Gallagher & Walter, 2016). This is particularly relevant in the context of RPE cells, which require efficient protein quality control and robust lysosomal function to maintain photoreceptor outer segment (POS) clearance and overall retinal integrity.

In vitro studies have validated the mechanism of Ceapin-A7, with data showing that the compound induces the formation of discrete ATF6α-positive foci in the ER (Gallagher & Walter, 2016). Moreover, the reversible nature of its action implies that Ceapin-A7 may offer a controllable therapeutic window, enabling fine-tuning of UPR modulation in a clinical setting (Gallagher & Walter, 2016). The involvement of peroxisomal protein ABCD3 in a neomorphic tethering mechanism further differentiates Ceapin-A7 from other UPR modulators by introducing a novel means of sequestering ATF6α (Torres et al., 2019). Such specificity is particularly compelling because it suggests that Ceapin-A7 can mitigate the chronic ER stress observed in dry AMD without interfering with other UPR branches (such as IRE1 or PERK), which are essential for normal cellular adaptation to transient stress.

However, there are notable limitations and challenges that warrant careful evaluation. First, despite the extensive preclinical work in cell lines and non-retinal systems, Ceapin-A7 has yet to be thoroughly evaluated in RPE-specific models or in vivo systems relevant to AMD (Gallagher & Walter, 2016). Second, the full spectrum of off-target effects is not yet fully characterized. While Ceapin-A7 shows selectivity for ATF6α, the influence of its induced neomorphic tether between ATF6α and ABCD3 on peroxisome function remains to be fully elucidated. Although available evidence suggests that Ceapin-A7 does not interfere significantly with ABCD3’s normal transporter function (Torres et al., 2019), the robustness of these findings in the retinal context remains an open question.

Another potential caveat is the dual role that ATF6α may play in various tissues. Although chronic activation of ATF6α is thought to contribute to maladaptive ER stress and consequent cellular dysfunction in AMD, ATF6α also participates in adaptive responses by upregulating crucial ER chaperones that preserve proteostasis (Gallagher & Walter, 2016). Therefore, complete inhibition of ATF6α activity might have unintended consequences if not properly dosed or if the timing of inhibition is not carefully managed. An optimal therapeutic strategy might require a fine balance between sufficient ATF6α inhibition to restore lysosomal and phagocytic function in RPE cells and preserving enough ATF6α activity to maintain overall cellular homeostasis, particularly in tissues under variable stress dynamics.

Moreover, the pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic profiles of Ceapin-A7 in the ocular environment have not been established. For a drug candidate to be viable in treating dry AMD, it must be effectively delivered to the RPE with minimal systemic exposure, maintain a stable concentration over time, and be cleared without inducing local toxicity. The formulation challenges of ocular drug delivery, including crossing the blood-retinal barrier and achieving sustained release in the subretinal space, remain critical hurdles that must be addressed in future studies (Hetz et al., 2019; Gallagher & Walter, 2016).

Finally, long-term safety studies are essential. The reversible nature of Ceapin-A7’s effects is promising; however, chronic treatment in a degenerative condition like dry AMD necessitates an in-depth understanding of the potential cumulative effects or chronic alterations in ER stress responses over time. Safety profiles in animal models, particularly those that recapitulate the chronic oxidative stress and proteostasis defects seen in AMD, will be crucial for advancing Ceapin-A7 into clinical trials.

In summary, Ceapin-A7 holds significant promise as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration. Its precise mechanism—selectively inhibiting ATF6α activation by preventing its ER-to-Golgi trafficking and inducing a novel tether with ABCD3—positions it as a unique tool for rebalancing maladaptive UPR signaling (Gallagher & Walter, 2016; Torres et al., 2019). The expected therapeutic benefit in RPE cells is the restoration of adaptive autophagy, maintenance of lysosomal function, and enhanced phagocytic clearance of photoreceptor outer segments, all of which are critical to slowing or halting the progression of dry AMD (Gallagher & Walter, 2016).

Nevertheless, the lack of extensive in vivo data in retinal models and the potential for off-target effects or unintended suppression of adaptive ER stress responses are significant concerns that must be addressed before clinical translation (Gallagher & Walter, 2016). Rigorous investigation in RPE-specific systems, careful dose–response studies, pharmacokinetic profiling, and long-term safety evaluations are essential next steps. Overall, Ceapin-A7 is a mechanistically innovative candidate that merits further preclinical development as a novel intervention for dry AMD, provided that its complex interplay with ER stress, autophagy, and lysosomal function is thoroughly characterized in ocular tissues (Gallagher & Walter, 2016).

Below is a detailed evaluation report of the repurposing potential of GSK0660 for the treatment of dry age‐related macular degeneration (dry AMD). The report is organized into five main sections: (I) Overview of the Therapeutic Candidate, (II) Therapeutic History, (III) Mechanism of Action, (IV) Expected Effect in RPE Models, and (V) Overall Evaluation. Each section draws on the available literature and data from the provided context.

────────────────────────────────────────  
I. OVERVIEW OF THE THERAPEUTIC CANDIDATE  

GSK0660 is a synthetic small‐molecule inhibitor that gained prominence as the very first PPARβ/δ (peroxisome proliferator‐activated receptor beta/delta)–selective inhibitory ligand reported in the scientific literature (Toth et al., 2012). Its design represents a significant breakthrough in the field of nuclear receptor modulation by demonstrating that subtype selectivity within the PPAR family can indeed be achieved with a low molecular weight organic compound. Structurally, GSK0660 belongs to the thiophenecarboxylate chemical class and features a uniquely tailored molecular architecture that includes several key pharmacophores: a methoxy‐substituted 1,4‐diaminobenzene core thought to be essential for receptor binding; a 4′‐aminophenyl substituent that not only contributes to high‐affinity interactions with the receptor’s ligand‐binding domain but also offers a promising site for subsequent chemical modification; and a methyl thiophene carboxylate moiety that helps orient the molecule within the hydrophobic pocket of PPARβ/δ (Toth et al., 2012). Extensive structure–activity relationship (SAR) studies have demonstrated that modifications to portions of the molecule—particularly the 4′‐aminophenyl substituent by introduction of medium‐length n‐alkyl chains—can enhance binding affinity by up to tenfold compared to the original structure (Toth et al., 2012).

GSK0660 was originally synthesized through a multistep organic process that began with commercially available precursors, followed by key transformation steps such as nucleophilic aromatic substitution to install appropriate groups on a benzene ring, catalytic reduction to generate the requisite amine functions, and finally sulfonamidation reactions to yield the final compound (Toth et al., 2012). In essence, this compound was developed primarily as a research tool to dissect the specific biological roles of PPARβ/δ and does not itself originate from a natural product or traditional antibiotic source. Instead, its design and synthesis reflect a targeted medicinal chemistry strategy aimed at obtaining a high degree of receptor selectivity.

Belonging to the broader class of PPAR modulators, GSK0660 occupies a niche that is distinct from the more commonly encountered PPAR agonists. Whereas most efforts historically have focused on the development of agonists for metabolic disorders and anti‐inflammatory indications, GSK0660 and its close analogs are used primarily to achieve receptor inhibition. This selective antagonism is critical for experimental setups in which the contribution of PPARβ/δ to downstream gene regulation and cellular homeostasis is being evaluated (Toth et al., 2012). Furthermore, the structure of GSK0660 aligns with the more general trends in nuclear receptor ligand development, capturing several “drug‐like” properties that, despite known limitations in bioavailability, maintain its status as a high‐quality research compound in proof‐of‐concept investigations.

────────────────────────────────────────  
II. THERAPEUTIC HISTORY  

GSK0660 has been widely used as a chemical probe to examine the biological functions of PPARβ/δ in various preclinical models. In early studies, it served as the first selective antagonist for this receptor subtype and was instrumental in clarifying the roles of PPARβ/δ in lipid metabolism, cell proliferation, and inflammation (Toth et al., 2012). Its experimental applications have spanned a number of research areas. For instance, several investigations in models of neurodegeneration—particularly in Parkinson’s disease—have utilized GSK0660 in both in vitro experiments (using human neuroblastoma cell lines such as SH‐SY5Y) and in vivo rodent models. In these studies, GSK0660 was able to negate the neuroprotective effects of PPARβ/δ agonists by blocking the receptor’s activity, thereby providing compelling evidence for a detrimental role of PPARβ/δ activation under neurodegenerative stress conditions (Antonosante et al., 2023; Boya et al., 2023). Such data have contributed to a nuanced understanding of PPAR signaling in the brain, implying that under certain conditions receptor inhibition may be more desirable than activation.

Moreover, GSK0660 has also been evaluated in dermatological applications. In recent studies focusing on psoriasis‐like skin disease, GSK0660—when formulated topically—was shown to mitigate epidermal hyperplasia and reduce inflammatory markers without systemic drug accumulation, thus proving useful for localized treatment strategies (Hack et al., 2012). These dermatological studies not only underscored the compound’s ability to counteract PPARβ/δ‐mediated signaling in inflamed tissues but also highlighted practical challenges associated with its formulation. For example, its inherent chemical instability, manifesting as a tendency to undergo oxidation (where solutions of GSK0660 may turn green upon light exposure at room temperature), underscores issues related to its shelf‐life and stability in clinical formulations (Hack et al., 2012; Lieber, 2015).

Despite its usefulness in these diverse experimental models—ranging from neurodegenerative to inflammatory skin diseases—the therapeutic history of GSK0660 reveals a critical gap: there is no record within the available literature of its application in ocular diseases or in the treatment of dry AMD. A systematic search of clinical trial databases has confirmed that no human clinical investigations have been registered evaluating GSK0660 for indications such as retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) dysfunction, macular degeneration, or related ocular conditions (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). In other words, while the compound has been validated as a tool in non‐ocular systems, its repurposing for dry AMD is entirely uncharted territory. This lack of ocular‐specific data is a limitation that must be considered when assessing its potential for enhancing lysosomal function in RPE cells.

Furthermore, limitations inherent to GSK0660—most notably its poor systemic bioavailability and the requirement for relatively high concentrations to achieve effective antagonism—are recurring themes in its therapeutic history (Toth et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2016; Lieber, 2015). Such pharmacokinetic drawbacks have spurred efforts to develop improved derivatives that possess enhanced potency and bioavailability. For instance, SAR studies have evaluated modifications to the 4′‐aminophenyl substituent, yielding analogs with substantially higher binding affinities (Toth et al., 2012). Nonetheless, all available records indicate that GSK0660 itself has remained primarily as a research tool rather than advancing to clinical or even advanced developmental stages in any therapeutic domain beyond the proof‐of‐concept experimental setting.

────────────────────────────────────────  
III. MECHANISM OF ACTION  

At the molecular level, GSK0660 exerts its action by binding selectively to the ligand‐binding domain (LBD) of PPARβ/δ, thereby inhibiting receptor activation. This interaction is competitive in nature; GSK0660 occupies the receptor pocket, effectively blocking binding of endogenous ligands or synthetic agonists (Toth et al., 2012). The molecular determinants of this selective interaction have been elucidated through SAR studies. The methoxy‐substituted 1,4‐diaminobenzene core forms critical hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic contacts with specific residues within the LBD, while the 4′‐aminophenyl group and the methyl thiophene carboxylate moiety contribute additional electrostatic and van der Waals interactions that stabilize the binding complex (Toth et al., 2012).

A notable aspect of GSK0660’s pharmacology is its dual mode of action. In addition to functioning as a competitive antagonist, GSK0660 has been reported in some experimental contexts to act as an inverse agonist. Under basal conditions—where PPARβ/δ exhibits a low level of constitutive transcriptional activity—GSK0660 can further suppress receptor activity beyond mere inhibition by promoting the recruitment of transcriptional corepressors. These corepressors (including members of the NCoR/SMRT family and class I histone deacetylases) bind to the receptor‐corepressor complex, modifying chromatin structure and decreasing transcription of PPARβ/δ target genes (Lieber, 2015; Monsalve et al., 2013). Through these mechanisms, GSK0660 effectively shifts the balance away from gene activation toward transcriptional repression.

The detailed molecular interactions responsible for these phenomena have been characterized using a variety of biochemical assays, including competitive TR‐FRET binding studies and reporter assays in cell‐based systems (Toth et al., 2012). The ability of GSK0660 to inhibit transcriptional activation in response to exogenous agonists has been well demonstrated in several cell models—including skeletal muscle myoblasts where PPARβ/δ activates genes such as carnitine palmitoyltransferase‐1A or pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase‐4 (Monsalve et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2016). This cellular pharmacology underpins its potential to serve as an experimental “off‐switch” for PPARβ/δ‐mediated transcription.

In the context of the proposed repurposing hypothesis for dry AMD, the mechanistic emphasis shifts toward the regulation of lysosomal biogenesis through transcription factor EB (TFEB). Although direct evidence linking PPARβ/δ antagonism with the modulation of TFEB activity in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells is not yet established, the working hypothesis posits that PPARβ/δ normally exerts a repressive influence on a suite of genes involved in lysosomal function—the coordinated lysosomal expression and regulation (CLEAR) network. TFEB is recognized as the master regulator of lysosomal and autophagic gene expression and, upon activation, translocates to the nucleus to drive expression of critical lysosomal proteins such as LAMP1 and proteases such as Cathepsin D (Abokyi & Tse, 2025). By antagonizing PPARβ/δ, GSK0660 is hypothesized to relieve this repressive effect, thereby “releasing the brake” on TFEB activity. This would allow for enhanced transcription of lysosomal genes that are vital for the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) and the clearance of toxic lipofuscin constituents like A2E.

It is important to note that while the biochemical rationale is compelling, the specific molecular details linking PPARβ/δ inhibition to enhanced TFEB function have yet to be firmly established in ocular models. Nonetheless, the ability of GSK0660 to modulate receptor conformation and corepressor recruitment provides a credible mechanistic basis for the hypothesis, even as further studies must elucidate the crosstalk between PPARβ/δ signaling and the lysosomal gene network in RPE cells (Toth et al., 2012; Abokyi & Tse, 2025; Lieber, 2015).

────────────────────────────────────────  
IV. EXPECTED EFFECT IN RPE MODELS  

Dry AMD is characterized by gradual dysfunction and atrophy of the RPE, which plays an essential role in the daily phagocytosis and degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS). A central pathogenic mechanism in dry AMD is the accumulation of undigested POS material and the toxic byproduct A2E, which, in turn, leads to lipofuscin deposition, oxidative stress, and eventual RPE cell death. Critical to the maintenance of RPE homeostasis is the proper function of the lysosomal machinery responsible for cellular clearance. Lysosomal biogenesis, autophagic flux, and the efficient degradation of internalized debris are centrally regulated by transcription factor EB (TFEB), which activates the CLEAR network of genes encoding proteins such as LAMP1 (a lysosomal‐associated membrane protein) and Cathepsin D (a key lysosomal protease) (Abokyi & Tse, 2025).

Under normal conditions, PPARβ/δ appears to play a role in regulating gene expression through the recruitment of coactivators and corepressors. The hypothesis driving the repurposing of GSK0660 for dry AMD is that activated PPARβ/δ imposes a repressive signal on the CLEAR network genes, thereby limiting TFEB‐mediated lysosomal biogenesis in RPE cells. In an experimental paradigm based on A2E‐loaded RPE cell cultures—a standard in vitro model that mimics the cellular environment of dry AMD—it is anticipated that treatment with GSK0660 at concentrations approximating its receptor inhibition IC₅₀ (~200 nM) will alleviate PPARβ/δ‐mediated repression. This derepression is expected to promote the nuclear translocation of TFEB and upregulate its target genes, culminating in an enhanced lysosomal degradative capacity (Abokyi & Tse, 2025).

The expected cellular responses following GSK0660 treatment in RPE models can be summarized as follows. First, by interrupting the ligand‐induced activation of PPARβ/δ, GSK0660 should shift the balance between transcriptional coactivators and corepressors in favor of a transcriptional environment that supports lysosomal gene expression. This would lead to a measurable increase in the mRNA and protein levels of LAMP1 and Cathepsin D, both of which are critical for lysosomal function and for the degradation of POS components (Abokyi & Tse, 2025). Second, the enhanced expression of these proteins should translate into an improved capacity for POS degradation—a phenotype that can be monitored using assays that track the clearance of fluorescently labeled POS or the reduction in A2E accumulation. Third, improved lysosomal biogenesis and autophagic clearance are expected to reduce the chronic accumulation of lipofuscin, thereby mitigating oxidative stress and preserving RPE function over time.

In addition to these molecular and cellular endpoints, there is also the expectation that successful derepression of TFEB activity will indirectly contribute to improved cell viability and resistance to stress. The RPE, being highly active in terms of metabolic turnover and phagocytic activity, is particularly vulnerable to the detrimental effects of lysosomal dysfunction. Thus, a treatment that effectively restores lysosomal function is likely to bolster the RPE’s ability to manage accumulated debris and maintain metabolic homeostasis.

It should be acknowledged that one of the primary challenges will be the optimization of the effective dose of GSK0660 in the context of ocular cells. While the compound exhibits potent receptor inhibition in vitro, previous studies have identified limitations with its bioavailability and chemical stability (Toth et al., 2012; Strosznajder et al., 2021). These issues necessitate careful attention to formulation and drug delivery strategies tailored to the ocular environment. For example, controlled‐release formulations or nanoparticle‐based delivery systems might be required to ensure that effective local concentrations of GSK0660 can be maintained in the retina while avoiding systemic exposure and off‐target effects.

Moreover, despite the attractive theoretical framework linking PPARβ/δ antagonism to TFEB activation, direct experimental evidence in RPE cells is currently lacking. As such, the expected effect remains a hypothesis that must be rigorously validated through a series of in vitro assays—including quantitative PCR for lysosomal gene expression, immunoblotting for protein markers, and functional assays to assess the clearance of photoreceptor debris. Additional studies might also involve monitoring autophagic flux using established markers such as LC3-II and p62 to provide a more comprehensive picture of the compound’s impact on RPE cell homeostasis.

────────────────────────────────────────  
V. OVERALL EVALUATION  

GSK0660 stands out as a highly characterized PPARβ/δ antagonist with a well‐documented profile in non‐ocular applications. The compound’s discovery as the first selective ligand for PPARβ/δ established a benchmark in the field and has since made it a prominent research tool in studies of neurodegeneration, inflammation, and even dermatological applications such as psoriasis (Toth et al., 2012; Antonosante et al., 2023; Hack et al., 2012). From a medicinal chemistry perspective, the structural features of GSK0660—the methoxy‐substituted 1,4‐diaminobenzene core, the 4′‐aminophenyl substituent, and the methyl thiophene carboxylate moiety—endow the molecule with high selectivity for the receptor. SAR studies have demonstrated that modifications to these groups can further enhance binding affinity, offering prospects for optimization if needed (Toth et al., 2012).

The principal strength of the compound lies in its receptor selectivity and in its demonstrated capacity to function as both a competitive antagonist and an inverse agonist. This duality is central to the proposed mechanism for reversing PPARβ/δ‐mediated repression of TFEB, which in turn may enhance lysosomal biogenesis and improve the degradative capacity of RPE cells. Considering that lysosomal dysfunction and the resultant accumulation of undegraded POS and toxic byproducts such as A2E are recognized pathological features of dry AMD, the hypothesis that GSK0660 can restore a more robust lysosomal function is innovative and scientifically compelling (Abokyi & Tse, 2025).

However, significant caveats temper this optimism. One major limitation is that, to date, GSK0660 has not been studied in the context of retinal diseases or any ocular applications. Although extensive preclinical research has been undertaken in models of Parkinson’s disease and psoriasis, no direct evidence supports its efficacy in modulating RPE cell lysosomal function or in mitigating dry AMD pathology (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Lieber, 2015). This represents a considerable translational gap that would require substantial preclinical work to bridge.

Another critical challenge is the compound’s pharmacokinetic profile. GSK0660 is known to suffer from poor bioavailability, and it frequently requires relatively high concentrations to achieve its intended effects in vitro. Furthermore, the chemical instability of GSK0660—demonstrated by its tendency to oxidize and change color under conditions of light exposure and room temperature storage—poses additional obstacles for formulation development, especially in a sensitive environment such as the eye where prolonged stability and controlled drug release are paramount (Toth et al., 2012; Hack et al., 2012; Strosznajder et al., 2021).

The translation of these findings to an application in dry AMD would also necessitate a careful reexamination of dosing strategies and delivery mechanisms. For instance, while topical formulations have been effective in dermatological models (Hack et al., 2012), the ocular setting will require alternative approaches to bypass obstacles such as the blood‐retinal barrier and to achieve sustained local drug concentrations without systemic spillover. Innovative drug delivery platforms—perhaps involving biodegradable implants, nanoparticles, or hydrogels—will likely need to be developed to turn the promising molecular mechanism of GSK0660 into a clinically viable treatment option.

Furthermore, although the mechanistic rationale linking PPARβ/δ antagonism with the activation of TFEB is theoretically sound, the direct evidence supporting this specific link in RPE cells is limited. Existing literature on TFEB clearly demonstrates its role as a master regulator of lysosomal genes in retinal cells (Abokyi & Tse, 2025), yet none of the studies directly establish that PPARβ/δ provides a repressive signal to TFEB in this context. Thus, the entire repurposing hypothesis, while attractive, remains speculative until dedicated studies in RPE models confirm that inhibition of PPARβ/δ by GSK0660 indeed results in derepression of TFEB and a subsequent upregulation of lysosomal markers such as LAMP1 and Cathepsin D.

Lastly, while GSK0660 has garnered a robust reputation as a research tool, its historical use in non‐ocular tissues suggests that extensive medicinal chemistry optimization may be required to enhance its physicochemical properties for ocular therapy. In essence, the compound may serve as an excellent lead structure, but modifications that improve its bioavailability, chemical stability, and potency in the ocular microenvironment will be essential steps before considering any clinical translation.

In summary, GSK0660 embodies both promise and challenges as a candidate for repurposing to treat dry AMD. On the one hand, its well‐defined receptor selectivity and dual mode of inhibition provide a solid mechanistic foundation to hypothesize that, by antagonizing PPARβ/δ, it may relieve repression of TFEB and thereby restore lysosomal function in RPE cells. On the other hand, the lack of any direct ocular data, coupled with severe limitations in bioavailability and chemical stability, underscores that significant preclinical validation and formulation optimization will be required before GSK0660 can be considered a viable therapeutic candidate for dry AMD (Toth et al., 2012; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Zhang et al., 2016; Hack et al., 2012).

────────────────────────────────────────  
VI. CONCLUDING REMARKS  

Repurposing GSK0660 for dry AMD is underpinned by an innovative hypothesis that bridges nuclear receptor biology with lysosomal regulation—a convergence that is highly relevant given the central role of lysosomal dysfunction in RPE degeneration. The expected therapeutic mechanism is clear: by blocking PPARβ/δ activity, GSK0660 may relieve a repressive influence on the CLEAR network, thereby enabling TFEB to drive lysosomal biogenesis and enhance the clearance of toxic photoreceptor debris. Such a therapeutic approach would address a key pathogenic process behind the progressive accumulation of lipofuscin and other deleterious cellular materials in the RPE, which are hallmarks of dry AMD (Abokyi & Tse, 2025).

Nonetheless, several hurdles must be overcome for this conceptual strategy to move forward. First, the absence of any preexisting data linking GSK0660 to ocular applications necessitates a comprehensive set of in vitro experiments targeting RPE cells—including assays for gene expression, lysosomal function, and POS degradation. Second, the known limitations of GSK0660—poor bioavailability, chemical instability, and the requirement for high concentrations—must be addressed via improved drug formulations or through the development of optimized analogs. Third, it will be critical to investigate whether the proposed crosstalk between PPARβ/δ signaling and TFEB‐mediated lysosomal regulation holds true in the RPE microenvironment, potentially involving studies using animal models of dry AMD. Finally, given the highly specialized nature of ocular drug delivery, translational efforts may need to incorporate modern delivery strategies such as implantable controlled‐release devices, nanoparticles, or hydrogels to ensure sustained local efficacy while minimizing systemic exposure.

In its current form, GSK0660 remains a highly informative research tool with excellent selectivity for PPARβ/δ, yet its direct translation into an ocular therapeutic faces significant challenges. The compound’s historical utility in preclinical models of Parkinson’s disease and psoriasis attests to its potential to modulate critical signaling pathways; however, the leap from these systems to effective treatment of dry AMD will require concerted efforts in medicinal chemistry, formulation science, and rigorous preclinical testing (Antonosante et al., 2023; Hack et al., 2012; Boya et al., 2023).

Overall, the repurposing hypothesis for GSK0660 offers a high‐risk, high‐reward strategy. The innovative concept of enhancing lysosomal function via the relief of PPARβ/δ‐mediated repression of TFEB is attractive and represents a novel intervention point for restoring RPE homeostasis. Should preclinical studies confirm that antagonism of PPARβ/δ indeed leads to significant upregulation of lysosomal genes and a measurable improvement in POS degradation in RPE cells, GSK0660 or its optimized derivatives could provide the basis for a new therapeutic class targeting the underlying pathophysiology of dry AMD.

Moving forward, the research team should prioritize:  
1. Rigorous in vitro validation in human RPE models (such as ARPE‐19 cells or primary RPE cultures) to examine TFEB activation and lysosomal gene expression changes (e.g., increases in LAMP1 and Cathepsin D levels) following treatment with GSK0660 at appropriate concentrations.  
2. Detailed pharmacokinetic and stability studies, coupled with efforts to modify the chemical structure (e.g., by optimizing the 4′‐aminophenyl substituent as suggested by SAR studies) to improve both the potency and bioavailability of the therapeutic agent.  
3. Development of ocular delivery strategies that overcome the challenges posed by the eye’s protective barriers—ensuring that effective drug concentrations can be delivered locally while minimizing systemic exposure.  
4. In vivo studies in suitable animal models of dry AMD to evaluate both the safety and efficacy profile of GSK0660, with endpoints that include assessment of RPE cell function, clearance of photoreceptor debris, and overall preservation of retinal structure and function.

In conclusion, while GSK0660 holds promise as a novel modality for enhancing lysosomal biogenesis via PPARβ/δ inhibition, its transition from a research tool in neurodegenerative and dermatological studies to an effective treatment for dry AMD is contingent on overcoming significant pharmacokinetic and formulation hurdles. The ultimate success of this repurposing effort will depend on rigorous preclinical validation that demonstrates not only the expected molecular effects in RPE cells but also the clinical relevance of these observations in ameliorating retinal degeneration.

────────────────────────────────────────  
VII. SUMMARY  

To summarize, the evaluation of GSK0660 for dry AMD repurposing can be encapsulated as follows:

• Overview: GSK0660 is a synthetically derived, thiophenecarboxylate‐class molecule designed as the first selective PPARβ/δ antagonist. Its structure, defined by a methoxy‐substituted 1,4‐diaminobenzene core, a 4′‐aminophenyl substituent, and a methyl thiophene carboxylate moiety, is supported by extensive SAR data that also suggest avenues for chemical optimization (Toth et al., 2012).  
• Therapeutic History: Historically, the compound has been employed as a research tool in models of neurodegeneration and inflammatory skin diseases. No literature presently documents its use in ocular applications or in treating conditions resembling dry AMD, a gap that underscores both the opportunity and the risk inherent to its repurposing (Antonosante et al., 2023; Hack et al., 2012; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).  
• Mechanism of Action: GSK0660 works by competitively binding to the PPARβ/δ ligand‐binding domain and, in certain contexts, acting as an inverse agonist via recruitment of transcriptional corepressors. The repurposing hypothesis contends that by blocking PPARβ/δ, the repressive influence on TFEB is alleviated, leading to enhanced lysosomal biogenesis—a mechanism that, while plausible, awaits definitive validation in RPE cells (Toth et al., 2012; Lieber, 2015; Monsalve et al., 2013).  
• Expected Effect: In A2E‐loaded RPE cells, treatment with GSK0660 is anticipated to upregulate the expression of TFEB target genes such as LAMP1 and Cathepsin D. This should result in improved POS degradation and lysosomal clearance, which are crucial for countering the pathogenesis of dry AMD. Nevertheless, dose optimization and adaptation to the ocular milieu remain key challenges (Abokyi & Tse, 2025).  
• Overall Evaluation: While GSK0660 is conceptually compelling because of its selective PPARβ/δ antagonism and its innovative potential to unlock TFEB‐mediated lysosomal pathways, its poor bioavailability, chemical instability, and lack of ocular‐specific preclinical data temper enthusiasm. The candidate is best viewed as a valuable starting point that will require considerable further optimization—both chemically and in terms of delivery methods—before it can be advanced as a viable therapeutic for dry AMD (Toth et al., 2012; Hack et al., 2012; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

The repurposing of GSK0660 for dry AMD thus presents a visionary, albeit risky, strategy that could address an unmet clinical need if the central hypothesis is confirmed and associated pharmacokinetic challenges can be overcome.

────────────────────────────────────────  
VIII. FINAL CONSIDERATIONS  

Given the current state of evidence, it is clear that while GSK0660 boasts a strong mechanistic rationale due to its precise inhibition of PPARβ/δ and well‐characterized molecular interactions, significant gaps remain with respect to its application in ocular therapeutics. For instance, elucidating whether PPARβ/δ indeed represses the CLEAR network in RPE cells is critical to substantiate the therapeutic hypothesis. Equally important is formulating strategies to mitigate the compound’s bioavailability and stability issues in the highly sensitive ocular environment. Successful resolution of these challenges would not only validate the approach but might also allow GSK0660 or its improved derivatives to emerge as a pioneering therapy targeting lysosomal dysfunction—a central driver in the progression of dry AMD.

In light of these considerations, the repurposing strategy for GSK0660 should be pursued with a dual focus on mechanistic validation in relevant cellular models and on the parallel development of advanced ocular delivery systems. Such a multidisciplinary research effort would be essential to transform a promising preclinical compound into a candidate that can safely and effectively restore RPE lysosomal function in patients with dry AMD.

To conclude, while GSK0660 holds promise as a novel modality for enhancing lysosomal biogenesis via PPARβ/δ inhibition, its transition from a research tool in neurodegenerative and dermatological studies to an effective treatment for dry AMD is contingent on overcoming significant pharmacokinetic and formulation hurdles. The ultimate success of this repurposing effort will depend on rigorous preclinical validation that demonstrates not only the expected molecular effects in RPE cells but also the clinical relevance of these observations in ameliorating retinal degeneration.
