Proposal for Bryostatin-1 (PKC modulator; NIH repository)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Bryostatin‐1 is a naturally derived macrolide originally isolated from marine invertebrates and belongs to a class of compounds collectively known as bryostatins. These compounds exhibit potent modulation of protein kinase C (PKC) activity by binding to the enzyme’s diacylglycerol binding site on the regulatory domain. Bryostatin‐1 has been characterized as a partial agonist of PKC and is noted for its ability to both acutely activate and chronically down‐regulate specific PKC isoforms. The molecular architecture of bryostatin‐1 confers a unique binding profile that distinguishes it from phorbol esters; it induces translocation of target PKC isoforms to membranes without eliciting the full tumor‐promoting effects observed with phorbol esters. The compound is synthetically challenging to produce, yet semisynthetic methodologies have enabled its preparation in sufficient quantities for preclinical and early clinical applications. As a member of the marine natural products family, bryostatin‐1 is frequently investigated for its anticancer and neuroprotective properties, and its chemical structure serves as the basis for designing simplified analogs with improved pharmacological profiles (Kollár et al., 2014; Le Tourneau et al., 2007).  

Therapeutic History:  
Bryostatin‐1 has a long preclinical history that spans oncology and neurology. In oncology, bryostatin‐1 has been extensively studied for its role in modulating PKC in various tumor types and has been evaluated in numerous clinical trials addressing B‐cell malignancies and renal cancers. Despite promising preclinical results, its cancer‐directed clinical efficacy has been limited by suboptimal outcomes and adverse side effects such as myalgia. More recently, bryostatin‐1 has been repurposed in neurological contexts. Several studies have demonstrated its neuroprotective capabilities in models of Alzheimer’s disease, where it has shown to improve synaptic function, restore dendritic spine morphology, induce synaptogenesis through the upregulation of brain‐derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF), and enhance cognitive function. Phase II clinical trials in Alzheimer’s patients have provided translational evidence of its ability to modulate PKCε in the central nervous system (Chen et al., 2024; Nelson et al., 2017). However, a search of clinical trial databases has revealed that no formal clinical trials have been registered evaluating bryostatin‐1 in the setting of macular degeneration, retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) dysfunction, or Rab7 signaling‐related pathways (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). Although there is evidence supporting bryostatin‐1’s capacity to affect cellular pathways—such as inducing autophagy and promoting PKC‐mediated cell survival—in neuronal and cancer cells, its application to ocular diseases like dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) remains unexplored in the clinical context (Safarpour, 2009; Sarangarajan & Apte, 2005).  

Mechanism of Action:  
Bryostatin‐1 functions primarily as a modulator of protein kinase C, a family of serine/threonine kinases that play central roles in regulating cell proliferation, differentiation, apoptosis, and intracellular trafficking. On a molecular level, bryostatin‐1 binds competitively to the diacylglycerol (DAG) binding site located in the C1 domain of PKC isoforms. This binding event leads to the translocation of PKC from the cytosol to membranous compartments, thereby bringing the kinase into close proximity with its substrates. Unlike potent activators such as phorbol esters, bryostatin‐1 acts as a partial agonist. Short‐term exposure results in the activation of specific PKC isoforms, whereas prolonged exposure leads to their down‐regulation via proteasomal degradation. Structural studies have demonstrated that the complex hydrogen‐bond networks formed by the A- and B-rings of bryostatin‐1 contribute significantly to its isoform selectivity and binding affinity (Kollár et al., 2014; Le Tourneau et al., 2007).  

In the context of the hypothesized mechanism for dry AMD, it is proposed that bryostatin‐1 can activate atypical PKC isoforms at very low effective concentrations (EC₅₀ ≈ 0.1 nM), potentially including enzymes that are involved in the regulation of Rab7 signalling. Although bryostatin‐1 has been studied predominantly for its activation of classical (e.g., PKCα, PKCβ) and novel PKC isoforms (e.g., PKCδ, PKCε), several experimental reports suggest that PKC activity regulates various aspects of vesicular trafficking, including phagosome maturation. In phagocytic cell lines, enhanced PKC activation has been linked to improved phagolysosomal fusion, which is essential for the degradation of ingested material. This connection is of particular interest in RPE cells, where the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) via the phagosome–lysosome pathway is central to retinal homeostasis. The hypothesis extends this mechanism by proposing that the activation of PKC by bryostatin‐1 may lead to the phosphorylation of Rab7 effector proteins, which are known to control the late stages of phagosome maturation and lysosome fusion. Although direct experimental evidence connecting bryostatin‐1‐mediated PKC activation to Rab7 effector phosphorylation in RPE cells is limited, existing literature has established the importance of PKC in regulating phagocytic processes and intracellular vesicle trafficking (Saddala et al., 2020; Sarangarajan & Apte, 2005). Furthermore, mechanistic parallels drawn from studies in neuronal systems—where bryostatin‐1 has been shown to influence autophagic flux and promote synaptic health—support the feasibility of such a cellular response in other highly phagocytic cells like the RPE (Chen et al., 2024).  

Expected Effect:  
Dry AMD is characterized by the dysfunction of RPE cells, which leads to impaired clearance of POS and subsequent accumulation of toxic lipofuscin deposits. RPE dysfunction is associated with disrupted phagosome maturation and lysosomal degradation pathways, contributing to retinal degeneration and vision loss. The therapeutic hypothesis for bryostatin‐1 posits that its administration will enhance the maturation of phagosomes by stimulating PKC isoforms that, in turn, phosphorylate Rab7 effectors. Effective phosphorylation of these effectors is expected to facilitate late phagosome–lysosome fusion, thereby improving the trafficking and degradation of POS. Empirical studies in RPE cells have shown that defects in phagolysosomal fusion lead to the accumulation of nondegradable materials and are closely linked to the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Safarpour, 2009; Sarangarajan & Apte, 2005).  

The candidate mechanism suggests that, upon administration, bryostatin‐1 will rapidly bind to its target PKC isoforms in RPE cells, causing these kinases to translocate to relevant subcellular membranes. This translocation is anticipated to bring PKC in proximity to Rab7 effectors situated on late phagosomes. Activation of these kinases would then promote the phosphorylation of regulatory proteins that control vesicular fusion events. As a result, the impaired phagocytosis observed in dry AMD would be corrected through improved maturation of phagosomes and enhanced fusion with lysosomes. Such a cascade is expected to lead to enhanced clearance of POS debris and, ultimately, a reduction in lipofuscin accumulation, which is central to the pathophysiology of dry AMD. Although supportive evidence for this cascade exists in the context of non‐ocular phagocytic cells and in neuronal models of autophagy activation, it remains imperative to directly evaluate these effects in primary RPE cell cultures or relevant animal models to solidify the connection between PKC activation by bryostatin‐1 and Rab7‐mediated phagosome maturation (Saddala et al., 2020).  

Overall Evaluation:  
Bryostatin‐1 presents an intriguing therapeutic candidate for dry AMD owing to its potent modulation of PKC, a central regulator of intracellular signaling pathways that govern vesicular trafficking, phagocytosis, and autophagy. One of the key strengths of bryostatin‐1 lies in its well‐documented activity in modulating PKC isoforms that are critical in diverse physiological contexts, including neuronal function and cancer cell biology. Its demonstrated neuroprotective efficacy in Alzheimer’s disease clinical studies supports the compound’s translational potential and suggests that its PKC‐modulating effects might be harnessed in alternate tissues such as the retina (Chen et al., 2024). Additionally, the critical role of PKC in promoting phagosome–lysosome fusion has been substantiated in other cell types, which provides a strong theoretical basis for its application in RPE cells where phagocytic clearance is essential for maintaining retinal integrity (Saddala et al., 2020; Safarpour, 2009).

Despite these promising aspects, several challenges and weaknesses must be considered. Foremost, no direct studies to date have evaluated bryostatin‐1 in the context of dry AMD or in RPE cells. Clinical trial databases have not registered any studies for bryostatin‐1 in macular degeneration, underscoring the novelty of this repurposing strategy but also highlighting a significant gap in the literature (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). The hypothesis that bryostatin‐1 will stimulate atypical PKC isoforms to phosphorylate Rab7 effectors, although plausible, remains largely speculative. While various studies have linked PKC activity to phagosome maturation and autophagy regulation, the precise isoforms relevant to RPE cell function—and whether these isoforms are the same ones activated by bryostatin‐1 in neuronal or cancer models—have not been comprehensively elucidated. Therefore, it will be crucial to determine, through rigorous in vitro assays and animal models, whether the purported EC₅₀ of approximately 0.1 nM is achievable in RPE cells and whether this concentration effectively modifies the Rab7‐related molecular machinery.

Additional considerations include the potential for off‐target effects and systemic toxicity. Past clinical studies of bryostatin‐1, particularly in oncology, have reported adverse effects such as myalgia and thrombocytopenia. However, the pharmacokinetic profile observed in Alzheimer’s trials suggests that the dosing regimens used for neurological disorders might be translatable to ocular delivery with appropriate formulation strategies. Localized ocular delivery, such as intravitreal injection or controlled‐release implants, may enable targeted modulation of PKC in the retina while mitigating systemic exposure and associated adverse events (Chen et al., 2024; Nelson et al., 2017). Moreover, the challenge of achieving adequate drug penetration to the RPE in vivo is nontrivial. Approaches to enhance ocular bioavailability, including nanoparticle encapsulation or conjugation to targeting ligands, should be explored concurrently with the design of preclinical studies to better validate this therapeutic candidate.

From a mechanistic standpoint, the dual nature of bryostatin‐1—characterized by initial activation followed by downregulation of PKC isoforms—necessitates precise temporal control of its pharmacodynamic effects. In the context of phagosome maturation, transient activation may be beneficial to restore proper lysosomal fusion; however, prolonged downregulation might counteract the desired effect. It is therefore important that future studies carefully delineate the dosing regimen (both concentration and administration frequency) required to achieve an optimal therapeutic window in RPE cells. Additionally, the specificity of bryostatin‐1 for PKC isoforms implicated in Rab7 effector phosphorylation must be confirmed, as the RPE expresses a complex array of PKC isoforms that may play distinct roles in cellular homeostasis and stress responses (Kollár et al., 2014; Le Tourneau et al., 2007).

The breadth and diversity of bryostatin‐1’s effects in preclinical models have generated considerable interest, yet its repurposing for dry AMD remains at an early stage of conceptual development. Given that disruption of phagosome maturation in RPE cells is a well‐established contributor to the pathogenesis of dry AMD—and that PKC signaling has been implicated in regulating this process—the rationale for exploring bryostatin‐1 in this indication is scientifically sound. Nonetheless, the transition from a neuroprotective agent in Alzheimer’s disease to an effective modulator of RPE function in dry AMD will depend on new studies that specifically address the cellular context of the retina. In this regard, preliminary investigations using primary RPE cultures or animal models of dry AMD will be critical to validate the hypothesis that PKC activation by bryostatin‐1 can enhance Rab7‐mediated phagolysosomal fusion and improve POS clearance (Saddala et al., 2020; Safarpour, 2009).

In summary, bryostatin‐1 offers both significant promise and notable challenges as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age‐related macular degeneration. Its ability to modulate PKC in a manner that may restore essential phagolysosomal functions in the RPE positions it as an innovative approach to address a major unmet need in ocular therapeutics. The compound’s successful use in Alzheimer’s disease trials provides encouraging translational evidence of its safety and efficacy in modulating neuronal PKC activity. However, the absence of direct evidence in retinal cells, the uncertainty regarding which specific PKC isoforms are most relevant to RPE phagocytosis, and potential issues related to dosing and systemic toxicity form significant hurdles that must be overcome. Moving forward, it will be critical to conduct comprehensive in vitro studies to assess the effects of bryostatin‐1 on RPE phagosome maturation, coupled with robust in vivo experiments in established dry AMD models. Such studies should focus on confirming the expression and role of the putative target proteins, including Rab7 effectors, and determining whether the activation of these pathways can indeed translate into improved clearance of POS and reduced retinal degeneration (Saddala et al., 2020; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Chen et al., 2024; Sarangarajan & Apte, 2005).

In conclusion, the overall evaluation of bryostatin‐1 as a drug candidate for dry AMD reveals a compound with strong mechanistic rationale and significant translational potential based on its established pharmacological properties in PKC modulation and neuroprotection. The strengths of bryostatin‐1 include its potent activity at nanomolar concentrations, a unique mode of action that distinguishes it from classical PKC activators, and supporting evidence from clinical studies in neurological disorders. Conversely, its weaknesses lie primarily in the absence of direct studies in ocular tissues, uncertainty regarding the specific PKC isoforms involved in RPE phagosome maturation, and potential challenges in achieving localized delivery without systemic side effects. An interdisciplinary approach that integrates detailed molecular studies with innovative drug delivery strategies will be critical in validating bryostatin‐1’s viability for the treatment of dry AMD. Based on the current literature, investing in rigorous preclinical testing to confirm the hypothesized mechanistic link between PKC activation, Rab7 effector phosphorylation, and enhanced phagosome maturation in RPE cells is warranted before progressing to clinical evaluation (Saddala et al., 2020; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.; Safarpour, 2009; Chen et al., 2024).

answer:
Proposal for AGI-1067 (Probucol analog; Tocris Cat. No. 4672)

Below is a detailed evaluation of the candidate, AGI-1067, for potential repurposing in dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
AGI-1067 is a synthetic, small‐molecule derivative developed as an analog of probucol—a well‐known phenolic antioxidant originally discovered for its lipid‐lowering and antiatherosclerotic properties. Chemically, AGI-1067 is the monosuccinic acid ester of probucol. In its synthesis, the parent molecule probucol is modified using a reaction with succinic anhydride under basic conditions (typically in a solvent such as tetrahydrofuran with sodium hydride) to yield the monosubstituted ester derivative (Meng et al., 2002; Serebruany et al., 2007). This chemical alteration is key: by substituting one of the two phenolic hydroxyl groups with a succinate moiety, the molecule retains one essential antioxidant phenol while significantly enhancing its water solubility, cell permeability, and overall pharmacokinetic properties. Such modifications have been shown to mitigate the drawbacks of the parent compound—namely, its poor bioavailability, cardiotoxicity via QT interval prolongation, and unwanted HDL cholesterol lowering—while keeping the desirable antioxidant and lipid-modulating activities intact (Meng et al., 2002).

AGI-1067 belongs to the class of phenolic antioxidants, a group of compounds known for their ability to scavenge free radicals and interrupt the chain reactions that govern lipid peroxidation. Historically, phenolic antioxidants—including probucol itself—have been employed to counteract oxidative stress in cardiovascular disease, largely based on their capacity to protect low-density lipoprotein (LDL) particles from oxidative modification. More recently, AGI-1067 has been classified under the emerging category of “vascular protectants” as it additionally exhibits anti-inflammatory actions, such as the inhibition of VCAM-1 and MCP-1, which are central to inflammatory signaling within vascular tissues (Meng et al., 2002; Serebruany et al., 2007; Stix, 2003). The chemical design of AGI-1067 was informed by detailed structure-activity relationship studies—demonstrating that modification of the probucol scaffold can yield a compound with enhanced therapeutic indices—that is, with potency comparable to probucol in antioxidant assays, yet with a safer profile in vivo (Tardif, 2005; Meng et al., 2002).

The origins of AGI-1067 are rooted in medicinal chemistry strategies aimed at overcoming the known liabilities of probucol through targeted chemical modifications. In doing so, not only is the inherent bioactivity maintained, but delivery characteristics are improved substantially. AGI-1067 has been advanced through preclinical development and early-phase clinical trials in cardiovascular diseases, suggesting that the molecule has been thoroughly vetted for systemic safety and efficacy (Serebruany et al., 2007; Sundell et al., 2003). As a compound with robust antioxidant and anti-inflammatory capabilities, AGI-1067 is now being considered for applications beyond its original indication, with dry AMD emerging as a plausible target given the shared mechanisms of oxidative and inflammatory stress in both vascular and retinal degenerative diseases (Tardif et al., 2003a; Tardif, 2005).

Therapeutic History:  
The therapeutic lineage of AGI-1067 is intrinsically linked to that of probucol, a lipid‐soluble phenolic antioxidant first discovered in the 1960s. Probucol was initially explored and later used primarily for its cholesterol-lowering effects and its ability to protect LDL particles against oxidation. Its clinical use, however, was compromised by significant side effects, including marked reductions in HDL cholesterol and adverse cardiac electrophysiological effects (notably QT interval prolongation). Recognizing these clinical limitations, researchers embarked on a drug development program to modify the structure of probucol, thereby retaining its beneficial antioxidant properties while eliminating or reducing its untoward effects. AGI-1067 emerged from this program as a promising candidate due to its modified structure—specifically, the introduction of a succinic acid ester group—that confers improved pharmacokinetic and safety profiles (Meng et al., 2002; Serebruany et al., 2007).

In a series of preclinical studies, AGI-1067 demonstrated equipotent antioxidant effects compared to probucol, as measured by its ability to inhibit copper-induced oxidation of linoleic acid and to scavenge free radicals. More importantly, however, AGI-1067 showed enhanced anti-inflammatory properties in vitro: it potently inhibited TNF-α–inducible expression of VCAM-1 in endothelial cells with an IC₅₀ around 6 µM—a dramatic improvement relative to probucol, which shows minimal activity at concentrations greater than 50 µM (Meng et al., 2002). These encouraging preclinical findings spurred the progression of AGI-1067 into Phase II clinical studies for the treatment of cardiovascular diseases such as atherosclerosis, where its efficacy was not solely limited to antioxidant protection but extended to lipid modulation and inhibition of inflammatory gene expression (Serebruany et al., 2007; Sundell et al., 2003; Tardif, 2005).

Despite these developments, no prior studies have directly applied AGI-1067 to ocular diseases such as dry AMD. However, the key pathophysiological processes—in particular, chronic oxidative stress and inflammation—are central to both atherosclerosis and dry AMD. In dry AMD, the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) is subjected to chronic oxidative damage from light exposure, metabolic activity, and the accumulation of toxic lipofuscin byproducts like A2E. The success of AGI-1067 in inhibiting oxidative stress and inflammatory responses in vascular tissues thus provides a compelling rationale for investigating its utility in the RPE, where similar stressors contribute to cellular dysfunction and the consequent impairment of photoreceptor outer segment (POS) degradation (Meng et al., 2002; Serebruany et al., 2007; Siu, 2010).

Further supporting its therapeutic repurposing is the fact that AGI-1067, as an orally bioavailable agent with a well-established safety record in Phase II clinical trials, offers a distinct advantage over many novel drug candidates that often struggle with systemic toxicity or poor pharmacokinetics. The clinical history of AGI-1067 in cardiovascular trials demonstrates that its metabolic stability allows it to reach therapeutic plasma concentrations rapidly (in less than two weeks), a feature that might be beneficial when considering dosing strategies for chronic conditions like dry AMD (Tardif, 2005; Serebruany et al., 2007). Although the translation from cardiovascular disease to retinal degeneration represents a significant leap, the underlying mechanistic overlap—centered on oxidative and inflammatory damage—positions AGI-1067 as an attractive candidate for further exploration in ocular applications (Tardif et al., 2003a).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, AGI-1067 acts through a multitiered mechanism that combines robust antioxidant activity with selective anti-inflammatory signaling modulation. The phenolic structure, inherited from probucol, facilitates free radical scavenging by donating hydrogen atoms to neutralize reactive oxygen species (ROS). This chain-breaking antioxidant mechanism interferes directly with lipid peroxidation, a process known to damage cellular membranes and macromolecules. Importantly, the conservation of one phenolic group is critical; it provides the necessary redox chemistry without overwhelming the system with potentially toxic metabolites. The strategic conversion of the second phenolic group into a succinic acid ester not only reduces lipophilicity—thus enhancing aqueous solubility—but also increases cellular uptake, as this modification improves passage across cell membranes (Meng et al., 2002; Serebruany et al., 2007).

In vascular and inflammatory cell models, AGI-1067 has demonstrated an ability to suppress the expression of key inflammatory proteins. One of its most notable effects is the inhibition of vascular cell adhesion molecule-1 (VCAM-1) expression upon stimulation by TNF-α. VCAM-1 is a critical mediator of leukocyte adhesion and transmigration, and its upregulation is a hallmark of inflammatory vascular injury. AGI-1067 achieves this inhibition at low micromolar concentrations (IC₅₀ ≈ 6 µM), far surpassing the potency of probucol, which fails to significantly inhibit VCAM-1 even at concentrations as high as 100 µM (Meng et al., 2002). Similarly, agents in this class inhibit monocyte chemotactic protein-1 (MCP-1) expression, a chemokine that further perpetuates inflammation by recruiting monocytes to sites of tissue damage (Tardif, 2006; Tardif, 2005).

While some studies suggest that AGI-1067 may interfere with NF-κB activation—a central transcription factor that regulates a host of inflammatory genes—the exact interplay remains complex. There is evidence to suggest that the compound’s ability to inhibit the expression of adhesion molecules such as VCAM-1 is at least partially independent of traditional NF-κB nuclear translocation pathways. Nonetheless, the net result is a dampening of the inflammatory cascade that typically follows oxidative stimuli (Tardif, 2006; Sundell et al., 2003). In addition to these anti-inflammatory actions, AGI-1067 exerts mild antiplatelet effects. By modulating the expression and function of platelet surface receptors and decreasing the synthesis of pro-aggregation signals such as thromboxane, the compound helps to reduce platelet activation—a property that, while primarily beneficial for cardiovascular disease, may also contribute to a systemic reduction in inflammatory tone (Muldrew & Franks, 2009; Serebruany et al., 2007).

This comprehensive mode of action—combining free radical scavenging with the selective suppression of inflammation—makes AGI-1067 a prototypical multifunctional antioxidant. In many preclinical models, the compound’s capacity to block redox-sensitive signaling has been linked to decreased vascular smooth muscle cell proliferation, reduced inflammatory cell recruitment, and overall protection against tissue injury induced by oxidative stress. These molecular interactions are mediated through its phenolic backbone and are further enhanced by the succinic acid moiety, which allows for a more favorable distribution in aqueous environments and within the intracellular milieu (Meng et al., 2002; Tardif, 2005; Muldrew & Franks, 2009).

In the specific context of cellular metabolism, AGI-1067’s actions have been correlated with a down-regulation of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6, at least in vascular endothelial cells. While such studies have largely been conducted in non-ocular tissues, the ubiquitous nature of these signaling pathways suggests that similar molecular interactions would occur in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, which are known to be highly sensitive to oxidative and inflammatory stress (Siu, 2010; Sundell et al., 2003). Thus, the compound’s multifactorial mechanism positions it not only as an effective scavenger of ROS but also as a modulatory agent that disrupts the cycle of chronic inflammation—a critical pathogenic driver in both atherosclerosis and dry AMD.

Expected Effect in Dry AMD:  
Dry AMD is characterized by a gradual degeneration of the RPE and subsequent photoreceptor dysfunction, largely driven by chronic oxidative stress and low-grade inflammation. In the RPE, the continuous phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) leads to the accumulation of lipofuscin pigments such as A2E, which in turn disrupt lysosomal function by inducing pH changes and impairing the activity of degradative enzymes like cathepsins. Over time, these alterations diminish the cell’s ability to clear damaged POS, exacerbating oxidative damage and activating inflammatory cascades that further compromise retinal integrity.

Based on the known pharmacological profile of AGI-1067, it is hypothesized that the compound will exert a protective effect on RPE cells through several convergent mechanisms. First, by activating antioxidant pathways, AGI-1067 is expected to reduce intracellular ROS levels. Its potent free radical scavenging ability should directly counteract oxidative damage to cellular lipids and proteins, thereby preserving the integrity of the membranes that are essential for normal phagocytic and lysosomal function (Sundell et al., 2003; Meng et al., 2002). In vitro experiments in non-ocular cell models have demonstrated that AGI-1067 can safeguard cells from oxidative insults even at concentrations as low as 2 µM, suggesting that a similar effective concentration might be achieved in RPE cells (Meng et al., 2002; Tardif, 2005).

Second, AGI-1067 is postulated to inhibit NF-κB signaling in RPE cells. NF-κB is a key transcription factor that becomes activated in response to oxidative stress and drives the expression of numerous pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemokines. In the RPE, such activation would lead to an inflammatory milieu that not only damages the cells themselves but also disrupts the regulation of phagocytic receptors necessary for efficient POS uptake. By mitigating NF-κB activation, AGI-1067 may lower the production of cytokines like TNF-α and IL-1β, thus breaking the cycle of inflammation and oxidative stress (Tardif, 2006; Tardif et al., 2008). This anti-inflammatory effect would be critical for preserving lysosomal integrity, as excessive inflammation has been shown to interfere with lysosome acidification and enzyme activity—two processes that are essential for proper POS degradation.

Moreover, the compound’s ability to rescue cathepsin activity is of particular interest. In RPE cells, cathepsins are responsible for the breakdown of POS, and their inactivation (often due to lysosomal pH elevation induced by A2E accumulation) is a hallmark of dry AMD. The hypothesis, supported by recent in vitro data (Si et al. Biomolecules 2023), is that AGI-1067 can prevent A2E-induced increases in lysosomal pH, thereby maintaining cathepsin activity and ensuring the continued clearance of POS. This preservation of lysosomal function is expected to not only slow down the accumulation of toxic lipofuscin pigments but also maintain overall cellular health, reducing the propensity for RPE cell death (Sundell et al., 2003; Tardif, 2005).

In addition to these direct effects on oxidative stress and inflammation, AGI-1067 may also exert beneficial systemic effects that are indirectly relevant to dry AMD. For instance, its lipid-modulating properties could result in a more favorable systemic lipid profile, which has been associated with reduced risk of AMD progression in epidemiological studies. Although the primary focus in dry AMD is on local oxidative and inflammatory processes, a more balanced systemic lipid environment might lessen the burden of inflammatory lipids that can accumulate in the retina (Sundell et al., 2003).

Importantly, RPE cells express a range of receptors and intracellular signaling molecules that are sensitive to both oxidative and inflammatory cues. Studies in vascular endothelial cells have shown that AGI-1067 modulates the expression of adhesion molecules and inflammatory mediators; given the shared signaling pathways between endothelial and RPE cells, similar downstream effects can be expected in the retina (Siu, 2010; Sundell et al., 2003). Therefore, the anticipated effect of AGI-1067 in the context of dry AMD is multifactorial: reduction of ROS levels, normalization of lysosomal pH, preservation of cathepsin activity, and attenuation of inflammatory cytokine production. Together, these actions should promote better POS phagocytosis and degradation, slow RPE degeneration, and ultimately help maintain photoreceptor health.

Overall Evaluation:  
Taking into account the extensive body of preclinical and clinical data available for AGI-1067 in cardiovascular applications, along with its well-characterized multifaceted mechanism of action, the repurposing of AGI-1067 for dry AMD has considerable appeal. One of the strongest points in favor of this candidate is its dual functionality. Unlike conventional antioxidants that merely scavenge free radicals, AGI-1067 has been shown to simultaneously suppress inflammatory signaling—particularly by inhibiting the expression of adhesion molecules such as VCAM-1 and chemokines like MCP-1—in a highly selective manner (Meng et al., 2002). In the context of dry AMD, where chronic inflammation and oxidative stress interlace to drive RPE dysfunction and subsequent photoreceptor degeneration, such dual activity is likely to be highly beneficial. The preservation of lysosomal function and, by extension, the maintenance of effective POS degradation are especially critical endpoints given that impaired phagocytosis is a key pathogenic mechanism in dry AMD (Sundell et al., 2003; Tardif, 2005).

Another compelling aspect of AGI-1067 is its improved pharmacokinetic profile relative to its parent compound. Its enhanced water solubility and cell permeability mean that it achieves steady-state plasma levels more rapidly—a factor that could translate to more predictable and effective dosing regimens in a chronic condition like dry AMD (Serebruany et al., 2007; Stix, 2003). Moreover, the Phase II clinical data supporting its safety in applications for cardiovascular disease, where it was not associated with dangerous QT interval prolongation or significant adverse lipid profile alterations, reduces the translational risk when considering an alternative indication (Sundell et al., 2003; Tardif et al., 2003b).

Nonetheless, there are notable challenges that must be addressed before advancing AGI-1067 as a treatment for dry AMD. First, the bulk of the published work on AGI-1067 has been in vascular contexts; as such, direct evidence for its efficacy in ocular tissues, and specifically in RPE cells, is limited. The cellular environment of the retina is markedly different from that of vascular endothelium, and it will be essential to establish that the antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties of AGI-1067 translate effectively within RPE cells. Detailed in vitro studies using RPE cell lines or primary RPE cultures that examine key endpoints—such as ROS production, NF-κB activation, lysosomal pH regulation, and cathepsin activity—are crucial (Meng et al., 2002; Serebruany et al., 2007).

Second, the ability of AGI-1067 to penetrate the blood-retinal barrier remains an open question. While its enhanced water solubility is an advantage over probucol, the compound must still be demonstrated to reach therapeutic concentrations in the retina following systemic administration or via alternative routes, such as intravitreal injection. Pharmacokinetic studies in ocular models will be vital to define dosing parameters and ensure that the drug can exert its effects in situ without off-target toxicity (Tardif, 2005; Serebruany et al., 2007).

Third, while the hypothesis proposes that AGI-1067 inhibits NF-κB in RPE cells, the literature from the cardiovascular domain does not unambiguously confirm this effect in ocular tissues. The signaling pathways leading to NF-κB activation—although similar in many cell types—may have unique regulatory mechanisms in the RPE. As such, targeted studies evaluating the modulation of NF-κB and related inflammatory mediators in RPE cells treated with AGI-1067 will help clarify this aspect of its mechanism in the context of dry AMD (Tardif, 2006; Sundell et al., 2003).

Furthermore, while the systemic safety profile of AGI-1067 is relatively well established, the possibility of ocular-specific adverse effects cannot be dismissed. Retinal tissues have a unique sensitivity to certain pharmacological agents, and what is safe in the cardiovascular system might necessitate additional scrutiny in the context of the eye. Preclinical toxicology studies using relevant animal models of retinal degeneration would be required to assess any potential retinal toxicity, inflammation, or interference with normal RPE function (Serebruany et al., 2007; Tardif et al., 2003a).

In addition, the chronic nature of dry AMD implies that long-term dosing will be essential. AGI-1067’s ability to maintain efficacy over prolonged treatment periods without inducing tolerance or unexpected metabolic alterations will need to be carefully evaluated. Although the compound has demonstrated metabolic stability in cardiovascular trials, this must be validated in the long-term context of an ocular application (Tardif, 2005; Sundell et al., 2003).

In conclusion, AGI-1067 exhibits several properties that are highly attractive for the treatment of dry AMD. Its design as a repurposed probucol analog—with enhanced water solubility, improved cellular uptake, and an integrated antioxidant/anti-inflammatory mechanism—is well aligned with the pathogenic underpinnings of dry AMD, where oxidative stress and chronic inflammation play pivotal roles in RPE dysfunction. The molecular mechanisms by which AGI-1067 acts—inhibiting redox-sensitive signaling pathways, preserving cathepsin activity, and reducing inflammatory mediator expression—offer a sound scientific basis for the hypothesis that it could protect RPE cells and preserve the critical process of POS phagocytosis (Meng et al., 2002; Meng et al., 2002; Siu, 2010).

However, the current body of work on AGI-1067 has focused predominantly on its cardiovascular applications, meaning that substantial additional research is required to evaluate its efficacy in ocular models. Key next steps would include (1) in vitro studies using RPE cell cultures to confirm its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects at the proposed EC₅₀ of approximately 2 µM; (2) assessment of its ability to preserve lysosomal pH and cathepsin activity in the face of A2E exposure; (3) pharmacokinetic studies to ensure effective retinal penetration; and (4) in vivo efficacy and safety studies in animal models of dry AMD.

Overall, the multifaceted biological activities of AGI-1067—ranging from free radical scavenging and inhibition of inflammatory cytokine production to improved lipid handling and platelet inhibition—provide a compelling rationale for its repurposing. Its established clinical safety in Phase II trials for cardiovascular indications further diminishes the risk associated with translational development. Nevertheless, the absence of direct data in the context of the eye and the potential challenges posed by the unique microenvironment of the retina underscore the need for a rigorous preclinical evaluation before progressing to clinical trials in dry AMD patients (Tardif et al., 2003b; Serebruany et al., 2007; Tardif et al., 2008).

In summary, AGI-1067 stands out as a promising candidate for dry AMD therapy based on its robust antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties, optimized chemical design, and favorable safety profile. While there are clear challenges associated with adapting a cardiovascular drug for an ocular application—especially regarding retinal drug delivery and ensuring efficacy in RPE cells—the mechanistic rationale and preclinical success in related fields justify further investigation. Given the devastating impact that dry AMD has on quality of life and the limited therapeutic options currently available, repurposing a compound such as AGI-1067 could represent a significant advancement in the management of this complex degenerative disease (Meng et al., 2002; Tardif et al., 2002; Sundell et al., 2003).

On balance, the strengths of AGI-1067—including its multifunctional mode of action, established clinical safety, and enhanced pharmacological properties over its precursor—strongly support its evaluation in the context of dry AMD. Simultaneously, the potential weaknesses related to ocular bioavailability, direct effects on RPE-specific pathways, and the need for comprehensive retinal safety data warrant careful, targeted preclinical investigations. It is recommended that the drug development team pursue further in vitro and in vivo studies in models of retinal degeneration to clarify these points before proceeding to early-phase clinical trials. Such a stepwise approach would ensure that the promising attributes of AGI-1067 are fully leveraged while minimizing the risks associated with repurposing an agent developed for a different therapeutic domain (Serebruany et al., 2007; Tardif, 2005; Tardif et al., 2008).

In conclusion, based on the comprehensive review of the biomedical, clinical, and biochemical literature available through our current sources, AGI-1067 shows considerable potential as a repurposed therapy for dry AMD. Its capacity to reduce oxidative stress, inhibit key inflammatory mediators, and preserve the phagocytic and lysosomal function of RPE cells provides a strong scientific foundation for further exploration. Should subsequent studies confirm its efficacy in ocular models and demonstrate adequate retinal bioavailability and safety, AGI-1067 may ultimately serve as a valuable therapeutic option for patients suffering from dry AMD, a condition in urgent need of novel treatment strategies (Meng et al., 2002; Serebruany et al., 2007; Siu, 2010; Serebruany et al., 2007).

Each of these observations is supported by multiple studies in related fields, and while direct evidence in RPE cells remains to be generated, the mechanistic overlap between atherosclerotic and retinal degenerative processes encourages this promising translational pursuit.

hypothesis: Gla-domain peptide mimetic of Protein S (Synthetic 12-mer; Peptide 2.0 Cat. No. H-PS12)
answer:
Proposal for Gla-domain peptide mimetic of Protein S (Synthetic 12-mer; Peptide 2.0 Cat. No. H-PS12)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
The candidate under evaluation is a synthetic Gla‐domain peptide mimetic of Protein S, designated as a 12‐mer peptide (Peptide 2.0 Cat. No. H‐PS12). In its natural role, Protein S is a vitamin K–dependent protein that contains an N‐terminal gamma‐carboxyglutamic acid (Gla) domain responsible for binding phosphatidylserine (PtdSer) on apoptotic membranes and photoreceptor outer segments (POS), and a C‐terminal region that mediates receptor binding to MerTK. This peptide mimetic is engineered to reproduce the key functional motif of the Gla domain that is critical for MerTK engagement. The synthetic peptide belongs to the class of peptide‐based small molecules designed to mimic native ligand functions and to act as receptor agonists. Peptide mimetics have been explored in several therapeutic contexts – for example, peptides that mimic portions of larger proteins often prove advantageous because of their superior stability, lower immunogenicity, and enhanced tissue penetration relative to full‐length proteins. With respect to the ocular environment, the small size and chemical stability of H‐PS12 favor its application as a locally delivered drug via intravitreal injection or topical administration, particularly in diseases such as dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD) where targeting the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) is paramount (Parinot et al., 2024; Nandrot, 2018).

Therapeutic History:  
Extensive literature supports the pivotal role of native Protein S in mediating MerTK signaling in RPE cells and promoting POS phagocytosis. Several studies demonstrate that Protein S acts as a positive regulator of MerTK‐mediated phagocytosis in the retina and that decreased activity of this pathway contributes to the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Parinot et al., 2024). Although native Protein S is known to be a critical ligand for MerTK in RPE cells, its direct application as a therapeutic agent is impeded by its intrinsic lability; indeed, purification challenges and loss of bioactivity in recombinant formats have been reported (Prasad, 2006). By contrast, there is emerging evidence that synthetic peptide mimetics – designed solely from the key Gla domain – can overcome these limitations and reliably stimulate receptor phosphorylation. In macrophage models, such Gla‐domain peptides have been shown to trigger MerTK autophosphorylation within minutes at nanomolar concentrations, suggesting a dose‐responsive mechanism that might be recapitulated in RPE cells (Parinot et al., 2024; Prasad, 2006). To date, while there have been reports on the fundamental biology of Protein S and its role in retinal homeostasis, no synthetic Gla–domain peptide has been commercially developed or clinically evaluated specifically for dry AMD. Nonetheless, the concept of repurposing Protein S’s receptor–binding activity through a stable, small synthetic molecule has been theoretically supported by detailed mechanistic studies in vitro and in animal models (Albert et al., 2015; Nandrot, 2018).

Mechanism of Action:  
The mechanism of action proposed for H‐PS12 centers on recapitulating the critical interaction between the Gla domain of Protein S and the extracellular binding sites of the receptor tyrosine kinase MerTK. In the native state, Protein S engages MerTK by binding to its Ig‐like extracellular domains through specific gamma‐carboxylated glutamic acid residues. This binding requires calcium ions to stabilize the conformation of the Gla domain and mediate a proper interaction with phosphatidylserine on the target cell surface (Nandrot, 2018; Prasad, 2006). Binding of Protein S initiates receptor dimerization and autophosphorylation, an event which subsequently activates intracellular signaling cascades including PI3K‐ and PLCγ‐dependent pathways—processes that are requisite for cytoskeletal rearrangements and efficient phagocytosis of POS (Parinot et al., 2024; Prasad, 2006; Albert et al., 2015).

H‐PS12 is designed as a synthetic 12–amino acid peptide that mimics the critical Gla–domain sequence of Protein S, maintaining the γ–carboxylation motif necessary for calcium binding and ensuring the correct spatial orientation for receptor engagement. The hypothesis is that when this peptide is administered to RPE cultures, it will bind to the MerTK extracellular regions in a fashion indistinguishable from that of the native protein, thereby triggering receptor dimerization and autophosphorylation at an effective concentration (EC₅₀) estimated to be around 100 nM (Parinot et al., 2024; Prasad, 2006). This autophosphorylation event then propagates downstream signaling leading to reorganization of the actin cytoskeleton, an essential step for the engulfment of POS. Detailed structure–function analyses have provided evidence that mutations in the Ig–like domains of MerTK (such as G122R and K263I) significantly alter the binding and internalization responses to Protein S and Gas6, thereby establishing the binding specificity that H‐PS12 aims to replicate (Parinot et al., 2024). Additionally, calcium dependency and proper gamma–carboxylation are confirmed as pivotal for TAM receptor activation, emphasizing how H‐PS12’s mimicry of the Gla domain can facilitate stable receptor activation (Nandrot, 2018; Lieffrig et al., 2023).

Expected Effect:  
In the context of dry AMD, the failure of RPE cells to effectively phagocytose shed photoreceptor outer segments leads to accumulation of cellular debris and subsequent retinal degeneration. The expected effect of H‐PS12 is to restore or enhance this fundamental phagocytic process by acting as a MerTK agonist. When applied to RPE cell cultures – particularly those derived from CFH–mutant lines, which have been shown to exhibit impaired POS phagocytosis – H‐PS12 is anticipated to bind to MerTK, trigger receptor autophosphorylation, and thereby initiate early phagocytic signaling (Parinot et al., 2024; Prasad, 2006). This activation should, in turn, enhance the uptake and internalization of POS, mimicking the natural role of Protein S in maintaining retinal homeostasis (Parinot et al., 2024; Prasad, 2006).

At the molecular level, following MerTK activation, downstream signaling cascades that include PI3K and the FAK pathway are activated, leading to actin polymerization and phagosome formation. Such events are crucial for the internalization of POS and are known to be compromised in models of AMD where MerTK signaling is deficient (Prasad, 2006; Lieffrig et al., 2023). Moreover, by restoring efficient phagocytosis, H‐PS12 may reduce the formation of lipofuscin and drusen—hallmarks of dry AMD—and ameliorate inflammatory processes that are secondary to debris accumulation (Albert et al., 2015). Furthermore, the localized expression of both Protein S and MerTK in the RPE, particularly at the apical microvilli interfacing with POS, supports the rationale that direct stimulation of MerTK in these cells will yield the desired therapeutic outcome (Prasad, 2006).

Overall Evaluation:  
The scientific premise underlying H‐PS12 is founded on in–depth mechanistic insights into the biology of Protein S and its regulation of MerTK–mediated phagocytosis in the retina. One of the primary strengths of the candidate lies in its well–defined mechanism of action. By isolating the Gla–domain, which has been shown to be critical for engaging MerTK and initiating receptor autophosphorylation, the synthetic peptide addresses a fundamental defect in dry AMD—the impaired clearance of POS by RPE cells (Parinot et al., 2024; Nandrot, 2018). The small molecular size of the 12–mer peptide not only minimizes potential for immunogenicity but also enhances tissue penetration and stability in the ocular environment, which is a significant advantage over full–length recombinant proteins that have been plagued by stability issues during purification and storage (Prasad, 2006).

Furthermore, the therapeutic rationale is supported by experimental findings in macrophage models, where similar peptides have been demonstrated to stimulate MerTK phosphorylation rapidly, hinting at the translational potential of H‐PS12 from immune cells to RPE cells (Parinot et al., 2024; Prasad, 2006). In addition, evidence from studies using native Protein S in RPE phagocytosis underscores the relevance of the MerTK pathway in retinal degenerative processes, thereby validating MerTK as a promising therapeutic target for AMD (Parinot et al., 2024; Kaarniranta et al., 2018).

On the other hand, several challenges and potential weaknesses must be considered. First, while Protein S has been conclusively shown to stimulate MerTK phosphorylation in biochemical assays, functional studies have revealed that recombinant Protein S can sometimes fail to stimulate phagocytosis in RPE culture systems unless in the presence of serum or additional cofactors (Prasad, 2006). This discrepancy highlights the possibility that the mere activation of MerTK by H‐PS12, as measured by receptor phosphorylation, may not fully recapitulate the complex intracellular processes required for effective phagocytosis in RPE cells.  

Another concern pertains to the delicate balance between the functions of Protein S and Gas6 in modulating retinal phagocytosis. Studies have indicated that while Protein S acts as a stimulatory ligand, Gas6 can exert inhibitory effects at higher concentrations, suggesting that the endogenous ligand stoichiometry is critical for optimal MerTK function (Parinot et al., 2024). Consequently, the introduction of a synthetic peptide might perturb this balance if not properly dosed, potentially leading to unintended modulation of phagocytic activity or downstream signaling cascades. This is particularly important given that the RPE is subject to a finely tuned circadian rhythm in phagocytosis, and any exogenous modulation must be compatible with these natural regulatory cycles (Nandrot, 2018; Parinot et al., 2024).

Moreover, the transition from in vitro assays to in vivo models and ultimately to clinical application is fraught with challenges. Although the EC₅₀ of approximately 100 nM suggests a high potency of H‐PS12 in triggering MerTK activation, the pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic properties of the peptide in the ocular milieu need to be thoroughly characterized. Issues such as peptide stability in vitreous humor, clearance rates from retinal tissues, and potential off–target effects on other TAM receptors (e.g., TYRO3 and AXL) require detailed investigation (Prasad, 2006). In addition, the efficacy of H‐PS12 in restoring POS phagocytosis must be validated in animal models that closely mimic the human pathophysiology of dry AMD, including models that exhibit CFH mutations where defects in phagocytosis are prominent (Parinot et al., 2024; Palczewska et al., 2016).

A further limitation comes from the fact that dry AMD is a multifactorial disease. Although impaired phagocytosis and resultant debris accumulation at the RPE–photoreceptor interface are central to disease pathogenesis, other pathological mechanisms such as oxidative stress, inflammation, and complement dysregulation also contribute considerably to retinal degeneration (Parinot et al., 2024; Prasad, 2006; Lieffrig et al., 2023). As such, while H‐PS12 is mechanistically attractive from the standpoint of enhancing phagocytosis via MerTK activation, it may need to be integrated into a broader therapeutic regimen that addresses these additional aspects. The long–term outcome of MerTK activation on retinal inflammation, for instance, has yet to be fully determined, even though some studies suggest that active MerTK signaling is associated with anti–inflammatory effects (Albert et al., 2015).

Despite these challenges, the overall evaluation of H‐PS12 is positive. The mechanistic rationale is robust and rooted in fundamental observations of Protein S’s role in retinal homeostasis. The potential to restore or enhance RPE phagocytosis, thereby reducing the accumulation of POS debris—a key pathological hallmark of dry AMD—makes this candidate highly promising. In particular, the possibility of correcting phagocytic deficits in CFH–mutant RPE cultures represents a novel approach that can address one of the unmet needs in dry AMD therapy (Parinot et al., 2024; Nandrot, 2018; Albert et al., 2015; Prasad, 2006).

Moreover, the simplicity of a synthetic peptide compared to biologics such as full–length recombinant proteins offers advantages in terms of manufacturing, storage, and cost. The use of a 12–mer peptide also minimizes the risk of unwanted immunogenic reactions, which is especially pertinent in the immune–privileged environment of the eye (Parinot et al., 2024; Prasad, 2006). It is also worth noting that any adverse effects related to off–target activation can be monitored experimentally by assessing not only the phosphorylation status of MerTK but also by profiling the activity of related receptors and inflammatory markers in preclinical models (Albert et al., 2015).

In summary, the H‐PS12 synthetic peptide stands out as a promising therapeutic candidate for dry AMD based on its targeted mechanism of action, favorable biophysical characteristics, and the strong mechanistic data supporting the role of Protein S in RPE phagocytosis. Its development represents an innovative translation of basic mechanistic insights into a potentially viable therapeutic approach. Nevertheless, successful clinical translation of this candidate will depend on overcoming several challenges, including ensuring that receptor activation translates to meaningful functional improvements in POS clearance, optimizing dosing to maintain the physiological ligand balance, and rigorously evaluating the safety and efficacy in appropriate in vivo models. These considerations will be crucial in determining whether H‐PS12 can be advanced beyond the preclinical proof–of–concept stage (Parinot et al., 2024; Nandrot, 2018; Albert et al., 2015; Prasad, 2006).

Overall, while the current data are highly encouraging, further studies are needed to address the following key issues:  
1. Quantitative profiling of MerTK phosphorylation kinetics by H‐PS12 in RPE cells under varying conditions, including chronic exposure and in the presence of competing ligands such as Gas6.  
2. Evaluation of the functional outcomes of MerTK activation by H‐PS12 in RPE phagocytosis assays, particularly the efficacy of POS uptake and clearance in CFH–mutant RPE cultures.  
3. Detailed pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic studies in ocular models to assess the peptide’s stability, tissue penetration, and potential off–target effects.  
4. Integration of the peptide’s activity with other pathways implicated in AMD pathogenesis, such as oxidative stress and complement activation, to ascertain whether a combinatorial therapeutic strategy might be warranted.

Given these considerations, H‐PS12 merits further preclinical investigation as a potential therapeutic for dry AMD. Its development is grounded in well–established mechanistic insights regarding MerTK function and RPE photoreceptor maintenance, and its design as a stable, small peptide offers distinct advantages over native Protein S. With careful optimization and validation, H‐PS12 could represent a significant advance in the treatment of dry AMD, providing a novel means to restore the critical phagocytic function of the RPE, reduce debris accumulation, and ultimately slow the progression of retinal degeneration (Parinot et al., 2024; Parinot et al., 2024; Albert et al., 2015; Prasad, 2006).

In conclusion, the synthetic Gla–domain 12–mer H‐PS12 demonstrates a promising preclinical profile as a repurposed drug candidate for dry age–related macular degeneration. Its ability to specifically bind and activate MerTK through a mechanism that mirrors the native function of Protein S, combined with its enhanced stability and ease of ocular delivery, underscores the potential for a targeted therapeutic approach to correct the underlying phagocytic deficit observed in dry AMD. While challenges remain concerning the translation of in vitro receptor activation to in vivo functional efficacy, the foundational data reviewed here support continued investigation into H‐PS12 as a novel MerTK agonist. Future research addressing dosing, long–term safety, and integration with other therapeutic modalities will be essential in determining the ultimate clinical utility of this synthetic peptide in combating dry AMD (Parinot et al., 2024; Nandrot, 2018; Prasad, 2006; Albert et al., 2015).

Overall, despite the inherent complexities of dry AMD pathogenesis and the potential for variable responses owing to the interplay of multiple ligands at the MerTK receptor, H‐PS12 offers a rational, targeted, and innovative approach to restore RPE phagocytic function. It thereby holds considerable promise as a next–generation therapeutic candidate that addresses a critical, yet hitherto unmet, need in the management of dry AMD (Parinot et al., 2024; Albert et al., 2015; Prasad, 2006).

hypothesis: P110 (Drp1/Fis1 interaction inhibitor peptide; AnaSpec Cat. No. 77584)
answer:
Proposal for P110 (Drp1/Fis1 interaction inhibitor peptide; AnaSpec Cat. No. 77584)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
P110 is a synthetic, cell‐permeable inhibitory peptide specifically engineered to disrupt the pathological interaction between dynamin‐related protein 1 (Drp1) and its mitochondrial outer membrane receptor fission protein 1 (Fis1). It is synthesized via solid‐phase peptide synthesis methods and rational design strategies that mimic the native binding interface of these two proteins. As such, P110 belongs to the class of peptide-based mitochondrial fission inhibitors, a subclass of compounds that have been previously investigated in a variety of neurodegenerative and metabolic disorders, where aberrant mitochondrial fission is implicated in disease pathology. These types of compounds have historically been used experimentally to restore normal mitochondrial morphological dynamics and attenuate excessive fission triggered by oxidative stress. The concept builds upon evidence that an overactive fission process, largely mediated by elevated activity of Drp1 in response to cellular stressors, results in mitochondrial fragmentation, cytochrome c release, and subsequent cell death. In retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, which bear extremely high energy demands for functions such as photoreceptor outer segment (POS) phagocytosis, proper mitochondrial network integrity is essential. The peptide’s cell-permeability and selective inhibition of the Drp1/Fis1 binding suggest that P110 can efficiently penetrate ocular tissues and modulate mitochondrial dynamics locally, offering a promising approach to preserve mitochondrial function in the diseased retina (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Fisher et al., 2022).

Therapeutic History:  
Numerous preclinical studies have investigated the modulation of mitochondrial dynamics in models of oxidative stress and neurodegeneration, often employing broad-spectrum inhibitors such as mitochondrial division inhibitor 1 (Mdivi-1) or genetic silencing approaches using Drp1-specific siRNA. In several in vitro studies using ARPE-19 cells—a human RPE cell line—excessive mitochondrial fission triggered by oxidative stress (for example, via hydrogen peroxide exposure) was effectively ameliorated by Drp1 inhibition. This intervention preserved mitochondrial structure, maintained ATP production, and increased cell viability, thereby preventing the morphological transition from tubular to fragmented mitochondria (Yako et al., 2021). Although these investigations have provided robust proof-of-concept evidence that targeting Drp1-mediated fission can be beneficial in preventing RPE dysfunction, most of the studies have not directly tested P110 peptide for age-related macular degeneration (AMD). Instead, the literature has explored alternative approaches using compounds like Mdivi-1 and genetic knockdown modalities to decrease Drp1 activity, which indirectly supports the mechanistic rationale for using a targeted inhibitor like P110. The literature also shows that increased expression of mitochondrial fission factor (Mff) and elevated Drp1 levels in AMD donor tissues correlate with impaired mitochondrial homeostasis and defective phagocytosis in the RPE (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Fisher et al., 2022). There remains, however, a gap in direct evidence for P110’s use in AMD despite its clear conceptual alignment with the therapeutic strategy of reducing pathological mitochondrial fission. Clinical trials have emerged that investigate mitochondrial fission inhibitors in ocular conditions, yet the available database queries indicate that while there is clinical interest in Drp1-targeting approaches, specific details on the P110 peptide remain sparse (ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.). Thus, while the broader therapeutic paradigm—targeting aberrant mitochondrial fission—is well supported, P110 itself represents an innovative candidate that requires further preclinical validation in AMD-relevant models.

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, the pathological process underpinning excessive mitochondrial fission centers on the overactivation of Drp1, a GTPase that orchestrates mitochondrial scission. Under normal physiological conditions, Drp1 exists in the cytosol and is transiently recruited to the mitochondrial outer membrane by receptors such as Fis1, mitochondrial fission factor (Mff), and MiD49/MiD51. In response to oxidative and inflammatory stress—conditions known to be prevalent in the aging RPE and AMD—the interaction between Drp1 and Fis1 is upregulated, leading to excessive fission, mitochondrial fragmentation, and subsequent mitochondrial dysfunction. P110 is designed to selectively inhibit the Drp1/Fis1 binding interface, thereby attenuating the aberrant recruitment of Drp1 to the mitochondria. In doing so, it preserves the elongated and interconnected mitochondrial network, which is essential for optimal mitochondrial bioenergetics and the production of adenosine triphosphate (ATP). Biochemically, inhibition of this interaction prevents the oligomerization of Drp1 on the mitochondrial surface, a process that is otherwise necessary for the formation of constriction rings that facilitate organelle division (Zhao et al., 2025). By blocking Drp1 recruitment, P110 indirectly maintains mitochondrial membrane potential and reduces the likelihood of cytochrome c release—a key event in the apoptosis cascade that is frequently observed in stressed RPE cells (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Yako et al., 2021). Although many of the studies in the context of AMD have focused on Mdivi-1 as a Drp1 inhibitor, the specificity of P110 for the Drp1/Fis1 interaction might offer a distinct pharmacological profile, reducing off-target effects and preserving the physiological fission events necessary for maintaining overall mitochondrial quality control (Fisher et al., 2022; Yako et al., 2021). Furthermore, the fact that mitochondrial fission and fusion processes are tightly integrated with mitochondrial biogenesis and mitophagy pathways supports the prospect that modulating this specific interaction may lead to a net improvement in mitochondrial dynamics without completely abolishing essential fission events (Yako et al., 2021; Buonfiglio et al., 2024).

Expected Effect:  
Given the underlying hypothesis, the expected effect of P110 in AMD RPE cells would be to restore a balance in mitochondrial dynamics that has been disrupted by chronic oxidative stress. The assay proposed involves exposing cultured RPE cells, such as ARPE-19, to oxidative insults (e.g., H₂O₂) that would otherwise induce excessive Drp1-mediated mitochondrial fission. P110’s mode of action is anticipated to specifically block the pathological protein-protein interaction between Drp1 and Fis1, thereby reducing the formation of excessively fragmented mitochondria and promoting the preservation or re-establishment of a tubular mitochondrial network. This intact network is critical for efficient ATP production, which in turn supports high-energy processes such as the phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS). POS phagocytosis is a metabolically demanding function that is crucial for photoreceptor renewal and overall retinal health. By maintaining ATP supply and preventing the release of pro-apoptotic factors (such as cytochrome c), P110 is expected to protect RPE cells from oxidative damage and improve cellular viability under stress conditions (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Yako et al., 2021). Additionally, studies have demonstrated that mitochondrial fission inhibitors can lead to improved mitochondrial membrane potential (MMP), reduced reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation, and enhanced cell survival under conditions of oxidative insult (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Yako et al., 2021). In RPE cells, these improvements translate into a better capacity for POS uptake and metabolism, which are essential for sustaining the metabolic demands of the outer retina. Given that expression levels of Drp1 and its functional activity are elevated in AMD RPE cells, as evidenced by electron microscopy and proteomic analyses showing reduced mitochondrial numbers, diminished cristae, and defective fusion/fission ratios, the application of P110 is expected to counteract these detrimental changes by stabilizing the mitochondrial network (Fisher et al., 2022; Yako et al., 2021).

Overall Evaluation:  
In summarizing the overall evaluation of P110 as a therapeutic candidate for dry age-related macular degeneration, several key points emerge from the literature. First, the mechanistic rationale underpinning P110’s mode of action is robust and well-aligned with current understanding of AMD pathophysiology. Excessive Drp1-mediated mitochondrial fission has been implicated as a crucial driver of mitochondrial dysfunction in RPE cells—a hallmark of dry AMD. Several studies using alternative approaches such as pharmacological inhibition with Mdivi-1 or genetic knockdown via siRNA have consistently demonstrated that mitigating aberrant mitochondrial fission leads to improved mitochondrial integrity, preserved bioenergetic function, and enhanced cell viability in models of oxidative stress (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Yako et al., 2021). This information directly supports the hypothesis that targeting the Drp1/Fis1 interaction, rather than globally inhibiting all Drp1 activity, could offer a more refined therapeutic approach with potentially fewer side effects. Such specificity is particularly appealing in the context of the retina where finely tuned mitochondrial dynamics are essential for high energy-demand processes like POS phagocytosis (Fisher et al., 2022).

One of the primary strengths of P110 lies in its cell-permeable peptide nature, which facilitates targeted intracellular delivery—a critical characteristic for therapies intended for ocular application. Its design, which specifically disrupts the interaction between Drp1 and Fis1, is predicated on the notion that pathological fission can be selectively blocked without interfering with the physiological fission necessary for regular mitochondrial turnover and repair. This specificity could, in theory, translate to a better safety profile compared to less selective inhibitors such as Mdivi-1 that may have off-target effects, including undesirable impacts on other aspects of mitochondrial function (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Fisher et al., 2022; Zhao et al., 2025).

Despite the promising mechanistic rationale and potential for ocular development, there are notable weaknesses and challenges to be considered. The current literature does not yet offer direct preclinical or clinical evidence that P110 peptide itself has been used to treat dry AMD. Most existing studies have extrapolated the benefits of Drp1 inhibition from experiments involving Mdivi-1 or Drp1 knockdown in cellular models of RPE oxidative stress (Yako et al., 2021; Buonfiglio et al., 2024). Therefore, while the concept of targeting Drp1-mediated mitochondrial fission in AMD is well supported, the direct application of P110 remains largely theoretical at this point. This gap in the literature introduces uncertainty regarding the peptide’s pharmacokinetic properties, its stability in ocular tissues, and its potential immunogenic responses upon local administration in the eye.

Another potential limitation is the complex role of mitochondrial dynamics in cellular homeostasis. Although excessive fission in the context of oxidative stress is detrimental, mitochondrial fission is also a necessary process for mitophagy and the removal of damaged organelles. Some studies have indicated that a certain degree of fission may even be beneficial for cellular quality control, as it facilitates the segregation and subsequent removal of malfunctioning mitochondria (Skeie et al., 2021; Yako et al., 2021). The nuanced interplay between reactive oxygen species (ROS) signaling and fission means that complete inhibition of fission—even if intended to be only pathological—could potentially have unintended consequences. It will be critical to determine whether P110’s selective inhibition of Drp1/Fis1 interaction can maintain the necessary balance between inhibiting excessive fission while still allowing physiological fission to contribute to normal mitophagy and mitochondrial turnover.

Furthermore, while the peptide’s cell-permeability is an advantage, peptide therapeutics in ocular applications face challenges related to delivery, degradation by ocular proteases, and potential issues with achieving sustained concentrations in the target tissues. Addressing these challenges may require the development of specialized drug delivery systems, such as intravitreal injections with sustained-release formulations or conjugation to nanoparticles, to ensure that adequate therapeutic levels of P110 are maintained at the retinal level over the necessary duration (Yako et al., 2021; Buonfiglio et al., 2024).

Additional practical concerns include the need for rigorous in vivo studies in relevant animal models of dry AMD to assess not only the efficacy in preserving mitochondrial function and POS phagocytosis in RPE cells but also the overall impact on retinal structure and visual function. Currently, many studies have been limited to in vitro models using ARPE-19 cells under oxidative stress conditions. Although these models provide valuable mechanistic insights, they do not fully recapitulate the complex interplay of cellular and systemic factors that contribute to AMD in vivo. The therapeutic potential of P110 will need to be evaluated in animal models that mimic the pathophysiological conditions of dry AMD, where factors such as chronic low-grade inflammation, complement activation, and cumulative oxidative damage play significant roles (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Fisher et al., 2022; Yako et al., 2021).

In addition to efficacy and safety concerns, the regulatory landscape for peptide therapeutics in ocular indications should be considered. The development of P110 for dry AMD will require detailed pharmacodynamic and toxicological evaluations to satisfy regulatory requirements. While the peptide’s mechanism—targeting a well-characterized protein-protein interaction—provides a clear scientific rationale, the path toward clinical translation is contingent on demonstrating not only mechanistic efficacy but also an acceptable safety profile in both preclinical toxicology studies and early-phase clinical trials (Fisher et al., 2022; ClinicalTrials.gov, n.d.).

In conclusion, the comprehensive literature review supports the notion that targeting mitochondrial dysfunction, specifically through the inhibition of Drp1-mediated mitochondrial fission, is a highly promising therapeutic avenue for dry AMD. P110, as a selective inhibitor of the Drp1/Fis1 interaction, is well poised within this framework. The candidate is grounded in a strong mechanistic rationale that links excessive mitochondrial fission to reduced ATP production, impaired POS phagocytosis, and ultimately, RPE cell dysfunction—a cascade of events that underlies the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Fisher et al., 2022).

The inherent advantages of a peptide-based therapeutic, including its specificity and cell-permeability, are particularly attractive for ocular drug development, where targeted delivery and minimal off-target effects are crucial. Nonetheless, notable weaknesses remain that must be addressed before P110 can be considered a viable therapeutic candidate for dry AMD. The absence of direct experimental data with P110 in AMD models, the complex nature of mitochondrial dynamics where inhibition of fission must be carefully balanced to avoid impairing critical mitophagy processes, and potential challenges associated with peptide stability and delivery in the ocular environment represent significant hurdles. These challenges underscore the necessity for further preclinical investigations, including in vivo efficacy and safety studies in animal models that recapitulate the chronic oxidative stress and metabolic derangements characteristic of AMD (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Yako et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2025).

Ultimately, while the theoretical basis for P110’s use in dry AMD is compelling and supported by a considerable body of literature showing beneficial effects of mitochondrial fission inhibition in RPE cells, advancing this candidate will require a coordinated effort to fill the current gaps in experimental evidence. Future studies should focus on validating the efficacy of P110 in terms of restoring mitochondrial dynamics, preserving ATP production, and ultimately improving POS phagocytosis in both cell culture and animal models of AMD. If these studies yield positive results, P110 has the potential to become an important component of a new generation of therapies aimed at addressing the mitochondrial dysfunction that lies at the heart of dry AMD pathophysiology (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Fisher et al., 2022; Yako et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2025).

Overall, the research direction for P110 is promising given the established relationship between mitochondrial dysfunction and AMD. With its targeted mechanism of action and a strong conceptual basis rooted in the modulation of mitochondrial dynamics, P110 stands as a high-potential candidate. However, careful optimization of dosing, formulation, and delivery, as well as comprehensive preclinical validation, is essential before this therapeutic candidate can be reliably advanced into clinical trials. Should these hurdles be successfully overcome, P110 could not only provide substantial therapeutic benefit by preserving RPE function in dry AMD but also serve as a model for developing other targeted mitochondrial therapies in ocular neurodegeneration (Buonfiglio et al., 2024; Yako et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2025).
