Proposal for SB 290157 (C3aR antagonist; Sigma-Aldrich Cat. No. SML 0740)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
SB 290157 (N2-[(2,2-diphenylethoxy)acetyl]-L-arginine) is a synthetic, low–molecular-weight, nonpeptide ligand originally discovered in a SmithKline Beecham high-throughput radioligand displacement screen (~240,000 compounds) for inhibitors of human C3a binding to membranes from RBL-2H3 cells stably expressing C3aR; subsequent medicinal chemistry optimization of the initial hit (SKF 63649) yielded SB 290157 with markedly improved potency and cross-species activity at C3aR (human, mouse, guinea pig) (Ames et al., 2001). The compound is typically supplied as a trifluoroacetate salt by commercial vendors and has been used extensively as a pharmacological tool compound in vitro and in vivo, including ocular and non-ocular models (Li et al., 2021; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). Chemically, SB 290157 is an arginine derivative bearing a 2,2-diphenylethoxyacetyl N2-acyl substituent; synthetic steps reported by the discovery group used Fmoc/Boc protection of arginine on Wang resin, coupling of tert-butyl(2,2-diphenylethoxy)acetate via carbodiimide/DMAP, and final deprotection with TFA to give the target amide (Ames et al., 2001). In the original pharmacological characterization, SB 290157 behaved as a competitive C3aR antagonist in radioligand binding and functional assays in recombinant cells and primary neutrophils, with reported low-nanomolar functional potency in Ca2+-mobilization and platelet ATP-release assays; selectivity was claimed versus C5aR and other neutrophil chemoattractant GPCRs in those systems (Ames et al., 2001). The class of nonpeptide C3aR-directed small molecules has been pursued largely as research tools and preclinical probes of anaphylatoxin biology; SB 290157 is the prototypical representative and has been used across diverse inflammatory models to interrogate complement C3a–C3aR signaling (Ames et al., 2001).

Therapeutic History  
- Foundational pharmacology and in vivo anti-inflammatory activity: SB 290157 was reported in 2001 to inhibit C3a-induced responses in multiple cell systems and to reduce inflammation in rodent models, including decreased neutrophil accumulation in a guinea pig LPS-induced airway neutrophilia model and attenuation of paw edema in a rat adjuvant-induced arthritis (AIA) model when dosed intraperitoneally twice daily (b.i.d.) at up to 30 mg/kg (Ames et al., 2001). Pharmacokinetics in guinea pigs after a single 30 mg/kg i.p. dose showed high Cmax (~7000 ng/ml), sustained plasma levels (>100 ng/ml at 8 h), and a short apparent half-life (~0.9 h) (Ames et al., 2001). In ex vivo vascular assays, SB 290157 blocked C3a-induced increases in perfused rat caudal artery pressure and prevented receptor internalization in neutrophils, supporting functional antagonism in those readouts (Ames et al., 2001).  
- Ocular/retinal relevance: In an in vitro human fetal retinal pigment epithelium (hfRPE) transwell model, chronic recombinant human C3a exposure for two weeks drove sub-RPE extracellular matrix (ECM) accumulation and wide-spaced collagen deposition, which were prevented by co-treatment with SB 290157 at 10 µM (trifluoroacetate salt); the antagonist did not impair transepithelial resistance or monolayer morphology (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). Mechanistically in the same hfRPE system, C3a impaired ubiquitin–proteasome pathway (UPP) activity and selectively elevated basal MMP-2 activity without changing proteasome-subunit mRNA, while promoting deposition of collagens IV and VI; these C3a-driven effects were reported to be abrogated by a C3aR antagonist, consistent with C3aR-mediated pathology in RPE (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). In vivo, SB 290157 was used in a laser-induced retinal vein occlusion (RVO) mouse model where pharmacologic blockade of C3a/C3aR reduced fluorescein leakage, retinal thickness abnormalities, disorganization of inner retinal layers (DRIL), and serous detachment height, improved ERG b-wave and oscillatory potentials, and suppressed inflammatory gene programs (DEGs enriched for chemokine/NF-κB/IL-17 pathways); the authors explicitly note known pharmacological limitations of SB 290157 including potential off-target and agonist actions (Zhao et al., 2025). Genetic evidence relevant to ocular disease includes partial protection in light-damage models: global C3aR deletion decelerated retinal thinning after light insult, although photoreceptor apoptosis levels (TUNEL) were not significantly altered, suggesting C3aR contributes to retinal structural change but not necessarily acute photoreceptor death in that model (Behnke et al., 2025).  
- Broader in vivo applications and cautions: SB 290157 has been used to probe complement biology in diverse indications, with reported benefits in models of lupus nephritis, antibody-induced arthritis, thromboembolic stroke, and AD-related cognition; however, many of these reports predate or did not control for later-recognized pharmacology (partial agonism, off-targets), which complicates interpretation (Li et al., 2021; Coulthard & Woodruff, 2015). In a mouse cuprizone demyelination model, intraperitoneal SB 290157 at 1 mg/kg every other day modulated astrocyte reactivity (GFAP), TNF-α dynamics, and complement deposition (C3d), with the dosing choice explicitly motivated to minimize off-target C5aR engagement; nevertheless, the authors caution about SB 290157’s weak C5aR agonism and interpretability of systemic dosing (Frankle, 2023). In neuropathic pain (spared nerve injury), SB 290157 acutely reversed mechanical hypersensitivity but is limited by a short half-life (~1.5 h) and known off-target/agonist properties (Cook, 2019).  
- Pharmacological controversies and off-target receptor activity: Soon after its introduction, independent groups reported that SB 290157 exhibits C3aR agonist/partial-agonist activity in multiple cell systems, with potency dependent on receptor density and assay context; examples include near-maximal Ca2+ mobilization in transfected RBL cells, NAG release in differentiated U-937 cells, and ATP release in guinea pig platelets, whereas it appeared antagonistic in other systems (e.g., guinea pig platelets with very low receptor expression) (Mathieu et al., 2005). More recently, SB 290157 was shown to be a partial agonist at C5aR2 (β-arrestin recruitment EC50 ~16 µM; partial efficacy vs C5a) and to dampen C5a-induced ERK signaling in macrophages, introducing a mechanistically plausible anti-inflammatory off-target pathway at commonly used concentrations (Li et al., 2021). Practical dosing analyses indicate that in vivo exposures at commonly used doses (>10 mg/kg i.p. or >0.3 mg/kg i.v.) will engage both C3aR and C5aR2, and high-dose use has been associated with adverse effects in animals (neutropenia, transient hypertension, weight gain, hematopoietic effects, tachycardia) (Li et al., 2021). Finally, modern C3aR signaling work demonstrates SB 290157 is a potent C3aR agonist that drives Gi/o/z activation and strong β-arrestin–dependent internalization, which can masquerade as “antagonism” in Ca2+ flux assays by depleting surface receptors and calcium stores; this β-arrestin–driven internalization explains many prior contradictory results (Rodriguez et al., 2024).  

Importantly, no published animal model of drusen or geographic atrophy using SB 290157 is identified in the provided context; evidence for drusen/sub-RPE deposit modulation by SB 290157 is restricted to in vitro hfRPE systems, while in vivo ocular use has been reported in RVO, which is a vascular occlusive disease and mechanistically distinct from dry AMD (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018; Zhao et al., 2025).  

Mechanism of Action  
- Target and signaling context: C3aR (C3aR1) is a class A GPCR canonically activated by the complement anaphylatoxin C3a; it couples preferentially to Gi/o/z to inhibit cAMP, mobilize Ca2+, and recruit β-arrestins to mediate receptor internalization and signaling bias, with expression across immune and stromal cells, including microglia/macrophages, neutrophils, mast cells, and ocular cells (Müller cells, microglia, macrophages, vascular endothelium), and on human RPE in vitro (Rodriguez et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2025; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). C3a/C3aR signaling has been implicated in RPE dysfunction and retinal pathologies through both pro-inflammatory outputs (e.g., VEGF upregulation, leukocyte recruitment) and tissue remodeling (ECM deposition) (Kleinman & Ambati, 2016; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).  
- SB 290157 at C3aR: Original reports characterized SB 290157 as a competitive C3aR antagonist in binding and functional assays, demonstrating inhibition of C3a-induced Ca2+ mobilization (IC50 ~27.7 nM in human RBL-C3aR cells; low-nanomolar potency across species) and blockade of receptor internalization and smooth muscle contractile responses (Ames et al., 2001). Later work showed that SB 290157 can behave as a partial/full agonist in multiple expression systems, with potency strongly influenced by receptor density; in overexpression models (CHO-C3aR), SB 290157 induced ERK1/2 phosphorylation with an EC50 ~0.46 nM and near-maximal efficacy relative to C3a, while in some primary systems (e.g., HMDMs) it did not exhibit agonism up to 100 µM yet inhibited C3a-induced ERK with an IC50 ~236 nM (Li et al., 2021). Orthogonal signaling profiling confirmed that SB 290157 is a potent C3aR agonist across Gi/o/z subtypes and is highly efficacious at β-arrestin recruitment/internalization; antagonism observed in Ca2+ assays can arise from this strong internalization blocking subsequent G-protein signaling (effects unmasked by barbadin or Pitstop-2), i.e., SB 290157 acts as a biased agonist with dominant β-arrestin/internalization bias in many contexts (Rodriguez et al., 2024).  
- SB 290157 at other complement receptors: Counter-screening revealed no activation of C5aR1 in the tested ERK readout, but consistent partial agonism at C5aR2 (β-arrestin2 recruitment EC50 ~16.1 µM; ~31% efficacy vs C5a), with functional consequences including attenuation of C5a-induced ERK signaling in human and mouse macrophages; thus, SB 290157 can engage anti-inflammatory C5aR2 pathways at micromolar concentrations (Li et al., 2021). Importantly, in vivo exposures at common doses are predicted to co-engage both C3aR and C5aR2, complicating mechanistic attribution (Li et al., 2021).  
- RPE-specific pathomechanisms and C3aR blockade: In primary hfRPE, C3a binds basolateral C3aR and triggers a cascade leading to sub-RPE ECM accumulation: (i) decreased proteasome (UPP) activity without changes in proteasome-subunit mRNA, indicating post-transcriptional downregulation; (ii) dysregulation of ECM turnover via increased basal MMP-2 activity and reduced TIMP-3 (markedly reduced TIMP-3 with proteasome inhibitor MG-132), consistent with enhanced collagenase activity; and (iii) increased deposition of collagen IV and VI beneath the RPE monolayer (dose- and time-dependent), without changes in collagen I or EFEMP1 (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). C3a exposure increased C3aR expression/localization on RPE basolateral membranes, while a C3aR antagonist prevented the C3a-driven proteasome impairment, MMP-2 elevation, and accumulation of basal deposits in this model (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). Notably, C3a did not acutely alter intracellular calcium in these RPE cultures, suggesting RPE-specific signaling architecture differs from classic immune cell paradigms; the antagonist’s protective effects in RPE thus map to UPP/ECM modulation rather than Ca2+-dependent degranulation (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).  
- Potency considerations: Reported SB 290157 binding affinity to C3aR is in the low-hundreds of nanomolar range (competition IC50 ~500 ± 250 nM; Ki ~210 ± 90 nM in membrane binding), whereas functional potencies span 7–30 nM in many GPCR Ca2+ or platelet assays; in HMDMs, C3a-ERK inhibition IC50 ~236 nM has been reported, and in hfRPE studies the antagonist was used at 10 µM without a defined IC50 in that context (Mathieu et al., 2005; Ames et al., 2001; Li et al., 2021; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). These disparities emphasize system-specific pharmacodynamics and the need for concentration–response characterization in RPE.  

Expected Effect  
The proposed hypothesis is that SB 290157 will competitively inhibit C3aR on RPE (IC50 ~500 nM), thereby preventing C3a-driven proteasome dysregulation and sub-RPE deposit formation, restoring proteostasis and improving photoreceptor outer segment (POS) uptake and degradation in dry AMD RPE cultures. Available data from the hfRPE system strongly support the first two mechanistic links—C3a promotes basal deposit formation via UPP inhibition and MMP-2/TIMP-3 imbalance, and C3aR blockade with SB 290157 (10 µM) prevents those ECM/proteostasis changes and associated sub-RPE deposit formation without damaging the RPE monolayer (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). Specifically, in multi-week C3a exposures, antagonist co-treatment normalized ECM ultrastructure (SEM/TEM), blocked accumulation of collagens IV and VI beneath the RPE, prevented C3a-induced upregulation of C3aR expression, and preserved proteasome functional readouts, which together map to restoration of RPE proteostasis and ECM turnover in this model (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). These observations are consistent with the broader mechanistic framework that C3a–C3aR signaling at RPE can drive early AMD-like basal deposit formation and that C3aR antagonism can reverse the key biochemical drivers (UPP impairment and MMP-2/TIMP-3 dysregulation) underlying deposit accumulation (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).  
However, the “IC50 ~500 nM” statement matches binding competition in recombinant systems rather than functional antagonism in RPE; hfRPE studies used 10 µM without a reported potency or binding occupancy analysis in this cell type, and inhibitory potencies vary substantially across cell systems (7–30 nM in Ca2+ mobilization and platelet ATP-release assays, ~236 nM for ERK blockade in HMDMs) (Mathieu et al., 2005; Ames et al., 2001; Li et al., 2021; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). For the intended RPE assay, an empirical concentration–response curve is needed to establish the minimal effective concentration that prevents C3a-driven UPP and ECM changes, ideally bracketed below concentrations known to partially activate C5aR2 to avoid confounded anti-inflammatory signaling (Li et al., 2021). The claim that SB 290157 will improve POS uptake/degradation is not supported by the provided literature; neither the hfRPE work nor the broader SB 290157 pharmacology summarizes RPE phagocytosis or POS processing endpoints, and the signaling work documenting SB 290157 effects on phagocytosis pertains to microglia, not RPE (Rodriguez et al., 2024; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). Thus, while restoration of proteasome function may secondarily benefit proteostasis pathways relevant to POS degradation, this remains to be demonstrated in RPE and should be considered an untested hypothesis rather than an evidence-based expectation at this time (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).  
Expression of the pharmacological target in the assay system is established in vitro: C3aR is present on hfRPE basolateral membranes, is upregulated by C3a challenge, and mediates the proteasome/ECM phenotypes that are reversed by antagonist co-treatment (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). Complement-responsive cell types within the retina (e.g., Müller cells, microglia, macrophages, vascular endothelium) also express C3aR, providing mechanistic plausibility for in vivo effects of C3aR blockade in retinal disease models, although RVO pathobiology differs fundamentally from dry AMD (Zhao et al., 2025).  

Overall Evaluation  
SB 290157 engages a biologically compelling axis (C3a–C3aR) with direct mechanistic links to early dry AMD pathogenesis in RPE, but its complex and context-dependent pharmacology imposes significant risks for both interpretation and translational development. The totality of evidence supports continued use of C3aR antagonism as a mechanistic strategy in RPE, while casting doubt on SB 290157 as a development-grade candidate without substantial de-risking.  

Strengths  
- Disease-mechanism alignment in RPE: Chronic C3a exposure in hfRPE is sufficient to recapitulate sub-RPE ECM changes typical of early AMD (collagen IV/VI deposition, wide-spaced collagen, impaired UPP, elevated basal MMP-2), and C3aR antagonism with SB 290157 prevents these changes with preservation of barrier integrity, directly linking the pharmacological target to a core pathophysiology in dry AMD (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). This is among the strongest mechanistic anchors for any complement-modulatory strategy specifically at the RPE level in vitro.  
- Ocular in vivo proof-of-concept for C3aR blockade: In an RVO model (distinct from dry AMD), SB 290157 reduced clinical, imaging, and functional pathology and dampened retinal inflammatory transcriptional programs, supporting ocular efficacy when the C3a/C3aR axis is pathologically active in vivo (Zhao et al., 2025). Although RVO is not dry AMD, these data imply that C3aR antagonism can be delivered in vivo to the eye with measurable therapeutic impact on inflammation-driven retinal pathology.  
- Established discovery provenance and extensive preclinical use: The origin, synthesis, and extensive cross-species pharmacology of SB 290157 are well documented, facilitating procurement and standardized use as a pharmacologic probe in RPE assays; the compound is commercially available as a TFA salt and has been broadly applied in complementary models, enabling rapid head-to-head comparisons and orthogonal validation strategies (Ames et al., 2001; Li et al., 2021).  

Limitations and risks  
- Intrinsic pharmacology is not a clean “antagonist”: SB 290157 is a potent, biased C3aR agonist that robustly recruits β-arrestin and internalizes the receptor, and it partially activates C5aR2 at micromolar concentrations; both properties confound interpretation of putative antagonism and introduce off-target anti-inflammatory mechanisms at concentrations commonly used in vitro and in vivo (Rodriguez et al., 2024; Li et al., 2021; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). In particular, the 10 µM concentration effective in hfRPE lies in the range that can engage C5aR2, so anti-inflammatory effects may not be solely attributable to C3aR blockade (Li et al., 2021; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).  
- System-dependent behavior: SB 290157 displays agonism at C3aR in overexpression systems and certain endogenously expressing cells, but antagonizes readouts in others (e.g., human macrophages, guinea pig platelets), a pattern explained by receptor density and signaling bias; this variability raises concerns that RPE outcomes could depend on culture conditions (e.g., receptor upregulation by C3a) and surface expression levels in ways that shift net pharmacology (Mathieu et al., 2005; Rodriguez et al., 2024; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).  
- Dosing and translational exposure liabilities: In vivo, commonly used doses achieve plasma concentrations predicted to co-activate C5aR2 and/or trigger undesired systemic effects (neutropenia, cardiovascular changes); short half-life complicates chronic dosing paradigms, and ocular tissue exposure metrics are not defined for SB 290157 (Li et al., 2021; Ames et al., 2001; Mathieu et al., 2005; Zhao et al., 2025). While the RVO study demonstrates functional benefit, it also acknowledges SB 290157’s pharmacological limitations, emphasizing the need for sham controls and target validation beyond a single tool compound (Zhao et al., 2025).  
- Lack of in vivo dry AMD/drusen data: No in vivo evidence in the provided context demonstrates that SB 290157 reduces drusen or geographic atrophy in animal models; the in vitro hfRPE data are compelling but represent a reductionist system that does not capture subretinal immune cell interactions, Bruch’s membrane transport, or choriocapillaris alterations central to dry AMD pathogenesis (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).  
- POS uptake/degradation claim is unsubstantiated: The assertion that SB 290157 will improve RPE POS phagocytosis and degradation is not supported by the cited literature; no presented data quantify SB 290157 effects on RPE phagolysosomal function, and extrapolation from proteasome restoration to POS handling remains hypothetical (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).  

Recommendations for a decision path  
- Near-term, SB 290157 is suitable as a positive-control pharmacological tool for target validation in RPE culture under stringent controls, not as a development candidate. In hfRPE, reproduce and extend published findings under defined C3a challenges by:  
  • Determining a full concentration–response for SB 290157 (e.g., 30 nM to 10 µM) on UPP activity, basal MMP-2, TIMP-3 expression, and collagen IV/VI deposition, with parallel assessment of C3aR surface expression, to establish minimally effective concentrations and exclude pro-inflammatory or agonist-like effects at lower doses (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).  
  • Incorporating orthogonal target validation: C3aR knockdown/knockout in RPE (if feasible), and pharmacological controls to test C5aR2 involvement (e.g., C5aR2-selective agonism as a counter model, acknowledging that RPE C5aR2 expression is not defined here), plus use of alternative C3aR reagents (e.g., anti-C3aR antibodies) where practical (Li et al., 2021; Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).  
  • Adding phagocytosis endpoints (POS uptake, lysosomal degradation kinetics) to directly test the hypothesis that proteasome restoration by C3aR blockade enhances POS processing; these endpoints are currently unsupported (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018).  
  • Monitoring off-target and cytotoxicity signals, including β-arrestin–dependent internalization (if assayable) to correlate with functional outcomes and to avoid misinterpreting biased agonism as antagonism (Rodriguez et al., 2024).  
- For in vivo exploration, given the interpretability risks with SB 290157, de-emphasize systemic dosing and consider localized delivery paradigms and/or more selective C3aR agents if available. If SB 290157 must be used, constrain intraperitoneal dosing to ≤1 mg/kg to minimize C5aR2 engagement and track pharmacodynamic readouts consistent with RPE-centric mechanisms (e.g., basal laminar deposit markers, MMP-2/TIMP-3 balance) in AMD-relevant models, recognizing that no such drusen/GA mitigation data are currently available for SB 290157 (Li et al., 2021). Genetic models (C3aR deletion) provide partial support for retinal structural preservation after injury, but differ in mechanism and context from RPE-intrinsic deposit biology (Behnke et al., 2025).  
- Strategically, prioritize identification or design of true C3aR antagonists devoid of agonist/β-arrestin bias and C5aR2 activity, or evaluate upstream C3 blockade where ocular delivery and safety allow, as parallel development tracks. The need for improved C3aR ligands is highlighted repeatedly in the pharmacology literature due to SB 290157’s liabilities (Mathieu et al., 2005; Coulthard & Woodruff, 2015; Rodriguez et al., 2024).  

Conclusion  
On balance, C3aR antagonism remains an attractive target mechanism for early dry AMD based on robust RPE-centric in vitro data linking C3a–C3aR signaling to proteasome impairment, ECM dysregulation, and sub-RPE deposit formation, with SB 290157 acting as an effective tool compound to prevent these changes in hfRPE (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018). However, SB 290157’s complex pharmacology—potent biased C3aR agonism and partial C5aR2 agonism—creates substantial risks for misattributing mechanism and for translation, particularly at micromolar concentrations or systemic in vivo exposures where off-target signaling is likely (Rodriguez et al., 2024; Li et al., 2021). There is no in vivo evidence here that SB 290157 reduces drusen/geographic atrophy, and the claimed benefits for POS phagocytosis are unproven (Fernandez-Godino & Pierce, 2018; Zhao et al., 2025). As a result, I recommend using SB 290157 only as a controlled, short-term pharmacologic probe to (a) mechanistically validate the role of C3aR in RPE proteostasis/ECM biology and (b) set pharmacodynamic benchmarks for target engagement in RPE; in parallel, we should invest in sourcing or developing next-generation, selective C3aR antagonists with confirmed lack of agonism and C5aR2 activity for any advancement toward dry AMD models and, ultimately, clinical translation (Mathieu et al., 2005; Rodriguez et al., 2024; Coulthard & Woodruff, 2015).

hypothesis: Mdivi-1 (DRP1 inhibitor; Sigma-Aldrich Cat. No. M0199)
answer:
Proposal for Mdivi-1 (DRP1 inhibitor; Sigma-Aldrich Cat. No. M0199)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Mdivi-1 is a small molecule pharmacological agent originally discovered through high-throughput chemical screening in yeast models and subsequently characterized in mammalian systems as an inhibitor of mitochondrial fission. It is a quinazolinone derivative that belongs to a class of compounds targeting mitochondrial dynamics, with the specific intent of modulating the activity of dynamin-related protein 1 (DRP1) (Cassidy-Stone et al., 2008; Smith & Gallo, 2017). DRP1 is a large GTPase that mediates mitochondrial fission by undergoing self-assembly at constriction sites on the outer mitochondrial membrane and catalyzing membrane scission; under physiological conditions, this process is balanced by mitochondrial fusion activities to maintain mitochondrial morphology, bioenergetics, and quality control. Mdivi-1 was synthesized and later commercialized (e.g., Sigma-Aldrich Cat. No. M0199) because of its ability to selectively inhibit DRP1 activity, thereby shifting the balance away from excessive mitochondrial division and promoting a more interconnected, tubular mitochondrial network (Rosdah et al., 2016; Cassidy-Stone et al., 2008). This compound’s origins as a research tool in basic mitochondrial biology have led to its investigation in various disease models ranging from neurodegenerative conditions and cardiovascular ischemia to ocular disorders, where mitochondrial dysfunction is known to play a critical role. Its repurposing for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is of particular interest because of the emerging evidence linking chronic oxidative stress, mitochondrial fragmentation, and RPE (retinal pigment epithelium) dysfunction to AMD pathology (Yako et al., 2021; Somasundaran et al., 2020).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, Mdivi-1 has been extensively used in preclinical studies to interrogate the role of excessive mitochondrial fission in diverse pathological conditions. Initial seminal work demonstrated that inhibition of DRP1 activity by Mdivi-1 could prevent mitochondrial fragmentation, reduce cytochrome c release, and attenuate apoptosis in yeast and mammalian cell models (Cassidy-Stone et al., 2008; Rosdah et al., 2016). Following these foundational observations, several studies explored its utility in neuronal and cardiovascular systems. For example, preclinical investigations in models of ischemia-reperfusion injury, myocardial infarction, and neurodegeneration revealed that Mdivi-1 treatment increased cell survival and improved functional outcomes by preserving mitochondrial structure (Chen et al., 2023; Park et al., 2011).  

In the ocular domain, Mdivi-1 has been tested in models of retinal ischemia, glaucoma, and retinal detachment. Studies have shown that Mdivi-1 can increase the survival of retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) in settings of acute ischemic injury, and its administration in retinal detachment models improved photoreceptor survival by mitigating DRP1-mediated mitochondrial dysfunction (She et al., 2018; Park et al., 2011). Moreover, within RPE-specific research, there is evidence from ARPE-19 cell studies that Mdivi-1 can counteract H₂O₂-induced oxidative damage by preventing mitochondrial fragmentation and preserving mitochondrial membrane potential, thereby protecting cells from apoptosis (Yako et al., 2021). Although the majority of these studies have focused on acute oxidative stress paradigms, the use of Mdivi-1 in these diverse retinal models provides a strong rationale to explore its potential in treating dry AMD, a condition characterized by chronic RPE stress, impaired photoreceptor outer segment (POS) phagocytosis, and progressive mitochondrial dysfunction (Yako et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action:  
The molecular mechanism of Mdivi-1 centers on its inhibitory effect on DRP1, a critical regulator of mitochondrial fission. In a normally functioning cell, DRP1 resides in the cytosol and, upon activation—often triggered by cellular stress or proliferative signals—it translocates to the outer mitochondrial membrane. There, DRP1 self-assembles into oligomeric complexes that hydrolyze GTP to execute the fission process (Cassidy-Stone et al., 2008; Rosdah et al., 2016). Mdivi-1 acts by binding to an allosteric site on DRP1, thereby inhibiting its GTPase activity and preventing the oligomerization necessary for mitochondrial membrane constriction (Rosdah et al., 2016; Smith & Gallo, 2017). This inhibition not only prevents the excessive fragmentation of mitochondria under conditions of oxidative stress but also stabilizes mitochondrial membrane potential and curbs the release of pro-apoptotic factors such as cytochrome c (Yako et al., 2021).

At the biochemical level, studies using ARPE-19 cells have shown that Mdivi-1 treatment correlates with a significant reduction in markers of mitochondrial dysfunction—such as decreased cytochrome c leakage and improved maintenance of mitochondrial membrane potential—even when the cells are challenged with oxidative insults like H₂O₂ (Yako et al., 2021). These protective effects are central to the proposed hypothesis for dry AMD, where preservation of mitochondrial function in RPE is paramount for sustaining ATP production and supporting energy-demanding processes like POS phagocytosis.

It is important to note, however, that emerging evidence suggests that Mdivi-1’s actions may not be limited solely to DRP1 inhibition. Several studies have reported that Mdivi-1 also acts as a reversible inhibitor of mitochondrial Complex I of the electron transport chain (Marx et al., 2024; Avilan, 2023). This off-target effect can modulate reactive oxygen species (ROS) production and potentially influence cellular bioenergetics in a manner that might either contribute beneficially by reducing oxidative stress or detrimentally by impairing ATP production if the inhibition of Complex I is too pronounced. Such dual activity necessitates careful titration of Mdivi-1 dosing to ensure that the beneficial effects of DRP1 inhibition are not overshadowed by unwanted metabolic interference. Additionally, post-translational modifications of DRP1, such as phosphorylation at serine residues 616 and 637, modulate its activity and may influence the sensitivity of DRP1 to inhibition by Mdivi-1 in different cellular contexts (Yako et al., 2021). This complexity underscores the need for a thorough understanding of Mdivi-1’s molecular interactions in RPE cells and how these might translate to functional benefits in conditions like dry AMD.

Expected Effect:  
The central hypothesis guiding the proposed therapeutic application of Mdivi-1 in dry AMD is that by inhibiting excessive DRP1-mediated mitochondrial fission, the drug will preserve the integrity of the mitochondrial network in RPE cells. This preservation is critical because RPE cells rely heavily on mitochondria to generate ATP, which in turn is essential for energy-dependent processes such as the phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) (Yako et al., 2021). Under oxidative stress conditions—conditions that mimic the chronic environmental challenges faced by the RPE in dry AMD—excessive mitochondrial fragmentation leads to diminished ATP production and impaired phagocytic function. In vitro studies using ARPE-19 cells have provided evidence that treatment with Mdivi-1 can normalize mitochondrial morphology, preserve mitochondrial membrane potential, and reduce the release of cytochrome c, all of which contribute to maintaining cellular ATP levels (Yako et al., 2021).

In the context of the proposed assay, Mdivi-1 is expected to act at an effective concentration—hypothetically around an IC₅₀ of ~1 µM—to inhibit excessive mitochondrial fission in stressed RPE cells. By stabilizing mitochondrial dynamics, RPE cells should be able to sustain adequate ATP production even under conditions of oxidative challenge, thereby directly supporting the energy-demanding process of POS phagocytosis. This is critical because efficient phagocytosis is a cornerstone of RPE function; failure to clear shed photoreceptor debris leads to the formation of drusen and the accumulation of lipofuscin, both hallmark features of dry AMD pathology (Yako et al., 2021).

Moreover, improved mitochondrial function should also contribute to the normalization of lysosomal pH—a factor that is important for the proper degradation of phagocytosed material. Together, these effects are anticipated to not only preserve cellular viability in the face of chronic oxidative stress but also enhance the functional capacity of the RPE to process photoreceptor debris, which in turn could slow or halt the progression of dry AMD. However, it is crucial to achieve a delicate balance in dosing; while low concentrations might yield the desired protective effects by selectively inhibiting DRP1, higher concentrations run the risk of triggering off-target Complex I inhibition, with a subsequent decrease in ATP production that would be counterproductive in an energy-deficient cell (Marx et al., 2024; Avilan, 2023). Thus, while the expected effect is highly promising, it is contingent upon precise dose optimization and careful validation in both acute and chronic RPE models.

Overall Evaluation:  
Taken together, the literature supports the potential of Mdivi-1 as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry AMD, predicated on its capacity to inhibit DRP1-mediated mitochondrial fission and preserve mitochondrial network integrity in RPE cells. The compound’s strength lies in its well-documented ability to prevent mitochondrial fragmentation, maintain mitochondrial membrane potential, and reduce apoptotic signaling under conditions of oxidative stress, which are all pivotal factors in the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Yako et al., 2021). Preclinical studies in various retinal and neurodegenerative models further bolster the case for its broader applicability in ocular diseases; evidence from glaucoma and retinal detachment models, as well as in ARPE-19 cell studies, suggests that modulating mitochondrial dynamics can offer significant neuroprotective benefits (Cueva-Vargas et al., 2025; Park et al., 2011; She et al., 2018).

Nonetheless, several weaknesses temper the enthusiasm for Mdivi-1’s clinical translation in dry AMD. One of the primary concerns is the duality in its mechanism of action. Although Mdivi-1 is primarily characterized as a DRP1 inhibitor, multiple studies have raised valid concerns regarding its off-target effects, notably its inhibition of mitochondrial Complex I at higher doses (Marx et al., 2024; Avilan, 2023). This is particularly significant in the context of RPE cells, which are highly dependent on robust mitochondrial function and efficient ATP production to sustain their phagocytic and metabolic activities. Inadvertent inhibition of Complex I could lead to decreased ATP synthesis and an accumulation of ROS, thereby exacerbating rather than alleviating cellular dysfunction—an outcome that would be highly undesirable in a disease like dry AMD.

Another key issue is the apparent variability in effective dosing. While some studies report cytoprotective effects at concentrations around 1–10 µM, others have employed doses up to 50 µM to observe meaningful modulatory effects on mitochondrial dynamics (Yako et al., 2021). Such variability suggests that the effective therapeutic window might be narrow, and that even minor deviations in dosing could result in suboptimal efficacy or unintended toxicity. Notably, some in vitro studies using ARPE-19 cells have demonstrated that higher concentrations of Mdivi-1 can lead to cytotoxicity, raising concerns about its safety profile for long-term use in the retina (Shulman et al., 2010).

Additionally, while the hypothesis underlying the current proposal—that inhibition of excessive mitochondrial fission can restore ATP production and thereby improve POS phagocytosis—is mechanistically sound, direct evidence linking Mdivi-1 treatment to enhanced phagocytic function in RPE cells remains somewhat preliminary. Most of the existing literature has focused on acute protective effects in response to oxidative stress rather than on the chronic functional deficits observed in dry AMD (Yako et al., 2021). This gap in the literature signals a need for more targeted studies that evaluate not only the biochemical and morphological endpoints but also the functional outcomes, such as phagocytotic efficiency, in models that closely mimic the chronic nature of AMD.

Furthermore, the complex intracellular milieu of the RPE—characterized by high metabolic demand, ongoing phagocytosis of photoreceptor outer segments, and a finely balanced process of autophagy and lysosomal degradation—means that interventions must be precisely calibrated. Chronic inhibition of mitochondrial fission, if not tightly controlled, could disrupt normal mitophagy (the selective removal of damaged mitochondria) and impair cellular turnover processes, potentially leading to the accumulation of dysfunctional mitochondria over time (Lin et al., 2024; Rosdah et al., 2016). Therefore, while the short-term benefits of Mdivi-1 are encouraging, its long-term impact on overall mitochondrial quality control and cellular homeostasis in RPE cells remains an open question.

From a translational standpoint, Mdivi-1’s established use in several preclinical ocular models is a significant strength, as it facilitates the leveraging of existing data and methodologies in further studies designed to address dry AMD specifically (Cueva-Vargas et al., 2025; Park et al., 2011; She et al., 2018). Moreover, the absence of current effective treatments for dry AMD underscores the urgency of pursuing novel therapeutic approaches that target its underlying pathophysiology. In this regard, the idea of preserving mitochondrial integrity to support energy-dependent processes like photoreceptor outer segment phagocytosis is particularly compelling (Yako et al., 2021).

In conclusion, while Mdivi-1 exhibits several attractive features as a candidate for dry AMD therapy—including the ability to modulate mitochondrial dynamics, preserve ATP production, and reduce oxidative stress—the existing body of evidence also highlights critical challenges that must be overcome. These include resolving the controversy surrounding its off-target effects on Complex I, establishing a reliable and safe dosing regimen, and generating direct evidence linking its use to functional improvements in RPE phagocytosis in models that accurately reflect the chronic nature of dry AMD (Yako et al., 2021; Marx et al., 2024; Avilan, 2023). Provided that these challenges are addressed through rigorous preclinical studies and careful dose optimization, Mdivi-1 remains a promising candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD.

Overall, our evaluation indicates that Mdivi-1 holds considerable potential as a therapeutic agent for dry age-related macular degeneration by targeting the mitochondrial dysfunction that is central to RPE pathology. Its ability to inhibit DRP1 and thereby reduce oxidative stress-induced mitochondrial fragmentation could preserve critical cellular functions such as ATP production and photoreceptor outer segment phagocytosis, offering a novel mechanism of action to address this currently untreatable condition. However, the possibility of off-target Complex I inhibition and dose-dependent cytotoxicity underscore the need for further detailed mechanistic studies and dose-ranging experiments in both in vitro and in vivo models that better simulate the chronic progression of dry AMD. With these challenges appropriately managed, Mdivi-1 could potentially become an innovative mitochondrial-based therapeutic for a disease desperately in need of effective intervention (Yako et al., 2021; Marx et al., 2024; Avilan, 2023).

hypothesis: MCC950 (NLRP3 inhibitor; InvivoGen Cat. No. tlrl-mcc)
answer:
Proposal for MCC950 (NLRP3 inhibitor; InvivoGen Cat. No. tlrl-mcc)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
MCC950 is a synthetic diarylsulfonylurea small molecule originally identified from an IL-1β processing inhibitor chemotype and later defined as a highly potent and selective inhibitor of the NLRP3 inflammasome complex (Coll et al., 2015). Within the inflammasome‐inhibitor landscape, MCC950 is representative of sulfonylurea‐based NLRP3 inhibitors that block canonical and noncanonical NLRP3 activation while sparing other inflammasomes (AIM2, NLRC4, NLRP1) and upstream innate pathways (e.g., TLR-NF-κB priming) (Coll et al., 2015; Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018). Mechanistically, MCC950 acts directly on NLRP3 to prevent assembly of the adaptor ASC (apoptosis‐associated speck-like protein containing a CARD) into oligomeric “specks,” thereby preventing caspase-1 activation and maturation of IL-1β and IL-18 (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018). Follow-on mechanistic analyses indicate MCC950 binds the NLRP3 NACHT domain to inhibit its ATPase function and thereby prevent NLRP3 activation; mechanistic models include prevention of ASC oligomerization and disruption of required conformations for NEK7–NLRP3 cooperation during sensor activation (Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Zheng et al., 2023).

This class (selective NLRP3 inhibitors) has been broadly leveraged in preclinical inflammatory disease models to selectively blunt inflammasome‐driven IL-1 family cytokine maturation and pyroptosis without pan‐suppressing innate immune sensing, with documented in vivo efficacy in autoimmune encephalomyelitis, CAPS (NLRP3 gain‐of‐function), spontaneous colitis, atherosclerosis, and myocardial infarction models (Coll et al., 2015; Perera et al., 2018; Zeng et al., 2021; Wooff et al., 2020). In ocular biology, several sulfonylurea NLRP3 inhibitors—including MCC950 and chemically related CRID3/IFM compounds—reduce IL-1β secretion and cell lysis in human RPE models and ex vivo mouse RPE/choroid eye cups under diverse AMD‐relevant triggers (lysosomal membrane permeabilization, oxidative/photooxidative stress, and P2X7 activation) (Wang et al., 2019; Korhonen, 2024).

Therapeutic History  
Systemic and non‐ocular indications. MCC950 has repeatedly shown robust pharmacodynamic suppression of inflammasome outputs and disease modification in vivo. Oral dosing in a spontaneous colitis model suppressed IL-1β/IL-18 production ex vivo and improved clinical/histopathologic indices (Perera et al., 2018). In APC‐driven autoimmune encephalomyelitis and in CAPS, MCC950 reduced IL-1β production and ameliorated disease; in CAPS it rescued neonatal lethality (Coll et al., 2015). In ApoE-deficient mice, MCC950 reduced atherosclerotic plaque burden, intraplaque macrophages, and systemic TNF-α/IL-1β/IL-6/IL-18 (Zeng et al., 2021). Across these studies MCC950 demonstrates in vivo target engagement, cytokine suppression, and disease modification with high selectivity for NLRP3 (Coll et al., 2015; Perera et al., 2018; Zeng et al., 2021). However, translational reviews emphasize that many NLRP3 inhibitors—including MCC950‐class agents—face liabilities for organ penetration (including eye/brain) and potential liver toxicity, underscoring formulation/delivery and safety risks that must be addressed for ocular use (Ortega et al., 2024).

Ocular and retinal contexts. In the ischemic OIR model, MCC950 lowered retinal neovascularization and vascular leakage and shifted an aberrant cytokine balance (decreased IL-1β activity with increased IL-18 activity), with accompanying reductions in angiogenesis‐ and pericyte‐associated signaling molecules (VEGF, VEGFR1/2, MMP2/9, PDGFR-β, Ang2) and evidence of inflammasome activation localized predominantly to macrophages (F4/80+) over endothelium (Sui et al., 2020a; Sui et al., 2020b; Sui et al., 2020c). In a glaucoma model (DBA/2J), MCC950 reduced NLRP3 and cleaved caspase-1 in retina and mitigated retinal ganglion cell loss independently of intraocular pressure, indicating on‐target retinal neuroinflammation suppression (Li, 2020).

By contrast, in a laser‐induced CNV model (wet AMD), short‐course MCC950 lowered IL-1β transcript/protein but paradoxically increased total CNV lesion volume and recruitment of microglia and monocyte‐derived macrophages; ERG a- and b-waves were unchanged, suggesting no gross electrophysiological toxicity under those conditions (Dieckmann et al., 2024a; Dieckmann et al., 2024b). This aligns with genetic evidence that inflammasome–IL-1β signaling promotes CNV largely through macrophages/microglia and that non‐NLRP3 inflammasomes also contribute, implying that selectively inhibiting NLRP3 may have complex, context‐dependent effects in neovascular disease (Marneros, 2023a; Marneros, 2023b).

In dry‐AMD–relevant photo‐oxidative damage (PD), intravitreal MCC950 failed to rescue function/structure and high‐dose MCC950 worsened ERG amplitudes: 20 µM showed no functional change versus PBS and did not alter photoreceptor death or IBA-1+ microglia counts; 100 µM significantly reduced ERG function (Wooff et al., 2020b). In the same study, Casp1/11−/− mice exhibited strong protection, whereas Nlrp3−/− mice showed only partial functional preservation, and pharmacologic NLRP3 inhibition or Nlrp3 siRNA provided no benefit (and in some readouts reduced function), leading to the conclusion that downstream caspase-1 is a dominant driver whereas NLRP3 may be neither necessary nor sufficient in this model (Wooff et al., 2020a; Wooff et al., 2020b). The authors also highlighted uncertainties about NLRP3 localization (predominantly INL/GCL rather than RPE), protein detection sensitivity, and the absence of ocular pharmacokinetic data for MCC950 (Wooff et al., 2020b).

RPE cell and ex vivo ocular models. In IL-1α–primed ARPE-19 and primary human RPE (pRPE), sulfonylurea NLRP3 inhibitors reduced inflammasome activation and cell injury across diverse triggers relevant to GA, including LMP (Leu-Leu-OMe), oxidative stress (H₂O₂), lipofuscin/photooxidative insult (HNE-POS + blue light), and P2X7 activation (BzATP); in Abca4−/− eye cups, selective NLRP3 inhibitors suppressed IL-1β and LDH release and preserved RPE morphology after blue‐light irradiation (Wang et al., 2019; Korhonen, 2024). A 2024 synthesis that included MCC950 reports that MCC950, IFM-632, and IFM-514 each decreased IL-1α-primed RPE inflammasome activation independent of the activation trigger, consistent with target class effects in RPE models (Korhonen, 2024). These in vitro/ex vivo data strongly support that NLRP3 activity can be engaged in RPE and that selective, small‐molecule inhibition suppresses canonical outputs (IL-1β, LDH) under multiple AMD‐relevant insults. However, detailed analyses of autophagic flux restoration or lysosomal integrity rescue after MCC950 are not reported in these excerpts (Wang et al., 2019).

Emerging genetics for AMD‐relevant deposits. In a monogenic EFEMP1 R345W knockin model (ML/DHRD) that recapitulates basal laminar deposits (BLamDs), as well as in aged WT mice, whole‐animal deletion of Nlrp3 or Casp1 significantly reduced BLamD size/coverage, normalized proinflammatory retinal cytokine profiles, and reduced microglial activation; these data provide genetic causality linking NLRP3–caspase-1 activity to deposit formation and inflammatory milieu (Ortega et al., 2024a; Ortega et al., 2024b; Ortega et al., 2024c). The same preprint cautions that NLRP3 inhibitors frequently suffer inadequate ocular penetration and potential liver toxicity, and emphasizes the need to determine whether ocular‐local versus systemic NLRP3 suppression is required (Ortega et al., 2024b).

Mechanism of Action  
Molecular target and binding mechanism. NLRP3 is a tripartite sensor (PYD–NACHT–LRR) that oligomerizes upon priming and activation to recruit ASC via PYD–PYD interactions, which in turn polymerizes and recruits pro-caspase-1 via CARD–CARD interactions to form an active inflammasome; active caspase-1 cleaves pro-IL-1β and pro-IL-18 and the pore‐forming effector gasdermin D (GSDMD) to elicit cytokine secretion and pyroptosis (Coll et al., 2015; Ildefonso et al., 2016). MCC950 binds NLRP3 and prevents its ATPase activity (NACHT domain), disrupting a conformational step required for oligomerization and ASC speck assembly; in cellular systems, MCC950 suppresses both canonical (e.g., K⁺ efflux, lysosomal rupture, mitochondrial ROS) and noncanonical (caspase-11–triggered) activation pathways (Coll et al., 2015; Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018). Notably, MCC950 does not broadly interfere with upstream priming (NF-κB–dependent transcription of NLRP3 and cytokine precursors), K⁺ or Ca²⁺ flux, or NLRP3–ASC direct binding in simple biochemical assays; rather, it functionally prevents ASC oligomerization and caspase-1 processing, reflecting target engagement at the level of sensor activation/oligomerization (Coll et al., 2015; Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018). Selectivity is strong: activity against AIM2, NLRC4, and NLRP1 inflammasomes is not observed, and broad target screening reveals only weak off-target activity (Coll et al., 2015; Perera et al., 2018).

Cell-context specificity in the retina and RPE. Expression of NLRP3 and caspase-1 in the retina is cell-type and stimulus dependent. In vitro, microglia robustly upregulate Nlrp3, Casp1, and Il1b upon stimulation; Müller cells can increase Nlrp3 and Il1b without matching Casp1 elevation; photoreceptor‐line cells upregulate Nlrp3 while reducing Casp1; ARPE-19 cells often show undetectable NLRP3 protein and variable inflammasome readouts under some conditions (Wooff et al., 2020a). In situ, NLRP3 labeling is minimal in dim-reared mouse retinas but becomes detectable in the INL/GCL after PD, and AMD donor tissue shows NLRP3 in INL/GCL, suggesting inner-retina/microglial inflammasome contributions that complicate direct linkage to outer retina/RPE degeneration (Wooff et al., 2020a; Wooff et al., 2020b). Conversely, multiple human and preclinical reports demonstrate NLRP3 upregulation in macular RPE of AMD eyes with strong increases in pro-IL-1β and pro-IL-18 transcripts, co-localization of NLRP3 with autophagosome-like structures, and mitochondrial damage/autophagy signatures—though the literature is conflicted by antibody specificity and cell line variability (Wang et al., 2016a; Wang et al., 2016b; Marneros, 2023b). Taken together, these data imply that in AMD-relevant contexts, NLRP3 activation can occur in RPE and in inner-retinal microglia/Müller/immune cells; drug effects will be inherently cell-type dependent.

Pathway-level effects in retinal models. In ischemic retinopathy (OIR), NLRP3 activation (NLRP3/ASC/CASP1 upregulation and ASC specks) is observed primarily in macrophages and endothelium, and MCC950 reversal of an increased IL-1β/decreased IL-18 pattern is associated with reduced neovascularization and leakage, implicating vascular-cell responses to inflammasome cytokines as drivers of pathology (Sui et al., 2020a; Sui et al., 2020b). In wet AMD CNV, inflammasome activation is localized mainly to infiltrating macrophages and microglia, and IL-1β is a principal driver of lesion growth; however, pharmacological NLRP3 inhibition increased lesion size in one study despite reduced IL-1β, suggesting additional non-NLRP3 inflammasomes and compensatory mechanisms (or cell-intrinsic NLRP3 roles) shape outcomes (Marneros, 2023a; Dieckmann et al., 2024a; Dieckmann et al., 2024b).

Expected Effect  
Proposed assay and mechanism. The proposal posits that MCC950 will specifically inhibit NLRP3 assembly in RPE (IC₅₀ ~7.5 nM), reducing IL-1β/IL-18 secretion, preventing inflammasome-induced lysosomal damage, preserving autophagic flux, and thereby enhancing photoreceptor outer segment (POS) clearance. Mechanistic underpinnings exist for the first components of this cascade: (i) MCC950 demonstrates nanomolar potency and high selectivity for NLRP3 and suppresses downstream IL-1β/IL-18 (Coll et al., 2015; Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018); (ii) in IL-1α–primed RPE models (ARPE-19 and pRPE), sulfonylurea NLRP3 inhibitors—including MCC950 in compiled data—suppress IL-1β and LDH release across LMP, oxidative stress, lipofuscin/photooxidative, and P2X7 activation paradigms, and preserve ex vivo Abca4−/− RPE morphology under blue-light irradiation (Wang et al., 2019; Korhonen, 2024). These findings support the expected reduction of canonical inflammasome outputs in RPE assays under multiple AMD-like stimuli.

Lysosome/autophagy preservation and POS clearance. Autophagy is a key negative regulator of NLRP3 activation: it limits ROS and damaged mitochondria, targets assembled inflammasomes for degradation, and suppresses IL-1β responses; conversely, autophagy suppression increases inflammasome activation and pyroptosis in RPE (Celkova et al., 2015). AMD-relevant triggers—including lipofuscin bisretinoids (e.g., A2E) and oxidative stress—cause lysosomal stress/LMP and NLRP3 activation in RPE, and caspase-1 inhibition can prevent RPE death in LMP contexts (Ildefonso et al., 2016). However, direct evidence that MCC950 restores autophagic flux or lysosomal integrity in RPE is not reported in the cited primary RPE inhibitor studies; the RPE evidence centers on IL-1β and LDH suppression and morphological preservation in ex vivo tissue but does not include autophagy- or lysosome-specific readouts or POS phagocytosis assays (Wang et al., 2019). Therefore, while it is plausible that NLRP3 suppression will indirectly favor autophagy homeostasis in stressed RPE by damping inflammasome-driven pyroptotic signaling (and thereby reduce further lysosomal damage), the proposed “preservation of autophagy and enhanced POS clearance” remains unproven for MCC950 and should be tested explicitly (Celkova et al., 2015).

Disease- and cell-type context expectations. In dry AMD models that feature outer-retinal/RPE degeneration, the translation of RPE in vitro suppression of NLRP3 to in vivo benefit is uncertain. In PD (a dry-AMD–relevant model), intravitreal MCC950 failed to confer protection and at higher dose impaired retinal function; Nlrp3−/− mice showed only partial protection while Casp1/11−/− mice were strongly protected, arguing that downstream caspase-1 and/or other inflammasomes may be the dominant drivers in photoreceptor death (Wooff et al., 2020a; Wooff et al., 2020b). In EFEMP1 R345W and aged WT models, genetic inactivation of Nlrp3 or Casp1 reduced basal laminar deposit burden and inflammatory signatures, supporting target pathway relevance for drusen/BLamD biology, but pharmacological MCC950 efficacy in these genetic models has not been reported (Ortega et al., 2024a; Ortega et al., 2024b; Ortega et al., 2024c). Importantly, if inflammasome activation in vivo is dominated by subretinal macrophages/microglia in some contexts (e.g., autophagy-impaired RPE signals that activate macrophage inflammasomes), the expected pharmacologic effect of MCC950 may depend more on drug exposure to myeloid cells in the subretinal/choroidal space than on direct RPE engagement (Liu et al., 2016).

Finally, IL-18 biology is context-dependent: while IL-1β is broadly pro-angiogenic and disruptive, IL-18 can be protective/anti-angiogenic in neovascular settings, and AMD-relevant studies have reported discordant roles for IL-18 across disease phenotypes (Celkova et al., 2015; Ildefonso et al., 2016). Given that NLRP3 blockade reduces both IL-1β and IL-18, net effects on tissue outcomes may vary by disease stage and cell-type source; in OIR, MCC950 “normalized” an inverted IL-1β/IL-18 pattern and improved pathology (Sui et al., 2020a; Sui et al., 2020c), whereas in CNV, MCC950 increased lesion volume—implicating competing effects and non-NLRP3 inflammasomes (Dieckmann et al., 2024a).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- On-target potency/selectivity. MCC950 is among the most potent and selective NLRP3 inhibitors described, blocking canonical and noncanonical activation at nanomolar concentrations and sparing other inflammasomes and upstream pathways; it consistently suppresses IL-1β/IL-18 maturation and caspase-1 activation in primary macrophages and multiple in vivo models (Coll et al., 2015; Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018; Perera et al., 2018).  
- RPE-target class activity under AMD-relevant stimuli. Sulfonylurea NLRP3 inhibitors, including MCC950 in compiled datasets, reproducibly suppress IL-1β and LDH in IL-1α–primed ARPE-19 and primary human RPE triggered by LMP, oxidative/photooxidative stress, and P2X7 activation; ex vivo Abca4−/− RPE morphology is preserved by an NLRP3 inhibitor during photooxidative stress (Wang et al., 2019; Korhonen, 2024).  
- Genetic target validation in AMD-relevant deposit biology. Whole‐body Nlrp3 or Casp1 deletion reduces BLamDs and normalizes inflammatory signatures in EFEMP1 R345W mice and even prevents spontaneous deposits in aged WT, indicating the inflammasome pathway contributes causally to deposit formation and retinal inflammation (Ortega et al., 2024a; Ortega et al., 2024b; Ortega et al., 2024c).  
- Demonstrated retinal efficacy in ischemic models and neuroinflammation. MCC950 improves vascular pathology in OIR (reduced neovascularization and leakage with cytokine-pattern reversal) and rescues retinal ganglion cells in glaucoma, supporting retinal target engagement and functional protection in relevant pathologies (Sui et al., 2020a; Sui et al., 2020b; Li, 2020).

Liabilities and gaps  
- Lack of efficacy and potential toxicity in dry-AMD–relevant PD. Intravitreal MCC950 did not improve functional or structural outcomes in PD and at 100 µM worsened ERG amplitudes; Nlrp3 siRNA similarly failed to protect despite gene knockdown; Casp1/11 deletion was robustly protective while Nlrp3 deletion was only partially protective, arguing sensor-specific inhibition may be insufficient in photoreceptor death contexts (Wooff et al., 2020b; Wooff et al., 2020a).  
- Mixed effects in neovascular disease. MCC950 increased CNV lesion volume in LCNV despite lowering IL-1β, and Nlrp3−/− mice displayed larger lesions, raising concern that NLRP3 blockade may remove protective constraints in some inflammatory/angiogenic contexts; non-NLRP3 inflammasomes likely contribute, further complicating pharmacodynamics (Dieckmann et al., 2024a; Dieckmann et al., 2024b; Marneros, 2023a).  
- Uncertain ocular delivery, exposure, and safety margin. Ocular PK for MCC950 is not defined; the PD study underscores unknown intravitreal bioavailability and clearance, and preclinical reviews warn of poor eye penetration and potential liver toxicity with many NLRP3 inhibitors; high intravitreal dose impaired ERG function in PD (Wooff et al., 2020b; Ortega et al., 2024b). While ERGs were unchanged in one CNV study, that does not establish comprehensive ocular safety (Dieckmann et al., 2024a).  
- RPE biology heterogeneity and expression uncertainty. In vivo NLRP3 induction localizes largely to inner retina/microglia rather than RPE in PD; ARPE-19 NLRP3 expression is variable in the literature and some human studies report low/undetectable NLRP3 in RPE, with concerns about antibody specificity, suggesting that direct RPE targeting may not be universally relevant across models or donors (Wooff et al., 2020a; Wooff et al., 2020b; Marneros, 2023b).  
- Unproven restoration of autophagy/lysosomal function by MCC950. Although autophagy restrains inflammasome activation and lysosomal damage is a key trigger in RPE, direct evidence that MCC950 preserves autophagic flux, lysosomal integrity, or POS processing in RPE is absent in the cited studies; current RPE data document IL-1β/LDH suppression and morphology preservation but not autophagy or phagolysosomal kinetics (Celkova et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2019).  
- Pathway redundancy suggests downstream targeting may be superior. Strong protection in Casp1/11−/− mice versus weak/absent benefits from NLRP3 inhibition in PD argue for targeting the shared downstream protease (caspase-1) or gasdermin D rather than individual sensors in retinal degeneration (Wooff et al., 2020a).

Risk-adjusted development path and decision inflection points  
- Go/no-go evidence needed in dry-AMD–relevant RPE assays. Establish whether MCC950 preserves lysosomal integrity and autophagic flux in RPE under LMP/photooxidative/P2X7 triggers and whether it restores POS digestion. Required readouts: LC3-II/I and p62 kinetics with and without bafilomycin, lysosomal pH and cathepsin activity, galectin-3 puncta for LMP, ASC speck formation, caspase-1 activity (FLICA), GSDMD cleavage, IL-1β/IL-18 maturation, and POS ingestion/digestion assays in ARPE-19 and pRPE (Celkova et al., 2015; Ranta-aho et al., 2021).  
- Ocular PK/PD and safety. Quantify intravitreal half-life, retinal/RPE/choroid distribution, and exposure–response for inflammasome suppression with MCC950; determine maximum non-toxic intravitreal dose across species. Include ERG, OCT, histopathology, IBA-1/microglial activation, and cytokine profiling. Investigate sustained intravitreal delivery strategies (e.g., silica-based nanoparticles) that have shown extended ocular release and improved anti-inflammatory efficacy for MCC950 in non-AMD contexts, while generating ocular PK and biodegradation data (Sun et al., 2023).  
- Efficacy in chronic dry-AMD models. Test MCC950 in EFEMP1 R345W mice (BLamD) and aging WT (spontaneous BLamD) with local ocular delivery; endpoints: BLamD size and coverage, RPE/Bruch’s integrity, microglial recruitment (Iba1), and cytokine panels. Given PD negative findings, prioritize deposit/atrophy models where genetic Nlrp3/Casp1 loss is protective (Ortega et al., 2024a; Ortega et al., 2024b; Ortega et al., 2024c; Wooff et al., 2020b).  
- Cell-type–specific targeting and biomarkers. Because inflammasome activation is often myeloid-dominant in vivo, delineate whether MCC950’s ocular benefits, if any, require exposure to subretinal macrophages/microglia versus RPE. Use cell-specific pharmacodynamic markers (ASC specks in Iba1+ cells vs RPE65+ cells; IL-1β/IL-18 localization) to define pharmacologic engagement (Liu et al., 2016; Wooff et al., 2020a).  
- Comparative strategy. In parallel, benchmark a caspase-1 inhibitor (or GSDMD inhibitor) against MCC950 in the same models, given the superior genetic protection with Casp1/11 deletion and the possibility of non-NLRP3 inflammasome contribution (Wooff et al., 2020a; Marneros, 2023a).

Bottom line  
MCC950 has strong mechanistic rationale, exquisite target selectivity, and reproducible suppression of inflammasome outputs in RPE assays across diverse AMD-like triggers. Genetic data incriminating NLRP3–caspase-1 in deposit biology strengthen the target hypothesis in a subset of dry-AMD phenotypes. However, the most AMD-relevant in vivo pharmacology with MCC950 to date is not supportive: no benefit and possible functional toxicity in PD, and mixed signals in neovascular settings (benefit in OIR, harm in LCNV). The translational path is further complicated by variable NLRP3 expression in RPE in vivo, dominance of myeloid inflammasomes in many retinal contexts, uncertain ocular PK/penetration, and the untested premise that MCC950 restores RPE autophagy/lysosomal function and POS clearance.

Given these data, MCC950 should not advance directly to costly IND-enabling studies for dry AMD without targeted de-risking experiments. The highest-value next steps are (i) mechanistic RPE assays that test autophagy/lysosome rescue and POS processing, (ii) rigorous ocular PK/safety to define a therapeutic index and viable delivery modality, and (iii) efficacy in deposit/atrophy models where the genetic target is validated (EFEMP1 R345W, aged WT). If these studies confirm robust ocular exposure, a favorable safety margin, and disease modification, MCC950—or a chemically optimized ocular NLRP3 inhibitor—could warrant advancement for specific dry-AMD endophenotypes. If not, downstream inflammasome targeting (caspase-1/GSDMD) may represent a more effective and generalizable strategy for retinal degeneration.

Mechanism of Action (detailed)  
NLRP3 activation requires priming (e.g., NF-κB upregulation of NLRP3 and pro-IL-1β/IL-18) and a second signal (e.g., K⁺ efflux via P2X7, lysosomal rupture with cathepsin release, mitochondrial ROS) that promotes sensor oligomerization (Coll et al., 2015; Ildefonso et al., 2016). NLRP3’s NACHT domain cycles ATP and orchestrates a conformational change enabling PYD-driven nucleation of ASC, which polymerizes into higher-order filaments/specks that template pro-caspase-1 recruitment and activation; activated caspase-1 cleaves GSDMD to induce pyroptotic pore formation and processes IL-1β/IL-18 for secretion (Coll et al., 2015; Ildefonso et al., 2016). MCC950 binds NLRP3 to suppress its ATPase activity (NACHT), preventing the conformational activation needed for ASC oligomerization and caspase-1 activation; in functional assays MCC950 suppresses both canonical and noncanonical pathways and decreases processed caspase-1 p10/p20 in supernatants without altering upstream TNF-α secretion after TLR priming (Coll et al., 2015; Akhtar-Schäfer et al., 2018). Evidence from retinal disease states aligns with these mechanisms: MCC950 reduces NLRP3 and cleaved caspase-1 in glaucomatous retina (DBA/2J), and in OIR normalizes IL-1β/IL-18 signaling and reduces pathologic neovascularization and leakage (Li, 2020; Sui et al., 2020a).

Inflammasome biology in RPE and AMD is multifactorial. AMD-associated triggers—lipofuscin photooxidation, A2E/oxidative stress, drusen lipid adducts (CEP), Alu RNA accumulation from DICER1 deficiency, and lysosomal destabilization—induce NLRP3 activation in RPE or in recruited subretinal macrophages (Ildefonso et al., 2016; Celkova et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2016). Autophagy limits NLRP3 activation by removing damaged mitochondria and targeting assembled inflammasomes for autophagosomal degradation; autophagy blockade increases IL-1β production and pyroptotic susceptibility (Celkova et al., 2015). Pharmacologic NLRP3 blockade in RPE reduces IL-1β and LDH release under LMP, oxidative, photooxidative, and P2X7 activation, consistent with suppression of caspase-1 activation and pyroptotic lysis (Wang et al., 2019). Whether these biochemical effects in RPE suffice to modify chronic, multicellular retinal degeneration in vivo depends on drug delivery to relevant compartments (RPE, subretinal macrophages/microglia), on the relative contributions of non-NLRP3 inflammasomes, and on downstream cytokine biology (e.g., IL-18’s context-dependent effects).

Therapeutic History (detailed)  
- Preclinical systemic efficacy and selectivity: MCC950 exhibits nanomolar potency for NLRP3 in human/mouse macrophages, sparing AIM2, NLRC4, NLRP1; suppresses caspase-1 p10 and IL-1β secretion; improves disease in EAE and CAPS; PK characterized; off-targets largely excluded (Coll et al., 2015; Perera et al., 2018). In atherosclerosis, MCC950 decreased plaques, macrophage content, and circulating cytokines without overt systemic organ toxicity, though cross-indication reviews caution about liver toxicity risk for the class (Zeng et al., 2021; Ortega et al., 2024b).  
- Ocular ischemic/neovascular settings: In OIR, MCC950 reversed an increased IL-1β/decreased IL-18 pattern, reduced neovascularization and leakage, and modulated endothelial/pericyte signaling; inflammasome activity localized more to macrophages than endothelium (Sui et al., 2020a; Sui et al., 2020b; Sui et al., 2020c). In LCNV, MCC950 lowered IL-1β but increased lesion volume; ERG unchanged; genetic Nlrp3 loss also increased lesion size—collectively indicating a complex, possibly protective role of NLRP3 in CNV or compensation by other inflammasomes (Dieckmann et al., 2024a; Dieckmann et al., 2024b; Marneros, 2023a).  
- Dry-AMD–relevant PD and NLRP3 targeting: Intravitreal MCC950 did not protect PD retina; 100 µM reduced ERG amplitudes. Nlrp3 siRNA reduced transcript but not pathology; Nlrp3−/− protected partially; Casp1/11−/− protected robustly, pointing to caspase-1 as the better target (Wooff et al., 2020b; Wooff et al., 2020a).  
- RPE in vitro/ex vivo: CRID3/IFM inhibitors (sulfonylureas, same target class as MCC950) reduced IL-1β and LDH across LMP, H₂O₂, lipofuscin/photooxidation, and P2X7 triggers in ARPE-19/pRPE and preserved ex vivo Abca4−/− RPE morphology under photooxidation (Wang et al., 2019). Compiled 2024 data list MCC950 alongside IFM analogs as effective in IL-1α–primed RPE independent of trigger (Korhonen, 2024).  
- Genetic validations in chronic deposit models: Nlrp3 or Casp1 deletion reduces BLamD in EFEMP1 R345W mice and in aged WT, with reduced microglial activation and normalization of cytokine profiles (Ortega et al., 2024a; Ortega et al., 2024b; Ortega et al., 2024c). These models offer strong causal support for inflammasome targeting in GA-relevant pathology, albeit via genetic ablation rather than pharmacologic inhibition.

Expected Effect (detailed)  
In ARPE-19/pRPE assays primed with IL-1α, MCC950 should suppress NLRP3 activation triggered by:  
– LMP (Leu-Leu-OMe), where caspase-1 inhibition prevents RPE death and NLRP3 inhibitors reduce IL-1β and LDH release (Ildefonso et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2019).  
– Oxidative and lipofuscin/photooxidative stress (H₂O₂, HNE-POS + blue light), where NLRP3 inhibitors significantly lower IL-1β and LDH and preserve RPE morphology ex vivo (Wang et al., 2019).  
– P2X7 activation (BzATP), a canonical AMD-relevant danger signal leading to K⁺ efflux and inflammasome assembly; selective NLRP3 inhibitors attenuate IL-1β and LDH in Ca²⁺/Mg²⁺-free conditions (Wang et al., 2019).

Because autophagy restrains inflammasome activation and removes inflammasome complexes, a reduction in NLRP3 activity may secondarily stabilize autophagic flux under stress. Yet, this remains hypothetical for MCC950 in RPE; explicit autophagy and lysosomal readouts (LC3 flux, p62, LAMP1/2, cathepsin B/D activities, lysosomal pH, galectin-3 LMP puncta) have not been detailed in the RPE inhibitor studies referenced (Celkova et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2019). Therefore, while reduction of IL-1β/LDH and preservation of morphology are expected and supported, the proposed enhancement of POS clearance should be considered an untested hypothesis requiring targeted experimentation.

In vivo, efficacy expectations diverge by model:  
– Deposit/atrophy (EFEMP1 R345W, aged WT) are rational choices: genetic deletion of Nlrp3/Casp1 is protective, so MCC950 might reduce BLamD burden and retinal inflammation if adequate ocular exposure is achieved (Ortega et al., 2024a; Ortega et al., 2024b; Ortega et al., 2024c).  
– Photoreceptor acute degeneration (PD) may not respond to NLRP3 inhibition and may be sensitive to dose-related toxicity, favoring downstream caspase-1 inhibition or broader inflammasome suppression (Wooff et al., 2020b; Wooff et al., 2020a).  
– Neovascular models diverge: OIR improved with MCC950; CNV worsened. Dry-AMD-focused development should avoid neovascular endpoints initially, or stratify hypotheses based on IL-1β/IL-18 balance and myeloid contribution (Sui et al., 2020a; Dieckmann et al., 2024b; Marneros, 2023a).

Overall Evaluation  
MCC950 is a mechanistically compelling, best-in-class NLRP3 inhibitor with credible RPE-target class activity in vitro and strong genetic support for inflammasome involvement in deposit biology. However, the in vivo ocular pharmacology to date is mixed and generally unsupportive for broad dry-AMD application without further de-risking: failure and potential toxicity in PD, context-dependent effects in neovascular models, uncertain RPE expression/engagement in vivo, lack of ocular PK, and unproven restoration of autophagy/lysosomal function in RPE.

On balance, MCC950 merits continued investigation as a mechanistic probe and potential therapeutic lead for specific dry-AMD endophenotypes linked to deposit pathology and chronic inflammasome signaling—provided that the next tranche of studies addresses ocular PK/safety, cell-type exposure, and autophagy/lysosome outcomes. In parallel, downstream targeting (caspase-1) should be benchmarked given superior genetic protection and potential coverage of multiple inflammasome sensors. If MCC950 cannot meet ocular exposure and safety requirements, alternative delivery (e.g., sustained-release nanoparticles) or next-generation NLRP3 inhibitors with better ocular PK and safety profiles may be required (Sun et al., 2023; Ortega et al., 2024b).

In summary, MCC950 has plausible potential for dry AMD if—and only if— its ocular pharmacology can be tuned to the appropriate disease biology: chronic deposit/atrophy with documented inflammasome involvement, sufficient drug exposure at RPE/subretinal myeloid compartments, and a safety margin that avoids the functional liabilities observed at higher intravitreal doses in PD. Without these, the probability of technical success remains low relative to downstream inflammasome targets.
