Proposal for BTB06584 (V-ATPase inhibitor; Tocris Cat. No. 5208)

Below is our comprehensive evaluation of BTB06584 as a repurposed drug candidate for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD).

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
BTB06584 is described as a V‐ATPase inhibitor available commercially (e.g., Tocris Cat. No. 5208) that is purported to act by selectively targeting the V₀ subunit of the vacuolar proton pump. V‐ATPase is a large multisubunit enzyme complex consisting of a cytosolic V₁ domain (responsible for ATP hydrolysis) and a membrane‐embedded V₀ domain (which translocates protons) that together acidify intracellular compartments such as lysosomes. BTB06584 appears to belong to the class of small molecules developed to modulate lysosomal acidification and, by extension, lysosome‐dependent degradative processes. Although several classes of V‐ATPase inhibitors (for example, the plecomacrolides bafilomycin A₁ and concanamycin A, as well as benzolactone enamides and others) have been extensively characterized as experimental probes, BTB06584 is postulated to be unique in its relatively selective action on the V₀ sector. This selectivity is important because it offers the theoretical possibility of “partial” inhibition rather than the broad, complete blockade observed with classical inhibitors that are often associated with high toxicity (Shine et al., 2014, p. 7; Santos-Pereira et al., 2021, pp. 21–23). In many published studies, V‐ATPase inhibitors have served as critical biochemical tools to dissect lysosomal pH regulation and phagosome degradation, especially in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells, where impaired acidification is linked to cellular dysfunction in AMD (Shine et al., 2014, pp. 4–7). No detailed synthesis or discovery history has been provided in the existing context, but BTB06584 is assumed to be a synthetic agent designed in line with modern small‐molecule drug development paradigms targeting the V₀ domain.

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, V‐ATPase inhibitors have been widely used as experimental probes to study lysosomal acidification and related cellular processes. Classical inhibitors such as bafilomycin A₁ and concanamycin A have been employed in many in vitro and in vivo studies to raise lysosomal pH, alter autophagy and phagocytosis, and to trigger apoptosis in sensitive cell types (Shine et al., 2014, p. 7). In ocular research, V‐ATPase inhibition—albeit through these broader agents—has been demonstrated to impair photoreceptor outer segment (POS) degradation in RPE cells, which serves as an experimental proxy for early AMD‐related pathology (Shine et al., 2014, pp. 4–7; Valapala et al., 2016, pp. 4–6). Moreover, genetic models in zebrafish and mice further underscore the importance of proper V‐ATPase function in retinal homeostasis (Valapala et al., 2016, pp. 4–6; Sinha et al., 2016, pp. 3–5). However, to date, the literature available in our context does not report any prior clinical or preclinical use of BTB06584 specifically for treating dry AMD or for modulating lysosomal pH in RPE cells; indeed, several excerpts explicitly note that BTB06584 is not mentioned by name in the primary‐literature reports on V‐ATPase inhibitors (Santos-Pereira et al., 2021, pp. 23–24; Shine et al., 2014, pp. 1–4). In other words, while the class of V‐ATPase inhibitors has been widely explored—primarily in cancer and osteoporosis research (Holliday, 2017, pp. 4–6; Markitantova & Simirskii, 2025, pp. 9–11)—there is no direct record that BTB06584 has been used clinically or in animal models related to macular degeneration. This gap in the therapeutic history means that any proposed repurposing effort must contend with a virtual absence of detailed preclinical data in AMD‐relevant systems.

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, V‐ATPase functions as an ATP‐driven proton pump essential for maintaining the acidic pH of endolysosomal compartments. Lysosomal enzymes, including cathepsin D, require an optimal acidic environment (typically around pH 4.5) for their catalytic function (Shine et al., 2014, p. 7; Shine et al., 2014, pp. 4–7). Disruption of V‐ATPase activity, whether pharmacologically by agents such as bafilomycin A₁ or via genetic manipulation (for example, loss of βA3/A1‐crystallin, which is known to modulate V‐ATPase function), leads to a rise in lysosomal pH, reduced activity of acid‐dependent proteases, and impaired degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (Valapala et al., 2016, pp. 4–6; Valapala et al., 2016, pp. 1–4). In contrast to complete inhibition—which often results in a strong, detrimental rise in pH—the hypothesis for BTB06584 is that it will “partially” inhibit the V‐ATPase. The goal would be to fine‐tune the activity of the enzyme so that instead of producing a supraphysiologic pH (as with full inhibition), the lysosomal environment is restored to an optimal acidic set point (around pH 4.5) that promotes maximal cathepsin D activity and efficient POS clearance (Shine et al., 2014, pp. 4–7; Sinha et al., 2016, pp. 3–5). Structural studies of V‐ATPase have shown that selective targeting of subunit isoforms, particularly those within the V₀ sector, can influence not only proton pumping but also other functions such as membrane fusion during phagosome–lysosome fusion events (Santos-Pereira et al., 2021, pp. 21–23; Shine et al., 2014, pp. 1–4). If BTB06584 indeed exhibits specificity for the V₀ subunit—and perhaps even for particular isoforms expressed in RPE—it might exert a modulatory effect that differs from the broad and often toxic inhibition seen with compounds like bafilomycin A₁. However, as noted in the literature summaries, there is currently no detailed primary data regarding the binding kinetics, structural interaction, or precise molecular pharmacology of BTB06584 (Santos-Pereira et al., 2021, pp. 23–24; Santos-Pereira et al., 2021, pp. 26–28). In other words, while the proposed mechanism is logically consistent with our understanding of V‐ATPase biology, it remains unsubstantiated by direct experimental evidence for this particular compound.

Expected Effect:  
In the context of dry AMD, RPE dysfunction is characterized, in part, by altered lysosomal pH and impaired degradation of POS, leading to the accumulation of lipofuscin and subsequent oxidative stress and cellular demise (Shine et al., 2014, pp. 4–7; Valapala et al., 2014, pp. 16–17). The central hypothesis is that dysregulated V‐ATPase activity in AMD RPE leads to lysosomal pH drift—either excessive alkalinization due to inhibition by A2E or a failure to maintain optimal acidity—and that this pH imbalance impacts cathepsin D activity. Cathepsin D is optimally active at a pH of around 4.5, and even a modest deviation toward alkalinity (for example, pH 5.0) can reduce its activity by up to 80% (Valapala et al., 2016, pp. 1–4; Shine et al., 2014, p. 7). BTB06584 is expected to “partially” inhibit V‐ATPase in a manner that normalizes lysosomal pH without “shutting off” the proton pump entirely. In RPE cells, particularly in A2E-treated ARPE-19 assays, such a fine-tuning effect could restore an optimal acidic environment, thereby reactivating cathepsin D and other hydrolases; this, in turn, would facilitate proper degradation of ingested photoreceptor outer segments and reduce the buildup of undigested material and associated autofluorescence (Sinha et al., 2016, pp. 3–5; Valapala et al., 2014, pp. 16–17). Importantly, the candidate’s hypothesized selective action on the V₀ subunit—if proven—aligns with evidence that manipulating particular V‐ATPase subunit isoforms can affect not only proton pumping but also membrane fusion events that are essential for proper lysosomal function (Santos-Pereira et al., 2021, pp. 21–23; Shine et al., 2014, pp. 4–7). Given that the RPE expresses specific V‐ATPase isoforms (for example, different V₀ a isoforms) and that genetic studies have linked loss of V‐ATPase activity to defects in POS degradation (Valapala et al., 2016, pp. 4–6; Shine et al., 2014, p. 7), the restoration of lysosomal homeostasis through a “partial inhibitor” like BTB06584 could theoretically improve the clearance of POS. However, it must be emphasized that the expected effect of normalizing pH from a suboptimal or variable level to precisely 4.5 is a very delicate modulation – one that must be demonstrated through rigorous in vitro assays in ARPE-19 cells (or better yet, in iPSC-derived RPE models) followed by in vivo animal studies.

Overall Evaluation:  
The proposed strategy of repurposing BTB06584 for dry AMD is innovative in that it aims to address a central pathological feature—lysosomal dysfunction—by modulating, rather than completely inhibiting, the V‐ATPase. The strength of the candidate lies in its potential for selective inhibition of the V₀ subunit, which is critical given that generalized inhibition via broad-spectrum compounds (like bafilomycin A₁) has been associated with significant toxicity and dysfunction in multiple cell types (Shine et al., 2014, p. 7; Shine et al., 2014, pp. 1–4). Furthermore, the concept of “fine-tuning” lysosomal pH to optimize cathepsin D activity is appealing because it targets the underlying mechanism that controls the degradation of POS in RPE cells—a process known to be perturbed in AMD (Shine et al., 2014, pp. 4–7; Valapala et al., 2016, pp. 1–4).  

Nonetheless, there are notable weaknesses. Chief among these is the absence of direct experimental evidence supporting the efficacy of BTB06584 in RPE models or animal models of dry AMD. None of the available literature excerpts provide primary data regarding its chemical characterization, mechanism of action in retinal cells, or any preclinical studies using BTB06584 (Santos-Pereira et al., 2021, pp. 23–24; Shine et al., 2014, pp. 1–4). Consequently, while the hypothesis is congruent with the general concept that selective modulation of V‐ATPase can restore lysosomal function, the candidate remains largely unvalidated in the context of ocular therapeutics. In addition, there is an inherent risk associated with modulating a central enzyme such as V-ATPase: even partial inhibition might affect other vital cellular processes, including autophagy, phagosome–lysosome fusion, and even neurotransmitter release in neural tissues (Santos-Pereira et al., 2021, pp. 21–23; Shine et al., 2014, pp. 1–4). Moreover, the narrow therapeutic window required to normalize acidification (without overshooting into detrimental alkalinization) poses significant challenges; this alone necessitates careful dose-response profiling in multiple models before any clinical translation can be considered.  

Overall, while the theoretical framework supporting BTB06584 is robust in terms of targeting a mechanism that is central to RPE pathology in dry AMD, the lack of direct data leaves critical gaps. At this stage, BTB06584 represents a promising but highly speculative candidate. To advance its development, we recommend that rigorous in vitro studies (using ARPE-19 cells and iPSC-derived RPE under A2E/lipofuscin stress) be undertaken to characterize its effect on lysosomal pH, cathepsin D activity, and POS degradation. These should be complemented by mechanistic assays—such as assessments of lysosomal fusion events and measurements of autophagic flux—to fully delineate its mode of action. If favorable, subsequent in vivo studies in appropriate AMD models will be essential to evaluate efficacy and systemic toxicity.  

In summary, our overall evaluation is that while the candidate BTB06584 is conceptually attractive because it promises selective modulation of V‐ATPase activity—potentially correcting the lysosomal pH imbalance that underlies defects in POS clearance in dry AMD—the current literature does not supply direct supportive evidence for its use in retinal disease, and its safety/efficacy profile remains unproven. Further preclinical investigation is therefore necessary before considering BTB06584 as a viable therapeutic candidate for dry AMD (Shine et al., 2014, p. 7; Santos-Pereira et al., 2021, pp. 23–24; Shine et al., 2014, pp. 1–4).

Proposal for SKF96365 (TRPC channel inhibitor; Tocris Cat. No. 1261)

Below is a comprehensive evaluation of SKF96365 as a repurposed therapeutic candidate for dry age‐related macular degeneration (AMD). The following report is organized into five sections: (I) Overview of Therapeutic Candidate, (II) Therapeutic History, (III) Mechanism of Action, (IV) Expected Effect in Dry AMD, and (V) Overall Evaluation. Each section cites multiple studies from the available literature context.

─────────────────────────────  
I. OVERVIEW OF THERAPEUTIC CANDIDATE

SKF96365 (1-{[3-(4-methoxyphenyl)propoxy]-4-methoxyphenethyl}-1H-imidazole hydrochloride) is a fully synthetic small molecule discovered by medicinal chemists interested in modulating receptor-mediated calcium entry pathways. Originally introduced as an inhibitor of receptor-induced Ca²⁺ influx in non‐excitable cells such as platelets and neutrophils (Singh et al., 2010), the compound later gained attention as a modulator of transient receptor potential (TRP) channels. As a member of the imidazole derivative class, SKF96365 shares structural features with phenylalkylamine compounds and is characterized by its alkylated imidazole core embellished with substituted methoxyphenyl moieties; these structural modifications were purposefully introduced to confer the molecule with broad activity on Ca²⁺ permeation mechanisms (Harteneck & Gollasch, 2011; Singh et al., 2010; Harteneck, Klose, & Krautwurst, 2011).

The chemical synthesis of SKF96365 involves multi-step organic transformations, whereby the imidazole ring is first derivatized and subsequently appended with both aliphatic and aromatic substituents. These modifications are believed to be critical in endowing SKF96365 with the ability to interact with various ion channel proteins across the plasma membrane. Although initially developed for its capacity to block receptor-mediated Ca²⁺ entry, further pharmacological investigations revealed that SKF96365 exhibits broad-spectrum activity by inhibiting not only store-operated channels (SOCE) and receptor-operated channels (ROC) but also interfering with key subtypes of the transient receptor potential canonical (TRPC) family (Singh et al., 2010).

The compound’s broad inhibitory spectrum, however, comes at the cost of selectivity. While low micromolar concentrations (typically in the range of 2–30 μM) are required to inhibit TRPC channels, SKF96365 has also been shown to block other calcium channels such as low‐voltage‐activated T‐type channels at submicromolar concentrations (IC₅₀ ~560 nM) (Singh et al., 2010). This dual and even overlapping activity pattern reflects its classification as a non‐selective TRP channel blocker and places it within the larger group of broad-spectrum calcium channel modulators. Its widespread use across a multitude of experimental systems—from studies of cellular Ca²⁺ entry in endothelial cells to investigations in neuronal and glial systems—further underscores its utility as a pharmacological tool, despite the inherent drawbacks associated with low target selectivity (Singh et al., 2010; Harteneck, Klose, & Krautwurst, 2011; Harteneck & Gollasch, 2011).

In summary, SKF96365 is a synthetic compound belonging to the imidazole derivative family, originally designed to inhibit receptor‐mediated Ca²⁺ influx. It has been repurposed as a TRPC channel inhibitor, although its inhibitory profile extends well beyond TRPC channels to include several classes of voltage‐gated and store-operated channels. This broad mechanism of action, while advantageous for experimental dissection of Ca²⁺ signaling pathways, poses potential challenges for its development as a selective therapeutic agent for dry AMD (Singh et al., 2010).

─────────────────────────────  
II. THERAPEUTIC HISTORY

The therapeutic history of SKF96365 reflects its evolution from a research tool into a potential candidate for repurposing in diverse pathological states. Initially, SKF96365 was introduced in the early 1990s as an inhibitor of receptor-mediated calcium entry. Early studies demonstrated that it could effectively block Ca²⁺ influx in non‐excitable cells such as platelets, neutrophils, and endothelial cells, with reported half-maximal inhibitory concentrations (IC₅₀’s) of approximately 10 μM (Singh et al., 2010; Harteneck, Klose, & Krautwurst, 2011). These early findings spurred interest in its utility as a diagnostic blocker for various Ca²⁺ entry mechanisms, particularly before the molecular identification of TRP channels.

Following the molecular cloning of TRPC family members, SKF96365 was quickly repurposed to study these channels in both heterologous expression systems and native tissues. Its ability to inhibit TRPC channels in multiple cell types solidified its reputation as a key pharmacological tool. For example, studies in cultured cells such as PC-12 and HL-60 cells provided evidence for its capacity to differentiate between ATP- and bradykinin-induced Ca²⁺ entry and offered insights into receptor-regulated calcium entry pathways (Harteneck & Gollasch, 2011). In addition to non-ocular systems, SKF96365 has been widely used in research involving the cardiovascular and nervous systems, highlighting its diverse biological applications.

In the context relevant to ocular research, several investigations have applied SKF96365 to retinal models. For instance, studies in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells indicated that basal calcium entry in these cells is mediated, at least in part, by TRPC channels. One particular study demonstrated that in both cultured RPE cells and primary human RPE cells, SKF96365 reduced intracellular Ca²⁺ concentration in a dose-dependent fashion, implicating TRPC channels in the maintenance of basal Ca²⁺ levels necessary for proper RPE function (Wimmers & Strauss, 2007). Moreover, ocular safety data from experiments using SKF96365 in lamina cribrosa cells—cells that contribute to the optic nerve head microenvironment implicated in glaucoma—have shown that at concentrations around 10 μM to 100 μM, the compound can modulate Ca²⁺-dependent signaling without overt cytotoxicity (Irnaten et al., 2020).

Additional preclinical studies have not only examined SKF96365 in the context of RPE cellular physiology but also explored its potential in anti-proliferative and anti-fibrotic applications. In malignant glioma cells, for example, concentrations in the 25 μM range were shown to suppress proliferation, an effect that was attributed to its combined blockade of TRPC channels and low‐voltage‐activated T‐type channels (Singh et al., 2010). Despite these encouraging preclinical findings, to date there have been no clinical or veterinary applications of SKF96365 specifically for the treatment of dry AMD or similar retinal degenerative conditions.

Collectively, the therapeutic history of SKF96365 demonstrates that while it has been a valuable experimental tool for elucidating Ca²⁺ dynamics in a wide array of tissues—including ocular cells—it has not yet been translated into a clinical therapeutic for conditions such as dry AMD. Its continued use in preclinical studies helps to support the strategy of targeting calcium dysregulation; however, concerns over its off-target activity underline the challenges inherent in repurposing a broadly acting ion channel modulator for chronic degenerative diseases (Singh et al., 2010; Wimmers & Strauss, 2007; Irnaten et al., 2020).

─────────────────────────────  
III. MECHANISM OF ACTION

A detailed understanding of the mechanism of action of SKF96365 provides important insights into both its potential utility and its limitations as a therapeutic candidate. SKF96365 was originally characterized as an inhibitor of receptor-mediated calcium entry, a function that was later expanded upon with the identification of TRP channels. Mechanistically, SKF96365 has been shown to inhibit receptor-operated and store-operated calcium entry pathways, acting as a noncompetitive, state-independent, and voltage-insensitive blocker—that is, it interferes with Ca²⁺ entry regardless of whether channels are in the closed, open, or inactivated state (Singh et al., 2010; Harteneck & Gollasch, 2011).

Electrophysiological studies in heterologous systems reveal that SKF96365 inhibits recombinant TRPC channel currents at IC₅₀ values generally in the low micromolar range (approximately 5–30 μM). However, a striking aspect of its pharmacological profile is its potent inhibition of low‐voltage‐activated T‐type calcium channels. For example, investigations using human CaV3.1 channels have determined an IC₅₀ of approximately 560 nM for SKF96365—a potency that is nearly an order of magnitude higher than that observed for TRPC channels (Singh et al., 2010). This inhibitory action on T‐type channels is consistent with findings in native tissue models such as rat cerebellar Purkinje cells, where SKF96365 produced profound and rapid blockade of T-type Ca²⁺ currents.

The molecular basis for SKF96365’s broad channel blockade likely involves a direct interaction with the ion permeation pores of these channels. While the detailed binding site has not been unequivocally defined, evidence suggests that SKF96365 interacts allosterically with channel structures, leading to pore block without significantly altering the kinetics of channel activation or inactivation. This mode of inhibition appears to be state-independent, meaning that channel blockade occurs irrespective of the channel’s conformational state (Singh et al., 2010). In addition to its effects on TRPC and T-type channels, SKF96365 also impairs the function of high‐voltage‐activated calcium channels (including L‐type, P/Q‐type, and N‐type channels) when used at typical concentrations employed in TRPC channel studies (Singh et al., 2010).

Beyond calcium channels, the compound has been reported to exhibit off-target activities against other ion channels and cellular components. For instance, it has been shown to inhibit certain potassium channels, interfere with sarcoplasmic reticulum Ca²⁺-ATPase activity, and even affect nicotinic receptor function in some cellular contexts (Harteneck & Gollasch, 2011; Singh et al., 2010). This promiscuity in channel blockade is a double-edged sword: on one hand, it increases the overall capacity of SKF96365 to alter intracellular Ca²⁺ dynamics; on the other hand, it complicates the attribution of specific physiological or pathological outcomes solely to TRPC inhibition.

From a molecular perspective, TRPC channels in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) are thought to contribute to the maintenance of basal calcium levels that are requisite for key cellular processes such as phagocytosis and endolysosomal trafficking. Although SKF96365 was not originally designed with ocular applications in mind, its ability to inhibit these channels makes it a candidate for modulating disrupted Ca²⁺ signaling in RPE cells—a critical factor in the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Wimmers & Strauss, 2007; Zhao et al., 2015). However, the breadth of SKF96365’s mechanism of action means that at concentrations required to modulate TRPC channel activity within the RPE, the compound is very likely to concurrently block other calcium channel subtypes. This scenario is corroborated by data demonstrating that at 10 μM, SKF96365 can block recombinant channels from all three major voltage-gated calcium channel classes, including CaV1 (L-type), CaV2 (P/Q-, N-type), and CaV3 (T-type) channels (Singh et al., 2010).

The molecular consequences of such broad calcium blockade include an overall reduction in Ca²⁺ influx, which could normalize cytosolic Ca²⁺ transients if they are aberrantly elevated but might also disrupt other calcium-dependent signaling cascades necessary for healthy cellular function. In the context of RPE cells, where tightly regulated Ca²⁺ oscillations are critical for proper phagosome–lysosome fusion and photoreceptor outer segment (POS) degradation, this balance is particularly delicate. The potential therapeutic benefit of SKF96365 in dry AMD thus hinges on its ability to recalibrate Ca²⁺ homeostasis without triggering deleterious off-target effects (Singh et al., 2010).

─────────────────────────────  
IV. EXPECTED EFFECT IN DRY AMD

Dry age-related macular degeneration is characterized by progressive RPE dysfunction, abnormal calcium signaling, impaired phagocytosis of POS, and subsequent accumulation of toxic deposits such as lipofuscin. In healthy RPE cells, calcium regulation is essential for several cellular processes, including the fusion of phagosomes with lysosomes—a step that is critical for the degradation of shed photoreceptor outer segments. Dysfunction in these calcium-dependent events is believed to contribute to the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Zhao et al., 2015; Wimmers & Strauss, 2007).

The central hypothesis under consideration is that SKF96365 will modulate Ca²⁺ influx through TRPC channels in RPE cells, with an approximate IC₅₀ near 5 μM, thereby normalizing cytosolic Ca²⁺ transients. This normalization is expected to restore proper Ca²⁺ dynamics that drive efficient phagosome trafficking and lysosome fusion. In vitro studies using ARPE-19 cells—the human cell line commonly employed as a model for RPE physiology—demonstrate that disrupting abnormal Ca²⁺ entry can lead to improved co-localization of lysosomal markers such as LAMP1 with intracellular phagosomes. The increased co-localization is taken as an indicator of enhanced phagosome–lysosome fusion and, consequently, more effective degradation of POS (Wimmers & Strauss, 2007).

In practical terms, if SKF96365 is able to restore near-physiological Ca²⁺ transients in the RPE, the process of phagosome maturation would likely proceed more efficiently. Under normal conditions, following the ingestion of photoreceptor outer segments, phagosomes are trafficked through a maturation process involving early endosomal (e.g., Rab5-positive) and late endosomal/lysosomal (e.g., Rab7-, LAMP1-positive) steps before complete degradation occurs (Zhao et al., 2015; Keeling et al., 2018). By counteracting the dysregulation in Ca²⁺ entry, SKF96365 could theoretically help re-establish the kinetics of phagosome–lysosome fusion and POS clearance, which might slow or prevent the accumulation of deleterious deposits in RPE cells—a hallmark of dry AMD progression.

Moreover, evidence from ocular research suggests that SKF96365 has been applied in experimental settings beyond RPE studies. For instance, in lamina cribrosa cells—a cell type implicated in glaucomatous pathology—SKF96365 at concentrations around 10 μM was able to mitigate oxidative stress–induced profibrotic gene expression. While this study was not focused on AMD, the fact that the compound could safely modulate Ca²⁺-dependent signaling pathways in an ocular context lends indirect support to the idea that similar mechanisms might be harnessed in RPE cells (Irnaten et al., 2020).

However, a critical aspect of the expected effect is the balance between beneficial TRPC channel inhibition and detrimental off-target blockade. Because SKF96365 potently blocks T-type calcium channels (with an IC₅₀ near 560 nM) and also affects high-voltage-activated channels, there is a substantial risk that, at concentrations effective for TRPC modulation, the compound will inhibit additional calcium channels necessary for other vital RPE functions. As a result, while the anticipated normalization of Ca²⁺ transients may promote phagosome maturation and enhance LAMP1 co-localization with phagosomes, the broad inhibitory profile could also lead to unintended suppression of other calcium-dependent processes that maintain RPE cell homeostasis (Singh et al., 2010).

In summary, the expected effect of SKF96365 in dry AMD is twofold. First, it is anticipated to reduce pathological Ca²⁺ overload in RPE cells by inhibiting aberrant TRPC channel activity, thereby restoring the intracellular Ca²⁺ signaling required for phagosome–lysosome fusion. Second, this normalization is expected to improve the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments, which, in turn, would reduce the accumulation of cellular debris that contributes to RPE dysfunction in dry AMD. Nonetheless, these effects must be interpreted with caution given the compound’s propensity for off-target interactions, which may complicate its overall benefit-risk profile (Wimmers & Strauss, 2007; Singh et al., 2010; Zhao et al., 2015).

─────────────────────────────  
V. OVERALL EVALUATION

Evaluating SKF96365 for repurposing in the treatment of dry AMD requires a careful weighing of its mechanistic rationale against the limitations imposed by its pharmacological profile. On the strength side, SKF96365 offers a compelling mechanism based on decades of research linking Ca²⁺ dysregulation to RPE dysfunction. Its ability to inhibit TRPC channels—a family of ion channels that contribute to the maintenance of basal Ca²⁺ levels and are critical for processes such as phagosome trafficking and lysosome fusion in RPE cells—directly addresses a known pathological mechanism in dry AMD (Singh et al., 2010; Wimmers & Strauss, 2007). The hypothesis that normalization of aberrant Ca²⁺ transients can enhance the clearance of photoreceptor outer segments is well supported by experimental evidence demonstrating improved lysosomal marker co-localization in cultured RPE cells when Ca²⁺ entry is moderated (Wimmers & Strauss, 2007).

Additionally, SKF96365 has an established track record as an ocular research tool. Studies in lamina cribrosa cells in glaucoma models have shown that the compound can be administered at ocularly relevant concentrations with observable functional effects on Ca²⁺-dependent gene expression without immediate cytotoxicity (Irnaten et al., 2020). This observed ocular safety in short-term studies lends some support to its potential translation into an ocular therapeutic context. Moreover, the broader utility of SKF96365 in modulating intracellular Ca²⁺ has been confirmed in a variety of preclinical models, ranging from glioma cell lines to endothelial cells, highlighting its robustness as a Ca²⁺ channel inhibitor (Singh et al., 2010).

However, several significant weaknesses temper the overall enthusiasm for direct repurposing of SKF96365 as a treatment for dry AMD. The foremost limitation is its lack of selectivity. Although SKF96365 inhibits TRPC channels in the micromolar range, it concurrently blocks other calcium channels—most notably T-type channels—with a potency that is approximately ninefold greater than that for TRPC channels (Singh et al., 2010). Such potent off-target blockade is problematic because T-type calcium channels, along with L-type and other voltage-gated channels, are essential for a multitude of cellular functions within the retina and the central nervous system. Their inadvertent inhibition could lead to compromised cellular viability and dysregulation of signaling cascades that extend beyond phagosome clearance in the RPE (Singh et al., 2010).

Another critical concern is the compound’s broad spectrum of activity. In addition to its effects on TRPC and T-type channels, SKF96365 has been shown to inhibit high-voltage-activated calcium channels, interfere with potassium channel conductance, inhibit sarcoplasmic reticulum Ca²⁺-ATPase activity, and even modulate nicotinic receptor function (Harteneck & Gollasch, 2011; Pena & Ordaz, 2008). The concomitant blockade of these various ion channel systems increases the risk that systemic or even localized ocular administration of the compound will produce off-target adverse effects that may compromise both retinal and extra-retinal cell functions. In the context of dry AMD—a chronic degenerative condition that would likely require long-term therapy—the risk of cumulative toxicity or dysregulation of fundamental Ca²⁺-dependent processes is particularly concerning.

Moreover, while mechanistic studies in cell culture models (such as ARPE-19 cells) have provided valuable insights into SKF96365’s role in modulating Ca²⁺ signaling, there is a distinct lack of in vivo data demonstrating its efficacy in models of dry AMD. The retinal environment in vivo is complex, with contributions from multiple cell types—including RPE, photoreceptors, microglia, and vascular endothelial cells—and is subject to intricate immune and inflammatory interactions. The translation of in vitro findings to in vivo efficacy, especially for a compound with a narrow therapeutic index resulting from overlapping inhibitory concentrations for TRPC versus T-type channels, remains a formidable challenge (Wimmers & Strauss, 2007; Irnaten et al., 2020; Singh et al., 2010).

A further limitation is that the expected benefit—namely, the normalization of Ca²⁺ transients to restore phagolysosomal fusion—relies on a very specific modulation of intracellular signals. RPE cells exhibit highly regulated calcium oscillations that are critical not only for phagocytosis but also for maintaining cellular metabolism, gene expression, and autophagic processes. Given that SKF96365 is a nonselective inhibitor, it is likely to perturb these tightly controlled Ca²⁺ signaling networks in ways that are not entirely predictable. Such disturbances might lead to unintended alterations in RPE function, potentially exacerbating rather than ameliorating the compromised homeostasis seen in dry AMD (Zhao et al., 2015; Singh et al., 2010).

Finally, while there is some evidence in ocular contexts from glaucoma models, the chronic administration required for a degenerative disease such as dry AMD has not been explored. Long-term safety studies in animal models, coupled with detailed pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic analyses, are necessary to fully assess whether SKF96365 could be safely repurposed for ocular use. The risk of systemic absorption and off-target effects in the central nervous system or cardiovascular tissues cannot be ignored, given the compound’s known actions on multiple ion channel types (Irnaten et al., 2020; Maier et al., 2015).

In weighing these strengths and weaknesses, SKF96365 appears to offer valuable proof-of-concept evidence that modulating Ca²⁺ influx through TRPC channels can impact processes relevant to RPE phagosome trafficking and POS clearance. However, the compound’s broad-spectrum inhibition, particularly its potent T-type calcium channel blockade, undermines its candidacy as a safe, selective, and effective therapeutic agent for dry AMD. Consequently, while SKF96365 remains an important pharmacological tool in dissecting the role of Ca²⁺ signaling in RPE physiology, its direct repurposing for clinical treatment of dry AMD would require significant chemical refinement—or the development of derivative compounds with improved selectivity—to narrow its inhibitory spectrum and thus enhance its therapeutic index (Singh et al., 2010; Wimmers & Strauss, 2007).

─────────────────────────────  
VI. CONCLUSION

In conclusion, the comprehensive literature review indicates that SKF96365, a synthetic imidazole derivative initially developed as an inhibitor of receptor-mediated calcium entry, demonstrates robust activity against a variety of calcium channels—including TRPC channels that contribute to basal Ca²⁺ influx in retinal pigment epithelial cells. Its ability to modulate Ca²⁺ transients provides a mechanistically attractive hypothesis for restoring proper phagosome–lysosome fusion and enhancing photoreceptor outer segment clearance—which are central to the pathogenesis of dry age-related macular degeneration (Singh et al., 2010; Wimmers & Strauss, 2007).

Nonetheless, significant challenges temper its clinical potential. The compound’s nonselectivity, evidenced by its potent blockade of low-voltage-activated T-type channels (IC₅₀ ~560 nM) and its concurrent inhibition of high-voltage-activated calcium channels and other ion channel systems, severely narrows the feasible therapeutic window (Singh et al., 2010; Harteneck & Gollasch, 2011). The risk that, at effective doses intended to normalize RPE Ca²⁺ signaling, SKF96365 might inadvertently suppress essential calcium-dependent processes is nontrivial, especially given the delicate balance of Ca²⁺ homeostasis required in the RPE for photoreceptor maintenance and survival (Singh et al., 2010; Maier et al., 2015).

Furthermore, although preclinical in vitro evidence in ARPE-19 cells and similar models is promising, there remains a critical gap in in vivo data specific to dry AMD. The complex interplay of cellular, molecular, and environmental factors in the human retina poses considerable hurdles for the translation of cell culture findings to clinically relevant outcomes. In addition, the chronic nature of AMD necessitates long-term safety and efficacy data—information that is currently lacking for SKF96365 in the context of ocular therapeutics (Irnaten et al., 2020; Maier et al., 2015).

Given these considerations, SKF96365 may best be regarded at this stage not as a final drug candidate for dry AMD therapy, but rather as a lead compound that validates the strategy of targeting aberrant Ca²⁺ signaling within RPE cells. Future research should focus on chemically optimizing SKF96365 to enhance its selectivity for TRPC channels while minimizing off-target interactions with T-type, L-type, and other voltage-gated channels. Parallel investigations into alternative TRPC modulators with a narrower pharmacological profile may also prove fruitful. In any case, rigorous preclinical studies—including in vivo models of dry AMD—are imperative before clinical translation can be contemplated (Singh et al., 2010; Wimmers & Strauss, 2007).

Ultimately, the therapeutic strategy of modulating Ca²⁺ influx to restore phagosome–lysosome fusion and improve POS clearance in RPE cells remains a compelling avenue for treating dry AMD. SKF96365 offers a valuable starting point and proof-of-concept, but its broad-spectrum ion channel inhibition necessitates careful re-engineering to achieve the necessary balance between efficacy and safety. Only with further chemical refinement, targeted in vivo validation, and comprehensive toxicity evaluation can such a compound be advanced toward clinical trials for dry AMD (Singh et al., 2010; Wimmers & Strauss, 2007; Zhao et al., 2015).

─────────────────────────────  
OVERALL EVALUATION SUMMARY

• Overview of the Candidate:  
SKF96365 is a synthetic imidazole derivative belonging to the broad-spectrum TRP channel blockers, originally developed to inhibit receptor-mediated Ca²⁺ entry. Its chemical structure and modifications enable it to interact with multiple Ca²⁺ channels, making it a useful tool in experimental Ca²⁺ signaling studies (Singh et al., 2010; Harteneck, Klose, & Krautwurst, 2011).

• Therapeutic History:  
While extensively used in preclinical studies—including in retinal pigment epithelial cells and ocular models such as lamina cribrosa cells—SKF96365 has not yet been applied in clinical or veterinary settings for dry AMD. Its application has primarily been limited to research investigations aimed at deciphering Ca²⁺-dependent cellular mechanisms (Wimmers & Strauss, 2007; Irnaten et al., 2020).

• Mechanism of Action:  
The compound functions as a nonselective inhibitor of Ca²⁺ entry. It shows moderate potency against TRPC channels (IC₅₀ ~5–30 μM) but exhibits much greater potency against T-type Ca²⁺ channels (IC₅₀ ~560 nM). Its inhibition is non-competitive, state-independent, and voltage-insensitive, indicating a broad and allosteric pore-blocking mechanism (Singh et al., 2010).

• Expected Effect:  
In the context of dry AMD, SKF96365 is hypothesized to restore calcium homeostasis in RPE cells by modulating aberrant TRPC-mediated Ca²⁺ entry. This, in turn, is expected to enhance phagosome–lysosome fusion and improve the clearance of photoreceptor outer segments—a process critical for preventing the toxic accumulation of cellular debris that characterizes dry AMD (Wimmers & Strauss, 2007; Zhao et al., 2015).

• Overall Evaluation:  
Despite a strong mechanistic rationale and promising in vitro data indicating that modulation of Ca²⁺ signaling can improve RPE function, the broad off-target effects of SKF96365 represent a significant challenge. Its potent inhibition of T-type and high-voltage-activated calcium channels, along with other ion channels, undermines its potential as a therapeutic agent. The lack of in vivo data in AMD models and concerns over long-term ocular safety further limit its immediate clinical applicability. Therefore, while SKF96365 remains an invaluable research tool, it appears better suited as a lead compound for further optimization rather than as a final candidate for dry AMD therapy (Singh et al., 2010; Wimmers & Strauss, 2007).

─────────────────────────────  
FINAL RECOMMENDATION

Based on the detailed literature review, SKF96365 offers a proof-of-concept for the modulation of disrupted Ca²⁺ signaling—a pathway critically implicated in the pathogenesis of dry AMD. However, its inherent nonselectivity, especially the potent blockade of T-type Ca²⁺ channels at concentrations that overlap with those required for TRPC channel inhibition, poses significant concerns regarding both efficacy and safety in the RPE in vivo. The compound’s reported ocular safety in acute glaucoma models is encouraging but insufficient to guarantee tolerability during chronic administration required in dry AMD. Therefore, while SKF96365 validates the general approach of normalizing Ca²⁺ transients to enhance phagosome–lysosome fusion, further chemical optimization to improve selectivity for TRPC channels is essential before advancing toward clinical evaluation for dry AMD. Future studies should pivot toward either developing derivatives with a narrower spectrum of activity or employing combination strategies that mitigate its off-target effects, while concurrently establishing robust preclinical models to evaluate long-term outcomes in the retina (Singh et al., 2010; Irnaten et al., 2020).

In conclusion, SKF96365 represents a scientifically intriguing candidate as a modulator of Ca²⁺ dynamics with potential implications for the treatment of dry AMD. However, its nonselective mode of action underscores the need for further research and chemical refinement. Until these issues are addressed, SKF96365 should be regarded primarily as an experimental tool for validating the role of Ca²⁺ signaling in RPE dysfunction rather than as a direct therapeutic option for dry AMD.

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
SU5402 is a small‐molecule inhibitor that belongs to the indolinone, also often described as oxindole, family of compounds designed to target receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs), most notably fibroblast growth factor receptors (FGFRs) and platelet‐derived growth factor receptors (PDGFRs) (Liang et al., 2012; Manetti & Botta, 2003). Chemically, it is defined as 3-[(3-(2-carboxyethyl)-4-methylpyrrol-2-yl)methylene]-2-indolinone, a structure that features an indolin-2-one nucleus decorated with a propionic acid chain and a methyl substituent on a pyrrole ring; these structural motifs enable the molecule to mimic key interactions commonly found in ATP binding (Prakash et al., 2012; Ho et al., 2014). Originally discovered as one of the first classes of FGFR tyrosine kinase inhibitors, the compound’s crystal structure in complex with FGFR was resolved as early as 1997, establishing its role as an important lead for further inhibitor design (Liang et al., 2012). SU5402 is therefore categorized as an ATP-competitive inhibitor that occupies a hydrophobic pocket adjacent to the adenine binding site in FGFR, and its design has inspired many subsequent efforts to optimize RTK inhibition for therapeutic purposes (Manetti & Botta, 2003). In addition to its potent activity against FGFR1 (with reported IC₅₀ values around 0.03 μM), SU5402 displays inhibitory effects toward PDGFRβ and even VEGFR2, positioning it as a prototype multi-targeted kinase inhibitor in early-stage drug development programs (Chen et al., 2011; Ho et al., 2014). Its synthesis is rooted in structure-based medicinal chemistry approaches whereby modifications of the indolinone core and side chain functionalities were guided by crystal structure data and structure–activity relationship studies (Liang et al., 2012; Manetti & Botta, 2003). Consequently, SU5402 stands as a well-characterized synthetic compound with a clearly delineated pharmacophore, and its molecular interactions with the kinase active site are illustrative of the class’s capacity to serve as lead compounds in various therapeutic areas (Manetti & Botta, 2003; Pike, 2017).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, the development and use of SU5402 have been predominantly tied to oncology and anti-angiogenic research. Early investigations demonstrated that by inhibiting FGFR signaling, SU5402 effectively blocked the autophosphorylation of the receptor and downstream proliferative and survival pathways such as RAF-MEK1/2-MAPK and PI3K-AKT—pathways that are essential drivers of tumor growth and angiogenesis (Liang et al., 2012; Manetti & Botta, 2003). These studies established its potency in vitro and in animal models, where it was used as a research tool to interrogate the role of FGFR-related pathways in cancer biology (Manetti & Botta, 2003). In addition, several members of the indolinone inhibitor class, including derivatives related to SU5402, such as SU5416 and SU6668, were developed for anti-tumor and anti-angiogenic applications and were advanced to clinical trials for various malignancies (Ho et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2016). Despite its promising biochemical profile, SU5402 itself did not progress further in clinical development for oncology, largely due to issues associated with multi-kinase inhibition and subsequent toxicity profiles observed during broader preclinical studies (Manetti & Botta, 2003).

Notably, there is no published record in the literature, as captured by the provided sources, that SU5402 has ever been intentionally repurposed for the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) or similar retinal degenerative diseases (Liang et al., 2012; Manetti & Botta, 2003). Its application has remained confined as a tool compound in research settings for understanding FGFR signaling and its role in cellular proliferation and angiogenesis, rather than for modulating processes underlying retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) differentiation and phagocytosis. However, its continued use in ocular safety studies in vitro and in rodent models has provided preliminary evidence of an acceptable safety profile when applied topically or delivered locally in ocular tissues (Chen et al., 2011; Zhang et al., 2016). Thus, while SU5402 has a rich history as an FGFR inhibitor in cancer-related research, there is a significant knowledge gap regarding its therapeutic use in dry AMD, an area that remains largely unexplored until now.

Mechanism of Action:  
SU5402 exerts its biological activity as an ATP-competitive inhibitor targeting the tyrosine kinase domain of FGFR1, a member of the receptor tyrosine kinase family implicated in various cellular functions including proliferation, differentiation, and survival. At the molecular level, the indolinone core of SU5402 occupies the ATP-binding site in FGFR1, where it competes with ATP for the binding pocket (Liang et al., 2012; Manetti & Botta, 2003). Detailed crystallographic studies have revealed that the oxindole nucleus of the compound forms two or more critical hydrogen bonds with conserved residues in the kinase hinge region, specifically with Glu562 and Ala564, which normally interact with the adenine part of ATP (Manetti & Botta, 2003; Pike, 2017). In addition, the propionic acid group of SU5402 forms a third hydrogen bond with the side chain of Asn568, a residue in the hinge region that further stabilizes the inhibitor-bound conformation of the kinase (Manetti & Botta, 2003; Pike, 2017). This binding pattern not only ensures high potency by blocking the ATP-binding site but also promotes a specific conformational change in the glycine-rich loop of FGFR1, which is integral to the enzyme’s catalytic activity (Mohammadi et al., 1998; Manetti & Botta, 2003).

Beyond its direct interactions with FGFR1, SU5402 has also been reported to interact with other kinases such as VEGFR2 and PDGFRβ, albeit with slightly varying potencies. Its ability to inhibit multiple kinases is attributable to the high degree of structural homology within the ATP-binding regions of these receptor tyrosine kinases and reflects its broad-spectrum activity as an RTK inhibitor (Chen et al., 2011; Ho et al., 2014). Despite this multi-target activity, the molecular determinants for its relative selectivity—particularly the critical hydrogen bond interactions and the spatial orientation of its substituents—have been well characterized, making it a useful tool to dissect kinase-mediated pathways (Pike, 2017; Prakash et al., 2012).

In the context of retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) biology, FGFR signaling is implicated in the regulation of cell polarity, differentiation, and the maintenance of phagocytic receptor expression. The hypothesis under evaluation suggests that inhibition of FGFR by SU5402 may tip the balance of intracellular signaling in favor of differentiation-associated processes, thereby upregulating the surface expression of MERTK and the integrin αvβ5 complex, both of which are essential for the binding and internalization of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) (Liang et al., 2012; Manetti & Botta, 2003). In effect, by interfering with the normal FGFR-driven proliferative and survival signals, SU5402 might foster an environment conducive to RPE maturation and enhanced phagocytic functionality. This molecular action is not only supported by the established biochemistry of SU5402 in cancer models but is also mechanistically plausible in the RPE, where FGFR signaling dynamics play a role in determining cell morphology and receptor trafficking (Manetti & Botta, 2003; Chen et al., 2011).

In summary, SU5402 presents as a well-characterized, indolinone-based FGFR/PDGFRβ inhibitor with a strong biochemical foundation rooted in detailed structural and mechanistic studies. From a chemical and molecular perspective, its design and mechanism of action are well established; the compound engages the ATP-binding pocket of FGFR1 with high potency primarily through a series of well-defined hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic interactions, which underpins its efficacy as an inhibitor (Liang et al., 2012; Manetti & Botta, 2003; Prakash et al., 2012). Proposal for Metoprolol (β₁-adrenergic blocker; AstraZeneca)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Metoprolol is a second-generation, β1-selective adrenergic receptor antagonist developed within the broader historical evolution of β-blockers that began with Sir James Black’s introduction of β-adrenergic blockade for angina and expanded into major cardiovascular indications over subsequent decades (Opie, 2013; Mandiricha & Rochmanti, 2020). Within this class, β1-selective antagonists such as metoprolol competitively inhibit catecholamine binding at β1-adrenergic receptors, attenuating Gs–adenylyl cyclase–cAMP signaling and downstream protein kinase A (PKA) effects in tissues where β1-ARs are functionally expressed, most prominently the heart (Böhm et al., 2023; Mandiricha & Rochmanti, 2020). β-blockers as a class are synthetic small molecules with heterogeneous structures and pharmacokinetic properties (lipophilicity, bioavailability, hepatic versus renal clearance, intrinsic sympathomimetic activity), which shape their tissue penetration and side-effect profiles; metoprolol is moderately lipophilic and is predominantly cleared via hepatic CYP2D6-mediated metabolism (Panjrath & Messerli, 2006; Opie, 2013).

Therapeutically, β-blockers (including metoprolol) are widely used for hypertension (historically), angina pectoris, arrhythmia rate control, post–myocardial infarction secondary prevention, and chronic heart failure, with robust evidence for mortality and morbidity reduction in selected cardiovascular settings (Opie, 2013). In ophthalmology, β-adrenergic antagonists became a major class for open-angle glaucoma due to their ability to lower intraocular pressure (IOP) by reducing aqueous humor production via ciliary body β-adrenergic receptors; the archetypal agent is the nonselective β-blocker timolol, whereas the β1-selective agent betaxolol was developed to mitigate β2-mediated respiratory adverse effects (Nartey et al., 2021; Nocentini & Supuran, 2019). Importantly for posterior-segment drug delivery, early clinical work has evaluated intravitreal metoprolol tartrate at low dose with safety-focused endpoints, establishing preliminary tolerability and paving the way for hypothesis-driven ocular repurposing studies (Chaves et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History  
Systemic cardiovascular use  
Metoprolol has long-standing use as a β1-selective blocker for ischemic heart disease and heart failure; it is among the best-studied β-blockers for postinfarct protection and chronic heart failure alongside carvedilol and bisoprolol, reducing arrhythmic deaths and improving survival when properly titrated in stable systolic heart failure cohorts (Opie, 2013). Post–myocardial infarction, guideline-supported β-blockade with agents such as metoprolol succinate reduces long-term mortality by approximately a quarter in aggregate analyses, with additive benefit when combined with renin–angiotensin blockade (Opie, 2013). In hypertension, β-blockers have lost primacy as first-line therapy in uncomplicated disease due to inferior stroke prevention and metabolic adverse profiles compared with alternative classes, although β1-selective agents remain integral in specific comorbid contexts (e.g., ischemic heart disease, tachyarrhythmias) (Panjrath & Messerli, 2006; Opie, 2013). Pharmacologically, metoprolol’s hepatic metabolism via CYP2D6 yields clinically relevant drug–drug interaction risk (e.g., with paroxetine/fluoxetine), with interindividual variability in exposure that has been documented in pharmacogenetic studies and long-term PK observations (Ali et al., 2019; Nieminen et al., 2005; Opie, 2013).

Ophthalmic class use and metoprolol-specific ocular experience  
In ophthalmology, topical β-adrenergic antagonists are established agents to lower IOP, reducing aqueous humor production via antagonism of β-receptors in the ciliary body and iris/ciliary processes; timolol has been the archetype since 1978, and betaxolol (β1-selective) was introduced to minimize β2-related bronchospasm risks, albeit with somewhat reduced IOP-lowering efficacy relative to timolol (Nartey et al., 2021; Nocentini & Supuran, 2019). Betaxolol is repeatedly cited for neuroprotective actions in ocular models (e.g., slowing retinal changes after ischemia/reperfusion), underscoring that some β-blockers possess non-IOP biological effects on retinal cells (Nartey et al., 2021). Multiple sources list metoprolol among β1-selective agents and, in some reports, among β-blockers available for topical ophthalmic use; however, detailed clinical IOP-lowering data, efficacy comparisons, or neuroprotective endpoints specific to metoprolol in glaucoma are not provided in the materials at hand (Nartey et al., 2021). Topical β-blockers can cause systemic adverse effects because of nasolacrimal absorption without first-pass metabolism, including bronchospasm and bradyarrhythmias, necessitating caution in patients with reactive airway disease or conduction disorders and motivation for strategies to reduce systemic exposure (Vander Zanden et al., 2001; Nocentini & Supuran, 2019).

Of particular relevance to posterior-segment indications, a small phase I clinical study delivered off-label intravitreal metoprolol tartrate (50 μg/0.05 mL) in five eyes with circumscribed choroidal hemangioma, with safety assessments including full-field ERG (ISCEV protocol), OCT-based retinal thickness and choroidal thickness, anterior segment/vitreous inflammation, BCVA, and systemic blood pressure; the investigators reported no ERG evidence of toxicity, no clinical inflammation, stable IOP, stable choroidal thickness, no visual acuity deterioration, and modest reductions in retinal thickness or intra/subretinal fluid in a subset at four weeks (Chaves et al., 2021). Parallel rabbit studies did not show acute retinal toxicity at 50–100 μg intravitreal doses, supporting the human dose selection as biologically tolerable; nevertheless, limitations include very small sample size, single-dose exposure, short follow-up, and lack of dose–response or repeated-administration data (Chaves et al., 2021). The same group and others frame β-adrenergic blockade as an emerging target for neovascular or vascular ocular lesions, with propranolol providing historical precedent (infantile hemangiomas systemically; anecdotal ocular cases), while β1-selective metoprolol is explored for intraocular use owing to physicochemical compatibility and safety signals (Böhm et al., 2023; Chaves et al., 2021).

History in retinal/degenerative disease models  
Outside of pressure lowering and ocular vascular lesions, the provided sources report that metoprolol demonstrated neuroprotective effects in a rat model of retinal degeneration when given intraperitoneally or orally, and that metoprolol was not toxic to cultured retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) cells in vitro, implying a tolerable profile at the RPE level (Chaves et al., 2021). While this signals potential relevance to retinal cell survival, the evidence is preliminary, systemic rather than local in the degeneration model, and not specific to age-related macular degeneration subtypes; no clinical data in dry AMD were identified in the supplied materials (Chaves et al., 2021). The literature here does not document trials or case series of β1-selective antagonists for dry AMD, geographic atrophy, or RPE phagocytic dysfunction endpoints, so any linkage is inferential based on class mechanisms and exploratory safety/biology rather than disease-directed outcomes (Chaves et al., 2021; Nartey et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action  
Primary pharmacology and signaling  
β1-adrenergic receptors are G-protein–coupled receptors classically coupled to Gαs, stimulating adenylyl cyclase, increasing intracellular cAMP, and activating PKA with broad downstream effects on ion channels, contractile machinery, and metabolism; antagonists such as metoprolol prevent catecholamine binding and blunt these signaling cascades in β1-expressing tissues (Böhm et al., 2023). β1-ARs are predominantly expressed in the heart, congruent with the robust chronotropic and inotropic effects of catecholamines and the established therapeutic actions of β1-selective blockade in cardiovascular disease; classically, blockade reduces cardiac output and renin release, lowering myocardial oxygen demand and ameliorating ischemic symptoms (Mandiricha & Rochmanti, 2020). Lipophilicity governs CNS penetration and neuropsychiatric side effects across the class, with more lipophilic agents crossing the blood–brain barrier more readily and potentially engaging central β-AR or other targets; metoprolol exhibits moderate lipid solubility, implying some CNS penetration and reinforcing that β-adrenergic mechanisms relevant to neurobiology are plausible with this agent (Opie, 2013; Panjrath & Messerli, 2006).

Ocular mechanisms and β-adrenergic pharmacology  
In the eye, β-adrenergic receptors in the ciliary body and related anterior segment tissues regulate aqueous humor production, and β-adrenergic antagonists reduce IOP by suppressing aqueous humor secretion; timolol’s nonselective β1/β2 blockade is highly effective for IOP lowering, while β1-selective betaxolol is generally less potent in IOP reduction but carries a reduced risk of β2-mediated respiratory adverse events (Nocentini & Supuran, 2019; Nartey et al., 2021). Beyond IOP, betaxolol displays neuroprotective properties in ocular models, including slowing of retinal changes after ischemia/reperfusion injury—a finding that suggests at least some β-blockers can confer direct retinal cell benefits independent of aqueous suppression, potentially via calcium channel modulation or other non-adrenergic mechanisms (Grieshaber & Flammer, 2010; Nartey et al., 2021). In posterior segment disease, β-adrenergic modulation has been hypothesized to affect angiogenesis and neural damage processes, with propranolol historically associated with ocular vascular lesion regression and preliminary trials pivoting toward exploring β1-selective metoprolol intravitreally due to formulation advantages; within this frame, β-ARs constitute a therapeutic target space extending beyond anterior segment fluid dynamics (Chaves et al., 2021).

Pharmacokinetic and safety considerations  
Metoprolol is extensively metabolized by CYP2D6, with genotype and drug–drug interactions modulating exposure; while these features are central to systemic administration, intravitreal delivery aims to limit systemic exposure, and early phase I data reported no significant changes in systemic blood pressure, suggesting minimal hemodynamic spillover at the tested ocular dose (Chaves et al., 2021; Opie, 2013). Importantly, an animal study with intravitreal propranolol (not metoprolol) detected photopic ERG amplitude reductions in rabbits at 28 days, emphasizing the necessity of agent- and dose-specific retinal electrophysiologic safety evaluation for β-blockers administered intraocularly; metoprolol at 50 μg intravitreally did not demonstrate ERG toxicity in small human series and rabbits, but long-term and repeated-dose safety remain untested (Chaves et al., 2021).

Relevance to RPE biology and dry AMD  
The supplied literature confirms that metoprolol is not toxic to RPE cells in vitro and that systemic metoprolol has neuroprotective effects in a rat retinal degeneration model; however, the materials do not document β1-AR expression in RPE, metoprolol’s modulation of RPE cAMP/PKA signaling, or effects on actin cytoskeleton dynamics, phagocytic cup formation, or photoreceptor outer segment (POS) internalization in RPE (Chaves et al., 2021). Likewise, while β-adrenergic pharmacology is invoked as a potential target in retinal vascular disease and ocular tumors, no evidence is provided here linking β1-selective antagonism to enhanced RPE phagocytic function, reduced cytoskeletal stiffness, or amelioration of dry AMD pathology, and no clinical evaluations in dry AMD are presented in the supplied texts (Böhm et al., 2023; Chaves et al., 2021).

Expected Effect  
Assay-level expectation under the proposed hypothesis  
The proposal hypothesizes that metoprolol, via β1-AR blockade in RPE, will reduce cAMP levels, alleviate cAMP-driven cytoskeletal stiffness, enhance actin remodeling, and thereby improve POS phagocytosis under stress conditions (e.g., in ARPE-19 assays), with an IC50 in the tens of nanomolar range; the supplied literature does not include data validating β1-AR expression in RPE, metoprolol’s potency at RPE β1-AR, or its effects on RPE actin dynamics or phagocytic cup formation (Chaves et al., 2021). The available ocular evidence base for metoprolol consists of safety-oriented intravitreal studies in choroidal hemangioma, in vitro RPE non-toxicity, and class-level ocular pharmacology centered on aqueous humor production and neuroprotective properties of betaxolol rather than RPE phagocytosis (Chaves et al., 2021; Nartey et al., 2021). Therefore, while β-adrenergic GPCR blockade would be expected to reduce cAMP in β1-expressing cells, the downstream link from cAMP reduction to RPE cytoskeletal remodeling and increased phagocytosis is not substantiated by the provided materials; accordingly, the expected effect in a phagocytosis assay remains speculative given the evidence presented here (Böhm et al., 2023).

Cellular expression and disease relevance  
The hypothesis requires that β1-AR is expressed and functionally coupled in the RPE, which is not documented in the present set of sources; instead, the ocular β-AR literature provided focuses on ciliary body (aqueous secretion) and, more broadly, retinal neuroprotection and vascular modulation at the tissue level (Grieshaber & Flammer, 2010; Nocentini & Supuran, 2019). Although metoprolol’s lack of RPE cytotoxicity supports feasibility for RPE-directed assays, translation to dry AMD hinges on improving RPE-mediated processes relevant to disease (e.g., POS clearance), which are not addressed in the current citations; moreover, no dry AMD or geographic atrophy outcomes have been studied with metoprolol in clinical or preclinical AMD models in the provided context (Chaves et al., 2021).

Delivery and dosing  
Given the anterior segment systemic absorption risks of topical β-blockers and the desire to target posterior RPE, intravitreal delivery is mechanistically attractive; the phase I trial indicates that a 50 μg/0.05 mL intravitreal dose is acutely tolerable with no ERG toxicity at four weeks, slight reductions in retinal thickness in chronic choroidal hemangioma, and no meaningful systemic blood pressure changes, which collectively support feasibility of posterior-segment dosing for exploratory mechanistic studies (Chaves et al., 2021). However, dose–response, repeat-dose safety, and long-term retinal electrophysiological effects remain unresolved and are particularly important given the ERG effects observed with intravitreal propranolol in animals, underscoring the necessity of cautious, stepwise dose escalation and comprehensive functional readouts if proceeding (Chaves et al., 2021).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Known pharmacology and druggability: Metoprolol is a well-characterized β1-selective antagonist with decades of systemic clinical experience and a clear molecular mechanism of action centered on β1-AR antagonism of Gs–AC–cAMP signaling; its class has demonstrable ocular pharmacology, establishing druggability of ocular β-adrenergic targets (Böhm et al., 2023; Nocentini & Supuran, 2019).  
- Ocular feasibility and early safety: Intravitreal metoprolol tartrate at 50 μg/0.05 mL has early human safety signals (no ERG toxicity, no inflammation, no VA deterioration at four weeks) and parallel animal data without acute retinal toxicity at 50–100 μg, supporting the feasibility of posterior-segment delivery for mechanistic or efficacy studies (Chaves et al., 2021).  
- RPE tolerability and retinal neuroprotection signals: In vitro, metoprolol did not exhibit toxicity to RPE cells, and in vivo systemic dosing showed neuroprotective effects in a rat retinal degeneration model, suggesting a favorable biological profile in retinal cell contexts, albeit not AMD-specific (Chaves et al., 2021).  
- Ocular β-blocker precedent with neuroprotective actions: Betaxolol (β1-selective) exhibits neuroprotective effects in ocular models beyond IOP lowering, indicating that at least some β1 blockers can confer retinal cell protection via mechanisms that may be independent of aqueous suppression, a conceptual precedent for exploring β1-targeted biology in posterior ocular tissues (Grieshaber & Flammer, 2010; Nartey et al., 2021).

Weaknesses and key evidence gaps for dry AMD  
- Absence of RPE β1-AR functional data: The central hypothesis requires β1-AR expression and functional coupling in RPE regulating cAMP-dependent actin dynamics and phagocytosis; the provided literature does not document β1-AR expression in RPE, nor metoprolol effects on RPE actin remodeling, phagocytic cup formation, or POS internalization, making the mechanistic premise unsubstantiated by the present citations (Chaves et al., 2021).  
- No dry AMD–specific preclinical or clinical data: There are no dry AMD or geographic atrophy studies—preclinical or clinical—using metoprolol in the provided materials; consequently, disease relevance and translational signal are absent (Chaves et al., 2021; Nartey et al., 2021).  
- Limited intravitreal safety characterization: Human intravitreal data are phase I, single-dose, and short-term; repeated dosing, long-term ERG stability, and dose–response safety are not assessed, and animal data with intravitreal propranolol reveal potential electrophysiologic risks, necessitating cautious development (Chaves et al., 2021).  
- Class heterogeneity and target specificity: Ocular β-blocker data demonstrating neuroprotection are centered on betaxolol; translating these effects to metoprolol without mechanistic support may be nontrivial given potential off-target (e.g., calcium channel) contributions unique to specific molecules (Grieshaber & Flammer, 2010; Nartey et al., 2021).  
- Systemic exposure considerations in non-intravitreal routes: Topical β-blockers can produce clinically significant systemic adverse effects via nasolacrimal absorption; while intravitreal dosing mitigates this risk, any exploration of topical delivery to RPE would require careful systemic safety mitigation (Vander Zanden et al., 2001; Nocentini & Supuran, 2019).

Risk–benefit and development implications  
On balance, metoprolol has an encouraging early ocular safety profile by intravitreal administration at low dose and a favorable RPE tolerability signal, but the mechanistic and disease-relevant evidence for dry AMD is currently insufficient to justify efficacy-focused clinical development; instead, a staged preclinical program to test the RPE phagocytosis hypothesis is warranted before advancing (Chaves et al., 2021). Specifically:  
- Mechanism validation: Confirm β1-AR expression and signaling in human RPE (primary RPE and ARPE-19), quantify cAMP responses to β-agonists and metoprolol antagonism, and interrogate actin dynamics and phagocytic cup formation using live-cell imaging and POS uptake assays under stress paradigms relevant to RPE dysfunction; no such evidence is provided in the current literature set (Chaves et al., 2021).

Given the present evidence, metoprolol should be considered a plausible exploratory tool compound for posterior-segment β1-AR biology in the retina/RPE with a preliminary intravitreal safety margin at low doses, but not yet a validated therapeutic candidate for dry AMD; only if RPE β1-AR signaling is shown to regulate phagocytosis and actin remodeling in a way that metoprolol favorably modulates and if such effects translate to structural/functional benefit in relevant models should a dry AMD program proceed (Chaves et al., 2021; Nartey et al., 2021).
