The central hypothesis under investigation posits that Methylstat, by inhibiting histone demethylases in RPE cells, will enhance the transcription of autophagy and phagocytosis genes (e.g., TFEB and MERTK). Such a transcriptional upregulation is expected to promote the uptake of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) and improve lysosomal function, thereby ameliorating the cellular damage associated with oxidative stress in AMD (Nita & Grzybowski, 2023; Kaarniranta et al., 2023).

II. Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Methylstat is a small molecule inhibitor originally synthesized for its potent activity against the Jumonji C (JmjC) domain-containing family of histone demethylases. These enzymes catalyze the removal of methyl groups from lysine residues on histone proteins, a process that modulates chromatin structure and thereby influences gene transcription. As a synthetic compound, Methylstat was developed to interrogate the functional roles of histone demethylases in various cellular contexts and disease states. It belongs to a class of epigenetic modulators that have been broadly investigated in oncology and other diseases where epigenetic misregulation plays a critical role (Campello et al., 2021). Although the majority of research in retinal diseases has focused on inhibitors of histone deacetylases or activating lysosomal biogenesis via mTOR modulation (Kaštelan et al., 2024; Sinha et al., 2016), there is promising rationale to consider histone demethylase inhibitors as well. The candidate’s chemical structure and mechanism of enzyme inhibition suggest that it may increase levels of activating histone marks such as H3K4me3 at key gene promoters, ultimately facilitating a transcriptionally active chromatin state in RPE cells.

Importantly, repurposing Methylstat for ocular use leverages its established preclinical profile. In rodent models, preliminary ocular safety data suggest tolerability, providing an impetus to explore its potential application in diseases such as dry AMD (Campello et al., 2021; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023). By virtue of its synthetic origin and the ability to fine-tune its dosage and delivery, Methylstat offers a strategic advantage over compounds that require extensive de novo safety profiling. This advantage is complemented by its mechanistic promise: by altering the epigenetic landscape, Methylstat may restore proper regulation of genes critical for autophagy, phagocytosis, and lysosomal clearance that are known to be compromised in aging RPE cells (Kaarniranta et al., 2023).

III. Therapeutic History  
Prior to its consideration in the context of AMD, Methylstat has primarily been utilized as a chemical probe in studies aimed at understanding the biological function of the JmjC family of histone demethylases in several cellular systems. Traditionally, this class of compounds has been investigated for their antitumor properties due to their capacity to alter gene expression profiles that govern cell proliferation and apoptosis (Campello et al., 2021). In contrast, interventions in age-related retinal diseases have so far concentrated on modifying chromatin accessibility through histone deacetylase inhibitors (HDACi) and acetyltransferase modulators, with several groups reporting that targeting these epigenetic enzymes may mitigate retinal damage and slow functional decline (Campello et al., 2021).

The literature regarding histone demethylases—especially those within the JmjC family—indicates that their role in retinal pathophysiology is less well-defined. Notably, the Open Targets platform data provide only limited support for the implication of histone demethylases such as KDM4A and KDM4C in AMD (Buniello et al., 2025). Furthermore, current evidence suggests that these particular demethylases have low association scores with AMD phenotypes and a dearth of mechanistic studies validating their function in RPE health (Buniello et al., 2025). In light of these factors, the therapeutic exploration of Methylstat represents an innovative, albeit higher-risk, strategy. It aims to extend the paradigm of epigenetic therapy to a class of enzymes that has not been rigorously evaluated in the context of AMD, thereby potentially uncovering new biological insights and therapeutic windows (Campello et al., 2021).

IV. Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, Methylstat functions by inhibiting the catalytic activity of JmjC domain-containing histone demethylases. These enzymes are responsible for demethylating lysine residues on histone tails—a modification that can either activate or repress gene transcription depending on the residue involved and the degree of methylation. For instance, trimethylation of histone H3 at lysine 4 (H3K4me3) is generally associated with open chromatin and active transcription, particularly at gene promoter regions. Under normal physiological conditions, a dynamic equilibrium between methylation and demethylation controls chromatin accessibility and the transcriptional potential of a cell (Campello et al., 2021).

Methylstat’s inhibition of these enzymes is expected to lead to an accumulation of methylation marks such as H3K4me3. This buildup can render the chromatin more accessible to transcription factors and the transcriptional machinery, thereby upregulating the expression of genes involved in cellular homeostasis. Specifically, the hypothesis driving the use of Methylstat in dry AMD is that this drug will increase H3K4me3 levels at the promoters of key regulatory genes involved in autophagy and phagocytosis—most notably transcription factor EB (TFEB) and MER tyrosine kinase (MERTK) (Nita & Grzybowski, 2023).

TFEB is a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy. When its expression is upregulated, there is an increased transcription of a suite of genes that coordinate the formation of autophagosomes, lysosomal fusion, and the processing of intracellular debris (Kaarniranta et al., 2023). In parallel, MERTK is critically involved in the phagocytic function of RPE cells, particularly in the uptake and clearance of POS, which are regularly shed by photoreceptors as part of their normal renewal process. By enhancing the transcription of such genes, Methylstat may ultimately promote more efficient autophagic flux and phagocytic clearance, mitigating the accumulation of damaged proteins and debris that is a hallmark of dry AMD (Sinha et al., 2016).

At a biochemical level, the inhibition mechanism most likely involves Methylstat binding to the active site of the demethylase where essential cofactors such as Fe(II) and α-ketoglutarate are coordinated. By chelating or otherwise interfering with these cofactors, Methylstat prevents the oxidative demethylation reaction that would normally remove methyl groups from histone substrates. The net consequence is an epigenetic shift toward transcriptional activation of autophagy and phagocytosis genes (Grigoryan & Markitantova, 2025). Moreover, in the oxidative environment typical of stressed RPE cells, maintaining an active autophagic response is critical to counterbalancing the accumulation of cellular damage. The literature underscores that impaired autophagy and lysosomal dysfunction are pivotal to the progression of AMD, as these pathways are central to the degradation of oxidized proteins and other cellular waste products (Kaarniranta et al., 2023).

An additional layer of complexity in this mechanism is the interplay between histone methylation and the broader network of epigenetic modifications. Dysregulation of histone deacetylases (HDACs) in AMD has been well documented (Campello et al., 2021; Kaštelan et al., 2024), and it often results in a transcriptionally repressive chromatin state. By contrast, Methylstat’s action is aimed at promoting a transcriptionally permissive configuration through the sustained presence of methyl marks. Thus, combining Methylstat’s mechanism with insights into HDAC regulation could eventually lead to combination therapies that more comprehensively restore the epigenetic balance in damaged RPE cells (Zibetti, 2025).

V. Expected Effect  
In vitro assays utilizing cultured RPE cells exposed to oxidative stress are expected to provide the first line of evidence regarding the efficacy of Methylstat. Under conditions that mimic the stress encountered in the aging retina, RPE cells experience an overload of damaged proteins and dysfunctional organelles. This is typically exacerbated by impaired autophagy—a process that is essential not only for recycling cellular components but also for mitigating apoptotic signals and inflammatory responses associated with chronic stress (Kaarniranta et al., 2023).

It is anticipated that treatment with Methylstat will yield several measurable outcomes in these assays. First, there should be an observable increase in global levels of H3K4me3, particularly at promoters of autophagy- and phagocytosis-related genes. Chromatin immunoprecipitation studies could verify this epigenetic shift, providing direct evidence that the histone demethylase activity is being successfully inhibited (Nita & Grzybowski, 2023). Second, such an epigenetic change should correspond to upregulated transcription of TFEB, MERTK, and potentially other downstream effectors vital for lysosomal function and autophagosome formation (Sinha et al., 2016). Quantitative polymerase chain reaction (qPCR) and RNA sequencing approaches would likely reveal increased messenger RNA levels for these genes, reinforcing the expected mechanism of action.

Functionally, RPE cells exposed to Methylstat may exhibit enhanced clearance of photoreceptor outer segments. In the healthy eye, efficient phagocytosis of these outer segments by RPE cells is essential to maintain photoreceptor function and overall retinal integrity. Under oxidative stress conditions, compromised phagocytosis leads to the accumulation of debris, formation of lipofuscin, and subsequent cellular senescence (Campello et al., 2021; Kaarniranta et al., 2023). By promoting the expression of genes directly involved in phagocytic uptake and lysosomal degradation, Methylstat is hypothesized to boost the cells’ capacity to remove POS cargo effectively. This enhanced clearance could not only improve retinal function but also potentially slow or reverse the progression of dry AMD.

Furthermore, the expected increase in TFEB activity would likely lead to improved lysosomal biogenesis and function. Given that lysosomal fusion and clearance are critical to mitigating cellular damage within the RPE, enhanced TFEB-driven gene expression offers a compelling mechanistic rationale. In fact, several studies have indicated that restoration of autophagic processes and lysosomal function represents a promising therapeutic strategy to counteract the accumulation of cellular waste and the ensuing inflammatory cascade seen in AMD (Kaarniranta et al., 2023). The net result of these effects would be the preservation of cellular homeostasis and prevention of premature senescence in RPE cells, which is a critical upstream event in the development of AMD pathology (Nita & Grzybowski, 2023; Campello et al., 2021).

In summary, the expected effect of Methylstat in cell-based assays is twofold: (1) an epigenetic reprogramming event characterized by increased H3K4me3 levels and upregulation of key autophagy and phagocytosis genes, and (2) a physiological enhancement of POS uptake and lysosomal degradation processes, thereby potentially mitigating the deleterious sequelae of oxidative stress in the aging retina (Nita & Grzybowski, 2023; Kaarniranta et al., 2023).

VI. Overall Evaluation  
The assessment of Methylstat as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD involves a careful weighing of the theoretical strengths against practical challenges and gaps in current evidence. On the strength side, the concept of epigenetic modulation in restoring retinal cellular homeostasis is supported by a growing body of evidence. Studies have demonstrated that targeting chromatin modifiers—such as HDACs and acetylases—can confer therapeutic benefits in models of retinal degeneration (Campello et al., 2021). Methylstat extends this approach by specifically targeting JmjC histone demethylases, thereby offering a novel mechanism that could upregulate genes crucial for autophagy and phagocytosis. The proposed increase in H3K4me3 levels at promoters of TFEB and MERTK is especially attractive because these genes are central to maintaining the lysosomal integrity and phagocytic function of RPE cells, functions that are critically compromised in AMD (Nita & Grzybowski, 2023; Kaarniranta et al., 2023).

Another significant strength lies in the practical aspects of drug development. Methylstat has already been characterized in other contexts, and preliminary rodent ocular safety data add a level of confidence regarding its tolerability (Campello et al., 2021; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023). Given that drug repurposing can greatly accelerate the timeline from preclinical validation to clinical application, Methylstat represents an appealing candidate from a strategic standpoint. Additionally, its small molecular size and synthetic origins provide opportunities for chemical optimization that may improve its specificity for retinal targets while minimizing systemic toxicity (Campello et al., 2021).

However, there are notable weaknesses and challenges associated with this therapeutic strategy. Foremost among these is the limited evidence linking JmjC histone demethylases—specifically the ones targeted by Methylstat—with AMD pathology. The Open Targets data indicate that potential targets such as KDM4A and KDM4C have low association scores with AMD, and there is scant evidence of their expression changes or pathogenic involvement in the retinal pigment epithelium during disease progression (Buniello et al., 2025). This suggests that while the theoretical underpinning is sound, the direct relevance of these enzymes to the disease phenotype remains to be conclusively demonstrated. As such, there is a significant risk that inhibition of these targets may not yield the expected therapeutic benefits.

Furthermore, the complexity of epigenetic regulation in the retina cannot be understated. RPE cells are subject to a tightly coordinated network of epigenetic modifications that interact dynamically. Whereas histone demethylation plays an important role, it is but one component of a broader regulatory milieu that includes histone acetylation, methylation at different residues, and DNA methylation. Consequently, the inhibition of one enzyme class may lead to compensatory changes in others, potentially diluting or even reversing the intended outcome. For instance, while Methylstat may increase H3K4 trimethylation, other repressive histone marks might persist or even become upregulated in response, thereby limiting the net transcriptional activation of autophagy and phagocytosis genes (Kaštelan et al., 2024; Zibetti, 2025; Sinha et al., 2016).

There is also the challenge of off-target effects. Histone demethylases are broadly expressed and are involved in numerous cellular processes beyond autophagy and phagocytosis. Inhibition of these enzymes in non-target cells could lead to unforeseen side effects, potentially compromising tissue integrity or inducing aberrant gene expression profiles that might exacerbate inflammation or other deleterious processes. Given that the retina is a highly specialized tissue with a fine balance of metabolic and oxidative stresses, any off-target effects resulting from systemic exposure to Methylstat will need to be carefully evaluated in preclinical studies (Buniello et al., 2025).

Another practical consideration is whether the epigenetic modulation achieved by Methylstat will be of sufficient magnitude and duration to effect functional improvements in RPE cells. Upregulation of TFEB and MERTK is an attractive proposition; however, the transcriptional responses in cells under chronic oxidative stress may differ from those in controlled in vitro environments. Additionally, the kinetics of chromatin modifications can be highly cell context-dependent, and there remains uncertainty regarding how quickly and sustainably Methylstat-mediated chromatin changes will translate into improved autophagic flux. This is particularly relevant given that AMD is a chronic disease and any therapeutic intervention must yield long-term benefits to justify clinical use (Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023).

In light of these considerations, a phased and incremental research strategy is advisable. Initial studies should focus on establishing robust links between histone demethylase activity, H3K4me3 levels, and the transcriptional status of autophagy and phagocytosis genes in RPE cells. Advanced genomic techniques, such as ChIP-seq and RNA-seq, should be employed to detail the chromatin landscape before and after Methylstat treatment. Such studies will help to determine whether the predicted epigenetic changes are indeed occurring at the necessary target loci, and whether these changes correlate with improved cellular function.

Additionally, in vivo models of dry AMD should be used to validate the therapeutic effect of Methylstat in a physiologically relevant context. Rodent models that recapitulate key features of RPE dysfunction and oxidative stress are particularly valuable in this regard. Evaluations should include histological assessments of RPE integrity, measurements of lysosomal enzyme activity, and functional assays of photoreceptor viability. It will also be important to monitor potential systemic effects, given the widespread expression of histone demethylases throughout the body (Campello et al., 2021; Sinha et al., 2016).

Finally, combination therapies that target multiple aspects of the epigenetic network may be warranted. Given that other chromatin modifiers, such as histone deacetylases, have already shown therapeutic potential in AMD (Campello et al., 2021; Kaštelan et al., 2024), a synergistic approach that includes Methylstat along with HDAC inhibitors or mTOR modulators might provide a broader restoration of the epigenetic landscape in RPE cells. Such combinations would need to be carefully optimized to balance efficacy with safety, but they could ultimately offer a more comprehensive strategy to counteract the multifactorial etiology of AMD (Zibetti, 2025; Sinha et al., 2016).

VII. Conclusion  
In summary, Methylstat presents an intriguing candidate for repurposing as a therapy for dry age-related macular degeneration. The theoretical basis for its use rests on its ability to inhibit JmjC histone demethylases, leading to an accumulation of activating histone marks such as H3K4me3. This epigenetic reprogramming is hypothesized to enhance the expression of critical autophagy and phagocytosis genes—including TFEB and MERTK—in RPE cells, thereby improving the uptake and lysosomal clearance of photoreceptor outer segments. Should these cellular processes be successfully augmented, the downstream effect would be a reduction in oxidative stress–induced damage, preservation of RPE function, and ultimately a slowdown or reversal of AMD progression (Nita & Grzybowski, 2023; Kaarniranta et al., 2023).

The strengths of this approach include its innovative mechanism that builds on the established relevance of epigenetic dysregulation in retinal degeneration, as well as the practical advantages associated with drug repurposing. Methylstat’s synthetic nature, existing preclinical safety data, and capacity for chemical modification all contribute to its potential as a versatile therapeutic tool. Moreover, the focus on restoring autophagic and phagocytic pathways aligns well with current insights into AMD pathophysiology, which repeatedly highlight the importance of efficient waste clearance in maintaining retinal cell homeostasis (Campello et al., 2021; Kaarniranta et al., 2023).

Nevertheless, challenges remain. The current evidence directly linking JmjC histone demethylases to AMD pathogenesis is limited. Open Targets analyses indicate a low association of enzymes such as KDM4A and KDM4C with the disease phenotype, raising concerns about whether their inhibition will yield significant clinical benefits (Buniello et al., 2025). Moreover, the complexity of epigenetic regulation—and the potential for compensatory mechanisms among various chromatin modifiers—necessitates a cautious approach. Off-target effects, the kinetics of transcriptional changes, and the chronic nature of AMD all underscore the need for comprehensive preclinical evaluation before advancing Methylstat into clinical trials.

In conclusion, while Methylstat exhibits several compelling features that justify its further investigation as a therapy for dry AMD, it is clear that significant gaps in our understanding of the role of histone demethylases in retinal aging must be addressed. Rigorous in vitro studies, supported by in vivo animal model data, are essential to validate the proposed mechanism of action and to optimize dosage and delivery strategies. Only through such a multifaceted approach can the full therapeutic potential of Methylstat be properly ascertained. If these initial studies demonstrate robust, reproducible benefits in restoring autophagic, phagocytic, and lysosomal functions in RPE cells, then Methylstat may emerge as a valuable addition to the currently limited therapeutic arsenal for dry AMD (Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Nita & Grzybowski, 2023).

Overall, the proposal to repurpose Methylstat for dry AMD treatment is scientifically intriguing and mechanistically plausible. However, the journey from hypothesis to clinical efficacy will require careful validation of the compound’s epigenetic impact in the pathological context of AMD. With concerted efforts combined with stratified preclinical studies, this candidate may open new avenues for precision pharmacotherapy in age-related retinal diseases (Campello et al., 2021).

answer:
Proposal for NT-219 (Dual IGF1R/SHP2 inhibitor; Nanosyn research compound)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
NT-219 is a small-molecule inhibitor originally characterized as a novel attenuator of insulin/IGF signaling (IIS) that blocks the IGF1R→AKT axis via a dual mechanism: rapid reduction of IGF1 receptor autophosphorylation to prevent downstream AKT activation, and promotion of inhibitory Ser phosphorylation and degradation of IRS1 and IRS2 to sustain IIS suppression in cells (dual-step mechanism) (El-Ami et al., 2014). In the earliest in vitro characterizations, NT-219 inhibited IGF1-induced AKT phosphorylation, induced IRS1/2 Ser phosphorylation and degradation, and elevated expression of FOXO target genes such as p27 and MnSOD in human A375 and N2a cells, thereby functionally mimicking reduced IIS in mammalian cells (El-Ami et al., 2014). In vivo, NT-219 increased stress resistance and protected Caenorhabditis elegans from proteotoxic stress induced by human Aβ or polyQ models, without extending lifespan, consistent with partial IIS attenuation and downstream activation of DAF-16/FOXO and HSF-1 programs (El-Ami et al., 2014).

Beyond IIS, several oncology reports and abstracts describe NT-219 as suppressing IRS1/2 and phosphorylated STAT3, framing the compound as a dual inhibitor of IRS and STAT3 signaling with activity in murine melanoma and colorectal cancer (CRC) systems (e.g., B16 melanoma variants, CRC brain metastasis models) (Azevedo et al., 2023). In CRC work, NT-219 is presented as a first-in-class IRS2-targeting agent that triggers IRS2 Ser phosphorylation and degradation, reducing oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) gene expression and mitochondrial respiration in IRS2-expressing CRC cells, with antitumor synergy when combined with 5-FU in intracranial CRC brain metastasis mouse models (Greenberg et al., 2022a, 2022b).

With respect to provenance, author affiliations and disclosures indicate NT-219’s development by NovoTyr/TyrNovo; one source states that a company developing NT-219 positions it as a novel IRS1/2 inhibitor, noting it is “already being tested in clinical trials,” although details of those trials are not provided in the excerpt (El-Ami et al., 2014; Greenberg et al., 2022a). Available reports do not supply chemical synthesis routes, structural class information, formulation beyond use of 2-hydroxypropyl-β-cyclodextrin for solubilization in some experiments, or pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic details (El-Ami et al., 2014).

Therapeutic History  
The preclinical history of NT-219 spans two principal areas: (1) aging/neurodegeneration model systems in C. elegans and cell culture; and (2) oncology models in mice and human cancer cell lines. In nematodes, NT-219 reduced late-onset proteotoxicity in Aβ and polyQ models, increased stress resistance (heat shock, UV), induced DAF-16 nuclear translocation, and required DAF-16 and HSF-1 for its protective effects; the compound did not extend lifespan under the reported paradigms, distinguishing stress/proteostasis benefits from longevity effects (El-Ami et al., 2014). The authors explicitly called for testing NT-219 in vertebrate Alzheimer’s or Huntington’s disease models, emphasizing that efficient administration routes would need to be developed; the excerpt provides no evidence that such mammalian neurodegeneration studies were completed (El-Ami et al., 2014).

In oncology, multiple independent preclinical lines report NT-219’s ability to destabilize IRS2 protein, suppress OXPHOS genes, reduce mitochondrial respiration in IRS2-positive CRC cells, and synergize with 5-FU to inhibit CRC brain metastasis growth and extend survival in mice (Greenberg et al., 2022a, 2022b). Additional immuno-oncology abstracts describe NT-219 as a dual IRS/STAT3 inhibitor that increases tumor PD-L1 and improves the efficacy of anti–PD-1 or anti–CTLA-4 by reprogramming the tumor microenvironment toward higher CD8+ T-cell activation and reduced myeloid suppressor populations in murine melanoma models (Azevedo et al., 2023). One CRC preprint notes TyrNovo develops NT-219 and states it is “already being tested in clinical trials,” but the materials provided do not contain peer-reviewed clinical data, detailed safety/tolerability, or ocular exposure information (El-Ami et al., 2014; Greenberg et al., 2022a).

Critically, there is no report in the provided literature of NT-219 being used to treat dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), retinal degenerations, or any ocular disease; likewise, there is no published application to retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) biology, MerTK signaling, or photoreceptor outer segment (POS) phagocytosis (El-Ami et al., 2014; Greenberg et al., 2022a; Azevedo et al., 2023). Within the RPE field, the candidate is untested, and the extrapolation from cancer and nematode proteostasis contexts to RPE phagocytosis is speculative in the absence of ocular data.

Mechanism of Action  
Primary mechanistic characterization places NT-219 as an IIS/IGF1R pathway inhibitor acting through a dual-step process: early partial inhibition of IGF1R autophosphorylation that prevents AKT phosphorylation (Thr308, Ser473), followed by induction of inhibitory Ser phosphorylation of IRS1/2 and their proteasomal degradation, which produces a sustained IIS blockade (El-Ami et al., 2014). In human cells, this culminates in reduced AKT activity and a shift toward FOXO-dependent transcription (e.g., increased p27, MnSOD), indicative of stress-responsive and anti-proliferative programs typical of IIS attenuation (El-Ami et al., 2014). In C. elegans, IIS attenuation by NT-219 triggers DAF-16/FOXO nuclear translocation and HSF-1 activation to enhance proteostasis and stress resistance; protection from proteotoxicity requires these effectors, as daf-16 or hsf-1 RNAi abrogates benefits (El-Ami et al., 2014).

Mechanistic distinctions versus canonical IIS genetic knockdown are noted. For Aβ models, NT-219 promotes accumulation of higher molecular weight Abeta species (hyperaggregation) similar to IIS reduction by daf-2 RNAi, consistent with detoxification by sequestration of oligomers; for polyQ models, NT-219 reduces SDS-resistant aggregates but does not increase high-MW species to the same extent as daf-2 RNAi, implying compound-specific modulation of protein aggregation dynamics (El-Ami et al., 2014). Collectively, NT-219 acts upstream (IGF1R and IRS1/2) to suppress AKT and activate FOXO/HSF-1/NRF-like programs, with context-dependent modulation of aggregation states.

Oncology abstracts expand NT-219’s mechanism to include suppression of phosphorylated STAT3 and dual targeting of IRS1/2 and STAT3, which increases PD-L1, reduces suppressive myeloid cells, and synergizes with checkpoint inhibitors in melanoma models, and also anchors the agent’s proximal action to IRS2 degradation with downstream suppression of OXPHOS and β-catenin in CRC brain metastasis models (Azevedo et al., 2023; Greenberg et al., 2022a, 2022b). These oncology data reinforce IRS1/2 as validated proximal targets of NT-219 and suggest broader transcriptional/immunologic impacts via STAT3 in tumor contexts (Azevedo et al., 2023).

No evidence in the provided literature indicates that NT-219 directly inhibits SHP2 phosphatase activity; the compound is repeatedly characterized by its actions on IGF1R autophosphorylation and IRS1/2 degradation, with some reports adding STAT3 inhibition, but there is no description of direct SHP2 binding or enzymatic inhibition (El-Ami et al., 2014; Azevedo et al., 2023). Likewise, there is no evidence presented that NT-219 modulates MerTK phosphorylation or its dephosphorylation by any phosphatase.

Disease Biology Context and Relevance to Hypothesized Mechanism in RPE  
RPE clearance phagocytosis of POS is a receptor-integrated, actomyosin-driven process requiring both αvβ5 integrin and MerTK, with a choreography that separates POS recognition/binding from internalization and processing (Lieffrig et al., 2023; Müller & Finnemann, 2020). MFG-E8 bridges phosphatidylserine on POS to αvβ5 integrin, triggering FAK activation, which in turn promotes MerTK phosphorylation at light onset in vivo; RPE lacking αvβ5 fail to exhibit the coordinated FAK/MerTK phosphorylation cycle and display desynchronized phagocytosis (Lieffrig et al., 2023; Müller & Finnemann, 2020). MerTK activation then drives essential engulfment signaling toward the actin cytoskeleton, with protrusive actin assembly and myosin-II–based contractility required to form and close the phagocytic cup (Zihni, 2025).

Downstream of MerTK, multiple mechanistic routes engage the Rho family GTPases and PI3K signaling. Mer recruits PI3K and PLC-γ to generate PIP2/PIP3 and activate PKCs, while PIP3 species bind DOCK180 family GEFs (as complexes with ELMO) to activate Rac1 at the membrane; independently, Gas6–Mer signaling can phosphorylate Vav1 (a Dbl-family GEF), further promoting Rac1 activation (Wu et al., 2006). In parallel to this Mer-dependent axis, POS–MFG-E8–αvβ5 engagement activates Rac1 via a pathway that is independent of FAK and MerTK, indicating that Rac1 activation is integrin-driven and converges with MerTK-dependent cytoskeletal programs during cup formation (Lieffrig et al., 2023). Functional studies demonstrate that Rac1 activation is necessary, and that a coordinated increase of Rac1 activity with suppression of RhoA/ROCK signaling is independently required to assemble the F-actin phagocytic cup; perturbing either node (e.g., sema4D/plexin-B1 reducing Rac1, RhoA activation) impairs internalization (Lieffrig et al., 2023). Notably, in MERTK-deficient RPE, Rac1 activation upon POS challenge persists but F-actin phagocytic cups fail to form due to failure to downregulate the RhoA–ROCK pathway; pharmacological ROCK inhibition is sufficient to restore engulfment, acidification, and digestion in MERTK-lacking RPE, highlighting the primacy of the Rac1/RhoA balance for internalization and processing (Lieffrig et al., 2023).

PI3K–AKT signaling participates in RPE cytoskeletal regulation, but with nuance: AKT1/2 are expressed and activated in RPE by POS challenge; AKT inhibition increases POS binding while leaving internalization largely unaffected, and AKT controls F-actin recruitment by regulating myosin-II localization to phagocytic cups—myosin-II activity is required for internalization (Lieffrig et al., 2023). This suggests that complete blockade of AKT can alter cortical cytoskeletal dynamics in ways that may not improve (and might complicate) internalization, even if binding is increased (Lieffrig et al., 2023). More broadly in the retina and RPE, IGF-1/insulin receptors activate PI3K/AKT and are linked to cytoprotection; IGF-1R is tyrosine-phosphorylated by light stress in ROS membranes with associated PI3K binding, and PI3K–AKT activation protects RPE from oxidative injury, a key pathogenic driver in AMD (Rajala, 2010). Thus, systemically blocking IGF1R→AKT may deprive RPE of a cytoprotective pathway critical under oxidative stress conditions relevant to dry AMD (Rajala, 2010).

The hypothesis under consideration asserts that IGF1R activation recruits SHP2 to dephosphorylate MerTK, and that dual IGF1R/SHP2 inhibition by NT-219 would sustain MerTK phosphorylation and enhance PI3K/Rac1 signaling to improve POS internalization. The provided literature does not support this cross-talk model. While MerTK possesses domains that can recruit SH2-containing adapters and there is a plausible framework for SH2-mediated anti-inflammatory signaling, the specific involvement of SHP2 in dephosphorylation/regulation of MerTK in RPE is not demonstrated in the provided sources; indeed, multiple reviews explicitly note the absence of direct evidence for MerTK dephosphorylation or SHP2 activity in RPE/retina controlling phagocytosis or AMD-relevant outcomes (Ghosh et al., 2024; Albert et al., 2015; Ghosh et al., 2024; Lieffrig et al., 2023; Ghosh et al., 2024). Furthermore, none of the NT-219 sources implicate SHP2 as a target; rather, they define the compound’s proximal activity against IGF1R autophosphorylation and IRS1/2 degradation (and STAT3 in oncology abstracts), with no SHP2 pharmacology reported (El-Ami et al., 2014; Azevedo et al., 2023). Absent evidence that IGF1R activation suppresses MerTK via SHP2 in RPE, or that NT-219 inhibits SHP2, the central premise—to sustain MERTK phosphorylation by dual IGF1R/SHP2 inhibition—remains unsubstantiated in the current literature set.

Expected Effect  
Proposed assay: ARPE-19 (or primary human RPE) POS clearance phagocytosis with readouts for binding, internalization, Rac1-GTP, RhoA activity, F-actin cup formation, MERTK phosphorylation status, and myosin-II localization.

Mechanistic expectation from the literature:
- NT-219 will inhibit IGF1R autophosphorylation and reduce AKT phosphorylation; it will also induce IRS1/2 Ser phosphorylation and degradation, producing a sustained IIS blockade in RPE if the compound engages its canonical targets in this cell type (El-Ami et al., 2014).
- In RPE phagocytosis, AKT inhibition increases POS binding while leaving internalization largely unaffected; AKT controls myosin-II localization to cups and myosin-II activity is required for internalization; therefore, IIS blockade by NT-219 could alter binding and myosin-II dynamics without enhancing internalization, and might even risk impairing the coordinated contractility required for cup closure depending on the extent and timing of AKT suppression (Lieffrig et al., 2023).
- There is no evidence that NT-219 directly increases MERTK phosphorylation or sustains it by inhibiting a MerTK-directed phosphatase; FAK is the upstream effector known to promote MERTK activation after αvβ5 engagement, and Mer-driven PI3K/PIP3 production recruits DOCK180/ELMO to activate Rac1, while Vav1 provides a parallel route to Rac activation (Lieffrig et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2006).
- Rac1 activation required for cup formation is driven by αvβ5 ligation via a pathway independent of FAK and MerTK and is modulated by semaphorin/plexin signaling; there is no indication that IGF1R/IIS inhibition increases Rac1 activation or overrides antagonistic RhoA/ROCK signaling (Lieffrig et al., 2023). Indeed, cup formation requires both increased Rac1 and decreased RhoA activity; manipulating only IIS/AKT is unlikely to rebalance this axis favorably (Lieffrig et al., 2023).
- In MERTK-deficient RPE, failure to suppress RhoA/ROCK—not failure to activate Rac1—explains defective cup formation; pharmacological ROCK inhibition rescues engulfment and downstream maturation, underscoring that targeting ROCK can bypass some MerTK-dependent defects (Lieffrig et al., 2023).

Taken together, the most defensible expectation is that NT-219 will reduce IIS/AKT signaling in ARPE-19, potentially increase POS binding, and alter myosin-II localization to cups, without a clear mechanism to enhance internalization; effects on Rac1-GTP are unlikely to be directly augmented, and there is no sound mechanistic basis in the provided literature to expect sustained MerTK phosphorylation through SHP2 inhibition by NT-219 (El-Ami et al., 2014; Lieffrig et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2006). Given evidence that PI3K–AKT activation protects RPE from oxidative damage—a central feature of dry AMD pathophysiology—sustained IIS blockade could be deleterious outside of a narrow, carefully controlled window (Rajala, 2010).

Contextualizing with dry AMD biology and MerTK function:
- MerTK is essential for RPE internalization of POS; genetic loss causes failure to engulf POS and retinal degeneration in RCS rats and some mouse models, and MERTK/TYRO3 signaling redundantly maintains an anti-inflammatory RPE gene expression program that influences retinal viability (Müller & Finnemann, 2020; Albert et al., 2015; Ghosh et al., 2024).
- After ingestion, internalized POS phagosomes enter LC3-associated phagocytosis (LAP) and autophagy pathways required for efficient degradation; MerTK promotes autophagy and inhibits NLRP3 inflammasomes, constraining retinal inflammation (Ghosh et al., 2024). These functions are distinct from IIS modulation and point to MerTK-proximal strategies (e.g., enhancing MerTK activation, targeting RhoA/ROCK to restore cup formation) as more rational levers to improve phagocytosis than IGF1R inhibition (Lieffrig et al., 2023).
- In RPE lacking MerTK ligation, phagocytic cup formation is impaired even when Rac1 activation is intact, and ROCK inhibition restores engulfment and maturation—an actionable, pathway-proximal intervention that has empirical support in RPE systems (Lieffrig et al., 2023).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Pharmacologic definition and tractability: NT-219’s mechanism is well supported in mammalian cells by decreased IGF1R autophosphorylation, suppressed AKT phosphorylation, and sustained IIS blockade via IRS1/2 Ser phosphorylation and degradation, with downstream activation of FOXO-regulated gene expression (El-Ami et al., 2014).
- In vivo activity in worms and robust oncology preclinical signals indicate that NT-219 is bioactive and can produce meaningful phenotypes via IIS attenuation and IRS1/2 suppression; preclinical efficacy includes synergy with 5-FU in CRC brain metastasis and potentiation of checkpoint blockade in melanoma (El-Ami et al., 2014; Greenberg et al., 2022a; Azevedo et al., 2023).
- The compound’s formulation has precedent (2-HP-β-cyclodextrin) and dose ranges have been explored in cell and worm systems, offering starting points for exploratory dosing in vitro (El-Ami et al., 2014; Greenberg et al., 2022b).

Weaknesses and key risks for dry AMD  
- Mechanistic disconnect with the hypothesis: There is no evidence in the provided literature that IGF1R activation recruits SHP2 to dephosphorylate MerTK in RPE, nor that NT-219 inhibits SHP2; MerTK’s downstream anti-inflammatory signaling may involve SH2-adapter recruitment, but SHP2-mediated dephosphorylation of MerTK in RPE has not been demonstrated (Ghosh et al., 2024; Albert et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2006; El-Ami et al., 2014; Ghosh et al., 2024). The central premise—that dual IGF1R/SHP2 inhibition by NT-219 will sustain MerTK phosphorylation—is unsupported by current evidence (El-Ami et al., 2014; Ghosh et al., 2024).
- Risk of antagonizing protective signaling: IGF1R/IR→PI3K/AKT signaling protects RPE from oxidative stress, a driver of dry AMD; broad IIS/AKT inhibition could be cytotoxic or reduce resilience to oxidative injury in RPE (Rajala, 2010).
- RPE phagocytosis data argue against the expected pro-internalization effect: In RPE, AKT inhibition increases binding but leaves internalization largely unaffected, and AKT controls myosin-II localization required for internalization; sustained IIS/AKT blockade is not a rationale to boost internalization and may perturb the force-generation needed for cup closure (Lieffrig et al., 2023).
- Lack of ocular/RPE data: There are no reports of NT-219 in ocular tissues, RPE cells, or phagocytosis assays; the compound’s tolerability, pharmacology, and target engagement in RPE are unknown (El-Ami et al., 2014).
- More mechanistically proximal and validated levers exist: Cup formation requires increased Rac1 and decreased RhoA/ROCK; in MERTK deficiency, ROCK inhibition rescues engulfment and downstream events, whereas Rac1 activation cannot overcome high RhoA activity; targeting ROCK or MerTK activation itself is more directly supported to enhance POS internalization (Lieffrig et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2006).
- The candidate’s oncology-specific mechanistic breadth (IRS/STAT3 dual inhibition, β-catenin/OXPHOS modulation) introduces off-target immunologic and metabolic effects that could be undesirable in retina and RPE, where mitochondrial function and immune quiescence are tightly regulated (Greenberg et al., 2022a, 2022b; Azevedo et al., 2023).

Assessment of the specific mechanistic claims in the proposal:  
- “IGF1R activation recruits SHP2 to dephosphorylate MerTK”: The provided literature does not support this assertion. While MerTK contains domains that can engage SH2-containing proteins and may suppress NF-κB through SHP-related mechanisms in other phagocytes, specific demonstration of SHP2-mediated MerTK dephosphorylation or suppression in RPE is absent (Wu et al., 2006; Ghosh et al., 2024). No source shows that IGF1R recruits SHP2 to target MerTK in RPE.  
- “NT-219 is a dual IGF1R/SHP2 inhibitor”: None of the documents identify NT-219 as a SHP2 inhibitor. The compound acts on IGF1R autophosphorylation and IRS1/2 degradation, and some oncology abstracts add STAT3 inhibition; SHP2 is not listed among NT-219’s targets (El-Ami et al., 2014; Azevedo et al., 2023).  
- “Sustained MerTK phosphorylation and Rac1-GTP by NT-219”: MerTK activation is promoted by the αvβ5→FAK axis and by its ligation through GAS6/PROS1; downstream, Mer activates PI3K, DOCK180/ELMO, and Vav1 to elevate Rac1. IIS suppression by NT-219 does not obviously reinforce this cascade and, importantly, Rac1 activation required for cup formation is driven by αvβ5 signaling independent of FAK/MerTK, and inadequate suppression of RhoA/ROCK—not Rac1 deficiency—limits cup formation in MERTK-deficient settings (Lieffrig et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2006).

Recommendation  
Given the absence of supporting evidence for the proposal’s key mechanistic link (IGF1R/SHP2→MerTK dephosphorylation) and potential risks of IIS/AKT suppression in RPE cells under oxidative stress, NT-219 should not be prioritized as a repurposed therapeutic for dry AMD to enhance RPE phagocytosis. If the team wishes to explore this axis despite these concerns, initial work should be stringently gated to low-risk, mechanistically focused in vitro experiments in human RPE with explicit go/no-go criteria:

- Biochemical target engagement in RPE: confirm IGF1R autophosphorylation and AKT suppression, and assess IRS1/2 degradation at NT-219 exposures spanning reported active ranges in human cells, with parallel viability and oxidative stress-challenge assays (El-Ami et al., 2014; Rajala, 2010).  
- MerTK signaling: test whether NT-219 alters MerTK tyrosine phosphorylation after POS challenge or GAS6/PROS1 addition, with FAK-dependent activation as positive control; due to the lack of any SHP2 data for NT-219, include SHP2 activity readouts only as exploratory corollaries, not as assumed mechanisms (Lieffrig et al., 2023; Müller & Finnemann, 2020; Ghosh et al., 2024).  
- Phagocytosis function: quantify POS binding versus internalization; F-actin cup counts; myosin-II localization; Rac1-GTP and RhoA-GTP; include ROCK inhibition as a positive internalization control and sema4D as a Rac1-downregulating negative control (Lieffrig et al., 2023).  
- Autophagy/LAP and inflammatory readouts: measure LC3-II, p62, and NLRP3-related markers following POS feeding with/without NT-219 to detect adverse effects on LAP or pro-inflammatory signaling, as MERTK’s anti-inflammatory function via autophagy is integral to retinal homeostasis (Ghosh et al., 2024).

Absent clear, positive results across these mechanistic checkpoints, further development should be halted. Parallel investment is better directed toward pathway-proximal strategies with published efficacy signals in RPE:

- Rho kinase inhibition to restore cup formation and downstream processing in MerTK-compromised contexts (Lieffrig et al., 2023).  
- Direct MerTK pathway activation (optimized GAS6/PROS1 engagement, integrin→FAK reinforcement), guided by the well-defined αvβ5→FAK→MerTK signaling axis (Lieffrig et al., 2023; Müller & Finnemann, 2020).  
- Modulators that enhance LAP/autophagy to promote POS digestion and inhibit NLRP3, aligning with MERTK’s anti-inflammatory role (Ghosh et al., 2024).

Conclusion  
On balance, NT-219’s pharmacology is incompatible with the proposal’s mechanistic rationale and presents non-trivial risks in the RPE context. The evidence base does not support SHP2 involvement in MerTK dephosphorylation in RPE or NT-219 activity at SHP2, and IIS/AKT inhibition is unlikely to enhance POS internalization while potentially undermining RPE resilience to oxidative stress relevant to dry AMD (Ghosh et al., 2024; Albert et al., 2015; Ghosh et al., 2024; El-Ami et al., 2014; Rajala, 2010). The candidate lacks ocular data, and superior, pathway-proximal approaches exist with direct evidence for improving phagocytosis or downstream processing. Deprioritize NT-219 for dry AMD and redirect efforts to ROCK pathway modulation, MerTK pathway agonism, and LAP/autophagy enhancement strategies that align with established RPE phagocytosis biology (Lieffrig et al., 2023; Müller & Finnemann, 2020; Ghosh et al., 2024).

hypothesis: Geldanamycin (HSP90 inhibitor; Sigma-Aldrich Cat. No. G5939)
answer:
Proposal for Geldanamycin (HSP90 inhibitor; Sigma-Aldrich Cat. No. G5939)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Geldanamycin is a small-molecule inhibitor of heat shock protein 90 (HSP90) that originally garnered attention as a naturally derived product from Streptomyces species, and it belongs to the benzoquinone ansamycin class of compounds. As a natural product, geldanamycin was first isolated for its antibiotic properties and later found to exert potent effects on cellular protein homeostasis by binding the N-terminal ATP-binding pocket of HSP90. This mode of binding disrupts the chaperone function of HSP90, which is responsible for assisting in the stabilization and maturation of numerous client proteins, including signaling regulators and enzymes. Compounds of this chemical class have historically been investigated for their anticancer potential, given that HSP90 plays a central role in sustaining oncogenic signaling by stabilizing mutated or overexpressed proteins. In the context of ocular research, geldanamycin’s ability to modulate proteostasis and inflammatory cascades has prompted its investigation as a potential therapy for dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD), where dysregulated protein aggregation, impaired autophagy, and chronic inflammation are key pathological features (Piippo et al., 2018).

Therapeutic History:  
Historically, geldanamycin and related HSP90 inhibitors have been used primarily as research tools to interrogate the role of molecular chaperones in cancer, neurodegeneration, and cellular stress responses. In preclinical studies, geldanamycin demonstrated the capacity to induce a robust heat shock response characterized by the upregulation of HSP70 and concomitant modulation of client proteins that depend on HSP90. Its inhibition of HSP90 has been extensively explored in models of protein aggregation diseases and in studies of inflammasome regulation in retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells. For example, several reports have provided direct experimental evidence that HSP90 inhibition by geldanamycin prevents the activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome in human RPE models—specifically in ARPE-19 cells, human embryonic stem cell-derived RPE, and primary human RPE—by disrupting the protective HSP90–SGT1 complex that stabilizes NLRP3, thereby triggering autophagy-mediated clearance of the receptor (Piippo et al., 2018). In related studies, geldanamycin was also shown to induce an HSP70 response that can modulate proteostasis and reduce cellular inflammatory stress, although its high toxicity has consistently been reported as a barrier to clinical application in humans (Chen et al., 2021). While geldanamycin itself has not been approved for clinical use in dry AMD, its mechanistic insights have spurred research into repurposing HSP90 inhibitors for ocular indications, albeit with a need for derivatives or alternative candidates (Chen et al., 2021; Piippo et al., 2018).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, HSP90 functions as an ATP-dependent molecular chaperone that is critical for the correct folding, stabilization, and activation of a wide range of client proteins, including kinases, transcription factors, and components of the inflammasome complex such as NLRP3. Under basal conditions, HSP90, together with its co-chaperone SGT1, forms a complex with NLRP3 that maintains the receptor in an inactive yet activation-competent state. Geldanamycin binds to the N-terminal ATP-binding pocket of HSP90, thereby competitively inhibiting its ATPase activity and disrupting its chaperone cycle. This inhibition leads to the dissociation of the HSP90–SGT1 complex, releasing NLRP3. Once liberated from the protective chaperone complex, NLRP3 is highly unstable and becomes a substrate for intracellular degradation mechanisms. In the specific context of human RPE cells, experimental evidence has shown that geldanamycin preferentially promotes the autophagic clearance of NLRP3 rather than its proteasomal degradation. Mechanistic experiments that used proteasome inhibition with MG-132 and lysosomal/autophagy inhibition with bafilomycin A₁ or chloroquine revealed that when autophagy is intact, geldanamycin drives the degradation of NLRP3 via the autophagy pathway, resulting in a robust reduction in caspase-1 activity and IL-1β secretion (Piippo et al., 2018). This HSP90-dependent regulation of NLRP3 is particularly significant because inflammasome activation in RPE cells is implicated in the pathogenesis of dry AMD. In addition, geldanamycin induces the expression of HSP70, a cytoprotective chaperone that further contributes to maintaining proteostasis under stress conditions; however, the increase in HSP70 is a double-edged sword, as it reflects cellular stress responses that could have both beneficial and deleterious effects if dysregulated (Chen et al., 2021; Ryhänen, 2011). Notably, the timing of geldanamycin administration is critical: its inhibitory effect on IL-1β secretion is maximal when added immediately prior to the induction of proteasome or autophagy inhibition, indicating that the HSP90 inhibition must occur before the onset of overwhelming proteostatic stress to be effective (Piippo et al., 2018).

Expected Effect:  
Based on the mechanistic findings, the expected therapeutic effect of geldanamycin in a dry AMD model is multi-pronged. First, by binding to HSP90 and disrupting its stabilization of NLRP3, geldanamycin is anticipated to accelerate the autophagic clearance of NLRP3 complexes. This clearance is expected to blunt the assembly and activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome, thereby reducing the cleavage of pro-caspase-1 and ultimately diminishing the production and secretion of the pro-inflammatory cytokine IL-1β. In the context of dry AMD, where low-grade chronic inflammation and impaired clearance of damaged cellular proteins contribute to disease progression, the suppression of inflammasome activation is a desirable outcome that could help mitigate retinal inflammation and cell death (Piippo et al., 2018). Second, by reducing the persistent activation of the inflammasome, geldanamycin may help preserve lysosomal function, which is critical for the degradation of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) by the RPE. Lysosomal dysfunction and the resultant accumulation of lipofuscin are hallmark features in the pathogenesis of dry AMD; therefore, maintaining efficient lysosomal degradation is key to restoring RPE homeostasis. Although direct evidence linking geldanamycin to enhanced POS digestion is not comprehensively detailed in the current literature excerpts, there is reasonable mechanistic rationale to suggest that improved autophagic flux and decreased inflammatory burden could promote better phagocytic competence in RPE cells (Markitantova & Simirskii, 2025; Piippo et al., 2018). Finally, given that HSP90 inhibition via geldanamycin has been shown to reduce proteostasis stress and modulate key inflammatory pathways, its application in RPE models of dry AMD could result in improved cellular survival and function, potentially slowing or reversing aspects of the degenerative process. It is important to note that the hypothesized effective concentration (EC₅₀ around 500 nM) is based on in vitro studies in RPE cells, and achieving this efficacy in an in vivo ocular setting via intravitreal administration would require careful dosing and pharmacokinetic optimization to mitigate systemic toxicity (Piippo et al., 2018).

Overall Evaluation:  
Geldanamycin represents a promising candidate from a mechanistic perspective for treating dry AMD due to its unique mode of action as an HSP90 inhibitor. The strengths of this therapeutic approach include its ability to directly target a key regulatory protein that stabilizes the NLRP3 inflammasome, leading to downregulation of a major pro-inflammatory pathway implicated in dry AMD pathogenesis. Preclinical research in RPE models, including ARPE-19, hESC-derived RPE, and primary human RPE, has consistently demonstrated that geldanamycin can reduce caspase-1 activity and IL-1β secretion by promoting autophagic degradation of NLRP3, which is central to halting the vicious cycle of chronic inflammation (Piippo et al., 2018). This is further supported by studies indicating that proper timing of HSP90 inhibition is crucial to maximize the clearance of NLRP3 and achieve therapeutic benefits before proteostatic stress overwhelms the cellular degradation machinery (Piippo et al., 2018). Additionally, the induction of HSP70 following geldanamycin treatment may confer additional cytoprotective effects by promoting proper protein folding and assisting in the clearance of misfolded proteins, thus helping preserve lysosomal function and potentially improving photoreceptor outer segment (POS) digestion—a process that is compromised in dry AMD (Chen et al., 2021; Ryhänen, 2011).

However, significant challenges limit the clinical translation of geldanamycin. One of the major weaknesses of this therapeutic candidate is its well-documented toxicity profile. Numerous studies have reported that while geldanamycin is effective in modulating HSP90 and reducing inflammasome activation at low nanomolar doses, its inherent cytotoxicity and off-target effects make it unsuitable for direct clinical application. In several experimental settings, geldanamycin has been described as “too toxic for human administration,” with adverse effects observed in both in vitro and in vivo models (Piippo et al., 2018). Such toxicity is believed to arise in part from the quinone moiety of the molecule, which can engage in redox cycling and generate reactive oxygen species, thereby exacerbating cellular stress and impairing normal proteostasis. Furthermore, while the small-molecule nature of geldanamycin is an advantage in terms of drug delivery—especially for routes such as intravitreal injection—the narrow therapeutic window means that fine-tuning the dose to achieve the desired biological effect without incurring toxicity remains a significant hurdle. There is also the possibility that global inhibition of HSP90 could destabilize multiple client proteins beyond NLRP3, leading to unintended perturbations in vital signaling pathways and cellular homeostasis (Chen et al., 2021).

In addition, despite the promising preclinical data supporting the use of geldanamycin for reducing inflammasome activation in RPE cells, there is a noticeable gap in the literature concerning its impact on other critical aspects of dry AMD pathology—specifically, the direct enhancement of photoreceptor outer segment (POS) digestion. Although it is hypothesized that preserving lysosomal function via inhibition of chronic inflammasome activity should translate into improved phagocytosis of POS by RPE cells, definitive experimental evidence demonstrating that geldanamycin treatment leads to enhanced POS clearance in AMD models is lacking (Markitantova & Simirskii, 2025; Piippo et al., 2018). This represents an area where further targeted studies are required.

Overall, geldanamycin’s mechanism of action is compelling from a proof-of-concept perspective; it elucidates how HSP90 inhibition can modulate the stability of key inflammatory mediators such as NLRP3 and thereby attenuate detrimental inflammatory cascades in RPE cells. The detailed biochemical insights provided by studies using geldanamycin have been invaluable for understanding the interplay between proteostasis, autophagy, and inflammation in the context of dry AMD. However, the clinical translation of geldanamycin as a therapeutic candidate is considerably hampered by its toxicity profile and the potential for off-target effects. Consequently, while geldanamycin offers important mechanistic validation for targeting HSP90 as a strategy to modulate NLRP3 inflammasome activity, repurposing efforts for dry AMD would likely need to focus on less toxic analogues or more selective HSP90 inhibitors (such as TAS-116) that preserve the beneficial effects on proteostasis without incurring significant cytotoxicity (Piippo et al., 2018). In summary, geldanamycin is a scientifically sound candidate from the perspective of modulating key pathogenic mechanisms in dry AMD, yet its translational potential is limited by safety concerns that must be addressed either through structural modifications or by identifying alternative inhibitors within the HSP90 inhibitor class that demonstrate improved ocular and systemic tolerability.

hypothesis: SHP099 (SHP2 inhibitor; SelleckChem Cat. No. S8653)
answer:
Proposal for SHP099 (SHP2 inhibitor; SelleckChem Cat. No. S8653)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
SHP099 is a fully synthetic, small-molecule allosteric inhibitor of the protein tyrosine phosphatase SHP2 (PTPN11) discovered by Novartis through a target-biased screening paradigm that enriched for modulators of full-length, autoinhibited SHP2 and counter-selected catalytic-site binders, followed by structure-based medicinal chemistry optimization to stabilize the closed SHP2 conformation rather than engage the conserved active site (chemical identity: 6-(4-amino-4-methylpiperidin-1-yl)-3-(2,3-dichlorophenyl)pyrazin-2-amine) (PDB: 5EHR) (Fortanet et al., 2016; Kong & Long, 2022; Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021). In the 1.7 Å co-crystal, SHP099 occupies a central “tunnel” at the interface of the N-SH2, C-SH2, and PTP domains present only in the autoinhibited state; its aminopyrazine/amine motif forms hydrogen bonds to Arg111 and Phe113 in the SH2 linker and to Glu250 in the PTP domain, while a 2,3-dichlorophenyl moiety engages hydrophobic residues (Leu254, Gln257, Pro491, Gln495), thereby clamping the interdomain interface and disfavoring opening/activation (ligand volume ~262 Å3; tunnel ~464 Å3) (Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021). Biochemically, SHP099 is potent and selective (SHP2 enzymatic IC50 ≈ 0.070–0.071 µM; no detectable activity across panels of 21 phosphatases and 66 kinases, including SHP1) and translates to cellular pathway inhibition (p-ERK IC50 ≈ 0.250 µM), with high aqueous solubility, high permeability without efflux, and acceptable mouse oral exposure/bioavailability (~46%) (Fortanet et al., 2016; Kong & Long, 2022). Mechanistically, SHP099 functions as a “molecular glue” that stabilizes the closed, autoinhibited SHP2 conformation via a conformational selection mechanism; affinity is reduced for strongly activating SHP2 mutants (for example, E76K) that bias the open state, although high concentrations can re-close some mutants in vitro and in cells (Meem, 2022; Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021).

SHP099 belongs to the class of SHP2 “tunnel-site” (site 1) allosteric inhibitors that stabilize the autoinhibited state by engaging the N-SH2/C-SH2/PTP interdomain pocket; dual allosteric occupancy (site 1 plus a distal latch, site 2) is structurally and biochemically validated and produces cooperative inhibition when SHP099 is combined with a site-2 ligand (for example SHP244 analogs), underscoring the druggability of multiple noncatalytic surfaces on SHP2 (Fodor et al., 2018; Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021). Discovery and SAR established that the aminopyrazine ring amine is essential (Glu250 H-bond), the 4-amino-4-methylpiperidine motif is favored over piperazines for potency, and an ortho-chlorine on the phenyl ring is critical; a representative synthesis employs Suzuki–Miyaura coupling to install the dichlorophenyl substituent on a pyrazinamine core, followed by SNAr to append the Boc-protected 4-methylpiperidin-4-amine and final acid deprotection to the free base (Fortanet et al., 2016; Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021). Class-level development moved the SHP099 pharmacophore into diverse chemotypes (for example, pyrimidinones and fused bicyclic pyrazolopyrimidinones) and into clinical candidates (for example, TNO155, RMC-4630, BBP-398), reflecting translational momentum for SHP2 allosteric inhibition (Kerr et al., 2021; Tojjari et al., 2023; Yuan et al., 2020).

Therapeutic History  
SHP099 established in vivo proof-of-concept for allosteric SHP2 inhibition in oncology. In an EGFR-amplified esophageal squamous carcinoma xenograft (KYSE-520), oral SHP099 produced dose-dependent pathway suppression (tumor p-ERK), antiproliferative effects, and tumor growth inhibition up to stasis at 100 mg/kg, supported by measurable exposure and oral bioavailability (Fortanet et al., 2016; Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021). Additional preclinical efficacy includes activity in EGFR-driven xenografts and reduction of leukemic burden in FLT3-ITD–positive AML models after oral dosing, with no overt toxicity noted in those studies (Dempke et al., 2018). In glioblastoma models, SHP099 achieved brain exposure after 100 mg/kg oral dosing, reduced tumor growth and vascularity in orthotopic xenografts, and showed activity both as monotherapy and combined with temozolomide, demonstrating CNS penetration and antitumor pharmacology in mice (Mitra & Ayyannan, 2021). Class-wide, SHP2 allosteric inhibitors have shown single-agent and combination efficacy in RTK/RAS/MAPK-driven tumors, have been advanced into clinical studies across multiple solid tumors, and display mechanism-consistent biomarker modulation (for example, decreased p-ERK) in preclinical models (Kerr et al., 2021; Stanford & Bottini, 2023; Tojjari et al., 2023).

Within the materials provided here, there are no reports of SHP099 (or any SHP2 allosteric inhibitor) being used in dry age-related macular degeneration (dry AMD), retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) biology, photoreceptor outer segment (POS) phagocytosis models, or any ocular indication; multiple reviews focus on oncology/immuno-oncology and either enumerate preclinical tumor evidence or clinical oncology programs, without ocular/retinal data (Kerr et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2020; Yuan et al., 2020). Consequently, repurposing SHP099 for dry AMD would be a first-in-class application with no precedent in the supplied literature (Yuan et al., 2020).

Mechanism of Action  
SHP2 is maintained in an autoinhibited state by intramolecular engagement of the N-SH2 domain with the PTP catalytic domain; engagement of SH2 domains by bis-phosphotyrosyl motifs on receptors/adaptors relieves autoinhibition, allowing both catalytic and scaffolding functions that couple receptor tyrosine kinases (RTKs) to RAS activation and downstream MAPK/PI3K signaling (Fortanet et al., 2016; Kerr et al., 2021). SHP099 binds in a tunnel formed by the N-SH2, C-SH2, and PTP domains of autoinhibited SHP2 and locks this closed conformation: crystallography defines hydrogen bonds to Arg111 and Phe113 (SH2 linker) and Glu250 (PTP domain), and hydrophobic contacts to Leu254, Gln257, Pro491, and Gln495 that together stabilize the interface and preclude opening; pre-organization of Arg111 additionally supports a cationic–π interaction with SHP099’s dichlorophenyl ring (Fortanet et al., 2016; Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021). Selectivity over SHP1 is rationalized structurally by differences in SH2-linker/tunnel geometry that preclude analogous Arg/Phe contacts, consistent with lack of SHP1 inhibition in broad profiling (Diop et al., 2022). Binding follows conformational selection, with lowered potency against mutants that favor the open state (for example, E76K, D61Y), though high concentrations or dual-site allosteric occupancy can re-close certain mutants and enhance inhibition (Fodor et al., 2018; Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021). Class-level medicinal chemistry around SHP099 uncovered both optimization paths (for example, pyrimidinones, fused bicyclic scaffolds) and liabilities such as unexpected hERG inhibition in some derivatives and combination-dosing tolerability issues in mice, underscoring the need for careful safety pharmacology (Meem, 2022).

RPE POS phagocytosis is a ligand-directed, RTK-driven process with defined signaling architecture. Externalized phosphatidylserine on shed POS tips is opsonized (for example, by MFG-E8), engages apical αvβ5 integrin, and triggers a pathway in which MerTK (activated by Gas6 or Protein S) is essential for physiological engulfment in vivo; loss-of-function MERTK mutations in RCS rats or humans abolish POS internalization and cause rapid photoreceptor degeneration (Ghosh et al., 2024; Moran et al., 2022). At the cytoskeletal level, formation of the F-actin phagocytic cup beneath bound POS requires Rac1 activation and a concurrent decrease in RhoA/ROCK-mediated contractility; RhoA elevation blocks cup formation even when Rac1 is active, whereas ROCK inhibition is both necessary and sufficient to enable cup formation and POS internalization and can rescue engulfment and acidification in MerTK-deficient RPE ex vivo (Lieffrig et al., 2023; Mao & Finnemann, 2021). Mechanistically downstream of MerTK, Src is activated and (i) phosphorylates and activates focal adhesion kinase (FAK), recruiting the p130CAS/CRKII/DOCK180 module that activates Rac1, and (ii) phosphorylates GDP-dissociation inhibitor GDI1, promoting dissociation from Rab5 to facilitate Rab cycling needed for cup formation and early phagosome dynamics (Shelby et al., 2015). These pathways define measurable biochemical checkpoints (MerTK/Src/FAK phosphorylation, Rac1-GTP, RhoA/ROCK activity) and functional readouts (cup formation, internalization, phagolysosomal acidification) relevant to any attempt to modulate RPE phagocytosis pharmacologically (Lieffrig et al., 2023; Moran et al., 2022).

Expected Effect  
The working hypothesis is that SHP099 will inhibit SHP2 in RPE (biochemical IC50 ~70–75 nM), sustain MerTK phosphorylation, maintain Rac1-GTP, and thereby increase POS internalization. The supplied literature confirms that SHP099 potently and selectively inhibits SHP2 by stabilizing the autoinhibited state and blocks RTK→RAS/MAPK signaling in cells, but it does not demonstrate that SHP2 directly dephosphorylates MerTK in RPE or that SHP2 inhibition prolongs MerTK phosphorylation or increases RPE POS uptake (Fortanet et al., 2016; Kerr et al., 2021). Across systems, SHP2 acts as a positive transducer linking activated RTKs to RAS/ERK signaling; SHP2 allosteric inhibition decouples upstream RTKs from RAS activation, lowering RAS-GTP and p-ERK, which is consistent with a broad attenuation of RTK-driven outputs rather than prolonged receptor phosphorylation per se (Fortanet et al., 2016; Kerr et al., 2021). Within the provided ocular literature, the only experimentally demonstrated pharmacologic rescue of RPE POS uptake is acute ROCK inhibition, which operates downstream of MerTK to reduce actomyosin contractility and enable cup formation and internalization—even rescuing MerTK-deficient RPE ex vivo—whereas elevating RhoA blocks phagocytosis despite Rac1 activation (Mao & Finnemann, 2021). Thus, while SHP099 will almost certainly inhibit SHP2 in RPE if exposure is achieved, the predicted increase in POS internalization via prolonged MerTK phosphorylation and sustained Rac1-GTP is speculative and not supported by direct evidence in the materials provided here (Kerr et al., 2021; Yuan et al., 2020).

If the assay readout is POS phagocytosis in primary or iPSC-derived human RPE, the mechanistic checkpoints most directly supported by the literature are: phosphorylation kinetics of MerTK and Src/FAK; Rac1-GTP elevation coincident with cup formation; RhoA/ROCK suppression; and functional measures of cup assembly, POS internalization, and phagolysosomal acidification, with a ROCK inhibitor as a validated positive control (Lieffrig et al., 2023; Mao & Finnemann, 2021; Moran et al., 2022). Ocular pharmacokinetics for SHP099 are unknown in the provided corpus; although brain exposure has been documented after oral dosing in mice, retinal/RPE exposure should not be inferred and would need to be measured for systemic or local (for example, intravitreal) dosing paradigms (Mitra & Ayyannan, 2021).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths for repurposing consideration  
- Potent, selective, and structurally validated target engagement. SHP099 is characterized at atomic resolution (PDB 5EHR) with a coherent interaction network (Arg111, Phe113, Glu250; Leu254, Gln257, Pro491, Gln495) that rationalizes potency, selectivity versus SHP1, and conformational bias, increasing confidence that SHP2 inhibition will translate biochemically in RPE if drug exposure is achieved (Diop et al., 2022; Fortanet et al., 2016; Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021).  
- Drug-like properties and in vivo activity. SHP099 exhibits favorable physicochemical properties (high solubility; Caco-2 permeability without efflux), oral bioavailability (~46% in mice), dose-dependent pathway modulation in tumors, and robust xenograft efficacy; CNS exposure after oral dosing has been demonstrated in mice, indicating trans-barrier distribution is feasible with adequate exposure (Fortanet et al., 2016; Mitra & Ayyannan, 2021; Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021).  
- Class-level translational experience. Multiple SHP2 allosteric inhibitors derived from the SHP099 tunnel pharmacophore have entered clinical testing across solid tumors, enabling leverage of class pharmacology, safety learning, and combination strategies if ocular repurposing proceeds (Kerr et al., 2021; Stanford & Bottini, 2023; Tojjari et al., 2023).

Key weaknesses and risks specific to dry AMD/RPE phagocytosis  
- Mechanistic gap in RPE. The premise that SHP2 dephosphorylates MerTK to terminate phagocytic signaling in RPE, and that SHP2 inhibition will prolong MerTK phosphorylation and sustain Rac1 activation, is not supported by the supplied literature; no direct data link SHP2 to MerTK regulation in RPE or demonstrate SHP099-induced increases in POS uptake (Kerr et al., 2021; Yuan et al., 2020). In contrast, RhoA/ROCK suppression is a validated, decisive permissive event for cup formation/internalization and can rescue MerTK deficiency, suggesting that targeting ROCK remains a higher-confidence pharmacological route to enhance POS uptake (Mao & Finnemann, 2021).  
- Potential on-target countereffects on trophic RTK signaling. SHP2 broadly transduces RTK signals to RAS/ERK; allosteric SHP2 inhibition reduces RAS-GTP/p-ERK by disconnecting RTKs from downstream pathways, which could dampen beneficial RTK-mediated homeostatic signaling in RPE and choroid (for example, PDGFR, c-MET, IGF1R) even if MerTK phosphorylation were transiently increased, necessitating careful evaluation of RPE viability and stress responses in addition to phagocytosis endpoints (Fortanet et al., 2016; Kerr et al., 2021).  
- Ocular PK/tissue exposure unknown. There is no reported ocular distribution for SHP099 in the materials provided; CNS penetration does not ensure retinal/RPE exposure, and systemic dosing to achieve ocular levels may be limited by plasma protein binding, efflux, or tolerability, while intravitreal dosing introduces local safety and formulation challenges that would require de novo assessment (Mitra & Ayyannan, 2021).  
- Class liabilities and context-dependent potency. Medicinal chemistry around SHP099 identified derivatives with unexpected hERG activity and tolerability issues in some combination regimens; while not demonstrated specifically for SHP099 here, this flags a class risk requiring prospective cardiac and ocular safety pharmacology. Conformational-selection binding also means potency varies with SHP2 activation state, which is undefined in aging human RPE and could shift under inflammatory or oxidative stress present in dry AMD (Meem, 2022; Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021).  
- Lack of precedent in ocular models. No ocular, retinal, or RPE data for SHP099 or related allosteric SHP2 inhibitors are available in the supplied literature, increasing translational uncertainty for this repurposing (Yuan et al., 2020).

Program decision and de-risking experiments  
On the basis of the information provided, SHP099 is not yet a compelling repurposing candidate for dry AMD without foundational mechanistic validation in RPE. The central claim—that SHP2 inhibition prolongs MerTK phosphorylation and increases POS internalization—remains speculative in the absence of RPE data (Yuan et al., 2020). If the team elects to explore this hypothesis, a gated, mechanism-first workplan is advised:

- Define pathway engagement in RPE. Confirm SHP2 expression and activation state during phagocytosis in primary or iPSC-derived human RPE; assess whether SHP2 associates with MerTK/Src/FAK complexes upon POS challenge by co-immunoprecipitation or proximity assays (Shelby et al., 2015).  
- Biochemical time-courses ± SHP099. Quantify MerTK phosphorylation kinetics, Src and FAK activation, Rac1-GTP, and RhoA/ROCK activity after POS addition with a SHP099 concentration range bracketing its biochemical potency in enzyme assays; benchmark effect sizes against a ROCK inhibitor positive control, which is validated to rescue phagocytosis even in MerTK-deficient contexts (Mao & Finnemann, 2021).  
- Functional phagocytosis assays. Measure POS binding, F-actin cup formation, internalization, and phagolysosomal acidification under the same conditions, using established assays and timepoints aligned to the diurnal phagocytic peak where applicable (Lieffrig et al., 2023; Moran et al., 2022).  
- Ocular PK and safety. Establish retinal/RPE exposure after systemic and (if considered) intravitreal dosing, and perform ocular tolerability assessments (inflammation, ERG, histopathology) to identify potential on- or off-target liabilities early, mindful of class risks noted in optimization campaigns (Meem, 2022; Mitra & Ayyannan, 2021).

In summary, SHP099 is a potent, selective, and well-characterized SHP2 allosteric inhibitor with robust oncology pharmacology and drug-like properties, but the case for repurposing to dry AMD by enhancing RPE POS phagocytosis is unsubstantiated in the provided literature and carries meaningful mechanistic and translational risks. Prioritizing direct RPE mechanistic studies and ocular PK/tolerability before any disease-model investment is the appropriate next step; in parallel, ROCK pathway modulation remains the most evidence-backed pharmacologic lever to augment phagocytosis in this system and should serve as a positive control and a benchmark for effect size (Fortanet et al., 2016; Mao & Finnemann, 2021; Tripathi & Ayyannan, 2021).
