Proposal for Eculizumab (Anti-C5 mAb; Alexion Pharmaceuticals)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate  
Eculizumab is a recombinant, humanized monoclonal IgG kappa antibody that specifically binds complement component C5 and prevents its proteolytic activation into C5a and C5b, thereby blocking terminal pathway activity and membrane attack complex (MAC; C5b-9) assembly while leaving upstream C3-dependent functions largely intact (for example, opsonization and immune-complex handling) (Rother et al., 2007; Parker, 2009; Mantegazza & Cavalcante, 2020; West et al., 2024). It was discovered by screening large panels of murine anti-human C5 monoclonals for potent inhibition of C5 activation and terminal complement–mediated hemolysis; the parental murine antibody (5G1.1) was then humanized by CDR grafting into human germline frameworks and engineered to use a hybrid IgG2/IgG4 heavy-chain constant region to minimize Fcγ receptor binding and classical-pathway activation (reducing effector functions that could confound terminal pathway blockade) (Rother et al., 2007; Parker, 2009). Eculizumab binds human C5 with very high affinity (Kd approximately 120 pM) and sterically prevents convertase engagement with the MG7 domain of C5; epitope mapping identifies residues in the MG7 domain (including the KSSKC motif around Arg885) critical for binding, and Arg885His/Cys polymorphisms have been linked to clinical non-responsiveness in some patients, consistent with the structural epitope (Rother et al., 2007; Schatz-Jakobsen et al., 2016; Risitano et al., 2019).

As a drug class, complement inhibitors have been deployed to treat diseases driven by complement dysregulation, with C5 blockade representing a terminal-pathway strategy that ablates C5a signaling and MAC-mediated cytolysis while preserving many proximal complement functions; eculizumab was the first complement inhibitor approved for clinical use and catalyzed broad clinical development of C5, C3, and alternative pathway–targeted agents across hematology, nephrology, neurology, and, more recently, ophthalmology (West et al., 2024; Mantegazza & Cavalcante, 2020; Mannes et al., 2021). Eculizumab is administered intravenously, exhibits a long serum half-life (~272 ± 82 hours), a limited volume of distribution consistent with an intravascularly confined antibody, and shows pharmacodynamic correlation between serum trough concentrations and blockade of hemolytic activity; vaccination against Neisseria meningitidis is required due to increased susceptibility when terminal complement is inhibited (Rother et al., 2007; Smith et al., 2012; Parker, 2009).

Within ophthalmology, complement activation products and MAC deposition have been implicated in AMD pathogenesis, motivating clinical trials of complement inhibitors including C5-directed agents; eculizumab has been formally evaluated in a randomized phase 2 setting for non-exudative AMD (geographic atrophy and drusen cohorts) via systemic administration (Kassa et al., 2019; Yehoshua et al., 2014; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009; Halawa et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History  
Eculizumab has an extensive clinical record in systemic complement-mediated disorders. It revolutionized therapy for paroxysmal nocturnal hemoglobinuria (PNH), where it reduces intravascular hemolysis, decreases transfusion requirements, and improves quality of life; it is also approved for atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome (aHUS) and for neurologic autoimmune indications including anti–acetylcholine receptor–positive generalized myasthenia gravis and aquaporin-4–positive neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (West et al., 2024; Mantegazza & Cavalcante, 2020; Mannes et al., 2021). Early clinical pharmacology in PNH demonstrated that an induction regimen of 600 mg weekly for four weeks followed by 900 mg every other week maintained near-complete terminal pathway blockade and significantly reduced hemolysis and transfusion needs; these dosing principles align with its long half-life and the concentration dependence of hemolytic inhibition (Hillmen et al., 2004; Rother et al., 2007; Smith et al., 2012). Despite robust control of intravascular hemolysis, residual extravascular hemolysis can persist because C3 opsonization is not prevented by C5 inhibition, illustrating an important mechanistic limitation of terminal-pathway agents (Schmidt & Smith, 2023; West et al., 2024).

The drug’s safety profile is dominated by infection risk with encapsulated organisms—particularly meningococcal disease—necessitating vaccination; otherwise, eculizumab has shown acceptable tolerability across long-term use, with clinical programs incorporating monitoring of functional complement activity (CH50) to confirm pharmacodynamic blockade and dose adequacy (Smith et al., 2012; Parker, 2009; Eskandary et al., 2016). Mechanistically relevant sources also report pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic complexities: high-affinity binding at acidic endosomal pH encourages recycling of eculizumab:C5 complexes by FcRn, leading to accumulation of total C5 bound to the drug in circulation; next-generation engineering in ravulizumab introduced pH-dependent release to minimize cargo recycling and extend dosing intervals (Schmidt & Smith, 2023).

In ophthalmology, eculizumab has been investigated as a repurposed systemic therapy for dry AMD. The COMPLETE study (ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009), a single-center, randomized, double-masked phase 2 trial, evaluated intravenous eculizumab in two cohorts: geographic atrophy (GA) and intermediate AMD with high-risk drusen; patients were randomized 2:1 to eculizumab or saline over 24 weeks with follow-up to 52 weeks (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Park et al., 2021). In the GA cohort (n = 30 study eyes), eculizumab did not reduce GA enlargement versus placebo at 26 or 52 weeks (square-root–transformed growth 0.19 ± 0.12 mm vs. 0.18 ± 0.15 mm at 26 weeks, P = 0.96; 0.37 ± 0.22 mm vs. 0.37 ± 0.21 mm at 52 weeks, P = 0.93), and no drug-related adverse events were reported (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Park et al., 2021). In the drusen cohort (n = 30 total participants; 20 active, 10 placebo), eculizumab failed to meet the prespecified primary endpoint of a ≥ 50% reduction in drusen cube-root volume at 26 weeks; none of 18 treated eyes achieved this threshold, while one placebo eye did (10%; P = 0.36), and there was no detectable difference in mean drusen growth between arms through 26–52 weeks (Filho et al., 2014). Trial conduct included meningococcal vaccination and careful multimodal imaging; retention was high with 28/30 completing 52 weeks (Filho et al., 2014; Yehoshua et al., 2014; ClinicalTrials.gov, 2009). Independent evidence syntheses judged the certainty of evidence as low to very low due to small sample size, imprecision, and some risk of bias; overall, systemic eculizumab “may have made little to no difference” in BCVA and GA lesion growth in the available cohort (Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Mechanistically similar C5-directed agents have not shown positive phase 2 outcomes in GA when administered systemically or intravitreally (e.g., LFG316 failed in phase 2), whereas intravitreal C5 inhibition with avacincaptad pegol progressed to later-phase testing and regulatory review, suggesting that drug, route, and pharmacology may be important determinants of outcome; by contrast, intravitreal C3 inhibition (pegcetacoplan) demonstrated efficacy and has been approved for GA, underscoring the translational relevance of target selection and ocular delivery (Kassa et al., 2019; West et al., 2024). Multiple reviews conclude that systemic eculizumab is no longer in development for AMD and highlight delivery and mechanistic concerns as likely contributors to the negative results (Nadeem et al., 2023; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Mechanism of Action  
At the molecular level, eculizumab targets the MG7 domain of C5 and sterically prevents formation of the C5 convertase–substrate complex, thereby inhibiting the cleavage of C5 into the potent anaphylatoxin C5a and C5b, which nucleates membrane attack complex assembly with C6–C9 (Schatz-Jakobsen et al., 2016; Rother et al., 2007). Structural analysis of an eculizumab Fab bound to C5 resolved at 4.2 Å shows that five CDRs form the principal interface with MG7; mutational scanning of CDR residues identifies a network of contacts necessary for high-affinity binding, and kinetic assays confirm that these interactions prevent complement-mediated hemolysis in vitro (Schatz-Jakobsen et al., 2016). The epitope includes residues near Arg885, and clinical resistance due to Arg885His/Cys substitutions in C5 provides orthogonal validation of the binding site (Schatz-Jakobsen et al., 2016; Risitano et al., 2019).

Pharmacodynamically, eculizumab ablates terminal pathway function: it suppresses CH50 to near zero when trough serum concentrations exceed ~35 μg/mL; however, because proximal C3 activation continues, C3b deposition and downstream opsonins accumulate on surfaces, which can drive extravascular clearance and generate residual pathology even under complete C5 blockade in appropriate disease contexts (Rother et al., 2007; Schmidt & Smith, 2023). Additional mechanisms can undermine complete terminal pathway control: (1) during intense proximal activation, densely opsonized surfaces can support C5 activation by convertases in ways that partially bypass classical C5 convertase assembly or even promote conformational C5 activation on surface C3b clusters; such context-dependent activation can manifest as “pharmacodynamic breakthrough” despite apparently adequate free drug levels, and has been reported in clinical settings as residual terminal-pathway activity and elevated sC5b-9 in some patients (Mannes et al., 2021; Schmidt & Smith, 2023). (2) Eculizumab binds C5 with high affinity at both neutral and mildly acidic pH, allowing FcRn to recycle eculizumab:C5 complexes and potentially alter antigen disposition; ravulizumab’s pH-dependent binding was engineered to release C5 in endosomes and improve pharmacokinetics by avoiding cargo recycling (Schmidt & Smith, 2023). These features are germane to dose selection, monitoring, and potential resistance or escape during strong complement activation.

Rationale for C5 inhibition in AMD rests on abundant mechanistic and histopathological evidence that C5-derived effectors and MAC participate in retinal/choroidal injury. C5a is detected in drusen and acts as a chemotactic and proinflammatory mediator capable of inducing VEGF expression from retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells, while C5b initiates MAC assembly; MAC deposition in Bruch’s membrane and the choriocapillaris increases with aging and is elevated in AMD (Kassa et al., 2019). Sub-lytic and lytic MAC on choroidal endothelium causes cell injury and can trigger surviving endothelial cells to upregulate VEGF and matrix metalloproteinases, linking terminal pathway activation to both atrophic injury and pro-angiogenic remodeling; complement regulatory proteins such as CD59 are natural inhibitors of MAC formation and their dysfunction or insufficiency can predispose to damage (Kassa et al., 2019; Park et al., 2021). Complement dysregulation in AMD further includes genetic risk (e.g., CFH variants) and evidence of alternative pathway activation in ocular tissues, suggesting both proximal and terminal effector involvement in disease biology (Piri & Kaplan, 2023).

Importantly, proximal inhibition at C3 has shown the capacity to restore lysosomal function and reduce sub-RPE drusen-like deposits in human iPSC-derived RPE models carrying the high-risk CFH Y402H variant by reducing C3 turnover and lowering downstream MAC (C5b-9) localization at lysosomes; in this system, a compstatin analogue (Cp40) suppressed C3b and MAC deposition and reversed lysosomal abnormalities, whereas direct C5 inhibition has not been shown in this model to rescue lysosomal function, and clinical C5 blockade has failed in GA (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). These data reinforce that while terminal pathway effectors are present and likely pathogenic in AMD, distal blockade at C5 does not necessarily address upstream complement turnover that drives intracellular lysosomal stress in RPE, and proximal intervention may be required to normalize cellular homeostasis (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).

Expected Effect  
The hypothesis proposes that high-affinity C5 blockade with eculizumab will prevent MAC assembly on RPE, thereby reducing sub-RPE deposit–driven lysosomal stress and indirectly supporting photoreceptor outer segment (POS) phagocytosis in dry AMD. Mechanistically, preventing C5 cleavage would abrogate both C5a signaling and C5b-dependent MAC formation; given the documented presence of C5a in drusen and increased MAC deposition in Bruch’s membrane/choriocapillaris with age and AMD, terminal pathway inhibition is expected to reduce MAC-mediated endothelial and RPE injury, dampen MAC-induced VEGF/MMP signaling, and potentially mitigate inflammation (Kassa et al., 2019). In principle, if MAC-driven lysosomal injury contributes to RPE dysfunction, C5 inhibition could reduce new MAC deposition at the RPE surface and limit subsequent endocytosis of MAC into lysosomes, thereby lowering lysosomal burden (Park et al., 2021).

However, two key bodies of evidence temper this expectation. First, clinical testing of systemic eculizumab in GA and intermediate AMD failed to show benefit on primary anatomical endpoints (GA growth and OCT drusen volume) through 26–52 weeks, despite established systemic pharmacodynamic blockade; these negative outcomes argue that either (a) terminal pathway activity at C5 is not the principal driver of lesion growth/drusen regression during the studied disease stages/time horizon, or (b) pharmacokinetic compartmentalization limited ocular target engagement after intravenous dosing (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Park et al., 2021; Filho et al., 2014). Reviews explicitly highlight the compartment barrier problem—systemic dosing may not achieve therapeutic concentrations in the retina or sub-RPE space due to the blood–retina/Bruch’s membrane barriers and large molecular size—and note that eculizumab exposure shorter than six months is unlikely to show benefit in slowly progressive GA, compounding interpretation (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Wu & Sun, 2019). Second, cellular models directly linking complement dysregulation to lysosomal failure in high-risk AMD RPE show that upstream C3 inhibition, not terminal C5 blockade, restores lysosomal function and reduces deposit formation; this suggests that intralysosomal stress is driven by continuous C3 turnover and opsonization rather than MAC alone, and that distal C5 blockade may be insufficient to normalize these processes (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). Consequently, POS phagocytosis metrics may improve only marginally or not at all if the dominant insult is proximal complement turnover rather than MAC-mediated damage. The clinical failure to slow GA growth or reduce drusen volume with systemic eculizumab supports the inference that target engagement at C5, via the tested route and schedule, did not translate into macroscopic anatomical benefit in human AMD eyes within one year (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Filho et al., 2014).

If eculizumab were to be tested in vitro on human RPE, appropriate readouts would include: surface and intracellular MAC (C5b-9) quantification, lysosomal number/size and membrane integrity (e.g., LAMP2, Galectin-8), Cathepsin D activity, autophagic flux, and POS degradation kinetics; concomitant measurement of upstream C3b/iC3b/C3d deposition would be essential to interpret whether C5 inhibition is affecting the dominant pathogenic pathway in the assay (Cerniauskas et al., 2020). In vivo, ocular pharmacokinetic considerations dominate: intravitreal administration delivers drug to the retina and sub-RPE space but is not reported for eculizumab in the provided context and would carry different safety and dosing constraints; systemic dosing faces blood–retina barrier limitations that likely constrained ocular target engagement in COMPLETE (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Wu & Sun, 2019). Notably, nearly all complement inhibitors that have shown anatomical effects in GA have been delivered intravitreally, underscoring the importance of route of administration for ocular diseases (Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Overall Evaluation  
Strengths  
- Strong mechanistic rationale: C5a and MAC are present in AMD-relevant tissues; MAC deposition increases with age and AMD and can drive endothelial injury, VEGF/MMP upregulation, and potentially RPE dysfunction; blocking C5 should diminish these terminal effector signals (Kassa et al., 2019; Piri & Kaplan, 2023).  
- Potent, well-characterized biologic: Eculizumab binds human C5 with picomolar affinity, has a well-defined structural epitope in the MG7 domain, and reliably ablates terminal pathway function systemically with a large clinical safety database outside ophthalmology (Rother et al., 2007; Schatz-Jakobsen et al., 2016).  
- Clinical feasibility and tolerability: In AMD trials, intravenous eculizumab was well tolerated without drug-related adverse events and with no clear signal for increased neovascular conversion or ocular infection within one year, supporting general safety of systemic C5 blockade in this population under vaccination protocols (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Park et al., 2021; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Weaknesses and Risks  
- Negative clinical efficacy in AMD: The randomized phase 2 COMPLETE trial showed no reduction in GA growth and no meaningful reduction in drusen volume through 26–52 weeks; certainty is limited by small sample size but confidence intervals and replication across endpoints argue against a large treatment effect (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Filho et al., 2014).  
- Compartmentalization barriers for systemic dosing: Blood–retina and Bruch’s membrane barriers likely limit ocular exposure to intravenously administered eculizumab; multiple reviews cite inadequate ocular penetration as a plausible reason for failure, and systemic eculizumab is no longer being pursued in AMD (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Nadeem et al., 2023; Wu & Sun, 2019).  
- Target selection may be too distal for RPE lysosomal rescue: Human iPSC-RPE data indicate that complement-driven lysosomal pathology and drusen-like deposits are reversed by C3 inhibition, with concomitant reduction of downstream MAC, while C5 blockade alone has not been shown to restore lysosomal metrics and did not slow GA clinically; this suggests that proximal complement turnover is the dominant driver of RPE lysosomal stress (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).  
- Mechanistic escape and incomplete terminal control: Under strong activation, C5 can be activated on dense C3b clusters with features of convertase bypass or conformational priming; stoichiometric C5 inhibitors can form long-lived C5:antibody complexes on surfaces, potentially allowing residual terminal activity, and clinical “pharmacodynamic breakthrough” has been documented (Mannes et al., 2021; Schmidt & Smith, 2023).  
- Genetic and biochemical determinants of response: C5 polymorphisms (e.g., R885H/C) can abolish binding and confer resistance; while prevalence in AMD populations is unknown here, such variants are important risk factors for nonresponse (Schatz-Jakobsen et al., 2016; Risitano et al., 2019).  
- Safety/logistics: Terminal complement blockade mandates meningococcal vaccination and vigilance for invasive infections; while acceptable systemically in selected diseases, risk–benefit in a chronic, slowly progressive ocular disorder is less favorable, and the cost and infusion burden are high (Smith et al., 2012; Parker, 2009).

Contextualization with alternative complement strategies  
- C5 vs C3: Clinical success in GA has emerged at the level of C3 (pegcetacoplan), consistent with cellular data showing rescue of lysosomal function by upstream blockade; by contrast, systemic C5 inhibition with eculizumab and other C5-directed agents failed to meet GA endpoints in early trials, and LFG316 also did not demonstrate efficacy in GA (West et al., 2024; Kassa et al., 2019; Cerniauskas et al., 2020).  
- Route of administration: Most agents demonstrating anatomical effects in GA are delivered intravitreally; eculizumab’s large size and systemic administration likely limited ocular penetration in COMPLETE, and no intravitreal eculizumab data are provided here to support local delivery (Tzoumas et al., 2023).  
- Risk of adverse ocular remodeling: Complement modulation has complex, context-dependent effects; in some models, complement inhibition or modulation can alter macrophage polarization and influence CNV formation, underscoring that indiscriminate or poorly targeted complement blockade could have unintended consequences; while the eculizumab AMD trials did not show a neovascular signal, vigilance is warranted when selecting targets and doses (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Park et al., 2021).

Decision Implications  
- As a repurposed systemic therapy for dry AMD, eculizumab has a low probability of success based on randomized clinical evidence, pharmacokinetic compartment limitations, and mechanistic considerations indicating that distal C5 blockade may not correct the proximal complement turnover driving RPE lysosomal pathology (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Filho et al., 2014; Cerniauskas et al., 2020).  
- If C5 remains a target of interest, local ocular delivery and alternative molecular formats designed for intravitreal pharmacokinetics (e.g., smaller C5-binding entities, RNAi to intraocular C5 production, or intravitreal C5 inhibitors such as avacincaptad pegol) are more plausible routes; indeed, avacincaptad has advanced in GA, while systemic eculizumab has been discontinued in AMD (Kassa et al., 2019; Nadeem et al., 2023; West et al., 2024).  
- For assays aimed at lysosomal stress and POS phagocytosis, prioritizing proximal complement inhibitors (e.g., C3-targeting) is more aligned with human RPE data and recent clinical experience, whereas C5 inhibition alone is unlikely to fully normalize lysosomal function or confer robust structural benefit (Cerniauskas et al., 2020; West et al., 2024).

Conclusion  
Eculizumab provides a clear mechanistic means to extinguish terminal complement effectors implicated in AMD biology, but the totality of evidence—negative randomized clinical data in GA and drusen, route-of-administration barriers to ocular exposure, mechanistic escape during high activation, and cellular evidence favoring proximal over distal inhibition for lysosomal rescue—argues against further development of systemic eculizumab for dry AMD (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Filho et al., 2014; Tzoumas et al., 2023; Cerniauskas et al., 2020). The program should be deprioritized in favor of intraocularly suited agents and proximal complement targets, unless a compelling, testable strategy emerges to achieve effective intraocular C5 blockade with eculizumab (which is not supported by the present context) (Nadeem et al., 2023; Tzoumas et al., 2023).

Mechanistic Appendix: Biochemical and Pathobiologic Evidence Relevant to the Hypothesis  
- Complement activation and terminal effectors in AMD:  
  - C5a is present in drusen and induces VEGF from RPE; MAC deposition increases with age and AMD; MAC induces endothelial lysis and sub-lytic survival signaling that upregulates VEGF and MMPs (Kassa et al., 2019).  
  - Alternative pathway dysregulation is central in AMD; genetic and experimental data implicate factor H and alternative pathway components in AMD and CNV models; inhibition of C3a, C5a, CFB, MAC or supplementation with CD59/CFH blocks CNV in animals (Piri & Kaplan, 2023).  
- Eculizumab structure–function:  
  - Epitope on MG7 with steric convertase blockade; high-affinity binding and resistance polymorphisms at Arg885; CDR function validated by mutational scans (Schatz-Jakobsen et al., 2016).  
  - PK/PD: long half-life, vascular distribution, CH50 suppression threshold, FcRn recycling of C5:eculizumab complexes; ravulizumab engineering to improve recycling and dosing (Rother et al., 2007; Schmidt & Smith, 2023).  
  - Breakthrough mechanisms: convertase bypass and surface-induced conformational activation on dense C3b clusters; residual TP activity despite inhibitors under strong activation (Schmidt & Smith, 2023; Mannes et al., 2021).  
- Clinical AMD trials:  
  - COMPLETE GA cohort: no slowing of GA growth at 26 or 52 weeks; well tolerated (Yehoshua et al., 2014; Park et al., 2021).  
  - COMPLETE drusen cohort: no ≥ 50% reduction in drusen volume in treated eyes at 26 weeks; no significant change in drusen growth vs placebo (Filho et al., 2014).  
  - Critical appraisals: small sample, imprecision, risk of bias; systemic delivery may not achieve retinal levels; eculizumab no longer in AMD development (Tzoumas et al., 2023; Nadeem et al., 2023).  
- RPE lysosomal biology:  
  - In high-risk Y402H iPSC-RPE, excessive C3 turnover increases MAC internalization and overloads lysosomes; C3 inhibition with Cp40 reduces both C3b and MAC, reverses lysosomal defects, and reduces drusen-like deposits; direct C5 inhibition is not shown to restore lysosomal function in this model (Cerniauskas et al., 2020).

Operational Recommendation  
- Do not advance systemic eculizumab for dry AMD. If C5 remains a strategic target, consider intravitreal agents designed for ocular PK and evaluate them head-to-head against proximal inhibitors in RPE lysosomal-function assays that quantify both MAC and C3 fragment deposition, with translational go/no-go predicated on alignment with known clinical signals in GA (Kassa et al., 2019; West et al., 2024; Cerniauskas et al., 2020).

hypothesis: SB431542 (TGFβR1 inhibitor; Tocris Cat. No. 1614)
answer:
Proposal for SB431542 (TGFβR1 inhibitor; Tocris Cat. No. 1614)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
SB431542 is a well‐characterized, synthetic small molecule inhibitor originally developed through medicinal chemistry efforts by researchers at GlaxoSmithKline. Its chemical structure, formally denoted as 4-(5-benzo[1,3]dioxol-5-yl-4-pyridin-2-yl-1H-imidazol-2-yl)-benzamide, incorporates a benzodioxole moiety linked to a pyridyl-imidazol core and terminated by a benzamide group, placing it within the imidazole class of compounds (Laping et al., 2002). SB431542 belongs to the class of transforming growth factor-β (TGFβ) type I receptor kinase inhibitors (commonly referred to as ALK5 inhibitors) that inhibit ATP-dependent receptor activation. Initially designed as an improvement over less-selective kinase inhibitors—such as early p38 MAPK inhibitors that exhibited off-target ALK5 inhibition—SB431542 emerged from a rational structure–activity relationship (SAR) campaign aimed at optimizing both potency and selectivity (Laping et al., 2002). Its discovery has been pivotal in establishing a molecular tool for dissecting TGFβ signaling, and its chemical synthesis reflects a focused effort on achieving high-affinity, ATP-competitive inhibition of the TGFβ receptor. This compound has been extensively used in preclinical research to study fibrotic mechanisms and cellular differentiation, thereby marking its reputation as a “gold standard” in TGFβ pathway inhibition (Laping et al., 2002).

Therapeutic History:  
The therapeutic history of SB431542 is primarily rooted in its application as a research tool rather than as a clinical drug candidate. In numerous preclinical studies, SB431542 has been consistently used to inhibit TGFβ-induced processes such as extracellular matrix (ECM) synthesis, Smad protein activation, and the induction of a fibrotic phenotype in various cell types including renal epithelial cells, fibroblasts, and even certain cancer cell models (Laping et al., 2002). Biochemical studies have shown that SB431542 effectively blocks the phosphorylation of Smad3 with an IC50 of approximately 94 nM, thereby preventing the downstream transcriptional activation of cytokines and matrix proteins (Laping et al., 2002). Its anti-fibrotic effects have been extensively characterized in in vitro assays, where it reduced the expression of collagen I α1, fibronectin, and plasminogen activator inhibitor-1 (PAI-1) mRNA, thus providing compelling evidence that the compound modulates TGFβ-induced ECM remodeling (Laping et al., 2002).

While SB431542 has been applied in many experimental models to study pathways implicated in fibrotic diseases such as glomerulonephritis, diabetic nephropathy, liver cirrhosis, and pulmonary fibrosis, there is scant direct evidence of its historical use in ocular pathologies, particularly dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) (Akhund et al., 2023; Nyati et al., 2011). However, TGFβ signaling has been implicated in retinal pathologies and in the mesenchymal transition of retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells from which some studies have emerged using general TGFβ inhibitors to reverse such pathological changes (Radeke et al., 2015). Although SB431542 itself has not been used in clinical trials for AMD, its mechanistic profile and reported efficacies in other fibrotic and ECM remodeling contexts make it a promising candidate for repurposing to address the abnormal matrix remodeling observed in dry AMD. Preclinical studies in non-ocular tissues have established that targeted inhibition of TGFβ signaling leads to substantial reductions in fibrotic markers, suggesting that similar approaches could mitigate Bruch membrane (BrM) alterations in AMD (Laping et al., 2002).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, SB431542 functions as an ATP-competitive inhibitor selectively targeting the kinase domain of the TGFβ type I receptor (TGFβRI, also known as ALK5). Its mechanism of action centers on binding to the ATP-binding pocket of TGFβRI, thereby preventing the phosphorylation of key intracellular effectors, primarily the Smad2 and Smad3 proteins (Laping et al., 2002). In normal TGFβ signaling, binding of the ligand (e.g., TGFβ1) to its receptors induces the formation of a heteromeric complex consisting of TGFβRI and TGFβRII, leading to the phosphorylation and activation of Smad2/3. These phosphorylated Smad proteins then form a complex with Smad4, translocate to the nucleus, and activate the transcription of pro-fibrotic genes, including those involved in ECM protein synthesis such as collagen, fibronectin, and PAI-1 (Laping et al., 2002).

Detailed molecular interaction studies have revealed that SB431542 makes critical hydrogen bonding contacts within the ATP-binding site of TGFβRI. For example, the benzodioxol moiety is reported to form a hydrogen bond with the amide nitrogen of His283, while additional interactions with Lys232 and other hydrophobic residues stabilize the inhibitor within the binding pocket (Leonardo-Sousa et al., 2025). This precise molecular engagement confers its high selectivity, as even minor substitutions in the binding region—such as mutations at the gatekeeper residue—can significantly alter inhibitor efficacy (Laping et al., 2002; Leonardo-Sousa et al., 2025). Furthermore, while SB431542 shows potent inhibition against ALK5, it also inhibits closely related receptors such as ALK4 and ALK7 with only modest differences in potency (IC50 for ALK4 is approximately 140 nM), and it exhibits negligible activity against BMP-activated receptors (ALK2, ALK3, and ALK6) (Laping et al., 2002). This selective inhibition ensures that the canonical TGFβ/Smad pathway is targeted without significantly perturbing other pathways that could be essential for cellular homeostasis, such as the BMP signaling cascade (Nyati et al., 2011; Akhund et al., 2023).

In addition to its inhibition of Smad2/3 phosphorylation, SB431542 has been shown to disrupt the subsequent nuclear translocation of these transcription factors, thereby halting the transcription of downstream ECM components. Such inhibition is critical because overactivation of the TGFβ pathway is a central driver in fibrotic diseases and leads to excessive deposition of ECM proteins, which in turn contribute to tissue stiffness and impaired cellular function (Laping et al., 2002). Overall, the molecular mechanism of SB431542 is well-delineated; its high selectivity for TGFβRI and the resulting blockade of Smad-mediated transcription form the foundation for its potential use in addressing aberrant ECM remodeling.

Expected Effect:  
The hypothesis for repurposing SB431542 in dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is built on the concept that excessive TGFβ signaling within the retinal microenvironment leads to an abnormal accumulation and remodeling of ECM components in the Bruch membrane (BrM). In the context of dry AMD, such ECM changes are believed to increase membrane stiffness and disrupt the diffusion of critical phagocytic ligands—specifically MFGE8 (Milk Fat Globule Epidermal Growth Factor 8) and Gas6—which play key roles in facilitating the integrin αvβ5-mediated binding and uptake of photoreceptor outer segments (POS) by retinal pigment epithelial (RPE) cells (Radeke et al., 2015).

By inhibiting TGFβRI, SB431542 is expected to block the TGFβ-driven phosphorylation of Smad proteins, thereby directly reducing the transcription of genes that encode for fibrotic and ECM-related proteins such as collagen I α1, fibronectin, and PAI-1 (Laping et al., 2002). In doing so, SB431542 should restore a more balanced ECM composition in the BrM. This normalization of ECM deposition is anticipated to reduce BrM stiffness, thereby enhancing the diffusion of phagocytic ligands like MFGE8 and Gas6 across the membrane. The improved ligand diffusion is expected to restore the optimal microenvironment required for integrin αvβ5 on the RPE surface to effectively bind and internalize POS, a process that is critically impaired in dry AMD (Radeke et al., 2015; Nyati et al., 2011).

Furthermore, by attenuating the fibrotic response within the retina, SB431542 may help preserve the native architecture and function of the RPE layer. This indirect modulation of phagocytosis, achieved through the normalization of ECM characteristics, represents a novel therapeutic angle that bridges the gap between ECM pathology and receptor-mediated cellular processes. In essence, the expected effect of SB431542 is a dual benefit: first, it directly inhibits pathological TGFβ signaling to reduce further fibrotic damage, and second, it indirectly normalizes phagocytic function by restoring the proper presentation of ligands critical for RPE-mediated clearance of POS (Laping et al., 2002; Radeke et al., 2015).

At the cellular and molecular level, the proposed assay is likely to measure a reduction in fibrotic markers (e.g., collagen I α1, fibronectin) and an improvement in assays of POS binding and internalization by RPE cells. Given that RPE cells express integrin αvβ5 and are responsive to TGFβ signaling, the application of SB431542 should result in a shift from a fibrotic, mesenchymal phenotype towards a more differentiated epithelial state that is conducive to normal phagocytic activity (Radeke et al., 2015; Akhund et al., 2023). This outcome would be mechanistically consistent with the known roles of TGFβ in modulating ECM dynamics and cellular differentiation. Consequently, if the hypothesis holds true, SB431542 would not only prevent further ECM deposition and stiffening of the BrM but would also support the resolution of existing pathological ECM alterations, thereby improving the overall homeostasis of the retinal microenvironment.

Overall Evaluation:  
The evaluation of SB431542 as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD requires careful consideration of its well-established biochemical profile alongside the translational challenges emerging from its current use primarily as a research tool. On the positive side, SB431542 is a potent and selective inhibitor of TGFβRI, with extensive preclinical evidence demonstrating its capacity to block TGFβ-induced Smad2/3 phosphorylation and consequently reduce the expression of fibrotic markers (Laping et al., 2002). Its high potency (with an IC50 in the low nanomolar range) and favorable selectivity profile—particularly with more than 100-fold selectivity over p38 MAPK and minimal activity against BMP receptors—render it an attractive candidate for targeted modulation of TGFβ signaling in tissues where fibrosis is a major pathogenic factor (Laping et al., 2002). These strengths are of particular relevance in the context of dry AMD, where BrM thickening and ECM remodeling are central features that compromise RPE function.

Moreover, the proposed mechanism underlying the therapeutic hypothesis is compelling. Excessive TGFβ signaling has been implicated in the aberrant remodeling of the BrM, which in turn impairs the presentation of critical phagocytic ligands necessary for efficient POS uptake by the RPE (Radeke et al., 2015). By inhibiting TGFβRI, SB431542 could theoretically restore the balance between collagen and proteoglycan production, thereby normalizing BrM stiffness and improving the diffusion of factors such as MFGE8 and Gas6. In doing so, the drug would indirectly enhance integrin αvβ5-mediated phagocytosis—a process that is essential for the maintenance of photoreceptor health and overall retinal integrity. This innovative indirect approach could represent a significant advancement in the treatment of dry AMD, addressing the disease from both a fibrotic and a functional perspective.

However, several considerable challenges and weaknesses must be acknowledged. First, the bulk of the supporting data for SB431542 comes from studies in non-ocular cell types or animal models of general fibrosis and cancer, with limited direct evidence in ocular systems. Although TGFβ inhibitors have been proposed as therapeutic agents in retinal diseases, there remains a significant gap in data specific to dry AMD or related retinal degenerative conditions (Akhund et al., 2023; Nyati et al., 2011). The absence of ocular pharmacokinetic studies, detailed data on retinal tissue penetration, and long-term safety evaluations in the eye poses a major hurdle for the clinical translation of SB431542 for AMD.

Furthermore, TGFβ signaling is a double-edged sword in many tissues, including the retina. While excessive TGFβ activity drives pathological ECM deposition and fibrosis, TGFβ also participates in immune regulation and cellular homeostasis. Therefore, complete or prolonged inhibition of TGFβ signaling may have unintended consequences, such as impairing normal wound healing or altering the immunological milieu of the retina (Akhund et al., 2023; Gupta et al., 2023). The delicate balance between therapeutic efficacy and potential adverse effects necessitates that any systemic or even locally delivered TGFβRI inhibitor be subject to rigorous dosing and toxicity studies. In this regard, the narrow therapeutic window often encountered in kinase inhibition therapies could be a limiting factor for SB431542’s adoption in an ophthalmic setting.

Another significant concern is the delivery method. The current literature on SB431542 primarily documents its use in cell culture assays or systemic administration in animal models; however, the ocular environment presents unique challenges due to barriers such as the inner limiting membrane, the blood-retina barrier, and the anatomical constraints of the retina. To achieve therapeutically relevant concentrations in the sub-retinal space or at the level of the BrM, innovative delivery strategies—such as topical formulations, intravitreal injections, or sustained-release devices—must be developed and validated (Hachana & Larrivée, 2022; Radeke et al., 2015). The pharmacokinetics and biodistribution of SB431542 in ocular tissues remain largely unexplored, which represents a critical gap in current knowledge.

Additionally, although the indirect mechanism of action—namely, the normalization of ECM to facilitate proper ligand–receptor interactions—is scientifically plausible, it is inherently more challenging to measure and validate compared to direct cellular responses. Assays designed to monitor changes in BrM stiffness, ECM composition, and the diffusion characteristics of MFGE8 and Gas6 must be highly sensitive and reproducible, and these endpoints have not been extensively characterized in available preclinical models of AMD. Furthermore, the redundancy within TGFβ signaling pathways raises the possibility that compensatory mechanisms might mitigate the effects of ALK5 inhibition over time, potentially limiting the efficacy of SB431542, particularly in a chronic, slowly progressive disease like dry AMD (Laping et al., 2002; Akhund et al., 2023).

From an efficacy standpoint, while numerous studies demonstrate that SB431542 effectively reduces TGFβ-induced fibrotic responses in various cell types (Laping et al., 2002), extrapolating these findings to the complex microenvironment of the aged retina is not straightforward. The retina and RPE possess distinct cellular and molecular characteristics that may respond differently to TGFβ signaling modulation. For example, in RPE cells, TGFβ signaling not only regulates ECM deposition but is also involved in the maintenance of epithelial phenotype and may even exert neuroprotective effects under certain conditions. Hence, unspecific inhibition of TGFβ signaling in the retina could conceivably result in a loss of beneficial effects that are essential for retinal homeostasis (Radeke et al., 2015; Akhund et al., 2023).

In summary, while SB431542 exhibits a robust, well-characterized mechanism of action as a TGFβRI inhibitor and has demonstrated potent anti-fibrotic effects in preclinical models of ECM remodeling, its repurposing for dry AMD must overcome several significant challenges. The strengths of SB431542 lie in its high potency, selectivity, and extensive preclinical validation in non-ocular models. Its molecular interactions are well understood, and its ability to inhibit Smad phosphorylation offers a clear mechanistic rationale for reducing pathological ECM deposition. Consequently, if applied to the pathological process associated with dry AMD, SB431542 could, in theory, mitigate the excessive ECM remodeling that impairs ligand diffusion and consequently restores the capacity for integrin αvβ5-mediated POS uptake by RPE cells (Laping et al., 2002; Radeke et al., 2015; Nyati et al., 2011).

On the other hand, the weaknesses of this approach are substantial. There is limited evidence of SB431542’s efficacy in ocular models, and its pharmacokinetics, ocular tissue penetration, and long-term safety profile have yet to be rigorously evaluated. Additionally, the complexity of TGFβ’s biological roles raises concerns regarding the balance between therapeutic benefit and potential interference with normal retinal physiology. The indirect nature of the hypothesized effect—mediated by ECM normalization—adds further layers of complexity to both preclinical testing and eventual clinical translation. Finally, challenges related to drug delivery to the retina, along with the potential for compensatory signaling pathways to undermine the inhibitor’s efficacy, suggest that significant additional research is warranted before SB431542 can be advanced as a therapeutic candidate in an AMD setting (Akhund et al., 2023; Akhund et al., 2023; Gupta et al., 2023).

Overall, SB431542 presents a biologically plausible and mechanistically sound candidate for repurposing in the treatment of dry age-related macular degeneration, particularly given its demonstrated ability to modulate TGFβ-driven fibrotic pathways. However, its successful translation to an ophthalmic therapeutic will hinge on a series of focused preclinical studies that address ocular biodistribution, safety in retinal tissues, and the optimization of dosing regimens tailored to the unique anatomical and physiological challenges of the eye. Only after these critical issues have been resolved can SB431542 be considered a viable strategy to restore ECM homeostasis in the Bruch membrane, normalize phagocytic ligand availability, and ultimately enhance integrin-mediated POS uptake in RPE cells affected by dry AMD (Laping et al., 2002; Radeke et al., 2015; Nyati et al., 2011). In conclusion, while SB431542 has strong potential and a compelling mechanistic rationale, further dedicated ocular research is required to fully validate its therapeutic promise in the context of dry AMD before it can be recommended for clinical development.

hypothesis: Trichostatin A (HDAC inhibitor; Sigma-Aldrich Cat. No. T1952)
answer:
Proposal for Trichostatin A (HDAC inhibitor; Sigma-Aldrich Cat. No. T1952)

Overview of Therapeutic Candidate:  
Trichostatin A (TSA) is a naturally occurring compound originally isolated from fermentation cultures of Streptomyces species (Grayson et al., 2010). Belonging to the hydroxamate class of histone deacetylase (HDAC) inhibitors, TSA possesses a distinct molecular architecture characterized by three critical structural motifs: a hydroxamic acid moiety, a hydrophobic linker, and a bulky polar cap. These elements cooperate to enable TSA’s high‐affinity binding to the zinc ion within the catalytic site of HDAC enzymes, thereby blocking deacetylation reactions (Grayson et al., 2010). Unlike many newer synthetic compounds, TSA’s discovery dates back several decades, where it was initially identified for its antifungal properties yet quickly found utility as a potent epigenetic modulator in various research fields, including oncology and neurobiology (Grayson et al., 2010; Hamid et al., 2021). Within this class, HDAC inhibitors are well recognized for their ability to alter chromatin configuration; by preventing the removal of acetyl groups from histone tails, these compounds induce chromatin relaxation and, as a consequence, facilitate robust transcriptional activation of genes that are otherwise epigenetically repressed (Grayson et al., 2010; Hamid et al., 2021). In the context of ocular research, TSA has been exploited primarily as a tool compound to dissect the role of epigenetic modifications in retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) function and has been applied in studies examining angiogenesis, apoptosis, and inflammatory responses in RPE cells (Hamid et al., 2021). Its availability from commercial suppliers such as Sigma-Aldrich (Cat. No. T1952) underscores its utility as a research-grade standard for HDAC inhibition studies, making it an attractive candidate for drug repurposing efforts aimed at diseases such as dry age-related macular degeneration (AMD) where impaired transcription of clearance and autophagy genes plays a pivotal role (Grayson et al., 2010; Hamid et al., 2021).

Therapeutic History:  
TSA has garnered extensive attention over the years in the biomedical literature due to its potent HDAC inhibitory function. Originally explored for its antifungal properties, subsequent studies rapidly shifted focus toward its ability to cause histone hyperacetylation, thereby rekindling interest in epigenetic regulation as a therapeutic strategy for various pathologies (Grayson et al., 2010; Hamid et al., 2021). In oncology, for instance, TSA and its synthetic derivatives have been used to induce cell cycle arrest and apoptosis in cancer cells, ultimately leading to the development of newer, more selective HDAC inhibitors that have reached clinical trials and even regulatory approval for certain hematological malignancies (Grayson et al., 2010). In ocular research, TSA has been employed in experimental models involving retinal pigment epithelial cell lines, such as ARPE-19, where its application has led to notable changes in the transcription of genes involved in inflammation, angiogenesis, and cellular stress responses (Hamid et al., 2021). Although TSA itself has not been approved for clinical use in any ocular disease, its ability to modify gene expression through HDAC inhibition has provided valuable insights into potential interventions for retinal degenerative conditions, including both wet and dry forms of AMD (Hamid et al., 2021; Falcão et al., 2025). Moreover, preliminary safety studies—such as those performed using topical formulations in animal models for corneal wound healing—have demonstrated that TSA can be applied at low nanomolar concentrations with minimal cytotoxicity, suggesting that careful dose titration could allow its repurposing for RPE-targeted therapies without incurring the severe systemic toxicities observed in some cancer studies (Sharma et al., 2009). However, it is important to note that despite the promising preclinical data in ARPE-19 cells and related ocular models, there remains a significant gap in clinical evidence directly linking TSA treatment with efficacy in dry AMD, meaning that its repurposing for this indication remains experimental and largely hypothesis-driven at this stage (Kaarniranta et al., 2023; Hamid et al., 2021).

Mechanism of Action:  
At the molecular level, TSA is known to inhibit histone deacetylases by binding to the zinc ion in the enzyme’s catalytic pocket, thereby preventing the removal of acetyl groups from lysine residues on histone tails (Grayson et al., 2010; Hamid et al., 2021). In normal physiological conditions, HDACs contribute to the formation of tightly packed chromatin by deacetylating histones, which leads to decreased transcriptional activity at specific gene promoters. TSA’s ability to inhibit this process results in a “relaxed” chromatin structure that is more accessible to transcription factors, leading to enhanced gene expression (Grayson et al., 2010; Hamid et al., 2021). In the context of the RPE, several genes critical for autophagic flux and phagocytic function—such as lysosomal‐associated membrane protein 1 (LAMP1) and the receptor tyrosine kinase MERTK—are thought to be epigenetically regulated and may be transcriptionally upregulated upon HDAC inhibition (Boya et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025). Importantly, the transcription factor EB (TFEB) is recognized as a master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy, controlling the expression of a suite of genes organized within the coordinated lysosomal expression and regulation (CLEAR) network (Falcão et al., 2025). In RPE cells, where efficient degradation of phagocytosed photoreceptor outer segments (POS) is dependent on both lysosomal function and autophagy, the upregulation of TFEB through enhanced chromatin accessibility could theoretically result in improved expression of LAMP1 and, by extension, better phagocytic capacity via receptors such as MERTK (Boya et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025). Moreover, TSA’s inhibition of HDACs also affects non-histone substrates; for example, it increases the acetylation of α-tubulin—a modification that can influence microtubule dynamics and vesicular transport processes (Grayson et al., 2010; Hamid et al., 2021). However, this action comes with a potential caveat: excessive tubulin acetylation has been reported to impair autophagosome trafficking, which is a critical step in the autophagic clearance pathway (Toops et al., 2015; Tan, 2018). Therefore, while TSA’s global HDAC inhibition can promote the transcription of genes essential for lysosomal biogenesis and POS degradation, careful titration of its concentration is necessary to ensure that the beneficial effects on gene transcription do not get overshadowed by disruptions in cytoskeletal dynamics and autophagosome motility (Grayson et al., 2010; Hamid et al., 2021). At the same time, TSA has been shown in some studies to downregulate pro-inflammatory and pro-angiogenic mediators such as HIF-1α and IL-1β while upregulating factors like IL-18, which may contribute additional neuroprotective benefits to the RPE (Hamid et al., 2021). Together, these multifaceted actions underline TSA’s potential to reprogram the epigenetic landscape of RPE cells, theoretically reinstating the expression of key genes involved in autophagic and phagocytic function (Boya et al., 2023; Hamid et al., 2021).

Expected Effect:  
Based on the working hypothesis, the expected effect of TSA in RPE cells is twofold. First, by inhibiting HDAC activity, TSA is anticipated to elevate overall chromatin accessibility, thereby stimulating the transcription of genes that are vital for proper lysosomal biogenesis and phagocytosis. In particular, the upregulation of LAMP1, a well-established marker of lysosomal membranes, should lead to an increase in the number and activity of lysosomes. Simultaneously, enhanced expression of MERTK, which plays a central role in mediating the binding and internalization of POS, should result in an improved phagocytic rate of these essential outer segment components (Boya et al., 2023). In RPE cells, where the daily burden of POS phagocytosis is critical for maintaining retinal integrity, such enhancements could potentially mitigate the accumulation of undigested cellular debris—a phenomenon that is closely linked with the progression of dry AMD (Falcão et al., 2025; Tan, 2018). Second, TSA is expected to promote the activation and nuclear translocation of TFEB. This transcription factor is normally sequestered in the cytoplasm when phosphorylated by mTORC1, but under conditions of stress or when mTORC1 activity is reduced, TFEB enters the nucleus and drives the expression of genes involved in lysosomal function and autophagy (Falcão et al., 2025). By facilitating an HDAC inhibition–mediated de-repression of the genes governing TFEB activity, TSA may help drive a feed-forward loop that enhances the cellular capacity for lysosomal degradation and autophagy. Given that RPE cells exhibit compromised autophagy and deteriorating lysosomal function in the pathogenesis of dry AMD, the net effect of TSA treatment should be an improvement in POS uptake and degradation, leading to better clearance of lipofuscin and other deleterious cellular debris (Garcia-Garcia et al., 2022; Falcão et al., 2025). Furthermore, some studies using ARPE-19 cells have reported TSA-induced changes in the expression of other oxidative stress and inflammatory markers—for example, a decrease in HIF-1α expression and a corresponding increase in antioxidant enzymes such as SOD2 and GPX3 (Hamid et al., 2021)—which may contribute to an overall protective environment that diminishes the progressive degeneration of RPE cells. The expected cascade of molecular events—from HDAC inhibition through increased histone acetylation, enhanced transcription of TFEB, LAMP1, and MERTK, to improved lysosomal biogenesis and phagocytic function—forms the basis of the therapeutic rationale for repurposing TSA in the context of dry AMD (Boya et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025).

Overall Evaluation:  
Evaluating TSA as a therapeutic candidate for dry AMD requires an in-depth analysis of both its promising attributes and its inherent limitations. One of the primary strengths of TSA lies in its well-characterized mechanism of action. As a proven, potent pan-HDAC inhibitor, TSA can recast the epigenetic landscape of RPE cells by enforcing hyperacetylation of histone proteins and upregulating transcription of ordinarily silenced genes (Grayson et al., 2010; Hamid et al., 2021). Considering that dry AMD is marked by severe dysfunction in protein clearance, lysosomal degradation, and autophagic flux, TSA’s capacity to activate TFEB—the master regulator of lysosomal biogenesis—and to potentially enhance the expression of key phagocytic receptors such as MERTK and lysosomal markers like LAMP1 offers a compelling pharmacological strategy to restore cellular homeostasis (Boya et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025). The cascading effect of promoting both lysosomal biogenesis and autophagy could improve the clearance of photoreceptor outer segments (POS), thereby mitigating the accumulation of toxic by-products like lipofuscin that contribute significantly to the pathogenesis of dry AMD (Falcão et al., 2025; Tan, 2018).

Furthermore, TSA’s history as a research compound in various cell culture models, including ARPE-19, provides a solid preclinical foundation for its repurposing. Studies have demonstrated that TSA can modulate the expression of inflammatory and apoptotic markers, reduce oxidative stress, and, importantly, alter the expression of genes that control cellular clearance pathways (Hamid et al., 2021). These data support the hypothesis that TSA might improve RPE function, a critical factor given that RPE degeneration is a driving force behind AMD progression. Preliminary ocular safety assessments, particularly in corneal models, indicate that TSA can be administered topically at carefully controlled low doses without significant toxicity (Sharma et al., 2009). Such findings are encouraging in light of the longstanding challenges associated with delivering effective therapeutics to the posterior segment of the eye; however, it must be emphasized that safety profiles established in corneal applications may not fully translate to the intricate microenvironment of the retina and RPE (Kaarniranta et al., 2023).

On the other hand, several weaknesses temper the enthusiasm for TSA as a repurposed treatment for dry AMD. Foremost among these is its broad-spectrum activity; as a pan-HDAC inhibitor, TSA does not differentiate between enzyme isoforms. This lack of selectivity raises the possibility of off-target effects that could disrupt not only histone modifications but also the acetylation status of numerous non-histone proteins, including α-tubulin (Grayson et al., 2010; Hamid et al., 2021). In RPE cells, proper microtubule dynamics are essential for the trafficking of autophagosomes to lysosomes. Excessive tubulin acetylation—an effect that is purportedly enhanced by agents such as TSA, and observed in conditions mimicked by lipofuscin bisretinoids—can impede autophagosome mobility, potentially undermining the very autophagic flux that TSA is intended to improve (Toops et al., 2015; Tan, 2018; Toops et al., 2015). This paradoxical effect suggests that while increasing transcription of lysosomal genes is beneficial, alterations in cytoskeletal regulation might counteract these benefits if not precisely calibrated.

Another concern arises from the conflicting roles of HDAC activity in the context of AMD. Some studies have observed that specific HDAC activities, such as those mediated by HDAC3, are already reduced in the RPE of AMD patients (Chatterjee et al., 2024; Hamid et al., 2021). This raises the possibility that further inhibition of these enzymes might exacerbate a preexisting imbalance rather than re-establish homeostasis. In other words, if the pathological state of AMD is associated with diminished HDAC activity, then TSA’s further suppression could potentially lead to unintended and deleterious transcriptional changes that might compromise cell survival (Chatterjee et al., 2024; Hamid et al., 2021).

Moreover, despite encouraging in vitro data, there remains a paucity of information regarding TSA’s effects on the specific gene targets central to the proposed mechanism—namely, the upregulation of phagocytic receptors like MERTK and lysosomal membrane proteins such as LAMP1. While the rationale is built upon sound principles of epigenetic regulation and the critical role these proteins play in ensuring efficient POS uptake and degradation (Boya et al., 2023), direct evidence linking TSA treatment to enhanced expression of these markers in RPE cells is yet to be conclusively demonstrated. This gap in the literature makes it difficult to fully endorse TSA as having the predicted beneficial impact on RPE phagocytic function and lysosomal biogenesis without further, targeted investigations (Tan, 2018; Garcia-Garcia et al., 2022).

In addressing the translational potential of TSA, one must also consider its pharmacokinetic and toxicity profiles. Although ocular studies—particularly those focusing on corneal wound healing—have suggested that TSA is safe at low nanomolar concentrations (Sharma et al., 2009), its use in chronic conditions such as dry AMD would likely require long-term administration. The potential cumulative toxicity of TSA, given its broad activity and historical association with off-target effects in other tissues, remains a serious concern. The challenge will be to reconcile the need for sufficient HDAC inhibition to achieve therapeutic upregulation of autophagic and phagocytic genes with the imperative to minimize adverse side effects that could compromise either the safety or the efficacy of the treatment (Grayson et al., 2010; Hamid et al., 2021).

Overall, TSA is a compelling candidate for repurposing in dry AMD due to its robust epigenetic modulatory effects, which align well with the therapeutic goal of enhancing lysosomal biogenesis and phagocytic clearance in RPE cells. Its ability to interfere with HDAC activity has been demonstrated to affect not only histone acetylation but also the transcription of genes involved in cellular stress responses and degradation pathways. In theory, such modifications could reverse or mitigate several of the pathological features of dry AMD, including the accumulation of undigested POS and subsequent lipofuscin buildup that drive RPE degeneration (Boya et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2025). The elevation of TFEB, a master regulator of lysosomal gene expression, through TSA-mediated chromatin relaxation offers a particularly attractive avenue for restoring the autophagy-lysosome machinery, thereby enhancing both cellular clearance and the overall health of RPE cells (Falcão et al., 2025; Falcão et al., 2025).

Nonetheless, the candidate’s broad-spectrum nature and potential to disrupt processes such as microtubule dynamics present significant challenges. The risk of impaired autophagosome trafficking due to aberrant tubulin acetylation (Toops et al., 2015; Tan, 2018) must be weighed against the expected benefits of improved lysosomal function. Moreover, the heterogeneity of HDAC activity in AMD pathology—with some reports indicating already compromised HDAC function in diseased RPE—complicates the prospect of using a pan-HDAC inhibitor without a carefully defined therapeutic window (Chatterjee et al., 2024; Hamid et al., 2021). The absence of definitive data linking TSA treatment to increased expression of MERTK and LAMP1 in RPE cells further underscores the need for additional research to validate the proposed mechanism of action (Tan, 2018; Garcia-Garcia et al., 2022).

In light of these considerations, our evaluation supports the continued exploratory investigation of TSA as a repurposed intervention for dry AMD, with the understanding that several critical questions remain unanswered. Future studies should aim to:  
1. Directly measure the impact of TSA on the expression levels of key phagocytic and lysosomal genes, such as MERTK and LAMP1, in RPE cells using both transcriptional and protein-level assays.  
2. Delineate the dose-response relationship in RPE cells to identify concentrations that achieve optimal activation of the CLEAR network and TFEB-mediated transcription without inducing detrimental levels of tubulin acetylation that could impede autophagosome mobility.  
3. Assess the long-term safety and pharmacokinetics of TSA in ocular tissues, particularly in animal models of dry AMD, to determine whether its beneficial effects on autophagy and phagocytosis can be sustained without incurring off-target toxicity or systemic side effects.  
4. Explore the possibility of developing more selective HDAC inhibitors or targeted delivery systems that concentrate TSA’s effects specifically within the RPE, thereby minimizing the risks associated with its broad-spectrum activity.

Ultimately, while TSA’s established role as an epigenetic modulator makes it an attractive candidate for addressing the underlying cellular dysfunction in dry AMD, careful balancing of its beneficial transcriptional effects against its potential to disrupt critical cellular processes is essential. The data reviewed herein provide a strong mechanistic rationale for TSA’s utility, yet underscore the necessity for rigorously designed preclinical studies to confirm its efficacy and safety in the context of retinal degeneration (Grayson et al., 2010; Hamid et al., 2021; Boya et al., 2023; Falcão et al., 2025).
